Accordingly, he begins from the more gloomy utterances, but the necessary ones, such as "I will kill," then, having killed, "and I will make alive; I will strike, and I myself will heal"; for "whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives." First he strikes, and after this he heals; "for he himself makes to feel pain and again restores." And so also here: "I have set you this day over nations and kingdoms, to root up and to pull down and to destroy and to build up again and to plant." Yet the first thing is that those evil things be taken away from us. God cannot build in the place of the evil building. "For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? What fellowship has light with darkness?" The evil must be rooted up from the foundations, the building of evil must be consumed away from our soul, so that after these things the words of God may build and plant; for I cannot understand otherwise the things that are written: "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth." What do the words do? "Root up and pull down and destroy." Words root up "nations," words pull down kingdoms—but not those bodily and worldly kingdoms. Worthily of words that pull down, worthily of words that root up, understand the things rooted up by words, the things pulled down by words. Is there not, then, right now in the things being spoken a power, if God grants it (according to the saying "the Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the good news with great power"), a power that roots up, if there be any unbelief, if any hypocrisy, if any wickedness, if any licentiousness? Is there not one that pulls down, if anywhere an idol-temple has been built up in the heart—so that, when that has been pulled down, a temple of God may be built, and the glory of God may be found in the temple built up again, and there may come to be not a grove, but a planting, a paradise of God, where the temple of God is in Christ Jesus; to whom is the glory and the might unto the ages of the ages. Amen.

They refused to yield to the sentence of fifty bishops passed against them. They declined to resign the government of their Churches although the number of bishops assenting to the decree for their deposition was so many, on the alleged ground that they were not partakers of the Holy Ghost, and were not governing their Churches by the grace of God, but had clutched their dignity by the aid of human power, and through lust of vain glory. Now they are for receiving the men consecrated by these same persons as bishops. I should like you to ask them in my stead, (although they despise all mankind, as bereft of eyes, ears, and common sense), to perceive the inconsistency of their conduct, what sentiments they do really entertain in their own hearts. How can there be two bishops, one deposed by Euippius, and the other consecrated by him? Both are the actions of the same man. Had he not been endowed with the grace bestowed upon Jeremiah to pull down and build again, to root out and to plant, he certainly would not have rooted the one out and planted the other. Grant him the one and you must grant him the other.

Isaiah, again, beheld the glory of the seraphim, and after him Jeremiah, who was entrusted with great power against nations and kings. The one heard the divine voice and was cleansed by a live coal for his prophetic office, and the other was known before his formation and sanctified before his birth. Paul, also, while yet a persecutor, who became the great herald of the truth and teacher of the Gentiles in faith, was surrounded by a light and acknowledged him whom he was persecuting, and was entrusted with his great ministry and filled every ear and mind with the gospel.
ON THE DEATH OF HIS FATHER, ORATION 18:14

And in the beginning of Jeremiah too something of the kind is written: Behold, I have put my words into your mouth; behold, I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to root up and to undermine, and to destroy, and to build, and to plant. A very bad building is destroyed so that afterwards a good building may be put up; a wicked planting is rooted up so that a planting may be set in its place.

Behold, I have set you today over the nations and over the kingdoms, to pluck up and to destroy and to ruin and to scatter and to build and to plant. This, which we have added from the Hebrew, 'scatter' or 'put down', is not found in the LXX. And it must be considered that two joyful things follow four sad ones. For good things could not be built unless evil things had been destroyed, nor the best things planted unless the worst were rooted out. For every planting which the heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted out, and the building which does not have its foundation upon the rock but has been raised upon the sand is undermined and destroyed by the word of God. And that which Jesus will consume with the spirit of his mouth and will destroy by the coming of his presence, namely every sacrilegious and perverse doctrine, he will ruin forever. Further, the things which are lifted up against the knowledge of God and trust in their own wisdom, which is foolishness with God, he will scatter and put down, so that lowly things may be built in their place, and in the place of the former things, which have been destroyed and plucked up, the things which accord with the truth of the Church may be raised and planted, and that may be fulfilled which the Apostle says: you are God's building, God's husbandry. Many understand this place of the person of Christ. For 'Jeremiah' means 'the exalted one of the Lord', who destroyed the kingdoms of the devil, which the devil had shown him on the height of the mountain, and who brought to ruin the adverse powers, blotting out on the cross the handwriting of errors. Of these the psalm too, after the truth of the history, speaks tropikōs [figuratively]: why have the nations raged and the peoples meditated vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes gathered together into one. In place of these, plucked up, destroyed, ruined and dragged down to lower things, the Church of God is built and planted. But concerning the person of Jeremiah there is no doubt; for we read in what follows that he takes in his hand a cup full of unmixed wine and is commanded to give drink to all the nations round about.

In such wise Thou sayest, I build, as not to destroy: for some Thou destroyest and buildest not; and some whom Thou destroyest Thou dost rebuild. For unless there were some who were destroyed to be rebuilt, Jeremiah would not have written, “See, I have this day set thee to throw down and to build.” And indeed all who formerly worshipped images and stones could not be built up in Christ, without being destroyed as to their old error. While, unless some were destroyed not to be built up, it would not be written, “He shall destroy them, and not build them up.”

But you should know that we must make an effort with a twofold purpose in our exertion; both for the expulsion of vice, and for the attainment of virtue. And this we do not gather from our own conjecture, but are taught by the words of Him who alone knows the strength and method of His work: "Behold," He says: "I have set thee this day over the nations and over kingdoms, to root up, and to pull down, and to waste, and to destroy, and to build and to plant." He points out that for getting rid of noxious things four things are requisite; viz., to root up, to pull down, to waste, and to destroy: but for the performance of what is good, and the acquisition of what pertains to righteousness only to build and to plant. Whence it is perfectly evident that it is a harder thing to tear up and eradicate the inveterate passions of body and soul than to introduce and plant spiritual virtues.
The First Conference of Abbot Nesteros, Chapter 3

Now our rod is the Word of God, Jesus Christ, as Jeremiah saw him as an almond rod. So everyone that spares his son a word of rebuke hates his son. Therefore teach your sons the word of the Lord. Punish them with lashes. Subdue them by your word of religion from their youth.

It is written in the book of the prophet, "Take a branch from a nut tree." So we must consider why the Lord said this to the prophet, for it is not written without a purpose, since we also read in the Pentateuch that the nut tree of Aaron, the priest, blossomed after it had been laid away for a long while.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: What do you see, Jeremiah? And I said: I see a watching rod, and the Lord said to me: You have seen well, for I will watch over my word, to perform it. For 'watching rod' the LXX translated 'staff of nut-wood'. We must therefore take pains that the Latin reader may briefly understand the Hebrew etymologian [etymology]. 'Saced' is said for 'nut', while 'watch' or 'watchful' or 'to watch' is called 'soced'. Hence also in later passages the watching leopard is set down under this name. So from the word for 'nut', because of the likeness of the word, the name has played upon the sense of 'watchful'. This indeed is written also in Daniel according to Theodotion, where from the trees schinu and prinu, namely the holm oak and the mastic, cutting asunder and sawing asunder is decreed for the adulterous elders. Besides, at the beginning of Genesis too, from 'man', which is called 'is', woman is called 'issa', as it were a kind of virago, because she was taken from man. For 'staff of nut-wood' Aquila and Symmachus translated 'watching rod', but Theodotion 'of almond'. And the rod watches, considering all the sins of the people, so as to strike and rebuke the transgressors. Hence the Apostle too writes to those who sin: what do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and the spirit of gentleness? This is the rod or staff of which David too speaks: your rod and your staff, they have comforted me. And beautifully he put 'have comforted'; for the Lord rebukes to this end, that he may amend. And just as the nut or the almond has a very bitter rind and is enclosed in a very hard shell, so that, when the harsher and hard parts are stripped away, a very sweet fruit is found, so every rebuke and the labor of continence seems bitter indeed for the present, but brings forth very sweet fruits. Hence there is also that old saying: 'the roots of letters are bitter, the fruits sweet'. Some understand the 'watching rod' and 'of nut-wood' as the Lord, of whom Isaiah says: a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse. Hence too the rod of Aaron, which was thought dead, is related to have blossomed in the resurrection of the Lord.

In the mystery of prophetical revelation, Christ is symbolized especially by means of sight. The prophet saw "a branch of the watching-tree." Christ is symbolized through prophetical visions, and this in different ways: for one saw Christ as "a branch of the watching-tree," another saw Him "seated on a high and lofty throne," while yet another saw Him "dressed."

But let it set this candlestick of lamps in the south, that it may look toward the north. For, the light being kindled, that is, with a watchful heart, it ought always to look toward the north and to observe "him who is from the north"; just as the prophet also says that he sees "a kindled cauldron, or pot, and its face from the face of the north"; for "from the north are kindled the evils of all the earth". Let it therefore, watchful and solicitous and burning, ever behold the cunning devices of the devil and ever look from what quarter temptation is about to come, from what quarter the enemy rushes in, from what quarter the foe creeps up. For the Apostle Peter also says that "your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about seeking whom he may devour".

And the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying: What do you see? And I said: I see a pot set on fire, and its face is from the face of the north. And the Lord said to me: From the north evils shall be opened — or shall blaze up — upon all the inhabitants of the earth. By certain degrees torments are assigned to sinners, so that they may come little by little to salvation: those who will not be amended when the rod strikes are sent into the bronze pot set on fire, of which Ezekiel writes more fully, which is kindled from the face of the north, signifying the Babylonian king and the city of Jerusalem.

The blessed Jeremiah also saw a boiling pot tilted away from the north. So he means that Manasseh will recover its own land, Ephraim regain its former power and Judah be renamed king of all, whereas the Moabites will be subject to them, observing their invincible strength—and not only they but also Edomites and foreigners.
In the mystery of prophetical revelation, Christ is symbolized especially by means of sight: the prophet saw "a boiling cauldron" and other things also.

And beautifully it is added: from the north evils shall blaze up upon all the inhabitants of the earth — either of the land of Judea or surely of the whole earth —, of whom it is written in Revelation too: woe upon all the inhabitants of the earth. For the saints are not inhabitants of the earth but strangers and sojourners, of whom one says: I am a stranger upon the earth and a sojourner, as all my fathers were, and another: few and very evil are my days, in which I sojourn on the earth. Hence Peter too writes his catholic epistle to the strangers and sojourners of Pontus, Galatia and Cappadocia. And according to the mystical senses Solomon says: the north wind is a harsh wind, but by name it is called right-handed, that is, by those who have grown stiff with its cold and have lost the warmth of faith.

For behold, I will call together all the families of the kingdoms of the north, says the Lord, and they shall come, and each one shall set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, and upon all its walls round about, and upon all the cities of Judah. And I will speak my judgments with them concerning all the wickedness of those who have forsaken me and have poured libations to foreign gods and have worshiped the work of their own hands. No one doubts that many nations, and the kings of the several nations, were subject to the Babylonian king; who, when Jerusalem was besieged, set round about, and especially at the outlets of the gates, their throne and tents, so that none of those who were shut in could break out; and that not only Jerusalem but all the cities of Judea were hemmed in by a like siege.

'And when', he says, 'the city has been taken, then I will speak to them, that my judgments were right and that each one received what he deserved, not for the other vices to which the human condition is subject, but above all for idolatry, through which, forsaking me, they worshiped the works of their own hands'. Some take this place in a good sense, namely that those who have been boiled in the bronze pot through torments and purged will afterward be princes of Jerusalem, and that, after the Lord has had mercy on them, he will then reproach them because, having forsaken him, they venerated images. But this is a forced and perverse interpretation; let not an unlearned expounder raise a false charge.

He emphasizes the justice of what has been done by adding, "I shall pronounce my judgment against them because of all their wickedness in forsaking me. They sacrificed to foreign gods and worshiped the works of their hands." What could be more foolish than this kind of godlessness? What could be more righteous than retribution? Consider that they, for their part, forsook their own maker and turned things of their own making into gods. He, by contrast, after demonstrating his patient mercy for such a long time, finally deprived them of his characteristic grace. Once deprived of it, they became enslaved to unholy people.

You therefore gird up your loins, and arise, and speak to them all things which I command you. Job too is commanded to gird up his loins, and the apostles, with loins girded — which Elijah and John the Baptist mortified with girdles of skin —, to hold lamps in their hands, namely those of the preaching of the Gospel. Whoever therefore is to speak the words of God ought to gird up his loins, knowing that all the strength of the devil is in the loins, and that the righteous man says in the psalms: my loins are filled with illusions. And when he has girded his loins, let him hear that which is written: arise, you who sleep, and be lifted up, and Christ will enlighten you, so that, always watching and rising up from sleep, he may speak the things which God has commanded him.

Do not be afraid of their face; for I will not make you fear their countenance, or, as the Seventy and the other translators have: lest perhaps I make you fear. And the sense according to our translation is: 'do not be afraid of their face; for with me as your helper you will not be able to fear them'; according to the Seventy: 'do not be afraid of their face, have confidence in my command; for if you do not offer what you have, so as to cease to fear, I will forsake you and hand you over to fear, and I shall in a manner seem to make you fear, while I leave you to dread'. And this signifies that truth is always bitter, and that the multitude of men is not to be feared, who, when rebuked, do not bear correction but lay snares for him by whom they are corrected. And what follows according to the Seventy: for I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord, is not found in the Hebrew. And the sense is: 'I will rescue you, not in this, that no one lies in wait for you, but in this, that by enduring snares you do not transgress'.

For I have given you today — or behold, I have set you on this day — as a fortified city, as an iron pillar and as a bronze wall over all the land: to the kings of Judah, to its princes and to the priests and to the people of the land. And they shall fight against you and shall not prevail, for I am with you, says the Lord, to deliver you. The divine word describes why the prophet ought not to fear. I, he says, have set or have given you today — that is, in the present life, while it is called today — as a very strong city, not as a single house, nor a tower or some walls, but as a whole city, which, set upon a mountain, cannot be hid, of which it is written: glorious things are spoken of you, city of God, and: I am a strong city, a city which is besieged. And as a pillar, he says, of iron, of which the Apostle writes: the pillar and ground of the truth. Hence Peter and John, who were reputed pillars of the Church, gave to Paul and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship. Nor is this enough, but as a wall, he says, of bronze, which is marred by no rust, nor perishes when beaten by rains, but becomes stronger with age. And you shall be such against kings and princes and people, not of any place whatever, but of the land, who savor earthly things and do not know heavenly things, who bear the image of the earthy and not of the heavenly; these, he says, shall fight against you and shall not prevail. Why, I ask? What is the cause of such great strength, that neither kings nor princes nor priests nor peoples prevail against one man? It follows: for I am with you, says the Lord, to deliver you. If ever the kings of Judah, which means 'confession', and its princes and priests and peoples, that is, bishops and presbyters and deacons, and the base and ignoble common crowd, should wish to rise up against a holy man, let him have firmness of faith and cease to fear, for with the Lord's help he will overcome.
2: The prophets say, "And the Word of the Lord came to me." … All these messages proscribe in every light the Arian heresy and signify the eternity of the Word, and that he is not foreign but proper to the Father's essence.

Consider by how many testimonies the Word of the Lord urges us to recite the Holy Scriptures in order that we may possess through faith what we have repeated with our mouth.… And elsewhere it is written, I remembered the mercy of your youth.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem, saying. This is not found in the Seventy, but was added under asterisks from the edition of Theodotion, who translated the Hebrew word 'carath', for which we said 'cry' or 'preach', as 'read'. For by its ambiguity it signifies reading and crying out and preaching. But the ears of Jerusalem we ought to take as the ears of its inhabitants.

Thus says the Lord: I have remembered you, pitying your youth and the love of your betrothal, when you followed me in the wilderness, in a land that is not sown. LXX: thus says the Lord: I have remembered the mercy of your youth and the love of your perfection. This is said more fully in Ezekiel, when the Lord joins Jerusalem to himself in marriage and, under the person of a wife, unites her to his embraces, or, to show a more ardent affection, calls her a girl and a young maiden and betrothed; for what we have not yet obtained, we desire the more to obtain. 'When', he says, 'you followed me in the solitude, and in the manner of betrothal gifts and a dowry I distributed to you the ornaments of the law and the necklaces of words'. And all this he refers not to her merit but to his own mercy, through which love too followed. This also, which we have set down: in the wilderness, in a land that is not sown, is not found in the Seventy.
Israel is a false wife, but Her heavenly Husband cannot forget the happier days; "I remember thee, the kindness of thy youth, the love of thy espousals, when thou wentest after Me in the wilderness."

Israel is holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his crops; all who devour him shall transgress; evils shall come upon them, says the Lord. When he calls Israel the firstfruits of the Lord's crops, he shows that the people gathered from the nations comes after the firstfruits, according to that which is written in another place: Remember your congregation, which you have possessed from the beginning. But firstfruits are owed to the priests and not to enemies. What follows: all who devour him shall transgress; evils shall come upon them, says the Lord, has this sense: just as those who devour the firstfruits, being in no way of priestly stock, are guilty of a crime, so those who defile Israel will be subjected to evils, according to that which the holy man says in Psalm 26 (27): While the harmful draw near against me to eat my flesh, those who trouble me, my enemies themselves have become weak and have fallen. For they will not be immune from punishment on the ground that they carry out God's sentence, and evils will come upon them; for it must needs be that offences come, but woe to him through whom offences come!

Hear the word of the Lord, house of Jacob and all the families of the house of Israel. Thus says the Lord: What iniquity did your fathers find in me, that they went far from me and walked after vanity and became vain? Another prophet too testifies to this sense: My people, what have I done to you, and how have I been troublesome to you? Answer me; for I brought you out of the land of Egypt and freed you from the house of servants. Now both names — Israel too — are set down, not according to the two and ten tribes, but for the whole people, since Jacob himself too was afterwards called Israel. And he traces the offense from the fathers, not so that the sins of the fathers are imputed to the sons, but so that the sons too, having the likeness of their fathers, are punished both for their own crime and for their parents'. We often read that God has mercy on sons for the sake of holy fathers. Now the fathers of the sinful people forsook God — and not briefly, but for a long time — and instead of God followed vanity, namely idols, which profit their worshipers nothing, and they became like them, according to that which is written: Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.

Again, elsewhere he says, "What fault have your fathers found in me?" That which is said is great and marvelous, because what he says means, "What wrong have I done?" God tells human beings, "What sin have I committed?"—something that not even slaves tolerate that their master utter.

And elsewhere again, "What transgression have your fathers found in me?" And again, "O my people, what have I done unto thee? and wherein have I grieved thee?" showing their thankless disposition, and that when in the enjoyment of all things, they requited it by the contraries; but here He expresses it with yet greater force. For He doth not plead, Himself, saying, "What ought I to have done that I have not done?" but brings in themselves to judge, that nothing hath been wanting, and to condemn themselves.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 68:2

God in the Old Testament expostulates with men on the basis of their own conceptions of gratitude, fidelity, and fair play: and puts Himself, as it were, at the bar before His own creatures--"What iniquity have your fathers found in me, that they are gone far from me?"

And they did not say: Where is the Lord, who made us go up from the land of Egypt, who led us across through the wilderness, through a land uninhabitable and pathless, through a land of thirst and the image of death, through a land in which no man walked nor did a human being dwell? For 'human being' the Seventy translated 'son of man', and for 'image of death' 'shadow of death' was added from Theodotion. Since this is plain according to the history, this must be considered according to anagōgēn [the higher, spiritual sense]: that as long as we are in this world and are being led out of Egypt, we go up little by little, and first we cross deserts and a land uninhabitable, which the holy man ought not to inhabit, and pathless, to show the difficulty of the journey; through a land of thirst, where we always desire greater things and are not content with things present, and the image or shadow of death — for we always stand in danger, and everywhere the devil sets his snares —, through a land in which no man walked, who is of the perfect age in Christ — for we shall all rise again to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ — ; nor does he who is a man of God, or a son of man, ever dwell in it, but he always hastens on to greater things. From this it is clear that perfection is not on the way, but at the end of the way and in the dwelling that is prepared for the saints in the heavenly places, and to whom it is said: you who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. In vain, therefore, does the new heresy sprung from the old suppose that perfect victory is here, where there is battle and contest and an uncertain outcome of things to come.

And I brought you into the land of Carmel, that you might eat its fruit and its good things, and having entered you defiled my land and made my inheritance an abomination. 'For the toil of a very hard journey I gave you an abundance of all things'; for this is what 'Carmelus' signifies, which in Hebrew is called 'Chermel' and in our language sounds as 'knowledge of circumcision'. And as that people polluted and violated with idolatry the holy land, fertile in all things, so we, receiving the knowledge of the true circumcision, eat its fruit and, if negligence creeps in, defile the land of God and make his inheritance abominable.

God has also entrusted a deposit to us: the brothers' way of life. While laboring on their behalf, we look forward to future rewards, lest this be said of us as well, "Let this people go," and lest, if we forsake the traditions of our ancestors, this be hurled at us: "Those who have my law do not know me; the shepherds have rebelled against me."

Jeremiah was known before he was formed, and sanctified from the womb. … He longs for water over his head and a fountain of tears for his eyes that he may adequately weep for Israel. No less does he lament the depravity of its rulers. God speaks to him to rebuke the priests: "The priests did not say, 'Where is the Lord?' Those who handle the law did not know me; the rulers transgressed against me." Again he says to him, "The shepherds are stupid, and do not inquire of the LORD; therefore they have not prospered, and all their flock is scattered." Again, "Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard, they have trampled down my portion, they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness." He further attacks the pastors again: " 'Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!' says the LORD. Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the shepherds who care for my people: 'You have scattered my flock, and have driven them away, and you have not attended to them. Behold, I will attend to you for your evil doings, says the LORD.' "
IN DEFENSE OF HIS FLIGHT TO PONTUS, ORATION 2:67-68

The priests did not say: Where is the Lord? And those who held the law did not know me, and the shepherds transgressed against me, and the prophets prophesied by Baal and followed idols. After such great benefits they turned the privileges of their dignity into contempt, so that the priests did not seek the Lord, the teachers of the law, who ought to have taught others, did not know him, and the shepherds became transgressors through negligence, and the prophets, who discourse among the peoples, speak not for God but for an idol, and venerate their own fabrications. These words must be used against the teachers of our own order, who devour the people of God like bread for food and by their evil works do not call upon the Lord.

Therefore I will still contend with you in judgment, says the Lord, and with your sons I will dispute. Lest he seem to strike through power, he contends by reason as with equals, according to that which David sings and the Apostle adopts: that you may be justified in your words and may prevail when you are judged. And in setting down 'still', he testifies that he has often done so; and in adding 'with your sons', he shows a like obstinacy also in the sons of the wicked. And covertly he signifies that their sons too, at the coming of the Lord, followed the ancient denial of God.

But they forsook Him, and worshipped idols, as Jeremiah said concerning them:—Go to the distant isles, and send to Kedar, and consider well and see, whether there has been (anything) like this, whether the nations change their gods, those that are no gods. But My people has changed My honour for that which is not profitable. Be astonished, ye heavens, at this; and quake and fear greatly, saith the Lord; because My people have done two wickednesses; they have abandoned Me, the fountain of the water of life, and they have gone and dug for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns which cannot hold water. For the broken cisterns are the fear of images and idols. And He calls the heavens to astonishment, because they worshipped the hosts of the heavens. And the heavens shall receive as a penalty, that they shall be rolled up as a scroll, and all the host of them shall fall down.

Even that last horror has come to pass which I shrink from saying, and yet cannot leave unsaid, for it is as a burning and blazing fire in my bones, and I am undone and cannot endure. You have taken the members of Christ and made them the members of a harlot. This is an evil with which no other can be matched. This outrage in life is new. “For pass over the Isles of Chittim and see; and send unto Chedar and consider diligently, and see if there be such a thing. Hath a nation changed their gods which are yet no gods.” But the virgin has changed her glory, and her glory is in her shame. The heavens are astonished at this, and the earth is horribly afraid, saith the Lord, for the virgin has committed two evils; she has forsaken Me, the true and holy Bridegroom of holy souls, and has betaken herself to an impious and lawless destroyer of body and soul alike. She has revolted from God, her Saviour, and yielded her members servants to uncleanness and to iniquity. She forgot me and went after her lover from whom she will get no good.

Pass over to the islands of Kittim and see, and send to Kedar and consider earnestly, and see whether such a thing has been done: if a nation has changed gods — or its gods — ; and surely they are not gods. But my people has changed its glory into an idol or, for that from which nothing will profit it. He makes a comparison of a thing that is incomparable, and sets the true God beside lying ones. 'Go', he says, 'to the islands of Kittim', which we ought to take as those either of Italy or of the western regions, from the fact that the island of Cyprus, in which a city is called by this name, is near the land of Judea; from it too came Zeno, the chief of the Stoics. Kedar, however, is a region of the wilderness and of the Ishmaelites, whom they now call Saracens, against which a prophecy of this very prophet is woven in his final parts, and which David mentions, saying: I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has long been a sojourner. And the sense is: 'Either go to the west or send into the wilderness, and see whether any nation has done what you have done. For none of them has spurned its gods, nor, by comparison with golden ones, exchanged its wooden and stone ones; but following its ancient error it has kept what it had received from its ancestors; and this surely, although none of them is a god, but they are images fashioned by the hand of men. But my people has changed the truth for a lie and preferred to me an idol, which will not be able to profit them in the time of need'. We can say this also against those who follow vices with greater zeal than virtues, whom the Apostle admonishes, saying: I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. As you yielded your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now yield your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification.

Those who are not saved always are taking care of those things that do not profit or benefit them in any way. So what kind of excuse is there for a Christian who withdraws from the assembly of the church? Such a person does not even imitate the Gentiles but by reason of his absence grows indifferent and careless. He stands aloof and does evil. The Lord said, … You have not walked in my statutes or kept my ordinances, and have not even acted according to the rules of the nations that are all around you, "you were more corrupt than they in all your ways." How, then, shall the indifferent excuse himself, since he has no zeal for the assembly of the church? If anyone takes the occasion of worldly business to withdraw, let him know this: the trades of the faithful are called works of surplus, for their true work is religion. Pursue your trades, therefore, as a work of surplus, for your sustenance, but let your true work be religion.

For since you are not persuaded out of the Scriptures, I am compelled to shame you by them that are without. This God also did unto the Jews, when He said, "Go ye forth unto the Isles of Chittim, and send unto Kedar, and know if nations will change their gods; which yet are no gods." And to the brutes likewise He sends us oftentimes, saying on this wise, "Go to the ant, thou sluggard, and emulate her ways:" and "go forth to the bee."
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 17:6

And what wonder? for He permitted opinions erroneous, and unworthy of Himself, to prevail, as that He was a body formerly, and that He was visible. In opposition to which He says, "God is a Spirit." Again, that He delighted in sacrifices, which is far from His nature. And He utters words at variance with His declarations of Himself, and many such things. For He nowhere considers His own dignity, but always what will be profitable to us. And if a father considers not his own dignity, but talks lispingly with his children, and calls their meat and drink not by their Greek names, but by some childish and barbarous words, much more doth God. Even in reproving He condescends, as when He speaks by the prophet, "Hath a nation changed their gods?", and in every part of Scripture there are instances of His condescension both in words and actions.

Let us further inquire whether the Lord took any care to foreshadow the water [of baptism] and the cross. Concerning the water, indeed, it is written, in reference to the Israelites, that they should not receive that baptism which leads to the remission of sins, but should procure another for themselves. The prophet therefore declares, "Be astonished, O heaven, and let the earth tremble at this, because this people hath committed two great evils: they have forsaken Me, a living fountain, and have hewn out for themselves broken cisterns. Is my holy hill Zion a desolate rock? For ye shall be as the fledglings of a bird, which fly away when the nest is removed."
The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter XI

For where the Church is, there is the Spirit of God; and where the Spirit of God is, there is the Church, and every kind of grace; but the Spirit is truth. Those, therefore, who do not partake of Him, are neither nourished into life from the mother's breasts, nor do they enjoy that most limpid fountain which issues from the body of Christ; but they dig for themselves broken cisterns out of earthly trenches, and drink putrid water out of the mire, fleeing from the faith of the Church lest they be convicted; and rejecting the Spirit, that they may not be instructed.

Reproof is the bringing forward of sin, laying it before one. This form of instruction God employs as necessary in the highest degree by reason of the feebleness of the faith of many. For he says by Isaiah, "You have forsaken the Lord and have provoked the holy One of Israel to anger." He says also by Jeremiah: "Heaven was astonished at this, and the earth shuddered exceedingly. My people have committed two evils. They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and have hewn out for themselves broken cisterns that will not be able to hold water."

Who that witnessed these things, or that has merely heard of them, will not be greatly amazed, and cry aloud unto the Lord, saying, 'Wilt Thou make a full end of Israel?' Who that is acquainted with these proceedings, will not with good reason cry out and say, 'A wonderful and horrible thing is done in the land;' and, 'The heavens are astonished at this, and the earth is even more horribly afraid.' The fathers of the people and the teachers of the faith are taken away, and the impious are brought into the Churches? Who that saw when Liberius, Bishop of Rome, was banished, and when the great Hosius, the father of the Bishops, suffered these things, or who that saw so many Bishops banished out of Spain and the other parts, could fail to perceive, however little sense he might possess, that the charges against Athanasius also and the rest were false, and altogether mere calumny? For this reason those others also endured all suffering, because they saw plainly that the conspiracies laid against these were founded in falsehood.

Be astonished, O heavens, at this, and, its gates, be utterly desolate, says the Lord; for my people has done two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns, which cannot hold waters. LXX: the heaven was astonished at this and shuddered beyond measure and exceedingly, the rest likewise. The heaven, to which it was said: Give heed, O heaven, and I will speak and: Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, seeing the precepts of God trampled underfoot, shudders and cannot hide its astonishment. For every creature groans together and grieves together over the sins of men. Now the people of God has done two contrary things: first, that they forsook God, who is the fountain of life and gave the precept, saying: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt; second, what is written in the same place: You shall have no gods in my sight; instead of which it followed demons, whom he calls broken cisterns because they cannot keep the commandments of God. And this must be noted, that the fountain is perpetual and has life-giving waters, but cisterns and pits are filled either from torrents or from the turbid waters of the earth and from rains. And he calls those the gates of the heavens of which it is also written in Psalm 23 (24): Lift up, O gates, your heads, and the king of glory shall enter; for which the Seventy translated: Lift up your gates, O princes; of these more will be said fully in its proper place. And let it trouble no one that Aquila and Symmachus translated 'heavens', but the Seventy and Theodotion 'heaven'. For the Hebrew 'samaim' is of common number, and both 'heavens' and 'heaven' are called by the same name, like Thebes, Athens, Salonae.

And our hearts are thus circumcised from evil, so that we are happy to die for the name of the good Rock, which causes living water to burst forth for the hearts of those who by Him have loved the Father of all, and which gives those who are willing to drink of the water of life. But you do not comprehend me when I speak these things; for you have not understood what it has been prophesied that Christ would do, and you do not believe us who draw your attention to what has been written. For Jeremiah thus cries: "Woe unto you! because you have forsaken the living fountain, and have digged for yourselves broken cisterns that can hold no water. Shall there be a wilderness where Mount Zion is, because I gave Jerusalem a bill of divorce in your sight?"

Hence also Jacob, as I remarked before, being himself a type of Christ, had married the two handmaids of his two free wives, and of them begat sons, for the purpose of indicating beforehand that Christ would receive even all those who amongst Japheth's race are descendants of Canaan, equally with the free, and would have the children fellow-heirs. And we are such; but you cannot comprehend this, because you cannot drink of the living fountain of God, but of broken cisterns which can hold no water, as the Scripture says. But they are cisterns broken, and holding no water, which your own teachers have digged, as the Scripture also expressly asserts, "teaching for doctrines the commandments of men."

Nor do we receive that useless baptism of cisterns, for it has nothing to do with this baptism of life. Wherefore also God has announced that you have forsaken Him, the living fountain, and digged for yourselves broken cisterns which can hold no water.

By reason, therefore, of this laver of repentance and knowledge of God, which has been ordained on account of the transgression of God's people, as Isaiah cries, we have believed, and testify that that very baptism which he announced is alone able to purify those who have repented; and this is the water of life. But the cisterns which you have dug for yourselves are broken and profitless to you. For what is the use of that baptism which cleanses the flesh and body alone? Baptize the soul from wrath and from covetousness, from envy, and from hatred; and, lo! the body is pure.

This "tree" is a mystery. In ancient times, Moses sweetened the bitter water with it. The people who were perishing of thirst in the desert drank and were revived because of it. We do this, too. We were drawn out from the calamities of the world in which we were lingering, perishing with thirst (that is, deprived of the divine Word). We drank "by the faith which is on him," the baptismal water of the "tree" of the passion of Christ. We have revived the faith from which Israel has fallen away, as foretold through Jeremiah, who says, "Send, and continue to ask whether such things have been done, whether nations will change their gods (and these are not gods!). But my people have changed their glory for that which does not profit. Be appalled at this, O heavens!"—and when were they appalled? Undoubtedly when Christ suffered—"and be shocked," he says, "utterly desolate."

When we were together in council, dearest brethren, we read your letter which you wrote to us concerning those who seem to be baptized by heretics and schismatics, (asking) whether, when the), come to the Catholic Church, which is one,4 they ought to be baptized. On which matter, although you yourselves hold thereupon the truth and certainty of the Catholic rule, yet since you have thought that of our mutual love we ought to be consulted, we put forward our opinion, not as a new one,5 but we join with you in equal agreement, in an opinion long since decreed by our predecessors, and observed by us,-judging, namely, and holding it for certain that no one can be baptized abroad outside the Church, since there is one baptism appointed in the holy Church. And it is written in the words of the Lord, "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out broken cisterns, which can hold no water."

But since many heresies have existed and the people of God have been torn apart at the instigation of demons, the truth must be briefly exposed by us and placed in its own peculiar dwelling place, so that if any one shall desire to draw the water of life, he may not be born to broken cisterns that hold no water but may know the abundant fountain of God. Watered by this fountain, he may enjoy perpetual light.

Is it right to say that what is God's offspring and proper to him exists out of nothing? Or, is it reasonable in the very idea that what is from God has accrued to him, that someone should dare to say that the Son does not always exist? For in this again the generation of the Son exceeds and transcends human thoughts, that we become parents of our own children in time, since we ourselves first did not exist and then came into being. But God, in that he always exists, is always Father of the Son. And the origination of humankind is brought home to us from parallel experiences. However, since "no one knows the Son but the Father, and no one knows the Father but the Son, and the one to whom the Son will reveal him," therefore the sacred writers to whom the Son has revealed him have given us a certain image from things visible, saying, "Who is the brightness of his glory and the expression of his person"; and again, "For with you is the well of life, and in your light shall we see lights." And when the Word chides Israel, he says, "You have forsaken the fountain of wisdom," and this is the fountain that says, "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters." Although the illustration is rather ordinary and vague compared with what we would like, it is still nonetheless possible from it to understand something above humanity's nature, instead of thinking the Son's generation is on a level with ours. For who can even imagine that the radiance of light ever did not exist so that he should dare to say that the Son has not always existed or that the Son did not exist before his generation? Or who is capable of separating the radiance from the sun or to conceive of the fountain as always void of life that he should madly say, "The Son exists from nothing," when it is the Son who says, "I am the life"? Or, who can conceive of him as "alien to the Father's essence," who says, "He that has seen me, has seen the Father"? For the sacred writers, wishing us to understand things in this way, have given these illustrations. It is unseemly and truly irreligious, when Scripture contains such images, to form ideas concerning our Lord from others that are neither in Scripture nor have any religious bearing.

"He has opened a pit and dug it." We do not find the name of "pit" ever assigned in the divine Scriptures to something good or a "well" of water to something bad. That into which Joseph was thrown by his brothers is a pit. There is a slaughter "from the firstborn of Pharaoh to the firstborn of the captive woman that was in prison." In the Psalms, "I am counted among those who go down to the pit." In Jeremiah it is said, "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug to themselves cisterns, broken cisterns that can hold no water."

Friends godly and well beloved, do, I implore you, beware of the shepherds of the Philistines; let them not choke your wills unawares; let them not befoul the purity of your knowledge of the faith. This is ever their object, not to teach simple souls lessons drawn from Holy Scripture, but to mar the harmony of the truth by heathen philosophy. Is not he an open Philistine who is introducing the terms “unbegotten” and “begotten” into our faith, and asserts that there was once a time when the Everlasting was not; that He who is by nature and eternally a Father became a Father; that the Holy Ghost is not eternal? He bewitches our Patriarch’s sheep that they may not drink “of the well of water springing up into everlasting life,” but may rather bring upon themselves the words of the prophet, “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water;” when all the while they ought to confess that the Father is God, the Son God, and the Holy Ghost God, as they have been taught by the divine words, and by those who have understood them in their highest sense.

Yea, rather with us is the living water, the very water which springeth from Christ; but thou, separated from the everlasting Fountain, whence receivest thou thy birth? Nor hath the Holy Spirit departed from the chief mother; whence then came He to thee? Unless perchance He hath followed one that is in strife, and abandoning so many priests, nor pleased to abide in His consecrated dwelling-place, hath preferred the broken cisterns of an adulterated fountain? Whence have your people the Spirit, not having been sealed by an anointed priest? Whence the water, being separated from its mother's womb? Whence renewal, who have lost the cradle of Bridal Peace?
Letter 3: Against the Treatise of the Novatians

So she went down to the fountain of wisdom, whether the Church or the soul, to fill her entire vessel and to draw from the pure disciplines of wisdom that the Jews refused to draw from the flowing fountain. Who is this fountain, listen to the one saying: "They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water." To this fountain ran the thirsting soul of the prophets, as David also says: "My soul thirsts for the living God"; so that it could quench its thirst with the richness of divine knowledge and wash away the blood of foolishness with the flow of spiritual waters.

So when the whole world was parched with the drought of Gentile superstition, then came that dew of the heavenly visits on the fleece. But after that the lost sheep of the house of Israel (whom I think that the figure of the Jewish fleece shadowed forth), after that those sheep, I say, "had refused the fountain of living water," the dew of moistening faith dried up in the breasts of the Jews, and that divine Fountain turned away its course to the hearts of the Gentiles. Whence it has come to pass that now the whole world is moistened with the dew of faith, but the Jews have lost their prophets and counsellors.

Still the Anomoeans have another well-rehearsed argument. What is that? Scripture says, "God is spirit." Tell me, then, does that bring his essence to light? Will anyone accept that argument if he has even drawn a little way near to the doors of the divine Scriptures? According to that argument, God will also be fire, just as it has been written that God is spirit, so has it been written, "Our God is a consuming fire," and again, "a fountain of living water." Not only will God be a spirit and a fountain and a fire; he will also be a soul, a wind, a human mind, and other things far more absurd than these.
O blessed change! Once the body wept, but now laughs forevermore. Once it desired the broken cisterns of which the prophet speaks, but now it has been satisfied in the Lord, the fountain of life.
Let him "possess his vessel in sanctification and honor," let him drink of his own wells, not out of the dissolute cisterns of the harlots that cannot hold within them the pure waters of chastity.

Between a well and a pit, that is, a cistern, there is this difference: a well has perpetual waters, flowing from a living spring; a cistern, which keeps water cool, holds waters that are external and brought in from outside. Hence God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves cisterns which cannot hold water.

Doubtless the heretics, who follow the teachings of demons, who think up false systems under the impulse of their spirit, who let it be known that they have seen visions that they have not seen and by their deadly arguments sow their seed in foolish and credulous hearts—doubtless these are the ones who do not hold the head, namely, Christ, the source of truth. Whatever is opposed to his teaching is without sense, and these are the "blind, leaders of the blind," of whom I think it is said, "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that can hold no water."

Iniquity lies to itself either by corrupting the nature you have made and ordained or by perverting it. It lies to itself when it practices an immoderate use of things permitted or when it burns for things forbidden to that use which is against nature. It lies to itself when convicted, raging with heart and voice against you as it kicks against the goads, or when—breaking through the pale of human society—they audaciously rejoice in private cliques or divisions on the basis of whether they have been pleased or offended. These things happen whenever you are abandoned and whenever, from a self-willed pride, they choose to align themselves instead with something false that they cherish instead of you, O Fountain of life, the one, true Creator and Ruler of the universe.

The arrogance of pride, the pleasure of lust and the poison of curiosity are the motions of a dead soul. It is not that it is dead in such a way as to lack all movement; rather, it dies by "abandoning the fountain of life" and thus is taken up by the transitory world and is conformed to it.

Now, here he clearly reveals to us the mystery of the holy Trinity: he called the only-begotten Word of God a fountain of life. This is the name, too, remember, God personally gave himself through the prophet Jeremiah: "They have forsaken me, a fountain of living water, taken their leave and dug for themselves cracked cisterns incapable of holding water."

The reason why it can never succeed is this. God made us: invented us as a man invents an engine. A car is made to run on petrol, and it would not run properly on anything else. Now God designed the human machine to run on Himself. He Himself is the fuel our spirits were designed to burn, or the food our spirits were designed to feed on. There is no other. That is why it is just no good asking God to make us happy in our own way without bothering about religion. God cannot give us a happiness and peace apart from Himself, because it is not there. There is no such thing.

That is the key to history. Terrific energy is expended—civilisations are built up—excellent institutions devised; but each time something goes wrong. Some fatal flaw always brings the selfish and cruel people to the top and it all slides back into misery and ruin. In fact, the machine conks. It seems to start up all right and runs a few yards, and then it breaks down. They are trying to run it on the wrong juice. That is what Satan has done to us humans.
Mere Christianity, Book 2, Chapter 3: The Shocking Alternative

Why then has he become a prey? Lions have roared over him and given their voice; they have made his land a wilderness, and his cities have been burned, and there is none who dwells in them. The divine word asks so that it may itself reply. And by lions he means the princes of Babylon, who made his land a wilderness and destroyed his cities by fire. Or at any rate, according to anagōgēn, let us understand the lions as the adverse powers or the leaders of the heretics, who, desolating the land of the Church, have laid waste all its cities with heretical fire, and with that fire of which it is written: All committing adultery, their hearts are like an oven. For they truly give their voice, and in this same prophet, under the person of the partridge, they cry out and gather what they did not bring forth, and they make riches not with judgment. But for this reason its cities have been laid waste and destroyed, because they do not have God as their inhabitant, as Scripture says: and there is none who inhabits them.

Is Israel a slave, or one born in the house? I think it was from this passage that the Jews, puffed up with pride, said to the Savior: We are the seed of Abraham and have never been slaves to anyone; how do you say: You shall be free?, not knowing that everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin, and that each one serves him by whom he is overcome. Born, then, of Abraham, the friend of God, by their own vice they became as it were sons of Ham, to whom it was said: Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a slave to his brothers.

The sons also of Memphis and Tahpanhes have debauched you even to the crown of the head. Has not this been done to you because you forsook the Lord your God at the time when he was leading you along the way? This, which we said: at the time when he was leading you along the way, is not found in the Seventy. Now he names two very great cities of Egypt, Memphis and Tahpanhes, and says that their sons debauched Israel even to the crown of the head, in that sense in which Isaiah set it down: From the sole of the foot even to the crown of the head there is no soundness in him. And so great was the lust of the Egyptians, who are great of flesh, that they spared no member but debauched everything. According to the letter, refer it to the idols of the Egyptians; according to the spiritual understanding, to the teachers of perverse doctrine, who pollute the purity of the Church with their own filthiness. And these things will befall him for this reason, because he forsook the Lord his God, and that above all at the time when he ought to have followed him as his guide.

Truly, I fear that our parents according to the flesh will be found to condemn us and to quote the words of Scripture, "How have you become wretched, greatly put to shame? Great is your affliction; a fire is kindled on you; your branches have become useless." For this cause they have become a prey. The lions have roared at it and have given out their voice against it. For this reason, the beloved are like the abhorred and the crown of your head is taken away. Cities that face the south, how are you shut off? There is nobody to give access to you. Let indeed the wicked be removed, that he may not see the glory of the Lord.

My child, flee to God, for it is he who created you. It was for you that he underwent these sufferings. For he said, "I gave my back to the whips and my cheek to the slaps. I did not turn my face away from the shame of spittle." O mortal, what is the good of your going to Egypt, to drink the water of the Geon that is churned up?

Woe to you, devil, or Antichrist, or perverse doctrine of the heretics, who with your teachings and your turbid potion make drunk the peoples of the deceived, and overturn their former faith, giving them a potion not from Siloam, not from the Jordan, not from the springs of Israel, but from the brook Kidron, and from the river of Egypt, of which Jeremiah says: What have you to do with the way of Egypt, that you should drink the water of Gihon? For this in the Hebrew is written sior, that is, turbid and muddy; for although the rivers of Egypt are believed to go out from the paradise of the Scriptures, yet because they are trampled by the feet of Pharaoh, they have lost their splendor, and, defiled by the Egyptian mud, have been turned into torrents, at having escaped which the holy one rejoices, saying: Our soul has passed through the torrent.

And now what do you want on the way of Egypt, to drink the water of Sior? And what have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the water of the river? For 'Sior' we translated 'turbid', which is what the Hebrew word signifies; for it the common edition has 'Geon'. Since, then, he had set down above the sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes, who debauched Israel even to the crown of the head, he now names Egypt itself more plainly. And no one doubts that the Nile has turbid waters, and that by the river of the Assyrians he signifies the Euphrates, as Scripture says that the land of promise extends from the torrent of Egypt even to the great river Euphrates. But those who have forsaken Christ, the fountain of life, and have dug for themselves the pits of the heretics, which cannot hold the waters of doctrines, must needs be subjected to the lions, who reduce their land to a wilderness and destroy all the churches, and be polluted even to the crown of the head, and drink turbid waters and the streams of the Assyrian river and of the north, whence evils blaze up upon the earth.

If we are not false servants of God, if there is in us a spark of that fire whereby "charity seeks not its own," we certainly should make our good works appear, not only before God but even before people, for fear that, while drinking of quiet waters in our own conscience, we should be constrained by careless feet to drive the sheep of the Lord to drink the troubled waters.

But if thou remainest in the desert, thou wilt not be tested. For thou seest no woman in the desert nor anything that does harm to thy behaviour, nor [doest thou hear] evil sounds. What hast thou to do with the ways of Egypt and with drinking water from the Nile? Understand what I say.

It is fitting first to take in Scripture, then to chew it, and finally to assimilate it. What does it serve a man to drink dirty water? "And now what hast thou to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the troubled water?" Drink instead healthy water, that is, wisdom.

The Lord has therefore endured all these things on our behalf, in order that we, having been instructed by means of them all, may be in all respects circumspect for the time to come, and that, having been rationally taught to love God, we may continue in His perfect love: for God has displayed long-suffering in the case of man's apostasy; while man has been instructed by means of it, as also the prophet says, "Thine own apostasy shall heal thee;" God thus determining all things beforehand for the bringing of man to perfection, for his edification, and for the revelation of His dispensations, that goodness may both be made apparent, and righteousness perfected, and that the Church may be fashioned after the image of His Son, and that man may finally be brought to maturity at some future time, becoming ripe through such privileges to see and comprehend God.

When he does not convince with his word, God many times permits the experience of things to be the teaching, something that he also said to the Jews. When he expended myriads of words though the prophets, he neither persuaded nor embraced the Jews. Allowing them to be educated through punishment, he said to them, "Your apostasy shall correct you, and wickedness shall reprove you."

Your malice shall reprove you — or your transgression shall instruct you — and your turning away shall rebuke you. Know and see that it is an evil and bitter thing that you have forsaken the Lord your God and that the fear of me is not with you, says the Lord God of hosts. It must be noted that malice too, or transgression, after it has glutted the transgressor and, like the quails, has come to the point of nausea, instructs the one who does repentance; and he is commanded to see what he has forsaken, what he has followed, and how, spurning good and sweet things, he has chosen evil and bitter ones. And all this happened because he forsook the Lord his God, and the fear of him is not with him. For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; and because he did not have it, he is handed over to evil and bitterness.

"Know and see that it is evil and bitter that you have forsaken the Lord your God, and that the fear of me is not in you." If you do not fear God, you have lost grace, you have lost justice, and you have lost true wisdom. "See" therefore "how evil and bitter it is that you have forsaken the Lord your God." Where there is no fear, there is neither wisdom nor justice nor grace.

From of old you have broken my yoke — or your —, you have burst my bonds — or your — and said: I will not serve. For on every lofty hill and under every leafy tree you lay prostrate as a harlot or there you poured yourself out in fornication. He speaks to Israel as to a harlot, because she broke the marriage covenant and said: I will not serve — 'the Lord' or 'the husband' is understood —, but on every lofty hill and under every leafy tree lay prostrate to idolatry; for pleasant and lofty places are always dedicated to idols. This can also be said to him who, a Christian from the beginning and in part instructed in the sacred letters, afterwards, through desire for secular literature, which is signified in the hills, and for the pleasant things of eloquence, which are shown in the leafy trees, prostrates himself to demons, who, under the pretext of learning and lofty knowledge, pollute the souls of believers and make them spread their feet for every passer-by.

Let us try, therefore, to discuss the third exposition also, according to the moral topic. If there is anyone who, while evils increase and vices overflow, is able to turn himself away from fluid and perishing and falling things and to hear the word of God and the heavenly precepts, this one builds within his heart an ark of salvation and consecrates within himself, so to speak, a library of the divine word, and places in it length and breadth and height — faith, charity, and hope. He stretches the faith of the Trinity to the length of life and immortality, he founds the breadth of charity by the affection of pardon and kindness, he raises the height of hope to the heavenly and lofty things; for, walking upon the earth, he has his "conversation in the heavens." But the sum of his acts he brings back to one. For he knows that "all indeed run, but one receives the prize" — namely, the one who has not been manifold through the variety of thoughts and the instability of mind. But this library he builds not out of rough and unpolished timbers, but out of squared ones directed according to the line of equity — that is, not out of the volumes of secular authors, but out of the prophetic and Apostolic ones. For these are the ones who, hewn by diverse temptations, with all vices cut away and excised, keep a squared life balanced on every side. For the authors of secular books can indeed be called "lofty timbers" and "shady timbers" — for "under every lofty and leafy tree" Israel is accused of having committed fornication — because they indeed speak lofty things and use flowery eloquence, yet they did not act as they spoke; and therefore they cannot be named "squared timbers," because in them life and word by no means balance out.

The God who "brings forth the sun on the evil and the good" is a desert to no one. To no one is he who "rains on the just and unjust" ever a land made dry. How is he a desert, when he brings forth the day and causes the night to rest? How is he a desert, when he causes the land to bear fruit? How is he a desert, when he provides for each person in his soul so that it is endowed with reason, so that it can grasp knowledge and exercise its intelligence, and in the body so that it has healthy sense faculties? And so with respect to the way of what is universal, God is not a desert.

"God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living; for he created all things that they might exist, and the generative forces of the world are salutary, and in them there is no poison of destruction, nor is the kingdom of Hades upon the earth." Then, passing over a little of the text, I will say whence death entered: "but by the envy of the devil death entered into the world." If, then, God has made everything that is best concerning us, while we ourselves have created for ourselves wickedness and sins — for this reason here too the beginning of the reading in the prophet says, as it were in a manner of raising a difficulty, to those who have acquired in their soul a bitterness contrary to the sweetness which God fashioned for it: "How were you turned to bitterness, O alien vine?" As if it said: God did not make lameness, but made all men sound of foot; what, then, has become the cause of those who are lamed? And God made all the members sound at the outset, but what has become the cause of some suffering harm? In the same way the soul came to be "according to the image" not of the first man only, but of every man. For the words "let us make man according to our image and likeness" reach unto all men. And just as in Adam there is that which is prior — which most people understand as the "according to the image" of what was taken up together with him, when because of sin he bore "the image of the man of dust" — so in all men the "according to the image of God" is prior to the worse image. We, being sinners, "have borne the image of the man of dust"; let us, repenting, "bear the image of the heavenly man." Yet the creation came to be in the image of the heavenly man. Here, then, the word is at a loss, speaking reprovingly to those who sin: "How were you turned to bitterness, O alien vine? For I planted you a fruit-bearing vine, wholly true." It has been said in what precedes, and taking up a few points again I will persuade you that God planted a good vine, the soul of man, but each one, having turned aside, has become contrary to the will of the one who created him. "But I planted you a fruit-bearing vine, wholly" — not "true" in part, nor partly true and partly false, but — "I planted you a fruit-bearing vine, wholly true; how were you turned?" — When I made you wholly a true vine, how were you turned to bitterness and become an alien vine?

Just as Paul too glories that the observances of the law, and all the glory of the Jewish institution, were to him only as dung, that he might be found in Christ not having his own righteousness which is of the law, but the righteousness which is of God. As Paul, therefore, having received the faith of Christ, did not keep his own vineyard — namely, the observances of the Jewish tradition; and perhaps he did not keep it because, when the true vine had been planted by God, it was turned into the bitterness of a strange vine, and their vineyard was already the vine of Sodom, and their branch from Gomorrah, and the cluster of bitterness in them, and their wine the fury of dragons, and the incurable fury of asps.
COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 2

So also God is introduced by the prophet as saying to the person who had become evil by his own choice, "Yet I had planted you a fruitful vine. How have you turned back into a wild vine?" Anywhere it is said that evils happen to the wicked from God, it must be understood as an accidental coincidence of name. This name is given to the chastisements that God in his goodness is said to send not for the hurt of those who are chastised but for their benefit and profit, in the same way that a physician might be thought to apply bad things in his painful and bitter remedies to save the sick.

Sin is a terrible thing, and the most grievous disease of the soul is iniquity, which corrupts the fiber of the soul and makes it liable to eternal fire. It is an evil freely chosen, the product of the will. The prophet clearly declares that we sin of our own free will: "I had planted you, a choice vine of fully tested stock; how could you turn into bitterness, a spurious vine?" The planting was good, but the fruit coming from the will is evil. So the planter is blameless, but the vine will burn with fire since it was planted for good and bore evil fruit of its own will.

Learn this also, that before the soul comes into the world, it has committed no sin. But though we came into the world sinless, we now of our own choice commit sin.… Remember also how God again accuses them and says, "I have planted you a choice vine, wholly of pure seed; how then have you turned degenerate and become a wild vine?"

Yet if the husband's power allures you, pray tell me who it was that spoke in the prophet, saying, "O Lord, make it known to me that I may know. Then I saw their thoughts. I was led as a harmless lamb to the slaughter and knew it not. They took counsel together against me, saying, Come, let us throw wood into his bread." For if the Son here spoke of the mystery of his coming incarnation—because it was blasphemous to suppose that the words are spoken concerning the Father—then surely it is the Son who speaks in an earlier passage: "I have planted you as a fruitful vine—how did you become bitter, and a wild vine?"

Hence God gave the gift of prayer. But this He doth, not as Himself standing in need of entreaty, but that we might not, from being saved without effort, grow indifferent. ... Wherefore to Jeremiah also He said, "Pray not for this people, for I will not hear thee," not as wishing to stop his praying (for He earnestly longeth for our salvation), but to terrify them: and this the prophet also seeing did not cease praying. And that you may see that it was not through a wish to turn him from it, but to shame them that He said this, hear what it says. "Seest thou not what these are doing?" And when He says to the city "Though thou wash thee with nitre, and take thee much soap, yet thou art stained before Me," it is not that He may cast them into despair that He so speaks, but that He may rouse them to repentance. For as in the case of the Ninevites, by giving the sentence without limitation, and holding out no good hope, He scared them the more, and led them to repentance, so He doth here also, both to rouse them, and to render the prophet more venerated, that in this way at least they may hear him.

And they gave him wine mixed with gall to drink, and when he had tasted it he would not drink. God speaks to Jerusalem: I planted you a true vine; how have you turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine? A bitter vine makes bitter wine, which it gives the Lord Jesus to drink, so that what is written might be fulfilled: They gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. But what is said: when he had tasted it he would not drink, indicates that he tasted indeed the bitterness of death for us, but on the third day he rose again.

But I planted you a choice vineyard, wholly a true seed; how have you been turned for me into what is crooked, a strange vineyard? LXX: But I planted you a fruitful vineyard, wholly true; how have you been turned into bitterness, a strange vine? For the 'choice' or 'fruitful' vineyard the Hebrew has 'sorec', which is set down in the song of Isaiah. Now it is a kind of the finest vine, with which slip the Lord says he planted Israel too, and he marvels how the true seed and choice vineyard has been turned into bitterness and has therefore become a strange vineyard. And let no one be secure, if both the planting of the Lord and the true seed and the vineyard sorec is so changed by its own vice that through bitterness it withdraws from the Lord and becomes a strange vine. And in this the clemency of the Creator must be considered, that he who said in the Gospel: I am the true vine, granted also to his disciples and to the people believing in him to be a choice or true vine, if it wills to remain in that in which it has been planted.

All they that refuse Christ for King become strangers. Wherefore strangers are they made? Because even that vine, though by Him planted, when it had become sour what heard it? “Wherefore hast thou been turned into sourness, O alien vine?” It hath not been said, My vine: because if Mine, sweet; if sour, not Mine; if not Mine, surely alien.

Now, those who were called children and were enrolled in the ranks of children made themselves foreign by proving ungrateful for favors done, limping in respect of the faith and abandoning the path of godliness. Thus God said through the prophet Jeremiah, "How did you turn into bitterness to me, a foreign vine, whereas I planted every vine to be genuine and fruitful?"

God through Jeremiah reproaches the evil of the human will in such a way that he teaches that it is foreign to him. He says, "Yet I planted you as a choice vine.… How then did you turn degenerate and become a wild vine?" He says that the vine is foreign to him not because of some defect in the divine creation but by the avoidance of his own will, which is justly blamed because it brought forth bitterness, something God did not produce in it. It had the bitterness not from God's predestination or from God's work but from the evil of its own will. Because of that bitterness, God rebukes it a second time through the prophet mentioned above: "Know and see that it is evil and bitter for you to forsake the Lord your God: the fear of me is not in you." Since, therefore, it is evil and bitter for a person to have left the Lord and not to have in him a fear of God, who is contrary to the truth in such a way that he thinks it comes from a good and kind God.

After this let us look at the words: "though you wash yourself with nitre and multiply soapwort for yourself, you are stained in your iniquities before me, says the Lord." Did some sinful soul suppose that, by taking nitre and washing herself with perceptible nitre, she would cease from the stain and cease from sin? And did someone imagine that, by taking this soapwort which springs up from the earth, and washing and scrubbing himself with it, his soul would be cleansed — since here the word says to her who was turned to bitterness and became an alien vine: "though you wash yourself with nitre and multiply soapwort for yourself, you are stained in your iniquities before me, says the Lord"? But one must know that the word has every power; and just as it has the power of every writing, so the word has the power of every medicine, and it is the power of everything that cleanses, and is most effective for scouring: "for the word of God is living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword." And whatever you may say, where there is need, this lies in the power of the word. There is, then, a certain word that is nitre, and there is a certain word that is soapwort, which, when spoken, cleanses such filth. But since not every sin is healed by such a word which is nitre, and by such a word which is soapwort — but there are sins that need neither nitre nor soapwort — it is said to her who thinks she has sins such as can be washed away by nitre and soapwort: "though you wash yourself with nitre and multiply soapwort for yourself, you are stained before me in your iniquities, says the Lord." And just as of wounds there are some that are healed with a poultice, and others healed with oil, and others need a bandage and are thus made whole, but there are other wounds concerning which it is said: "there is no poultice to apply, nor oil, nor bandages; but your land is desolate, your cities burned with fire" — so there are certain sins which defile the soul, and for these sins a man needs a word of nitre, a word of soapwort; but there are certain sins which are not healed in this way, for they are not even comparable to filth.
