Therefore the Lord in Isaiah, knowing the differences of sins, see how he says: "the Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse away the blood from their midst by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning." Filth and blood: filth by a spirit of judgment, blood by a spirit of burning. If you have sinned, though not "unto death," you are defiled. "The Lord will wash away," then, "the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse away the blood from their midst." Then there is the correspondence: for "the filth" a "spirit of judgment," and for "the blood" a "spirit of burning"; and the many of us, when we commit worse sins, have need not of nitre nor of multiplying soapwort, but of the spirit of burning.

For this reason Jesus baptizes (perhaps now I find the meaning) "in [the] Holy Spirit and fire." Not that he baptizes the same person "in the Holy Spirit and fire," but the holy one "in the Holy Spirit," while the one who, after believing, after being counted worthy of the Holy Spirit, has again sinned, he washes in "fire" — so that the same person is not baptized by Jesus "in the Holy Spirit and fire." Blessed, then, is the one baptized in the Holy Spirit and having no need of the baptism that comes from fire. But thrice-wretched is that one who has need to be baptized with fire. Yet Jesus has both. For "there shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse, and a flower shall come up out of the root." A "rod" upon those who are punished, a "flower" upon the righteous. Thus "God is a consuming fire," and "God is light": a consuming fire to sinners, light to the righteous and holy. And "blessed is the one who has a part in the first resurrection," the one who has kept the baptism of the Holy Spirit. Who is the one saved in another resurrection? The one who has need of the baptism that comes from fire, when he comes to that fire, and the fire tests him, and that fire finds wood, hay, and stubble, so as to burn them up. Therefore, since these things are said, let us with all our power gather together the words of the Scriptures, and lay them up in our heart, and try to live according to them, if perchance we may be able to become pure before our departure, and, having prepared our works for the departure, may go forth in those very good things and be taken up in them and be saved in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the might unto the ages of ages. Amen.

If you wash yourself with nitre and multiply for yourself the herb borith, you are stained with your iniquity before me, says the Lord God. For 'herb borith', which we have rendered as it is set down in the Hebrew, the Seventy translated poan, to signify the fullers' herb, which, after the manner of the province of Palestine, grows in green and moist places and has the same power for washing away dirt as nitre does; but our 'nitre' and 'fullers' herb' is repentance. The preaching of the Church too, which reproves and rebukes and corrects the offender, has the likeness of a more biting nitre. He who is stained with the light dirt of sins is cleansed by lighter admonitions. But grave sins, which drag to death, can be washed away neither by nitre nor by the herb borith, but need heavier torments. For each one's work, of what sort it is, the fire will test, and in fire it will be revealed. And beautifully he added: you are stained with your iniquity in my sight, because, even if you seem clean to men, you are not clean to me, who know the consciences of each one. Hence too in another place it is said: no one living shall be justified in your sight.

A light runner unfolding her ways, a wild ass accustomed to the wilderness, in the desire of her soul has drawn in the wind of her love; none shall turn her away. All who seek her shall not fail; in her monthly courses they shall find her. LXX: toward evening her voice howled, she widened her ways over the waters of the wilderness, in the desire of her soul she was borne by the spirit, she was handed over. Who will turn her back? All who seek her shall not toil; in her humiliation they will find her. In this passage the Seventy's edition disagrees greatly with the Hebrew truth; yet each has its own sense. Because above she said: I am not defiled, and he was speaking as if to a woman who had behaved shamefully, he describes her fornication. 'As', he says, 'a light roe' — which we called 'runner' in the common gender, and which Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion translated more expressively dromas kouphē [a light runner, in the feminine] — 'unfolds her ways and is carried swiftly to the pastures, and as a wild ass accustomed to the wilderness draws in, in the desire of her soul, the wind or spirit of her love' — for among the Hebrews both 'wind' and 'spirit' are called by one name, 'ruha' —, 'so too Israel, or Jerusalem, was borne with all her impetus toward the desire of lust and burned with every love of idols, and there is no one who can turn her from this impetus by his warnings, not that the inability of the prophets brought this about, but the perverse malice of her who desires'. Whoever, he says, seek her will not toil greatly; in her monthly courses and in her uncleanness they will find her, for which Aquila translated neomēnian, that is, 'the Kalends', Symmachus 'month', the Seventy and Theodotion 'humiliation'. But according to the Seventy this is the sense: the harlot Jerusalem, like that woman who is described in Proverbs, toward evening howled with her voice and provoked lovers to lust, opened the ways of her shamefulness, and spread her feet for every passer-by. And there was a place having the pleasantness of flowing waters, which becomes more delightful when there is solitude all around, so that no one sees her fornicating. In the desire, he says, of her soul epneumatophoreito [she was borne along by a spirit], or by a perverse spirit she was led, or she drew the refreshment of love, or at any rate she sang the songs of her shamefulness. She was handed over, he says, to her vices and to lust; no one will be able to turn her back. All who wish to find her will find her in the humiliation of her shamefulness, so that she can never be sated with the love of pleasure.

How do you say: I am not defiled, I have not gone after the Baals? See your ways in the vale or valley, which in Hebrew is called 'ge' and by the Seventy is translated polyandrion, which in our language can be called 'the tomb of a multitude'. 'In vain', he says, 'are you unwilling to confess your crimes, and do you boast of cleanness, you who are polluted with the filth of idolatry, and shamelessly deny that you worshiped the idol of the Baals. Look back at the vale of the sons of Hinnom, which is watered by the springs of Siloam, and there you will see the shrine of Baal, whom you venerated, having forsaken God'. And what is added: know what you have done, opens the closed eyes of her who denies, so that she may see what she blushes to look upon. According to tropology, let us refute by their works the shameless brow of those who will not confess their vices. For men of this kind do not walk in the strait and narrow way that leads to life, but in the broad and spacious one, by which very many enter, which leads to death. Hence too it was significantly named polyandrion, or else according to the history, because there a multitude of the people was slain and perished through the evil of idolatry.

Nothing makes God as angry as when people from despair of better things cling to those that are worse. Indeed, this despair in itself is a sign of unbelief. One who despairs of salvation can have no expectation of a judgment to come. For if he dreaded such, he would by doing works prepare to meet his Judge. Let us hear what God says through Jeremiah: "Withhold your foot from a rough way and your throat from thirst," and again, "shall they fall, and not arise? Shall he turn away, and not return?"

Restrain your foot from nakedness and your throat from thirst. And you said: I have despaired, by no means will I do it; for I have loved strangers, and after them I will walk. LXX: turn back your foot from the rough way and your throat from thirst. She said: I will act manfully, because she loved strangers and walked after them. Those who are about to keep the Passover are commanded to have shoes on their feet. And the Apostle proclaims shod the feet of those who are prepared by the Gospel, lest, while they walk through the wilderness of this world, they lie open to venomous creatures, which ought to be trampled and crushed by the Gospel foot. We restrain the throat from thirst when we receive the precepts of the Savior, who says: Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink. She, out of despair of better things, denied that she would do what the Lord commanded, and set out the reason, saying: I have loved strangers, and I will follow them, thinking by a shameless confession to escape her crimes. But according to the Seventy, the way of sinners is rough, and it is turned by the Lord into a level way. Whoever follows heretics is branded by the verdict of these verses, because he has said: I have despaired — or, in an evil purpose, I will act manfully — and in my error I will be strengthened. And it is necessary that whoever follows a doctrine strange to the Church's should love strangers and follow their footsteps, either demons or the leaders of the heretics, because they are strangers to God.

As a thief is confounded when he is caught, so are the house of Israel confounded, they and their kings, princes and priests and their prophets. Although the face of thieves is shameless and bold, yet it blushes when it has been caught in theft. And so Israel too, saying to wood: You are my father, and to stone: You have begotten me, so as to call those his parents whom he himself had fashioned, is confounded when he has been caught in his idolatry. And lest we think that he says this of the common people, he sets down kings and princes and priests and their prophets. Let us use this testimony if ever our princes, and those who are reckoned leaders in the Church, are caught in shameful sins.

It is adultery, if you abandon the ecclesiastical and true knowledge and the opinion about God, and consent to false and incompatible opinion, either by deifying any created object or by making an idol of anything that does not exist, so as to overstep, or rather step away from, knowledge.… For this reason, the noble apostle calls one of the kinds of fornication, idolatry. In following the prophet says, "My people have committed fornication with wood and stone. They have said to the wood, 'you are my father' and to the stone, 'you have begotten me.' "

With unspeakable mercy, God deigned to be called the Father of humankind. He is in heaven, they on earth. He is the eternal Maker. They are made in time. He holds the earth in the hollow of his hand. They are like grasshoppers on the earth. Yet people forsook their heavenly Father and said to wood, "you are my father, and to the stone, you have begotten me." And for this reason, I think, the psalmist says to humankind, "Forget your own people as well, and your father's house."

How is a person wise who looks not for his Maker but says to a stone, "You are my father"? Who says to the devil as the Manichaean does, "You are the author of my being"? How is Arius wise, who prefers an imperfect and inferior creator to one who is a true and perfect one? How can Marcion or Eunomius be wise, who prefer to have an evil rather than a good God? And how can one be wise who does not fear his God? For "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom."
On the Duties of the Clergy 1.25.117

They have turned to me the back and not the face. Those who cast the words of God behind them themselves turn their back against him and not their face. For when a master gives instruction, it is a sign of one who obeys if he listens with his head bowed before him; but if he turns his back, it is a sign of one who despises, as it is written in another place: and they turned to me a withdrawing shoulder. 'So far', says God, 'have they despised my precepts that they would not even hear, but showed the swelling of their mind by the gesture of their body'.
And in the time of their affliction they will say: Arise and deliver us. Those who did not perceive God through benefits, let them perceive him through torments.

Where are your gods, which you made for yourself? Let them arise and deliver you in the time of your affliction. It is a shameless request, in time of need and distress, to seek help from him whom they despised in peace. And it is to be read with the feeling of one rebuking: 'Let your gods, which you made for yourself, deliver you; so that, since God is the creator of men but man has made a god, necessity may prove what they can do whom you formerly worshiped when you were secure.'

According to the number of your cities were your gods, O Judah. The several cities worshiped either the same gods or single and different ones, so that they did not seem to have agreement even in impiety, but a superstition fighting against itself followed diverse error. And what follows: and according to the number of the streets of Jerusalem they sacrificed to Baal, was added by the Seventy.

Why do you wish to contend with me in judgment? You have all forsaken me, says the Lord. Human perversity is prone to excuse itself, so that whatever men suffer deservedly they appear to suffer unjustly, and they refer their own fault to the judgment of God. 'In vain', therefore, he says, 'do you put forward complaints and plead that the judge is unjust, since what you suffer comes from your impiety.' And what follows: and you have all acted unjustly against me, was likewise added by the Seventy.

Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree. This refers to the three captivities in which the Israelites were taken away as captives, so that they might be chastened, but they were not chastened. In vain have I smitten your children, but they have not taken correction. To show that even after these things he was still patient, he said to the vinedresser, Cut it down. The vinedresser replied to him, Leave it, Lord, for another year. He agreed to be patient with the Israelites.

Like a ravaging lion is your generation. LXX: like a ravaging lion, and you did not fear. 'The sword', he says, 'which devoured your prophets' — there is no doubt that he means the soothsayers of Baal and of the idols —, 'has laid everything waste like a lion, and yet your generation, which ought to have been amended by the slaying of a few, has persevered entire in crime'. But according to the Seventy this is the sense: 'Thus the sword of the Lord, which has displayed the sword of the adversaries, has devoured and torn your false prophets like a lion, which most greedily tears the prey it has found, and yet not even by the punishment of your prophets could you be turned to better things.'

In vain have I struck your sons; they did not receive discipline, for which the Seventy set down: you did not receive. And the sense in the Hebrew is: 'They themselves, who were struck, were unwilling to receive discipline,' but in the Seventy: 'I struck your sons for this reason, that by their death you might be instructed. And lest perhaps you should say: You were unwilling to correct us when we sinned, learn from the blows dealt your sons that I desired to cure you with a harsher remedy.'

Your sword has devoured your prophets. 'Not my prophets but yours, and by no means my sword but yours, has devoured them, the sword which you suffered for your sins'. But the Seventy do not have 'your', but translated simply: the sword has devoured your prophets, 'so that it may be shown to be either the enemy's sword or my sword, by which I have pierced your sins.'

"Some of those measures do not succeed," you say. Is a remedy, then, to be discontinued because the illness of some patients is incurable? You are looking at those who are so hardened that they are not affected by such correction. Concerning these it has been written: "In vain have I struck your children. They have not received correction."

At the beginning of what has been read, the Lord says concerning Israel that he did not become a "wilderness" to him, nor "a parched land." Who then, coming to this passage, would not inquire, examining the intention of what is written? Grant that God did not become a wilderness in Israel, that he did not become in Israel a parched land: has the Lord then become a wilderness to Israel today, or is he now to him a parched land? And what of this: when to Israel he was neither a wilderness nor a parched land, was he to the nations a wilderness and a parched land? For if to all he is always not a wilderness, and to all he is always not a parched land, what need was there for it to be said to Israel in particular and by way of exception, "Have I become a wilderness to the house of Israel, or a parched land?" But it is possible to come first to the universal benefactions of God, and then, after his universal benefactions, to the particular ones.

To no one is God a wilderness, "making his sun to rise upon the wicked and" — and to no one is he a parched land, "sending rain upon" the just "and the unjust." How is he a wilderness, who makes the day to rise and the night for rest? How is he a wilderness, who makes the earth to bear fruit? How is he a wilderness, who administers each person according to the soul, that it may be rational, that it may take up knowledge, that its faculty of understanding may be trained with respect to the body, that it may have "the organs of perception" in vigor? Therefore, as regards the universal account, God is a wilderness to no one. But as regards the particular account, I come to the affairs of Israel and say: he was neither a wilderness nor a parched land, when in Egypt he was working the signs and the wonders for the people. But if there was any time when they were forsaken, he became, as it were, a wilderness to them — though he himself was not a wilderness. When, however, to Israel he was not a wilderness nor a parched land, to the nations, according to the particular account, he was a wilderness and a parched land. But when he turned away from Israel and became to that Israel a wilderness and a parched land, then the grace was poured out upon the nations, and Christ Jesus has now become to us not a wilderness but full, and not a parched land but bearing fruit; for "many are the children of the desolate one, more than of her that has the husband." And he threatens those to whom he did not become a wilderness nor a parched land, saying: I indeed have not become to you "a wilderness" nor "a parched land," but you have said, "We will not be lorded over; we will not come to you any longer." Have the sons of Israel then said, in their reckless folly, according to the wording, "We will not be lorded over" […]

See the word of the Lord: Have I become a wilderness to Israel, or a late-yielding land? Why then has my people said: We have withdrawn, we will come to you no more? LXX: hear the word of the Lord: thus says the Lord: Have I become a wilderness to Israel, or a land full of thorns, because my people said: We will not serve, nor will we come to you? Moses too saw the voice of God, and John the apostle says that he saw and handled the word of God. And he marvels how the people of Israel held God as a wilderness, while it followed idols as though they were the throng of cities. A late-yielding land is one that does not receive the rains of doctrines nor the discipline of the Gospel; and full of thorns, because it had not been cultivated. The people, then, that was once God's is the more wicked in this, that it withdrew from the Lord and is unwilling to return again to its God. It is a great offense to be unwilling to appease him whom you have offended.

It is the virgin Mary of whom God by the mouth of Jeremiah speaks, saying, "Can a maid forget her ornaments or a bride her attire?" Concerning her we read of a great miracle in the same prophecy—that a woman should compass a man and that the Father of all things should be contained in a virgin's womb.

The band covers the breast, and holds that place in women which the Rational holds in the High Priests. Of this breast-band Jeremiah too spoke in mystical speech: If a bride can forget her adornment, or a virgin her breast-band, I too will forget you, says the Lord (Jer 2:32). The virgin, such as the Apostle desires to present us to Christ (2 Cor 11), so long as she is not corrupted in Egypt and her breasts, which are bound with the breast-band, are not broken, is joined to the bridegroom; and though daily she bears sons of the virtues, she by no means ceases to be a virgin. But if at some time she has spread her feet to every passer-by and followed her lovers, and, according to the prophecy of Hosea, the Lord has hedged in her ways and shut off her paths, she will return to her former husband and will hear: Put off the garments of mourning, and put on the garments of your glory (Hos 2).

Will a virgin forget her ornament, a bride the band of her breast? But my people has forgotten me days without number. Through these words we learn that Christ is the bridegroom of the virgin Church, which has no spot or wrinkle. And if he himself is the bridegroom, the words are his, of whom John the Baptist also speaks: He who has the bride is the bridegroom. He, therefore, loses his ornament who withdraws from the Lord, and he loses the understanding of doctrines, which is signified in the breast. Hence also John the Evangelist reclines upon the breast of the Lord, and for the priests, among other things, the breast of the victims is set apart. But the greater the number of the times in which we forget God, the greater the penalty of the sin, because it could not be tamed even by the length of ages.

Why do you strive to show your way good, to seek love? You who moreover have also taught your wickednesses, your ways, and on your wings — or in your hands — has been found the blood of the souls of the poor and innocent. Not in pits did I find them, but in all these or under every oak. 'In vain', he says, 'do you desire to defend yourself by the art of words and to show your works as good, so as to merit love, you who besides have also taught others your ways and been an example of evil works to all. And on your wings indeed — or in your hands — has been found the blood of the innocent, whom you sacrificed to idols, or whose souls you destroyed by the likeness of sacrifices'. 'The poor' we set down from the Hebrew; they are not found in the Seventy. 'But these,' he says, 'poor and innocent ones I did not find slain in pits' — which usually happens through the ambushes of robbers —, 'but in all the things which I have mentioned above, or under the oak' — which in Hebrew is called 'ella,' which indeed also signifies 'these', so that the sense is: 'in all these, or under the oak and terebinth' —, 'under whose shade and leaves, as in pleasant places, you enjoyed the crimes of idolatry'.

And you said: I am without sin and innocent, and therefore let your fury be turned away from me. Behold, I will contend with you in judgment, because you said: I have not sinned. How exceedingly vile you have become — or since you have greatly despised — repeating your ways! These words must be used against those who will not acknowledge their sins, but in the time of affliction and distress say that they suffer unjustly what they suffer, and provoke the wrath of God the more, since it is another and greater sin not to mourn what they have done, but to put forward vain excuses for their sins. In judgment, he says, I will contend with you because you said: I have not sinned, as though it were something greater than this sin to hold one thing in the conscience and to utter another in speech. Let the new heresy sprung from the old hear that it is the very greatest wrath of God to be unwilling to confess sin humbly, and instead to boast shamelessly of righteousness.

And besides this we say, that it makes God angry for us to imagine that we are free from all impurity: for He is even found saying to one of those who led polluted lives, "Behold I have a lawsuit with you because you say I have not sinned, in that you have acted very contemptuously in repeating your ways." For the repetition of the way to sin is for us, when we are overtaken by offences, to refuse to believe that we are guilty of the defilement which arises from them.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

And you shall be confounded by Egypt, as you were confounded by Assyria; for from this one too you shall go out, and your hands shall be upon your head, since the Lord has crushed your confidence — or hope — and you shall have nothing prosperous in it. To avoid the onset of the Egyptians they fled for refuge to the Assyrians, whose protection was vain; for we read that they were conquered by the Egyptians. Again, to escape the wrath of the Assyrian they relied on the help of the Egyptians, who, as history relates, were overcome by the Assyrians. They are rebuked, therefore, because, abandoning hope in God, they rely on the help of men, which has all been crushed and so overthrown that they can find nothing of use in it. Hence he says: and from this one you shall go out, that is, from Egypt, as you went out from the Assyrians, and your hands shall be upon your head, and you will mourn that you vainly expected protection from the Egyptians. Let us recall the history, when Tamar, corrupted and violated by Amnon, her most wicked brother, placed her hands upon her head sprinkled with ash and so returned to her house.

Moreover, the experience of the Vandals was not dissimilar: when our people went against them in Spain and had as much confidence in a complete victory as they had recently against the Goths, the same overweening pride engulfed them in the same disastrous ruin. Then the words of the prophet were fulfilled for our army: "The Lord shall reject thy confidence and thou shalt not prosper in it."

For we trusted in our own wisdom and strength against the command of the Lord, who said: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither the mighty man in his might, but let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the Lord."

So we have not been conquered undeservedly, for the enemy sought better aid than we did. While we prided ourselves on arms and auxiliaries, on the side of the enemy the Book of the Divine Law opposed us. To its help most of all the fear and terror of the Vandals then resorted, to oppose to us the Divine Word and to open up to those who came against them in rivalry the writings of the Sacred Book which may be called the very voice of God.
On the Government of God, Book 7, Chapter 11
3: since indeed Scripture designates the sons of adulterers as imperfect. For such a soul, which, having deserted the conjunction of the spirit, prostrates itself wholly to the sense of the flesh and to bodily desires, as though turned away from God will impudently hear that "you have made yourself the face of a harlot, you have become without shame toward all." Therefore as a harlot she will be punished, and her sons are commanded to be prepared for slaughter.

Again He took up a parable against them and reminded them of that which is written in the law, and He wished that the law might speak falsely for the sake of their repentance. For He said: "When a man takes a wife and she shall go forth from him and shall be unto another man, and if the other man who took her shall die or shall dismiss her, and she shall return unto her first husband, it will not be possible for her first husband to take her again after she has been polluted; and if he shall take her, behold that land will surely be polluted. And now also I have taken thee, Jerusalem, to Myself, and thou hast become Mine, and thou hast gone from Me, and thou hast departed, and thou hast committed fornication with stones and trees. Now return unto Me, and I will receive thee, and in thy repentance I will loose the law" (Jere. 3: 1 sqq., and Dt. 24: 13 sqq., both loosely).

If a man living with a wife is not satisfied with his marriage and falls into fornication, I account him a fornicator, and prolong his period of punishment. Nevertheless, we have no canon subjecting him to the charge of adultery, if the sin be committed against an unmarried woman. For the adulteress, it is said, “being polluted shall be polluted,” and she shall not return to her husband: and “He that keepeth an adulteress is a fool and impious.” He, however, who has committed fornication is not to be cut off from the society of his own wife. So the wife will receive the husband on his return from fornication, but the husband will expel the polluted woman from his house. The argument here is not easy, but the custom has so obtained.

For this end he hath mentioned Ruth also and Rahab, the one an alien, the other an harlot, that thou mayest learn that He came to do away with all our ills. For He hath come as a Physician, not as a Judge. Therefore in like manner as those of old took harlots for wives, even so God too espoused unto Himself the nature which had played the harlot: and this also prophets from the beginning declare to have taken place with respect to the Synagogue. But that spouse was ungrateful towards Him who had been an husband to her, whereas, the Church, when once delivered from the evils received from our fathers, continued to embrace the Bridegroom.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 3:5

And you will find the prophets filled with examples of this kind, when they address Jerusalem; for she fell into fornication, and a novel form of it, even as Ezekiel says: "To all harlots wages are given, but thou hast given wages to thy lovers, and there hath been perversion in thee beyond all other women," and again another saith "Thou didst sit waiting for them like a deserted bird." This one then who hath committed fornication in this fashion God calls back again. For the captivity which took place was not so much by way of vengeance as for the purpose of conversion and amendment since if God had wished to punish them out-right He would not again have brought them back to their home. He would not have established their city and their temple in greater splendour than before: "For the final glory of this house" He said "shall exceed the former." Now if God did not exclude from repentance her who had many times committed fornication, much more will He embrace my soul, which has now fallen for the first time. For certainly there is no lover of corporeal beauty, even if he be very frantic, who is so inflamed with the love of his mistress as God longs after the salvation of our souls; and this we may perceive both from the divine Scriptures. See at least, both in the introduction of Jeremiah, and many other places of the prophets, when He is despised and contemned, how He again hastens forward and pursues the friendship of those who turn away from him; which also He Himself made clear in the Gospels saying, "O Jerusalem! Jerusalem! thou that killest the prophets and stonest them that are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not?"

It is commonly said — for which the Seventy translated only it is said — : if a man dismisses his wife, and she, departing from him, marries another man, will he return to her any more? Will she not be polluted and defiled, that woman — or that land — ? And you have committed fornication with many lovers or shepherds. For the word 'rehim', which is written with four letters, 'res, ain, ioth, mem', signifies both 'lovers' and 'shepherds'; and if we read 'rehim', it means 'lovers', if 'rohim', 'shepherds'.

Yet return to me, says the Lord or and you used to return to me, says the Lord. In the Hebrew he even receives her as a penitent after her fornication and exhorts her to return to him; but in the Seventy he does not call her to repentance, but rebukes the shamelessness of the harlot, in that after adultery she dares to return to her husband. And as to what he says: and that woman will be defiled, for which in the Hebrew we read 'land', he leaves the example and speaks more plainly of the land of Israel, which is compared to an adulterous woman. Let us use this testimony against those who, abandoning faith in the Lord and entangled in the errors of the heretics, after many fornications and the deception of souls, pretend to return to the former truth, not in order to lay aside the poisons of their breast, but in order to instill them into others.

Those who have experienced the sins of the flesh are to be admonished to observe vigilantly with how great a benevolence God opens the bosom of his pity to us, if after transgressions we return to him. He says through the prophet, "If a man puts away his wife, and she goes from him and becomes another man's, shall he return to her again? Shall not that woman be polluted and contaminated? But you have played the harlot with many lovers. Yet return again to me, says the Lord." So, concerning the wife who has played the harlot and has deserted, the argument of justice is put forward. Yet to us, returning after the fall, not justice but pity is displayed. Where we are surely meant to gather, how great is our wickedness if we return not, even after transgression, seeing that, when transgressing, we are spared with so great pity. Or what pardon for the wicked will there be from him who, after our sin, ceases not to call us.

Hence again under the figure of Judea it is said to every sinful soul: "If a man puts away his wife, and she departs and marries another man, will he return to her again? Will not that woman be polluted and contaminated? But you have fornicated with many lovers; nevertheless return to me, says the Lord." Behold, he gave the example of a shameful woman. He showed that after such shame she cannot be received back. But he overcomes by mercy this very example that he set forth, when he says that a fornicating woman can by no means be received back, and yet he himself waits to receive the fornicating soul. Consider, brothers, the weight of such great tenderness. He says what cannot be done, and demonstrates that he himself can do this even against custom. Behold, he calls, and those whom he declares to be defiled, he also seeks to embrace, those by whom he complains he has been abandoned.

And you have polluted — or killed — the land with your fornications and in your evils. Therefore the drops of the rains have been withheld, and there was no late rain or and you had many shepherds for your stumbling. The land was killed or polluted on account of the killing of those who perished by the fornication of idolatry; hence the blessing of all things was taken away, so that they suffered a drought of the word of God. Or she had shepherds through whom she offended God, so that those who ought to have been teachers, to keep others from error, became the authors of impiety.

Lift up your eyes straight ahead and see where you have not been prostrated; you sat in the ways waiting for them like a robber in the wilderness or like a deserted crow. In place of 'robber' and 'crow' in the Hebrew 'arabe' is written, which can also signify 'Arabs', a nation given to brigandage, which to this day raids the borders of Palestine and besets the roads for those going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, a thing the Lord too recalls in the Gospel. 'Lift up, therefore, your eyes, O Jerusalem, and look around this way and that, and see where you have not been by fornication prostrated. For just as robbers are accustomed, toward evening and in deserted places, to lay ambushes for travelers, so you, like the harlot of Proverbs, sat in the ways toward evening, to kill by your intercourse the souls of those who commit fornication; on account of which the whole land is polluted with your fornications'. And significantly, according to anagōgēn [the higher, spiritual sense], those who promise that they will abandon heretical errors are commanded to lift their eyes straight ahead. For unless they begin to see what is straight, they cannot condemn their former crookedness.

Accusation is censure of wrongdoers.… Of this help the divine Instructor made use by Jeremiah, saying, "You have a prostitute's forehead. You were shameless toward all. You did not call me to the house, I who am your father, and Lord of your virginity." "And a fair and graceful harlot skilled in enchanted potions." With consummate art, after applying to the virgin the disgraceful name of whoredom, he at once calls her back to an honorable life by filling her with shame.

And this again is the peculiarity of harlots that they are his who gives the gold. Even if he is a slave or a gladiator, or any person whatever, yet if he offers their hire they receive him. But the free, even should they be nobler than all, they do not accept without the money.… For that shamelessness makes harlots, hear the prophet saying, "You were shameless toward all. You had a harlot's countenance." This may be said to the covetous also, "You were shameless toward all," not toward these or those, but "toward all."
ON THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS 15:7

What then is one to do?… We ought not to apply punishment merely to the scale of the offense. Rather, keep in view the disposition of the sinner so that, while wishing to mend what is torn, you do not make the rent worse. Because you do not wish, in your zealous endeavors to restore what is fallen, to make the ruin greater. Weak and careless characters are addicted for the most part to the pleasures of the world. If they have the opportunity to be proud of their birth and position, they may yet, if gently and gradually brought to repent of their errors, be delivered, partially at least, if not perfectly, from the evils by which they are possessed. But if anyone were to inflict the discipline all at once he would deprive them of this slight chance of amendment. When the soul has been forced to put off shame, it lapses into a callous condition. It neither yields to kindly words, nor bends to threats nor is susceptible of gratitude but becomes far worse than that city that the prophet reproached, saying, "You had the face of a harlot, refusing to be ashamed before all men."

No, a widow must take every precaution not to overstep by an inch the bounds of chastity. For if she once oversteps them and breaks through the modesty that becomes a matron, she will soon riot in every kind of excess. So much so that the prophet's words shall be true of her, "You have a whore's forehead, you refuse to be ashamed."

When they go out, they do their best to attract notice and with nods and winks encourage troops of young fellows to follow them. Of each and all of these the prophet's words are true, "You have a whore's forehead. You refuse to be ashamed." Their robes have but a narrow purple stripe, it is true. And their headdress is somewhat loose, so as to leave the hair free.

The brow of a harlot woman has become yours, you were unwilling to blush. LXX: the face of a harlot has become yours, you have become without blushing toward all. Because he had said above: I have not sinned, and she had sinned the more by denying her crimes, therefore he now rebukes her as a brazen woman of excessive shamelessness, so that she is not borne with brazen face to one man and another only, but blushes before none. Let us use this word against the conventicle of the heretics, who glory in their errors.

For their own misery has taught them, which happiness had made negligent, alas, what an evil thing it is to fornicate against the Lord by presuming upon themselves; oh how good it is to cling to the Lord, always thinking humbly. For withdrawing from that simple and singular good into the multitudes of pleasures, and into the love of the world and corruptions of the earth, this is to fornicate against the Lord. To this one it is called out: "A harlot's face has been made for you, and you have become shameless in your entirety."

Therefore at least from now on call me: My father, you are the guide of my virginity; will you be angry forever, or will you persevere to the end? Let the heretics blush, who are unwilling to be turned to better things or to go back to the Father, their creator, and let them hear: at least from now on call me: my father, you are the guide of my virginity. He himself has betrothed your soul to his embraces and teaches how it ought to pray and to do repentance. But the more merciful he is who shows the way of salvation after fornication, the more wretched is the harlot who is unwilling to receive healing after her wounds.

Behold, you have spoken and done evil things, and you were able. 'In place of words of repentance you have blasphemed with words of pride, and you have fulfilled your evil thought and shown your strength against your husband, so that you can do what you handled in speech.'

The very wording of the passage that has been read has something obscure in it, which must first be understood; and after this, if God grants it, we shall come to know his mystical intent. Now he wants us to know this: that, as is written in the books of Kingdoms, the people were divided in the times of Rehoboam into the kingdom of the ten tribes under Jeroboam and into that of the two tribes under Rehoboam; and those under Jeroboam were called Israel, but those under Rehoboam Judah. And this division of the people has remained, so far as concerns the historical record, down to the present; for we know of no historical account that has gathered Israel and Judah together into one. Now Israel sinned first and more grievously — the people under Jeroboam and his successors — and sinned so much beyond Judah that they were condemned by Providence to become captives "into Assyria," as the Scripture says, "unto this day." After this the sons of Judah also sinned and were condemned to captivity into Babylon, not "unto this day" as Israel, but for "seventy years," concerning which Jeremiah prophesied, and which Daniel also mentioned. If we understand these things as spoken with reference to that people of that time, look at the words of the prophet, whether they do not indicate something of this sort. For he accuses, as it were, the sins of Israel, and says that, when so many sins had been committed by Israel, the congregation of Judah, having heard of their transgressions and in what manner I made them come to be in captivity, was not instructed but added to its sins, so that, because of this addition of sins when compared with the sins of Israel, righteousness was found in Israel over against Judah. Then, upon these things, the prophet is commanded to prophesy, since Judah had become worse than Israel, in order that after its sins it might turn back. So after the prophecy addressed to Israel commanding it to turn back, the prophet prophesies that Israel and Judah are going to come together and that there is at some time to be one kingdom of them both. Let whoever is concerned with the readings take up the words of the whole of today's reading, and then he will see that these meanings have been made plain.

"And the Lord said to me in the days of Josiah the king: Have you seen what the house of Israel has done to me" — not Judah, but Israel first? "She went up upon every high mountain and beneath every leafy tree and there played the harlot; and I said, after she had committed all this fornication: Turn back to me; and she did not turn back. And the faithless Judah saw her faithlessness," the faithlessness of the congregation of Israel. "And they saw" — those of Judah — "that for all the things in which the house of Israel had been caught, in which she committed adultery, I also sent her away and gave her a bill of divorce." Judah ought to have been instructed — for I sent away Israel, the congregation of Israel, I cast them out into the Assyrians "and gave her a bill of divorce into her hands" — "and the faithless Judah did not fear." But after so many things as I did to Israel, sending her away, giving her a bill of divorce, when the congregation of Judah ought to have been instructed by what those others suffered, they not only were not instructed but added to their sins, so that the sins of the congregation of Israel, by comparison with the sins of the congregation of Judah, seemed to be righteousness. "And I gave her a bill of divorce into her hands; and the faithless Judah her sister did not fear, and she went and played the harlot herself also, and her fornication became as nothing to her, and she committed adultery with wood and stone. And in all these things the faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood" she turned to me. She was not ashamed before me for what I had done to Israel, so as to turn completely; but though she ought to have turned in truth, she instead turned in falsehood. "And in all these things the faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood. And the Lord said to me: Israel has justified his soul as against the faithless Judah." The sins of Israel, compared with the transgressions of Judah, have become a justification of the soul of the congregation of Israel.

If, then, he says that first I sent away Israel because of its sins and sent it into deportation, but Judah, hearing what had happened to Israel, did not turn back, he speaks concerning our own sins. Since the things that befell Israel are read, and the transgressions concerning that people, we ought to fear, and: "if he did not spare the natural branches, how much more will he not spare us either; if that One who is both kind and at the same time loving to mankind, God, did not spare but cut off those who boasted to be a 'cultivated olive tree,' those rooted in 'the root' of the patriarchs Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, how much more will he not spare us." For he is not kind and yet not severe, nor severe and yet not kind. For if he were only kind but not severe, we would to a greater degree despise "his kindness." If he were severe but not kind, perhaps we would even despair over our sins. But as it is, as God — for we human beings need his kindness when we repent, but his severity when we persist in our sins — God is both kind and severe, and he speaks to us through the prophets and says: "Have you seen what the house of Israel has done to me?" Understand that Israel to be that people of mine: "She went up upon every high mountain and beneath every shady tree." If you see the Pharisee going up into the temple boastfully and not beating his own breast nor being anxious about his own evils, but saying: "I thank you that I am not as the rest of mankind, robbers, unjust, adulterers, or even as this tax-collector; I fast twice on the sabbath, I tithe my possessions" — you will see that he has gone up "upon every high mountain" in a blameworthy manner, having loved high-mindedness, and, according to his boasting and according to his arrogance, upon every high hill, and he has come to be "beneath every tree" that is not fruitful, but "leafy"; for the leafy tree is one thing, and another is the tree that men plant into groves. When they plant trees into groves, they plant not the fruit-bearing ones, not a fig tree nor a vine, but only barren trees for the sake of delight. Such you will find the words of the heterodox and the beauties of their persuasive arguments, which do not turn back those who hear. Whenever, then, someone gives himself over to such words, he has gone "beneath every leafy tree." He did not say "every tree" and fall silent, nor again did he add: every fruitful tree, but he said "beneath every leafy tree." Because of this you will understand what indeed the lawgiver means when he says: "You shall not plant any tree beside the altar of the Lord your God, and you shall not make a grove"; for you have also the very name of the grove forbidden.

And the Lord said to me in the days of King Josiah: Have you seen what averse Israel has done? She went off by herself upon every high mountain and under every leafy tree, and committed fornication there. And I said, when she had done all these things: Turn to me; and she did not return. And her sister, Judah the transgressor, saw that, because averse Israel had committed adultery, I had dismissed her and given her a bill of divorce; and the transgressor Judah, her sister, did not fear, but went and committed fornication, she too, and by the facility of her fornication she defiled the land and committed adultery with stone and wood. And in all these things her sister, Judah the transgressor, did not return to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood, says the Lord. The torments of some are the remedies of others; and when a murderer is punished, he himself indeed receives what he has done, but others are deterred from the crime. Thus, when the ten tribes, which were called Israel, had been captured by the Assyrians and carried over into Media, the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, which ought to have feared the like and to have been turned to God with their whole mind, surpassed the crimes of the ten tribes and followed idols to such a degree that they set up a statue of Baal in the temple of God, which in Ezekiel is called the idol set up to provoke the zeal and jealousy of the Lord. Now he speaks under the figure of two sisters, because they were begotten of the one stock of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, and he calls the first the averse one, the second the transgressor. For the former became wholly averse to God at once, when the golden calves were worshipped in Dan and Bethel; but the latter, with whom were the temple and the religion of the true God, by imitating her sister gradually withdrew from the Lord, and is therefore called the transgressor. But according to anagōgēn the prophecy concerns the heretics, who, while they imagine that they are pursuing with heretical subtlety the knowledge falsely so called, climb the mountain of pride and, beguiled by the pleasures of this flesh, display their fornication under every leafy and pleasant tree. And when they are handed over to the devil for the destruction of the flesh, it often happens that the house of 'Iuda', that is, of 'confession' and of the true faith, is by no means frightened by the example, but commits far greater things, and by the facility of its fornication defiles the land of the Church and commits adultery with stone and with wood, following those doctrines which are adverse to God. But if a man of the Church wishes to correct the one who errs, and to cut away the rotten flesh, and to draw back to repentance those who had followed falsehood, and they nonetheless, under the appearance of the Church's truth, follow their old error, it can be said of them: in all these things the transgressor Judah has not returned to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood. Now this prophecy is made in the times of Josiah, a righteous king, under whom Jeremiah also began to prophesy.

Those who place themselves far from your care and choose to serve idols will reap the destructive fruit of defection. He calls idolatry infidelity here. God likewise says also through Jeremiah, "She went up every high hill and under every green tree and was unfaithful there. I said, after all this infidelity of hers, 'Return unto me,' and she did not return." Again, "She committed adultery with tree and stone," meaning, "Leaving me, her spouse, she served false gods." Accordingly, here too he called the worship of idols infidelity.

"And she played the harlot there. And I said, after she had committed all this fornication: Turn back to me; and she did not turn back, and the faithless Judah saw her faithlessness." We too have been reproached — I mean those of us who sin and do not keep the covenants of God, nor look to the fact that those others destroyed the covenant though they were nobly born, being of Abraham, having received the promise. We ought, then, to reckon that, since those others fell out of the blessings and the promises and it profited them nothing to be from the fathers, how much more shall we, when we sin, be forsaken. "If you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham," the Savior says to them. And again John: "Do not begin to say among yourselves, We have Abraham as father; for I tell you that God is able out of these stones to raise up children to Abraham" — hinting by "stones" at us who have the stony heart and are hardened against the truth. And truly the powerful God has raised up children to Abraham from the stones, if we remain in the childbearing and keep the spirit of adoption. So the "faithless Judah" saw "her faithlessness," the faithlessness of the house of Israel — she who did not keep the covenants toward God — and she saw "that for all the things in which that one had been caught" (for we, who are Judah, behold all these things, if we read the Scripture): that concerning the things in which the house of Israel had been caught, in which she committed adultery, God sent her away and gave her a bill of divorce. We ought to be instructed by what he did to those others when he judged them according to their sins, forsaking them and delivering them into captivity and delivering them to slaughter and delivering them to their enemies; from these things we ought to turn back, and each of us ought to reckon that, if God did not spare the natural branches, how much more will he not spare us. If he thus drove out those from the fathers when they became sinners, what shall we who have been called from the Gentiles suffer — we who reckoned none of these things, though we were called in order that that people might be provoked to jealousy, seeing the slave honored, beholding the base-born one drawn near? And if those others suffered so many things, how much more, if we sin, shall we be forsaken?

"In the things in which the house of Israel committed adultery, I sent her away and gave her a bill of divorce into her hands; and the faithless Judah did not fear" the things I had done to the house of Israel, namely that "I sent her away and gave her a bill of divorce." She "did not fear" because of what had happened to those others. Someone entered into the house of a master of a household; he is newly bought, he inquires which of the former household servants the master honored and why, which of the servants he dishonored and why. Having carefully considered, if he wishes to remain in the house of the master, he guards against falling into those things which the former slaves did who sinned and were cast out and delivered over to punishment. Then, having learned what the former slaves did who were well approved, and upon what terms they obtained their freedom, he emulates those. And we too were not slaves of God, but of idols and demons, Gentiles; yesterday and the day before we drew near to God; let us read the Scripture, let us see who was justified, who was condemned, let us imitate those who were justified, let us guard against falling into those things into which those fell who were taken captive, who were cast out from God.

For this is a new kind of his goodness, that even after adultery he receives the soul, provided she returns and repents from the heart; as he himself also says through the prophet: "if a woman go out from her husband and sleep with another man, shall she return again to her husband? Shall she not be defiled with defilement? But you have fornicated with many shepherds, and yet you were returning to me". Likewise elsewhere he says: "and after you had fornicated in all these things, I said: return to me; and not even so did you return, says the Lord".

Then He directs His speech unto the city, in this way too being minded to correct His hearers, and saith, "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem!" What meaneth the repetition? this is the manner of one pitying her, and bemoaning her, and greatly loving her. For, like as unto a woman beloved, herself indeed ever loved, but who had despised Him that loved her, and therefore on the point of being punished, He pleads, being now about to inflict the punishment. Which He doth in the prophets also, using these words, "I said, Turn thou unto me, and she returned not."
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 74:3

For these two indeed are chief sins, engendered of violent lust, the one of sexual desire, the other of the desire of money.… Let no man then of them that live in vice despair; let no man who lives in virtue slumber. Let neither this last be confident, for often the harlot will pass him by; nor let the other despair, for it is possible for him to pass by even the first. Hear what God saith unto Jerusalem, "I said, after she had committed all these whoredoms, Turn thou unto me, and she returned not." When we have come back unto the earnest love of God, He remembers not the former things. God is not as man, for He reproaches us not with the past, neither doth He say, Why wast thou absent so long a time? when we repent; only let us approach Him as we ought. Let us cleave to Him earnestly, and rivet our hearts to His fear.… How many other such changes wouldest thou see, both to have taken place of old, and now taking place every day? For this reason then I say, Neither let him on the stave despair, nor let him in the church be confident. For to this last it is said, "Let him that thinketh he standeth, take heed lest he fall;" and to the other, "Shall not he that falleth arise?" and, "Lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees." Again, to these He saith, "Watch;" but to those, "Awake, thou that sleepest and arise from the dead." For these need to preserve what they have, and those to become what they are not; these to preserve their health, those to be delivered from their infirmity, for they are sick; but many even of the sick become healthy, and of the healthy many by remissness grow infirm.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 67:3-4

Have we provoked Him severely, so as no other man ever did? this is just the reason why we ought specially to abstain from our present deeds and to repent for the past, and exhibit a great change. For the evils we have once perpetrated cannot provoke Him so much as our being unwilling to make any change in the future. For to sin may be a merely human failing, but to continue in the same sin ceases to be human, and becomes altogether devilish. For observe how God by the mouth of His prophet blames this more than the other. "For," we read, "I said unto her after she had done all these deeds of fornication, return unto me, and yet she returned not."… Hear at least what He says by the mouth of the prophet: "Declare thou first thy iniquities that thou mayest be justified." Now this He demands from us in order to intensify our love towards Him.

Those who place themselves far from your care and choose to serve idols will reap the destructive fruit of defection. He calls idolatry infidelity here. God likewise says also through Jeremiah, "She went up every high hill and under every green tree and was unfaithful there. I said, after all this infidelity of hers, 'Return unto me,' and she did not return." Again, "She committed adultery with tree and stone," meaning, "Leaving me, her spouse, she served false gods." Accordingly, here too he called the worship of idols infidelity.

"And the faithless Judah did not fear, and she went and played the harlot herself also." Israel having played the harlot first, Judah too played the harlot afterward. "And her fornication became as nothing, and she committed adultery with wood and stone." Whenever we sin, we do nothing else than, becoming stony-hearted, commit adultery with "the stone." Whenever we sin and play the harlot "beneath every leafy tree," we too commit adultery with "the wood." "And the faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood." If we turned to God, but deficiently, we are charged as not having turned "with the whole heart." Therefore "the faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart." He did not say: and the faithless Judah turned, and stood firm, but: "and the faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood" she turned. The true conversion, then, is to read the things of old, to know those who were justified, to imitate them, to read those things, to see those who were blamed, to guard against falling into those blames, to read the books of the New Testament, the words of the apostles, and after reading to write all these things upon the heart, to live according to them, so that a bill of divorce may not be given to us also, but that we may be able to come to the holy inheritance, and, when the fullness of the Gentiles has been saved, then Israel may be able to enter in; for if the fullness of the Gentiles enters in, then all Israel shall be saved, "and they shall become one flock, one shepherd," teaching us to glorify God the Almighty in Christ Jesus himself, to whom be the glory and the might unto the ages of the ages. Amen.

"Go," therefore, "and read these words toward the north."

If the wording has been understood, let us see what it means to make plain in these things. The calling of the Gentiles took its beginning from the transgression of Israel, and the apostles, when they preached to the synagogues of the Jews, say: "To you the word of salvation was sent; but since you judge yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the Gentiles." And the apostle, knowing what he knows about these matters, says: "By their transgression salvation has come to the Gentiles, to provoke them to jealousy." So then the many sins of that people brought about that they were forsaken and that we came to the hope of life — we who were strangers to the covenants, aliens to the promises. For how does it come to me, who wherever I chanced to be born was a stranger to what is called the holy land, now to discourse about the promises of God, and to believe in the God of the patriarchs Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, and by the grace of God to receive Jesus Christ who was proclaimed beforehand by the prophets? If you understand these two peoples, the one from Israel and the one from the Gentiles, consider for me the deportation of Israel with regard to that people of Israel, and understand it written concerning that people: "I have sent her away and given her a bill of divorce"; for God sent away that people and gave it a bill of divorce. This is something of the following sort in the case of those who have married: if the wife is displeasing to the husband, the law of Moses says, a "bill of divorce" was made out from the husband and the wife was sent away, and it was permitted to the one who had sent away his former wife, because she seemed to have behaved unseemly, to marry another woman. Thus in the spiritual sense behold those people receiving a bill of divorce. And since they received the bill of divorce, therefore they were utterly forsaken. For where are there prophets any longer among them? Where are signs any longer among them? Where is the manifestation of God? Where is the worship, the temple, the sacrifices? They were cast out from their own place; so he gave Israel a "bill of divorce."

Then we, being Judah (and Judah because of the Savior who arose from the tribe of Judah; for it is plain that our Lord has arisen out of Judah), have turned to the Lord, and our last state — which may it not now already be — seems to be becoming much like their last state, if indeed it is not even worse.

For that such things will be also in our own case at the consummation of this age is plain from what was said by the Savior in the Gospel, in which he says: "Because iniquity is multiplied, the love of the many will grow cold. But he who endures to the end, he shall be saved"; and: "He will do signs and wonders so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect." Such will our own case be, so that the Savior says concerning his own coming, since among so many churches a faithful one is scarcely to be found: "Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he indeed find faith upon the earth?" And truly, if we judge matters by truth and not by crowds, and if we judge matters by moral choice and not by seeing many gathered together, we shall see that now we are not faithful. But they were faithful then, when the noble martyrdoms were taking place, when, having escorted the martyrs from the burial-places, we came to the assemblies, and the whole church attended, unafflicted, and the catechumens were catechized amid the martyrdoms and amid the deaths of those confessing the truth "unto death," "not frightened" nor troubled "before the living God." Then we know that they had also seen paradoxical signs and marvels. Then there were faithful — few indeed, but truly faithful — journeying the narrow and afflicted way that leads "unto life." But now, when we have become many, since it is not possible for the elect to be many (for he does not lie who said, Jesus: "Many are called, but few are chosen"), out of the multitude of those who profess godliness exceedingly few are those who attain to the election of God and to blessedness.

Let us now proceed to consider the mode of his loving discipline, with the aid of the prophetic testimony. Admonition, then, is loving care's censure and produces understanding. Such is Christ the Educator in his admonitions, as when he says in the Gospel, "How often would I have gathered your children, as a bird gathers her young ones under her wings, and you did not allow it!" And again, the Scripture admonishes, saying, "And they committed adultery with wood and stone and burned incense to Baal." For it is a very great proof of his love, that, though knowing well the shamelessness of the people who had kicked and bounded away, he notwithstanding exhorts them to repentance and says by Ezekiel, "Son of man, you live in the midst of scorpions; nevertheless, speak to them, if perhaps they will hear."

Admonition, then, is loving care's censure and produces understanding. Such is Christ the Educator in his admonitions, as when he says in the Gospel, "How often would I have gathered your children, as a bird gathers her young ones under her wings, and you would not!" And again, the Scripture admonishes, saying, "And they committed adultery with stock and stone and burned incense to Baal." For it is a very great proof of God's love that, though knowing well the shamelessness of the people who had kicked and bounded away, he nevertheless exhorts them to repentance. He says by Ezekiel, "Son of man, you dwell in the midst of scorpions. Nevertheless, speak to them, if by chance they will hear." Further, to Moses he says, "Go and tell Pharaoh to send my people forth, but I know that he will not send them forth."

It is not only bodily sin that is called fornication and adultery, but any sin you have committed, and especially transgression against that which is divine. Perhaps you ask how we can prove this. "They prostituted themselves," it says "with things they made." Don't you see an impudent act of fornication? And again, "They committed adultery with pieces of wood." Don't you see a kind of adulterous religion? Do not then commit spiritual adultery, while keeping your bodies chaste.
ON THE WORDS OF THE GOSPEL, 'WHEN JESUS HAD FINISHED THESE SAYINGS,' ORATION 37:19

Those who place themselves far from your care and choose to serve idols will reap the destructive fruit of defection. He calls idolatry infidelity here. God likewise says also through Jeremiah, "She went up every high hill and under every green tree and was unfaithful there. I said, after all this infidelity of hers, 'Return unto me,' and she did not return." Again, "She committed adultery with tree and stone," meaning, "Leaving me, her spouse, she served false gods." Accordingly, here too he called the worship of idols infidelity.

"And yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah has not returned to me with her whole heart, but feignedly." It is a smaller sin to follow evil that you think is good than not to venture to defend what you know for certain is good. If we cannot endure threats, injustice and poverty, how shall we overcome the flames of Babylon? Let us not lose by hollow peace what we have preserved by war. I should be sorry to allow my fears to teach me faithlessness when Christ has put the true faith in the power of my choice.

And the Lord said to me: Averse Israel has justified her soul in comparison with the transgressor Judah. 'More righteous,' he says, 'is Israel in comparison with Judah, because the former perished at once, at the beginning, while the latter could have been corrected by the torments of the former'. Let the new heresy sprung from the old take note that Israel is said to be justified in comparison with a worse one. Nor is this surprising of sisters of one nation, since Sodom too, in comparison with Jerusalem, receives the name of righteousness, as the Lord says through Ezekiel: 'Sodom has been justified by you', and the publican becomes righteous in comparison with the Pharisee.

And Scripture keeps up this comparison on the other side also, i.e., in weighing the merits of sinners, so that in comparison with the wicked it justifies those who have sinned less, saying: "Sodom is justified above thee;" and again: "For what hath thy sister Sodom sinned?" and: "The rebellious Israel hath justified her soul in comparison of the treacherous Judah."
The Third Conference of Abbot Theonas, Chapter 4

AGAINST NOVATIAN. — His disciples say to Jesus, “Lord, do you want us to say that fire should come down from heaven and consume them, as Elijah did?” And the Lord answered them, saying, “You do not know of what spirit you are. For the Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save them” (Luke 9:54–56). Although it was certainly fitting to take revenge on the Samaritans who did not receive him, nevertheless the Lord, who came to grant mercy, removed the sentence, so that those who were corrected afterwards might be changed. And the prophet Elisha, angered at the boys who insulted him, took vengeance on them with God as judge, so that in that place they were eaten by bears, where there is said to be no forest (2 Kings 2:23–24); but the Lord spared the prostitute who was brought before him, namely the one whom the leaders of the Jews said they had caught in adultery (Jn. 8:11), so that, since a loving declaration had begun, he might teach that she was not to be condemned, but pardoned. For the Law given through Moses, because it had justice directed to revenge, exercised severity in its beginnings. It took funeral revenge on the man who went out to gather wood on the sabbath (Num. 15:32–36); and similarly took punishment on the son of the Egyptian woman who had blasphemed God (Lev. 24:10–14); and in the matter of the molten calf struck the sons of Israel (Exod. 32:27). Each Law, then, in its very beginnings shows its full character: the old Law, because it was more ready to punish, appeared harsher in its early days, so that by instilling fear it might make its hearers diligent and watchful. But the new Law, because it is loving and inclined easily to mercy, showed its beginnings as most gentle and most compassionate, so that by this very charm and love it might call all to forgiveness. Afterwards, however, even that Law which seemed harsher, on account of the frailty of the human race, not only softened its severity, but also showed itself humane and loving, and this Law which seemed gentle at times took vengeance. For Ananias and his wife Sapphira were struck down by God (Acts 5:5, 10). And Elymas the magician, unbelieving and opposing the law of God, was blinded by the judgment and power of the Lord (Acts 13:8–11). And King Herod, because he did not give honor to the God of heaven, was struck by an angel of God and, swelling with worms, breathed his last (Acts 12:23). Lest, because mercy is preached, people should think there is absolutely no punishment and that they may sin with freedom, fear was imposed, showing that forgiveness of sins is given for this purpose: that, as if brought to life from the dead, they should afterwards abstain from the contrary things, so that it may be brought about that no one departs from here with guilt, because there will be a coming to judgment. For the sentence in which each person dies is what is credited to him. Since, therefore, the new Law has the fullness of mercy, lest it be treated with contempt by lovers of sin, it took vengeance on the above-mentioned persons. The old Law, though given for vengeance, nevertheless pardoned some, lest it be called wholly cruel; but it took vengeance on many, because its disposition is ready to punish. Without doubt, then, the grace of the new Law is greater than that of the old. If, therefore, the grace is greater, how is it denied that this Law can grant what that Law granted, which had less grace? For the former was more inclined to severity. Therefore, if that Law is proved to have forgiven the repentant, how can it be that this Law, which is gentle, does not receive the repentant? For even the Jews were called sons of God, who, as we read on the authority of the apostle Paul, were baptized through Moses in the cloud and in the sea (1 Cor. 10:2). Indeed, they are known to have been purified as they were about to receive the Law, so that afterwards they might give an account of the Law they had received, and if they sinned, they might reform themselves through repentance; as the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah, “Do penance, you who err, and be converted” (Isa. 45:22). But perhaps, on the contrary, it is said: Repentance indeed was preached, but not remission. If, therefore, repentance has been preached by God, there will be fruit for those doing repentance. For the Lord would not admonish this in vain. Moreover, since the Lord knew that remission of sins must be given to the converted, he commanded this; for he said, “I do not desire the death of the sinner, only that he be converted and live” (Ezek. 18:32). And therefore there is fruit of repentance, as has become clear, for those who are converted to God. Therefore, the assertion wickedly fabricated by Novatian is excluded, by which he overturns the meaning of the Lord’s words, saying, “The Lord said, Whoever shall deny me, I also will deny him” (Matt. 10:33); so that if any Christian, for whatever reason, has denied, he can no longer return, or certainly, if he does return, he is in no way received. And where, then, is the repentance that has been enjoined? When the Savior, after having pronounced this sentence, did not deny the apostle Peter who had denied him. Why? Because, with repentance following, he wept bitterly over his sin (Matt. 26:75), knowing, of course, that forgiveness is granted to those who are converted, and that they are reformed through repentance. But Novatian pretends that repentance is to be done. Because he does not openly dare to deny that repentance should be granted, being limited by the Law, he strives subtly to frustrate it. For when he says that whoever has denied will by no means have pardon, but will himself be denied before the angels of God, how does he not deceitfully profess that repentance is to be done? From this his fraud clearly appears, when he adds, saying, “Whoever shall sin against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither here nor in the future” (Matt. 12:32). Although one cause is that by which there is sin against the Holy Spirit, and another to deny the Lord Jesus, Novatian, nevertheless, in order to deny pardon for this sin, wants there to be one and the same meaning for the one who denies the Lord and for the one who sins against the Holy Spirit, so that by this fudging he may cut off the fruit of repentance. For if denying the Lord is the same as having sinned against the Holy Spirit, there is no pardon to be hoped for by those who deny, nor any fruit of repentance; because this sin, neither here nor in the future, the Lord’s oracles have promised to remit. From this it becomes clear that Novatian speaks deceitfully when he says that penance must be done. For why should one repent, if it is denied that the sin can be removed? For the sighs, tears, and weeping of repentance obtain this: that it both merits pardon and restoration. Therefore David, repenting and confessing his sin, both obtained forgiveness (2 Kings 12:13) and was restored to his former state; for he remained king and afterwards prophesied. This is clearly proven: for in the fiftieth Psalm he repented, and afterwards, having suffered persecution from his son, he prophesied. For the third Psalm according to the historical order is after the fiftieth. But perhaps it will be said that a king had to be forgiven, whereas the lowly must not be forgiven, although it seems that it is rather more difficult to forgive those who are more powerful. For God does not regard the person of a man (Rom. 2:11). The higher one is, the more, even if his sin is slight, it is a grave crime. For just as humility in a powerful man is lofty and noble, so also his fault must be regarded as a crime. Except for those sins which are clearly unlawful for all, not everything is permitted to the powerful that is allowed to the lowly. For it is disgraceful for a man of rank to bargain in trade, and entering a tavern is noteworthy. For senators, lending at interest is a disgrace. If therefore in these lesser matters they are found worthy of censure, how much more must they be held guilty if they sin? From this, then, it appears that David sinned very grievously, and in fact in a twofold way. Yet, when he turned back, he obtained forgiveness for both murder and adultery, and what is more, he was reformed with tears. For when he was rebuked by the prophet Nathan, he did not dare hide his sin, but confessed it, saying, I have sinned against the Lord. Then the prophet answered and said, The Lord has taken away your sin, and you shall not die, because you have repented. And because he is afterwards found to have prophesied, there is no doubt that he was restored. For also Ahab, rebuked by the prophet because of the death of Naboth, went about weeping, and tore his garments, and girded himself with sackcloth; and the word of the Lord came by the hand of His servant Elijah concerning Ahab, and the Lord said: Have you seen how Ahab is moved before my face? I will not bring the evil upon him in his days (1 Kings 21:27–29). And when the Ninevites wept for their sins, with death awaiting, their life was restored (Jonah 3:10). See how great is the progress of repentance. But perhaps it may be said in reply: Repentance was granted indeed, but not for the crime of idolatry; although these sins are grave, the crime of idolatry is greater. Nevertheless, Novatian’s assertion is rightly overthrown in no small part, since two grave crimes appear to have been granted to repentance. For if fornication ought not to be forgiven, as Novatian thinks, how much less murder or adultery? Yet here his vanity is evident, since those sins which are more serious are shown to have been forgiven. Therefore now it must be asked whether God has promised that forgiveness can be granted even to idolaters. For whatever has not been lawfully granted here cannot be granted in the future. For here, as the Lord said, sins are either bound or loosed (Matt. 16:19); but in the future there will be nothing else but reward or condemnation.
