Accordingly I fear, dearly-beloved, lest that utterance of the Prophet be addressed in rebuke to such men, which says, “thou hast scourged them and they have not grieved: thou hast chastised them, and they have refused to receive correction.” For what amendment is shown by them in whom such aversion to God’s service is found? One is ashamed to say it, but one must not keep silence: more is spent upon demons than upon the Apostles, and mad spectacles draw greater crowds than blessed martyrdoms. Who was it that restored this city to safety? that rescued it from captivity? the games of the circus-goers or the care of the saints? surely it was by the saints’ prayers that the sentence of Divine displeasure was diverted, so that we who deserved wrath, were reserved for pardon.

We are judged by the ever-present judgment of God, and thus a most slothful race has been aroused to accomplish our destruction and shame. They go from place to place, from city to city, and destroy everything. First they poured out from their native land into Germany, which lay nearest them, a country called barbarous, but under Roman control. After its destruction, the country of the Belgae burst into flames, then the rich estates of the luxurious Aquitanians, and after these the whole body of the Gallic provinces. This ruin spread gradually, however, in order that while one part was being visited with destruction, another might be reformed by its example. But when has there been any amendment among us, or what part of the Roman world, whatever its affliction, is corrected by it? As we read: "They are all gone out of the way, they are altogether become useless." And in like manner the prophet cried out to the Lord, saying: "Thou hast stricken them but they have not grieved; thou hast consumed them, but they have refused to receive correction; they have made their faces harder than a rock; they have refused to return.''

How truly this applies to us the present situation shows. Gaul long endured devastation; did Spain, her near neighbor, mend her ways? Not undeservedly, since they showed no fear whatever, and no reform, the people of Spain began to catch fire from the flames by which the Gauls were consumed. The worst and most evil aspect of all this is, as I have said before, that the fires which, to speak figuratively, consumed the bodies of these sinful men, did not burn away their vices.
On the Government of God, Book 7, Chapter 12

In my own case this is now the third year of my silence, and my boast has become like that of the Psalmist, “I was as a man that heareth not and in whose mouth are no reproofs.” Thus I shut up in the bottom of my heart the pangs which I suffered on account of the calumnies directed against me, for calumny humbles a man, and calumny makes a poor man giddy. If, therefore, the mischief of calumny is so great as to cast down even the perfect man from his height, for this is what Scripture indicates by the word man, and by the poor man is meant he who lacks the great doctrines, as is the view also of the prophet when he says, “These are poor, therefore they shall not hear;…I will get me unto the great men,” he means by poor those who are lacking in understanding; and here, too, he plainly means those who are not yet furnished in the inner man, and have not even come to the full measure of their age; it is these who are said by the proverb to be made giddy and tossed about.

Paul says about those who live in piety and prosperity, "I thank God that in every way you were enriched in him with all speech and all knowledge." And to those who are impious, the blessed Jeremiah says, "Maybe they are poor. For this reason, they could not hear the word of the Lord." Do you see that he calls poor those who have distanced themselves from piety? Therefore, God is merciful to those who sin because they are spiritually poor, and he places demands on those who act justly because they are spiritually rich. To the former he gives freely, on account of their poverty. From the latter he collects with great care, on account of their wealth of piety. That which he does to the righteous and to sinners, he does to both the rich and the poor.

But I said: Perhaps they are poor and foolish — or they could not — not knowing the way of the Lord, the judgment of their God. I will go therefore to the nobles and will speak to them; for they have known the way of the Lord, the judgment of their God. He speaks here of the poor and the nobles not in terms of want and riches; rather, he compares the people with the princes. And the sense is: 'Seeing the obstinacy of the unbelieving people, and that with hardened face it would not receive discipline, I was reasoning this out with myself: perhaps the ignoble common crowd cannot know the teaching of God and is therefore excusable, because through inexperience it is not able to know the commandments of God. I will go therefore to the priests and to those who preside over the people, and will speak to them; for they have known the will of the Lord and know the judgment of their God'. He says this in the language of one who doubts, according to that saying of the Gospel: I will send my son; perhaps they will reverence him, so that from the ambiguity of the statement and the suspense of the words the free will of man may be shown.

"Well-off" refers to the priests and the teachers of the law; "poor" refers to the rest, insofar as they did not possess the wealth of divine knowledge. Yet he accuses both of lawlessness, proceeding in this way, "They all alike broke the yoke, they snapped the bonds." It was not without purpose the prophet said this. Instead, since the Lord promised lovingkindness, provided he found someone "doing justice and seeking faith," he explains that though he went looking, as he was commanded to do, he found they had all broken the yoke of the law.

"I will go to the great ones and speak to them." Those who are great in soul are spoken of in praise. For among the Greeks too "greatness" (to hadron) is continually used to name the grandeur of the rational soul. For whenever someone undertakes great matters and has purposes worthy of account and always considers what is fitting — how he may live according to right reason, wishing and looking upon nothing lowly and small — such a one has the greatness and grandeur in his soul. These men, then, since they were poor — the former ones whom the word blamed — did not listen, says the prophet. For this reason they did not listen, because they are poor. "I will go to the great ones and speak to them." And if it is a blessed thing to speak "into the ears of those who hear," it is a blessed thing if one meets with a great and mighty hearer. Therefore, since these things are so spoken, knowing that it is no loss to those who speak, so much as to those who hear, not to accept the things announced, and that it accuses the poverty of their mind and of their understanding, let us beseech to receive from God, as the word increases greatness and grandeur in us in Christ Jesus, that we may be able to hear the sacred and holy words — to whom be the glory and the might unto the ages of ages. Amen.

And behold, these all the more together have broken the yoke, have burst the bonds. Therefore a lion from the forest struck them, a wolf at evening laid them waste, a leopard watching over their cities. Everyone who goes out from them will be taken, because their transgressions are multiplied, their turnings-away are strengthened. 'Those whom I thought to be teachers were found to be worse than the disciples; and the greater the authority among the rich, the greater the insolence of their sins'. For they broke the yoke of the law, as the Apostle says: Now therefore why do you tempt God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we are saved, in the same way as they also; and they burst the bonds of the precepts of God, and not of the Pharisees, of whom it is said in the second Psalm: Let us burst their bonds asunder, and cast away their yoke from us.

And the prophet of God reproacheth severely those who have broken the yoke, and cut the bands of the fear of God. Now Israel became rebels because there was no fear [in them]; and they trod under foot the commandments because they were not mindful of what was threatened; and they despised the law because they remembered not the penalty of Him that ordained it. For He Who ordained the law because He knew to whom He was giving the law, against [the breaking of] His commandments multiplied His threats in His wisdom, so that although freewill might hold the law in contempt, the fear which followed thereafter might incite [Israel] to the keeping thereof. And because he that received the law became a rebellious slave, He made him to labour in bondage in the fear of tribulation. Before his face He displayed all the various forms of punishment, so that as long as he looked thereupon he might take heed to the commandments, and keep the law.
13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 6 -- First Discourse on the Fear of God

[Passage quoted, Jer. v. 6-10.]

Here once more the charge against their whole race is shewn, and the siege that came on them, and the remnant again, which he names "the foundation" as belonging to the Lord. Because being inspired and strengthened by their faith in the Christ of God, they did not undergo such sufferings as the rest of their race.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

Jeremiah also speaks of sinners: A lion from the forest struck them, and a wolf destroyed them even to their houses; and a leopard kept watch over their cities. All who go out from them will be taken. In this, note that no one is taken except one who has gone out from the cities of God.

Because, then, they did these things, a lion from the forest struck them, namely the Babylonian kingdom; a wolf at evening laid them waste, signifying the Medes and Persians, in place of which in the vision of Daniel a 'bear' is set down, in whose mouth there were three rows; a leopard watching over their cities, prefiguring the onslaught of Alexander and his swift course from the west all the way to India. He calls him a leopard on account of his variegation, and because he fought against the Medes and Persians with very many nations subject to him. And there were, he says, four heads on the beast, and power was given to it. And because he is not prophesying of the future, but is weaving the history of the past or of things now on the very point of coming, for that reason he is silent about the Roman empire, of which perhaps it is said: Everyone who goes out from them will be taken. And he gives the causes why they suffered these things: because their transgressions are multiplied and they persevered in their transgressions. Hence it is said: and their turnings-away are strengthened. What we set down at the beginning, that the Hebrew word 'sacad' signifies 'watchfulness', is shown in the present place; for where we said 'a leopard watching', in the Hebrew is written 'nemer sacad'. According to tropology: those who are thought great in the Church, because they break the yoke and burst the bonds, are for that reason handed over to the disgrace of passions, so that they do the things that are not fitting.

We must conduct our festivals and rejoice with fear and trembling. A faithful Christian, the psalm says, must not sing the songs of the heathen or have anything to do with the principles and doctrines of strange assemblies. It may happen that through their songs, he might make mention of the names of idols, which God forbids the faithful to do. The Lord scolds certain people through Jeremiah and says, "Your children have forsaken me, and have sworn by those who are no gods."

On what ground shall I be able to be merciful to you? Your sons have forsaken me and swear by those who are not gods. I filled them, and they committed adultery, and in the house of the harlot they ran riot. They have become to me horses, lovers toward the females, and stallions; each one neighed after the wife of his neighbor. Shall I not visit for these things? says the Lord, and on such a nation shall not my soul take vengeance? A Katalogos [a catalogue] of the sins of Jerusalem, while God says that he does not know on what ground he could have mercy on her. 'The sons', he says, 'of yours have forsaken me: by no means mine, but yours, because they swear by those who are not gods. I filled them, and they committed adultery'. Let those hear this who, brooding over the riches they have received from the Lord, are slaves to luxury.

Those who do indeed reject the Spirit's counsel, and are the slaves of fleshly lusts, and lead lives contrary to reason, and who, without restraint, plunge headlong into their own desires, having no longing after the Divine Spirit, do live after the manner of swine and of dogs; these men does the apostle very properly term "carnal," because they have no thought of anything else except carnal things. For the same reason, too, do the prophets compare them to irrational animals, on account of the irrationality of their conduct, saying, "They have become as horses raging for the females; each one of them neighing after his neighbour's wife." And again, "Man, when he was in honour, was made like unto cattle." This denotes that, for his own fault, he is likened to cattle, by rivalling their irrational life. And we also, as the custom is, do designate men of this stamp as cattle and irrational beasts.

At another time, he speaks of us under the figure of a colt. He means by that that we are unyoked to evil, unsubdued by wickedness, unaffected and high-spirited only with him our Father. We are colts, not stallions "who whinny lustfully for their neighbor's wife," beasts of burden unrestrained in their lust. Rather, we are free and newly born, joyous in our faith, and hold fast to the course of truth. We are swift in seeking salvation, and we spurn and trample on worldliness.

If birth is an evil, then the blasphemers must place the Lord who went through birth and the virgin who gave him birth in the category of evil. Abominable people! In attacking birth they are maligning the will of God and the mystery of creation. This is the basis of Cassian's docetism, Marcion's too, yes, and Valentinus's "semi-spiritual body." It leads them to say, "Humanity became like cattle in coming to sexual intercourse." But it is when a man, swollen with lust, really and truly wants to go to bed with a woman not his own, that that sort of man actually becomes a wild beast. "They turned into stallions crazed for mares; each was whinnying for his neighbor's wife."

Rebuking censures what is base and highlights what is noble. This is shown by Jeremiah: "They were horses mad for females. Each one neighed for his neighbor's wife. Shall I not visit them for these things? says the Lord. Should not I avenge my soul against such a nation as this?" He everywhere interweaves fear, because "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of reason."

Angels do not change. Not one of them is a child, or a young man, or an old man, but in whatever state they were created, in the beginning, in that state they remain. Their substance is preserved pure and inviolate for them. But we change in our body, as has been shown, and in our soul and in the inner person, always shifting our thoughts with the circumstances. In fact, we are one sort of person when we are cheerful and when all things in our life are moving forward with the current. But we are another sort in precarious times, when we stumble against something that is not according to our wishes. We are changed through anger, assuming a certain savage state. We are also changed through our lusts of carnal things, becoming like beasts through a life of pleasure. "They become amorous horses," being madly in love with their neighbors' wives. The deceitful person is compared with a fox, as Herod was. The shameless person is called a dog, like Nabel the Carmelian. Do you see the variety and diversity of our change? Then, admire him who has fittingly adapted this title to us. For this very reason, a certain one of the interpreters seems to me to have handed over beautifully and accurately the same thought through another title. He says, "For the lilies," in place of, "For them that shall be changed." He thought that it was appropriate to compare the transitory state of human nature with the early death of flowers. But since this word has been inflected in the future tense (It is said, "For them that shall be changed," as if at some time later this change will be shown to us), let us consider whether there is suggested to us the doctrine of the resurrection, in which a change will be granted to us, but a change for something better and something spiritual.

Fasting can be utilized as a weapon against demonic armies: "For this kind does not come out except through prayer and fasting." Many good things come from fasting, but being satiated introduces the beginnings of insolence. It immediately rushes in alongside the delicacy you are eating and it accompanies rich sauces. All kinds of licentious behavior begin grazing at its table. After this, men start becoming "lusty horses" toward women because all this luxury begins to start a maddening itch that enters into their soul. Those who get drunk begin perverting themselves against nature, using a male like a female, or vice versa. Fasting, by contrast, reveals the proper boundaries for marriage. It curtails the excesses of even those things that may be permitted by law but that are abstained from by agreement so that the couple can devote themselves to prayer.But we should not limit the goodness of fasting only to abstaining from foods. True fasting, in whatever form, is the enemy of evil. "Loose the chains of injustice!" Forgive your neighbor when an offense occurs against you and forgive his debts. Do not "fast in order to bring about judgment and strife."14
You may not eat meat, but you devour your brother. You abstain from wine but hold on to insolence. You wait till evening to indulge [in a meal] but spend the day in court. "Woe to those who are drunk, but not from wine!" Wrath can also be a drunkenness of the soul, making it senseless, like wine. Grief can also feel like being drunk, weighing down the mind. Fear is another form of drunkenness whenever it fears something where there is no need for fear, because the psalmist says, "deliver my soul from the fear of my enemy." When taken together, each of these passions that allow the mind to be taken over and to go out of control is rightly termed drunkenness.… Guard against this kind of drunkenness, but do not be given over to the kind that comes from wine, either. Do not start being a water drinker just because you have been drinking too much. Do not let drunkenness be what leads you into fasting. The door that leads to fasting is not entered through drunkenness. Neither is greed the entryway into justice, nor is intemperance the way to sound judgment. In summary, evil never leads to virtue. There is another door into fasting. Drunkenness leads to intemperance. Contentment is what opens the door to fasting.

Humanity … did not understand and neglected to follow God and to become like his Creator. And becoming a slave of the passions of the flesh, "he is compared with senseless beasts and is become like them." Now he is like an amorous horse that neighs after his neighbor's wife. Now like a ravenous wolf, lying in wait for strangers, but at another time, because of his deceit toward his brother, he makes himself like the villainous fox. Truly, there is excessive folly and beast-like lack of reason that he, made according to the image of the Creator, neither perceives his own from the beginning nor even wishes to understand such great dispensations that were made for his sake. At least, he should learn his own dignity from them, but he is unmindful of the fact, and he throws aside the image of the heavenly, but he has taken up the image of the earthly.
The neighing horse depicts the recklessness of young men.

Yet for all this some are so cold and senseless, as to be always seeking only the things that are here, and uttering those absurd sayings, "Let me enjoy all things present for a time, and then I will consider about things out of sight: I will gratify my belly, I will be a slave to pleasures, I will make full use of the present life; give me to-day, and take tomorrow." Oh excess of folly! Why, wherein do they who talk so differ from goats and swine? For if the prophet permits not them to be accounted men, that "neigh after their neighbors wife," who shall blame us for esteeming these to be goats and swine, and more insensible than asses, by whom those things are held uncertain, which are more evident than what we see?
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 13:7

They have become horses, lovers toward the females. For 'stallions' in the Hebrew is written 'mosechim', which all with one accord translated helkontes, that is, 'drawing', so that the size of the genitals may be shown, according to that saying of Ezekiel: like the flesh of asses is their flesh. This is what is written in another place: they were likened to senseless beasts and became like them. And at the same time he shows so great a madness of lust that he calls it not the appetite of pleasure but chremetismon, that is, 'neighing', and keeps the metaphoran [metaphor] of horses raging for lust.

Perhaps I am doing an injustice in reckoning the actions of the rich as sins, for when they kill their poor slaves they consider it an act of justice, not a crime. Nor is this all; they also abuse their privilege in their vile breaches of chastity. What rich man keeps his marriage vows, who among them does not plunge headlong into passionate lust, who does not use his household slaves as harlots and pursue his madness against any one on whom the heat of his evil desires may light? They illustrate well the words of the Holy Scriptures about such men as they: "They are become as horses rushing madly on the mares." Is it not a proof of what I just said, that the average man wishes to make his own by physical union whatever his eyes have beheld with desire?
On the Government of God, Book 4, Chapter 5

When the master of the house acts as husband of the maidservants, the mistress is not far removed from the mean position of the slave. Who among the rich men of Aquitania did not so act? Who among them has not been considered by his shameless maids, and with good, reason, as either adulterer or husband? For, as the prophet said: ''They were as fed horses in the morning; everyone neighed after his neighbor's wife." Those of whom he spoke sinned perhaps less grievously, and, I think, with less intention of wrong than did our men. The Aquitanians more truly resembled the post horses: they whinnied not after a few women merely, but after all their household maids — that is, after their own herds — and, like those; beasts called the stallions of the herd, they waxed wanton with the heat of their intoxicating passion, and attacked whatever woman was first exposed to the onslaught of their shameless lust.
On the Government of God, Book 7, Chapter 4

'When you have done these things', he says, 'are you not deserving of a fitting visitation?' And note that here 'visitation' is put for penalty and punishments, according to what is written: I will visit their iniquities with the rod. And on such a nation shall not my soul take vengeance? After she has been bound by sins, she is no longer called the people of God, but a nation, from which the soul of God has withdrawn, according to what is written: your new moons and sabbaths and feast days my soul hates. But what in the Old Testament is said by way of affection, in the New is written as truth, as the Savior says: I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up.

Go up upon her walls — or bulwarks — and destroy, but do not make a full end! Take away her shoots — or props —, because they are not the Lord's! For with transgression the house of Israel and the house of Judah has transgressed against me, says the Lord. He commands the nations of which he had said above: a lion from the forest struck them, a wolf laid them waste, and a leopard in their cities, to go up upon the walls of Jerusalem, or its bulwarks, and destroy it, but not to make a full end, so that the remnant may be saved and there may be one to announce the glory of God among the nations; and he mingles clemency with severity. And as for what he added: take away her shoots or props, he orders all the aids to be removed which she lost by her own fault, because the house of Israel and the house of Judah transgressed against God, signifying the ten tribes and the two. Let the Church hear this: that the walls and bulwarks of those who have no hope in the Lord and transgress against him are quickly destroyed, but that nevertheless a full end is not made, on account of the clemency of the judge and not on account of the merits of the offenders.

Accusation is the censure of wrongdoers. This mode of instruction God employs by David, when he says, "The people whom I did not know served me, and when their ears heard they obeyed me. Sons of strangers came to me, and halted from their ways." And by Jeremiah: "And I gave her a divorce decree, but covenant-breaking Judah did not fear." And again: "And the house of Israel disregarded me. The house of Judah lied to the Lord."

They have denied the Lord and said: He is not — or these things are not — nor will evil come upon us; sword and famine we shall not see. The prophets have come to wind, and an answer — or a word — was not in them. These things therefore will come upon them. Because they have denied the Lord — or they have lied to the Lord — and said: 'He is not, by whose judgment all things come to pass, but all these things have happened by chance; and the things which the voices of the prophets threaten us with will not come, nor shall we see the sword, nor shall we endure the famine of a siege; and whatever the prophets spoke, they spoke to the wind, and all things have passed away void, nor did they have an answer, that is, an oracle, or the word of God was not in them', therefore they will endure what the following discourse describes. Let the Church hear this, when it is negligent and rejects the providence of God: that it will endure both sword and famine, unless it believes that the things which are spoken will come.

Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Because you have spoken this word, behold, I give my words in your mouth into fire, and this people into wood, and it will devour them. 'You said: The prophets have come to wind, and the things they threaten will not come; therefore, O prophet, I give my words in your mouth, which are to have the power of fire, and which are to turn this people into wood, so that the unbelieving may be burned up together by your discourse and prophecy.' So God is called a consuming fire, that he may consume in us whatever, upon the foundation of Christ, we have built of hay, wood, stubble.

Behold, I will bring upon you a nation from afar, O house of Israel, says the Lord, a strong nation, an ancient nation, a nation whose language you will not know, nor will you understand what it says. Its quiver is like an open sepulchre; all are mighty. And it will eat your crops and your bread, it will devour your sons and your daughters, it will eat your flock and your herds, it will eat your vine and your fig tree, and it will crush with the sword your fortified cities, in which you have confidence. Nevertheless in those days, he says, I will not make you into utter destruction. 'Not after a long time, nor, as you falsely believe, will the prophets speak to you into the wind; but even now I will bring upon you a nation of the Babylonians, which will come from afar, a strong nation' — for which in the Hebrew is written 'etham' —, 'an ancient nation' — over which Nimrod the giant once held dominion —, 'whose language you will not know or' — as is written in the Hebrew — 'nor will you understand what it says; for it is a solace in misfortunes if you have such enemies as you can entreat and as understand your prayers'.

And what follows: its quiver is like an open sepulchre, which is not said in the edition of the Seventy, signifies the Babylonian armament. Nor is there any doubt that the kingdom of the Assyrians, the Babylonians, the Medes and the Persians is most skilled in archery.

And at the same time he describes the devastation of the land of Judea and the slaughter of many, the driving off of cattle, the overthrow of cities and of walls: that all things are taken by the hostile sword, and that yet amid such great evils he does not destroy them to extermination, but keeps a remnant safe, either of those who were led into Babylon and released for the cultivation of the fields of the land of Judea, or of those who, after the heat of persecution, kept the faith of the Lord either by flight or by confession.

God, who judges "little by little," gives to those being chastised room for repentance, and does not, in punishing at the very moment of sin, bring the full completion of the punishment upon the one who has sinned. For this reason, "judging little by little," he chastises. And an example of this is in Leviticus; for in the curses against those who transgress the Law it is written, after the earlier punishments: "And it shall be, if after these things you do not turn back, says the Lord, I too will add to you seven plagues." And again he recounts another punishment: "And it shall be, if after these things you do not turn back, but walk toward me crookedly, I too will walk with you in crooked wrath." And you will find God measuring out punishments with sparing restraint, since he wishes to lead the one who has sinned to conversion, and does not repay them all at once. Such things, then, so far as the letter goes, had come about concerning the people; and the word, threatening them with what they will suffer, says after those things: "And it shall be in those days, says the Lord your God, I will not strike you unto complete destruction." But whether these things especially reach even to the punishments that are to come — if not, let the one who is able pass over from the things that befell the people in this life to those punishments as well; for I, being persuaded, would say that just as "they serve a copy and shadow of heavenly things," so it was with a copy and shadow of the true punishments that that people was punished for their own sins, so that every punishment according to the Law and the Prophets which concerns the people contains a shadow of the true punishments.

If, then, for those people no complete destruction came upon them for their sins, but at some point in the end there would be — nor will there ever fail to be, even after the departure, a punishment upon those who have sinned. But the complete destruction came upon Jerusalem when the captivity is that of Nebuchadnezzar. And yet someone will say that not even then was there complete destruction, nor even in the times of the Maccabees. But the complete destruction came upon the people at the coming of my Lord Jesus Christ. For as long as the Savior was not saying to them, "Behold, your house is forsaken to you," it was not forsaken. But when he wept over Jerusalem, saying, "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to her, how often have I wished to gather together your children, in the way a hen gathers together her chicks under her wings, and you would not? Behold, your house is left to you desolate," the house was forsaken, "Jerusalem was surrounded by armies," as the house had been forsaken, and "her desolation drew near." Then, after their transgression, salvation came to us. So those people were being chastised, and complete destruction did not reach them until the sojourn of my Lord Jesus.

But I consider whether such things may also be the case concerning us, and whether certain punishments come about, so that these here have no experience of second punishments but are content with the former, while others come even to the second, though not also to the third, and others will come even to the fourth. For the phrase "I will add seven plagues" indicates some mystery, since one plague comes, and a second, and a third, up to the seven that have been mentioned, upon certain people. But not all are struck with seven plagues; rather, I think some will be struck with six plagues, others five, others four, others three or two, while those most inferior of all in punishments I suppose will be struck with one plague. God, then, knows the things concerning the plagues as well. Therefore it is written here at the beginning of the reading: "And it shall be in those days," those concerning the things spoken of, "I will not make you unto complete destruction." But it is not in those days that complete destruction comes; for there are certain days, when he will make those whom he will make unto complete destruction.

"And it shall be, when you say, 'For what reason has the Lord our God done to us all these evils?' — and you shall say to them, 'Because you forsook me and served other gods in your land, so shall you serve in a land not your own.'" Let the letter be understood, and it suffices for the present to set forth the reminder from the letter for those able to hear. So then, the sons of Israel had the holy land, the temple, the house of prayer. They ought to have served God. But transgressing the divine commandments, they both practiced idolatry and took up the idols of Damascus, as it is written in the books of Kingdoms, and they took up other idols of the nations into the holy land. Through the idols of the nations which they took up, they made themselves worthy to be cast down into the land of the idols, to end up there where they worshiped the idols. So the word says to them according to the letter: "Because you forsook me and served foreign gods in your land, so shall you serve foreign gods in a land not your own." Everyone who deifies anything serves foreign gods. Do you make a god of foods and drinks? Your god is "the belly." Do you honor silver as a great good, and the wealth here below? Your god and lord is mammon. For Jesus called it lord of the lovers of money, saying: "You cannot serve God and mammon; no one can serve two lords." Therefore the one who honors silver and admires wealth and considers it to be a good, and welcomes the rich as gods, while despising the poor as not having their God — this one deifies silver. If anyone, being in the land of God, the Church, worships foreign gods, deifying the things not worthy to be deified, he will be cast out into a foreign land, and let him worship the gods whom he worshiped within. Let the lover of money be outside, cast out from the Church; let the glutton be outside, having been put out of the Church. These things according to one figurative interpretation, so that I may not now busy myself with what is beyond me — concerning the land, about which the Savior said, "Who will give you what is our own?" — and that, when worship has taken place in someone's land, God so arranged that some should be cast out from his own land and come to the land about which it is written: "Hear, O Israel, why is it that you are in the land of your enemies? You were reckoned together with those going down into Hades. You forsook the fountain of life, the Lord. If you had walked in the way of God, you would have dwelt in peace for time everlasting."

Now, then, we are in a foreign land, and we pray to do the opposite of what the sons of Israel did in the holy land. For they worshiped foreign gods in the holy land; but we, in a foreign land, worship the God who is foreign to the land, foreign to the affairs upon the earth. For the ruler of this age rules here, and God is foreign to his sons. But when I say "foreign," I do not mean this — not that he did not create the world, but that he is foreign to the lord of wickedness, foreign to the present sins. And yet, even wishing to worship the God who is foreign to the affairs of sin in this land of affliction, let us see what we do. Do we not say, "How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?" But rather: How shall we sing the song of the Lord not in a foreign land? We seek a place for this, of singing the song of the Lord, a place for worshiping the Lord our God in a foreign land. What, then, is the place? I have found it: he came to this land bearing the body that saves, taking up "the body of sin" "in the likeness of the flesh of sin," so that in this place, because of Christ Jesus who has sojourned here and abolished the ruler of this age and abolished sin, I might be able to worship God here, and after this I shall worship in the holy land. For if one who worshiped the idols in the holy land departed into the foreign land, one who has worshiped God in the foreign land will depart to the holy land in Christ Jesus, to whom be the glory and the might unto the ages. Amen.

But if you say: Why has the Lord our God done all these things to us? you shall say to them: As you have forsaken me and served a foreign god — or foreign gods — in your land, so you shall serve foreigners in a land not yours. Great is the folly of not knowing why they have suffered, when they have sinned so greatly; and brief is the answer to those who are in doubt: as you have served a foreign god — that is, Baal — or foreign gods of all the nations in the land of Judea, so you shall serve foreign gods in a land not yours, no doubt the Babylonians and Chaldea. 'For if a strange religion delights you, what need is there to take up an error from afar? Dwell with such people; nay rather, serve those whose gods you worship.' This can also be taken of heretics, of whom it is written: they went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us: that the Lord casts out of the Church the heretics who for a long time under his name have venerated the images of their own lies, so that they may worship outside what they formerly venerated inside, and the chaff may be separated from the wheat.

Declare this to the house of Jacob and make it heard in Judah, saying: Hear, O foolish people, who have no heart, who having eyes do not see, and ears and do not hear! In many ways he draws sinners back to salvation, and he calls foolish the people that has abandoned the author of wisdom, and he compares them to the images of which it is written: They have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear. Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them. Properly, however, he speaks to Judah and to the house of Jacob — for Israel had already for a long time been in exile among the Assyrians — and at the same time he gives us to understand that even without a precept we ought to understand by natural sense the things that are right.

And with the same meaning the Lord rebukes by the prophet the unnatural but freely chosen blindness of the Jews, which they by their obstinacy brought upon themselves, saying: "Hear ye deaf, and ye blind, behold that you may see. Who is deaf but My servant? and blind, but he to whom I have sent My messengers?" And that no one might ascribe this blindness of theirs to nature instead of to their own will, elsewhere He says: "Bring forth the people that are blind and have eyes: that are deaf and have ears;" and again: "having eyes, but ye see not; and ears, but ye hear not." The Lord also says in the gospel: "Because seeing they see not, and hearing they hear not neither do they understand." And in them is fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah which says: "Hearing ye shall hear and shall not understand: and seeing ye shall see and shall not see. For the heart of this people is waxed fat, and their ears are dull of hearing: and they have closed their eyes, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart, and be turned and I should heal them." Finally in order to denote that the possibility of good was in them, in chiding the Pharisees, He says: "But why of your own selves do ye not judge what is right?" And this he certainly would not have said to them, unless He knew that by their natural judgment they could discern what was fair.
The Third Conference of Abbot Chaeremon, Chapter 12

That it is the height of folly not to fear, the Lord says in Jeremiah: "Hear, O foolish people, who have no heart: who having eyes, see not, and ears, and hear not. Will you then not fear me, and will you not be grieved at my presence? I who have set the sand as the boundary of the sea, an everlasting decree, which it shall not pass beyond." Do you not fear me?

For ye are not ignorant that we, being exposed to all, as rocks running out in the sea, sustain the fury of the heretical waves, which, in that they break around us, do not cover the district behind. I say “we” in order to refer it, not to human power, but to the grace of God, Who, by the weakness of men shows His power, as says the prophet in the person of the Lord, ‘Will ye not fear Me, who have placed the sand as a boundary to the sea?’ for by the weakest and most contemptible of all things, the sand, the Mighty One has bounded the great and full sea.

For fear the water should spread beyond its bed, and in its successive invasions cover one by one all countries, and end by flooding the whole earth, it received the order to gather unto one place. Thus we often see the furious sea raising mighty waves to the heaven, and, when once it has touched the shore, break its impetuosity in foam and retire. “Fear ye not me, saith the Lord.…which have placed the sand for the bound of the sea.” A grain of sand, the weakest thing possible, curbs the violence of the ocean. For what would prevent the Red Sea from invading the whole of Egypt, which lies lower, and uniting itself to the other sea which bathes its shores, were it not fettered by the fiat of the Creator? And if I say that Egypt is lower than the Red Sea, it is because experience has convinced us of it every time that an attempt has been made to join the sea of Egypt to the Indian Ocean, of which the Red Sea is a part. Thus we have renounced this enterprise, as also have the Egyptian Sesostris, who conceived the idea, and Darius the Mede who afterwards wished to carry it out.
The Hexaemeron, Homily 4: Upon the Gathering Together of the Waters

Will you not then fear me, says the Lord, and will you not grieve before my face — or fear — ? I who set the sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting precept, which it will not pass. And they will be moved and will not be able — or it will be troubled and will not be able — and its waves will swell — or will sound — and will not pass over it. But to this people there has come to be an unbelieving and provoking heart, and they have withdrawn and gone away, and they have not said in their heart: Let us fear the Lord our God, who gives us the early and the late rain in its season, keeping for us the fullness of the yearly harvest! He recounts his benefits in order to convict the ungrateful. 'Me,' he says, 'you will not fear, I who have bestowed such great things on you? I do not ask for the love of the perfect, but for the fear of beginners, I who set the sand as a boundary for the sea, I who by my precept have reined in at the shores so mighty an element and the immense masses of the deeps, according to that which is written: He set a precept, and it will not pass.

And again God demanded from the Jews the fear of Himself by the hand of Jeremiah, and reproached them by the testimony of the dumb things in nature, which, though silent, trembled at the fear of Him, while the Jews despised His commandments. "Fear ye not Me? saith the Lord: will ye not tremble at My presence? For I have placed the sand for the bound of the sea, [by] an everlasting law, and it shall not pass over it." And here again the Creator demanded fear and trembling from created things, and because they forsook His fear they were reproached through the dumb things of nature, which feared and trembled at the Majesty of the Creator, while His commandments were despised by the children of men. And God in all places shewed the majesty of His nature by the hand of the Prophet, that He might cast the fear thereof into those who listened. For to those who would have despised His meekness—if it had been shewn unto them—He revealed the majesty of His nature that they might tremble thereat; and to others He shewed His gentleness and meekness, which at the report of His humiliation would increase [their] love [for Him].
13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 7 -- Second Discourse on the Fear of God

That it is the height of folly not to fear, the Lord says in Jeremiah: "Hear, O foolish people, who have no heart: who having eyes, see not, and ears, and hear not. Will you then not fear me, and will you not be grieved at my presence? I who have set the sand as the boundary of the sea, an everlasting decree, which it shall not pass beyond." Do you not fear me?

But there is another quarrel involved in which the young gentleman of culture comes into violent collision with the young lady of the cauliflowers. The first essential of the merely bookish view of the sea is that it is boundless, and gives a sentiment of infinity. Now it is quite certain, I think, that the cauliflower simile was partly created by exactly the opposite impression, the impression of boundary and of barrier. The girl thought of it as a field of vegetables, even as a yard of vegetables. The girl was right. The ocean only suggests infinity when you cannot see it; a sea mist may seem endless, but not a sea. So far from being vague and vanishing, the sea is the one hard straight line in Nature. It is the one plain limit; the only thing that God has made that really looks like a wall. Compared to the sea, not only sun and cloud are chaotic and doubtful, but solid mountains and standing forests may be said to melt and fade and flee in the presence of that lonely iron line. The old naval phrase, that the seas are England's bulwarks, is not a frigid and artificial metaphor; it came into the head of some genuine sea-dog, when he was genuinely looking at the sea. For the edge of the sea is like the edge of a sword; it is sharp, military, and decisive; it really looks like a bolt or bar, and not like a mere expansion. It hangs in heaven, grey, or green, or blue, changing in colour, but changeless in form, behind all the slippery contours of the land and all the savage softness of the forests, like the scales of God held even. It hangs, a perpetual reminder of that divine reason and justice which abides behind all compromises and all legitimate variety; the one straight line; the limit of the intellect; the dark and ultimate dogma of the world.
Alarms and Discursions, The Garden of the Sea (1910)

Things that have no sense of hearing hear me and perceive me; and the people once mine, made foolish by its own fault, not only despises but even provokes its sweet God. They have withdrawn,' he says, 'from me, and turned their backs on me, and gone away with hurried step, nor did a silent conscience draw them back, so that they should say in their hearts: Let us fear him who gives us the early and the late rain! — through all of which I have shown good things, the fullness of the yearly harvest', for which Aquila's first edition and Symmachus translated 'weeks'; for in the Hebrew is written 'sabaoth', which, owing to the ambiguity of the word, signifies both 'weeks' and 'fullness'.

Our iniquities have turned these things aside, and our sins have withheld good from us. Therefore, if at any time the sea both oversteps its boundaries and the rain is held back, by no means has the hand of the Lord been shortened, so as not to do these things; but our sins have turned aside these things as they were coming to us, so that they went on to others who had not sinned. 'And they have withheld,' he says, 'the good that was already coming to us, according to that which is written according to the letter: I will command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it'. But we can take the early and the late rain as the law and the Gospel, and as the various callings from the first hour to the eleventh, in which one reward of eternal life is promised to the laborers of the vineyard.

For among my people there have been found ungodly men lying in wait like fowlers, setting snares and traps to catch men! As a trap full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit. That the early and the late rain might turn aside from them and all good things might not come, the causes are added: because there have been found among his people 'ungodly men'. He did not say 'unjust' and 'sinners', as the new heresy would have it, but 'ungodly'. Ungodliness openly denies God; iniquity and sin, if it confesses its error, easily bends God to mercy. And for what we have said, lying in wait like fowlers, which is not found in the Seventy, Aquila and Symmachus translated the word 'iasir' as like the net of a fowler, because even he who among them seems good and upright lays snares like a fowler, while they hunt one another to death and fill their own houses with the losses and costs of others, so that that saying of the philosophers is fulfilled: Every rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man. And would that these things were done only by those who seem to be outside, and whom the Lord judges, and were not fulfilled in our own little assemblies by those whom avarice, the root of all evils, possesses, so that we look not at the faces of those who come to us, but at their hands!

Therefore they have been magnified and enriched. They have grown fat and sleek, and they have passed over my words most wickedly. They have not judged the cause, the cause — or judgment — of the orphan they have not directed, and the judgment of the poor — or of the widow — they have not judged. Shall I not visit for these things? says the Lord, or shall my soul not take vengeance on a nation such as this? If I should wish to note one by one the things that have been left out in the edition of the Seventy, it will become long. 'Those who lay snares,' he says, 'and rejoice in the nakedness of others, therefore they have been magnified and enriched.' Because they did the things above, they have grown fat and sleek, according to that which is written: He grew fat and sleek, and the beloved kicked. And they have passed over my words, because in the consciousness of their riches they said that saying from the Gospel: Soul, you have many goods laid up for very many years; rest, eat, drink, feast! Moreover, they passed over to their own harm, and, despising all men, they did not set the judgment of God before their eyes. They despised the orphan and the poor, for which the Seventy said 'widows', which is not found in the Hebrew; for 'hebionim' properly denotes 'poor', not 'widows'. But what follows, Shall I not visit for these things? says the Lord, or shall my soul not take vengeance on a nation such as this?, has already been discussed above.

Astonishment and wonders have come to pass in the land: the prophets prophesied a lie — or wicked things — and the priests clapped with their hands, and my people loved such things! What then will you do at the last — or after these things — ? Above he had said: I will go to the chief men and will speak to them; perhaps they have known the way of the Lord. And behold, these rather have together broken the yoke, they have burst the bonds; now he describes who the chief men are, namely the prophets and the priests, some of whom foretell things to come, while others determine from the law the things to be done. 'And behold,' he says, 'while those men prophesied a lie, the priests clapped with their hands.' And so that it may be shown that the people too is not without fault, which lets itself be led away by such men, it is written: and my people loved such things: once mine, but after it loved them, it ceased to be mine. What then will they do when the last time of judgment has come, or the necessity of captivity? Hence there are astonishment and wonders, because neither among the princes nor among the people was anyone found who thought rightly.
6: Be strengthened, sons of Benjamin, in the midst of Jerusalem, and in Tekoa sound the trumpet, and over Beth-haccherem raise a signal — or a standard —, for evil has been seen — or has appeared — from the north, and great destruction! No one is unaware that Jerusalem is situated in the tribe of Benjamin. That Tekoa too is a small village situated on a mountain, twelve miles distant from Jerusalem, we see daily with our own eyes. Between these is another village, which in the Syriac and Hebrew tongue is named Bethacarma, and it too is set on a mountain. What he says, therefore, is this: 'Since from the north Nebuchadnezzar is now on the very point of coming and captivity is near and threatening, O inhabitants of Jerusalem, seize your arms and sound the trumpet in Tekoa and in Beth-haccherem raise the standard', he says, 'so that you may be able to resist your enemies!' Beniamin means 'son of the right hand', Thecua 'trumpet', Bethaccarem 'estate of the vineyard'. Let us refer all these things to the Church, so that, if she has transgressed and the onslaught of persecution has come, she may prepare herself to resist.

I have likened the daughter of Zion to a beautiful and delicate woman. To her shepherds will come with their flocks; they have pitched — or they will pitch — their tents against her round about; each one will pasture those who are under his hand. Sanctify — or Prepare — war against her; arise, and let us go up at noon! The beauty of Jerusalem is described, which is Zion itself, so that the one name denotes the whole city, the other the citadel of the city. For Sion means 'citadel', that is, watchtower, and she is compared to a beautiful woman; and as lovers come together to the one, so shepherds are said to come together to the other. And quite elegantly in the Hebrew the word that is written with four letters, 'res, ain, iod, mem', if it is read 'reim', means 'lovers', if 'roim', 'shepherds', so that either, according to the metaphoran [metaphor] of a beautiful woman, lovers are understood, or, according to the overthrow of the city, shepherds: of whom the former hasten to defile a harlot, the latter to besiege and overturn a city. In the shepherds and their flocks let us perceive the princes and the army of the Chaldeans. And they will pitch their tents round about in the siege of the city, and each one will pasture those who are under his hand, that is, his own squadrons and companies.

These princes or shepherds will say to their flocks: 'Sanctify against Jerusalem war, for it is the command of the Lord. Arise, and let us go up at noon: let us fight not by night and by ambush, but in full daylight; for no one can resist us'.

Woe to us, for the day has declined, for longer have grown — or have failed — the shadows of evening. Arise, and let us go up by night, and let us destroy the houses — or foundations — of her! Those say: 'Arise, and let us go up at noon, and let us fight in clear daylight'; these reply: woe to us, for the shadows of evening have grown longer, according to that saying of Vergil: and now far off the rooftops of the farmhouses smoke, and greater shadows fall from the high mountains. And the sense is: 'If we suffer these things by day, what shall we suffer by night?'

And again those who had said above: 'Sanctify war against her and arise', now rouse themselves to battle, saying: 'Arise, and let us go up by night, so that our adversaries may know that the victory belongs not to the time of day but to strength, and let us destroy the houses, which are fenced in vain by the firmness of their walls'.

For thus says the Lord of hosts: Cut down her tree — or her trees —, pour out — or heap up — a mound around Jerusalem! 'Therefore', they say, 'we are secure of victory, because it is the command of the Lord, who orders the Chaldeans: cut down the trees and heap up a mound for the siegeworks to come!' By these words it is shown, before it comes to pass, that the city was not to be taken at once by an encircling ring of troops, but by a long siege, as we read afterwards.

This is the city of visitation — or the lying city —, all false accusation — or oppression — is in her midst. As a cistern makes cold — or a pit — its water, so she has made her wickedness cold. The Lord commands that the trees be cut down, that mounds be cast up round about, because the time of her visitation has come, that she may receive the due for her sins, the greatest of which is sykophantia, that she oppresses the innocent by false accusation.

Iniquity and devastation will be heard in her; before me continually are sickness and wound. Be instructed, Jerusalem, lest perhaps my soul depart from you, lest perhaps I make you a desert, an uninhabitable land! LXX: Ungodliness and misery will be heard in her before her face. Through every pain and scourge you will be instructed, Jerusalem, lest perhaps my soul depart from you, lest I make you a trackless land, which is not inhabited. Through these words we learn that the Lord scourges every son whom he receives; and for that reason Jerusalem is instructed by blows and torments, that she may be corrected, and that the soul of God may not depart from her and she be reduced to a wilderness. If ever, therefore, we lie under frequent distresses, let us recall for our consolation this little verse: through every pain and scourge you will be instructed, Jerusalem.

As, therefore, a cistern or pit makes its water cold, so in the midst of Jerusalem the wickedness that is in her has lost all the warmth of life. And this is to be noted, that the saints are called fervent in spirit, whereas evils are cold; whence that also is written, that in the last days, when iniquity has been multiplied, the love of many will grow cold. I think that this too means the same: I have been likened to those who go down into the pit. And let the Latin reader understand this, so that it may suffice to have said it once: that 'lacus' [pit] does not mean 'pool' according to the Greeks, but 'cistern', which in the Syriac and Hebrew tongue is called 'gubba'. In the present passage, however, for 'lacus', which all translated alike, in the Hebrew it is 'bor'.

See the mercy and the loving-kindness of the good God. When he wishes to have mercy, he says that he is indignant and angry, as through Jeremiah he says: "with grief and with scourge you shall be chastised, Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from you". If you understand these things, it is the voice of a God who has mercy, where he is angry, where he is jealous, where he applies griefs and scourges. "For he scourges every son whom he receives".

And another prophet, Jeremiah, says, "Turn to the Lord your God, as a grape gatherer to his basket, and you shall find mercy." The sayings in the Holy Scriptures regarding repentance are many, yes, countless. God always desires that the human race turn from all its sins.
Theophilus to Autolycus, Book III, Chapter XI

God invites us to knowledge also, when he says by Jeremiah, "If you had walked in the way of God, you would have dwelled forever in peace." … God grants pardon to those who have erred. He says, "Turn, turn, as a grape gatherer returns to his basket." Do you see the goodness of justice in that it advises us to repent?

Thus says the Lord of hosts: Even to the last cluster they will glean, as in a vineyard, the remnant of Israel; turn back your hand like a grape-gatherer to the basket! LXX: For thus says the Lord of powers: Glean, glean as in a vineyard the remnant of Israel; return like a grape-gatherer to his basket! Some take these words in a good sense, others in a bad. In the good sense: 'When Jerusalem has been laid waste, let the remnant be saved'. In the bad, thus: 'Let not even one cluster and small bunch of grapes remain in the vineyard; let everything be gathered; and whatever you find, throw into the basket like a grape-gatherer, so that, as he drags the clusters to the winepress, so you may drag the captives to Babylon'.

To whom shall I speak, and whom shall I solemnly warn, that he may hear? Behold, their ears — or your ears — are uncircumcised, and they cannot hear! Behold, the word of the Lord has become to them a reproach, and they will not receive it! They cannot hear because they were unwilling to circumcise their ears; yet the inability is not free of punishment, since it comes down from contempt and unbelief. If anyone, therefore, does not receive the words of God and has no understanding of his precepts, he is of uncircumcised ears. And at the same time it is to be noted that circumcision in the Scriptures is spoken of in three kinds: in the foreskin, in the heart, and in the ears; whence the Lord too says: He who has ears to hear, let him hear. It is by our own will, therefore, that we do not receive the word of God; and for that reason it becomes to us a reproach, so that what had been given for salvation is turned by our own fault into punishment.

Therefore I am full of the fury of the Lord; I have toiled in holding it in. LXX: And I have filled up my fury and held it in, and I did not consume it. According to the Hebrew it is said in the person of the prophet, that he foresees the wrath of God that is coming, and is full of the fury and anger of the Lord, and can hold it in no longer, nor dares to entreat the Lord for sinners. According to the Seventy, however, a new sense is set down: that the Lord himself speaks and says: I have completed my fury, by striking the sinful people, and yet that he restrained it and did not pour it all out, so that a remnant might be saved. This seems to me to be self-contradictory; for if he completed his fury, how did he hold it in so as not to complete it?

Pour out — or He poured out — upon the little child outside and upon the council of young men together; for man with wife will be taken, the old man with him who is full of days. And their houses will pass to others, their fields and wives alike. Either the prophet in the spirit commands the coming Chaldean to pour out the fury of the Lord upon the little children and to spare not even their innocent age, or else he relates what has been done upon the council of young men together, who had seized their arms to fight back. For man with wife will be taken: names most sweet to one another will alike feel captivity, the old man with him who is full of days. Therefore old age is not the last age, but that of those who are 'full of days', whom in our own speech we call 'depositos' [given up for dead] or 'decrepitos' [decrepit].

There follows: and their houses will pass to others through the evil of captivity, their fields and wives together, so that both wife and possession pass to the enemy. Whatever we understand according to the letter of Jerusalem, let us refer according to the spiritual understanding to the Church, if she has offended God.

For I will stretch out my hand over those who inhabit the earth, says the Lord. For from the least even to the greatest, all are devoted to avarice, and from prophet even to priest all practice deceit. And they were healing the breach of the daughter of my people with disgrace, saying: Peace, peace! And there was no peace. What in the Hebrew is said: I will stretch out my hand over sinners or the inhabitants of the earth, among the Seventy is always written 'I will lift up'; and each is the posture of one who strikes, according to what is written: and still the hand of the Lord is stretched out or lifted high. The inhabitants of the earth, moreover, are always in vice; whence in Revelation too it is said quite frequently: Woe to the inhabitants of the earth!

From the least even to the greatest, all are devoted to avarice, according to that saying of the Apostle: the root of all evils is avarice. And from prophet even to priest all practice deceit: the one by prophesying a lie, the other by perversely interpreting the law of God; for the prophet also says in another place: Seek the law from the priests.

Idol temples had fallen before the standard of the cross and the severity of the gospel. Now, on the contrary, lust and gluttony endeavor to overthrow the solid structure of the cross. And so God says by Isaiah, "O my people, they who bless you cause you to wander and trouble the paths of your feet." Also by Jeremiah, "Flee out of the midst of Babylon, and save everyone his life, and believe not the false prophets who say, 'Peace, peace,' and there is no peace." Who are always repeating, "The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord." "Your prophets have seen for you false and foolish things. They have not laid bare your iniquity that they might call you to repentance. They devour God's people like bread. They have not called on God." Jeremiah announced the captivity and was stoned by the people. Hananiah, the son of Azzur, broke the bars of wood for the present but was preparing bars of iron for the future. False prophets always promise pleasant things and please for a time.

'And though', he says, 'they were doing such things, they kept announcing prosperity of every kind to my people, and as it were desired to heal the wound and the disgrace of my daughter, saying: Peace, peace, when there was no peace at all'. This is properly to be understood of the priests and teachers who promise prosperity to the rich and to those whom they see set in the highest honor, and proclaim God to be merciful, rather preparing them for punishment and wrath.

Not all kinds of peace are compatible with all kinds of goodwill, nor do all those who say 'Peace, peace' inherit the blessing promised to the peacemakers. The real pacificus is he who promotes peace, not he who gasses about it. Peace, peace ... we won't be hard on you ... it was only a boyish prank . . . you had a neurosis . . . promise not to do it again . . . out of this in the long run I do not think either goodwill or peace will come. Planting new primroses on the primrose path is no long-term benevolence.
DELINQUENTS IN THE SNOW, from God in the Dock

Were they confounded because they committed abomination? Nay rather, they were not confounded with confusion, and they knew not how to blush. This is to be read more closely according to the Hebrew. 'And though', he says, 'they have done such things, were they at all confounded? Did they at all blush in their crimes? Nay rather, they increased their contempt, and they knew not how to blush' — and he put 'knew not' here for 'would not' — 'or else, through excessive contempt and the vice of an ingrained evil, they could not even understand'.

Therefore they will fall among those who fall; in the time of their visitation they will collapse, says the Lord. 'Since', he says, 'they knew not how to blush, and had not only not the deed but not even the knowledge and the sense of repentance, therefore those who formerly stood will fall among them; they will collapse through their own vices and, when the time of their visitation and punishment has come, they will be joined to all who fall'. And it is a great ungodliness not only not to guard against sins but not even to be willing to understand them, and to make no distinction between good and evil works.

Since the soul became too enfeebled for the apprehension of realities, we needed a divine teacher. The Savior is sent down—a teacher and leader in the acquisition of the good, as the secret and sacred token of the great Providence. "Where, then, is the scribe? Where is the searcher of this world? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?" it is said. And again, "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent," speaks plainly of those who are wise in their own eyes and contentious. Excellently, therefore, Jeremiah says, "Thus says the Lord, 'Stand in the ways, and ask for the eternal paths, what is the good way, and walk in it, and you shall find expiation for your souls.' "

And through Jeremiah, he provides further enlightenment in the truth for those who have erred: "Thus says the Lord, stand in the roads, and look. Ask for the eternal paths of the Lord. Look for the good path, and walk in it, and you shall find purification for your souls." He leads us to repentance in order to promote our salvation.

But what sprinklings shall we now employ, while we celebrate the feast? Who will be our guide, as we haste to this festival? None can do this, my beloved, but Him Whom you will name with me, even our Lord Jesus Christ Who said, ‘I am the Way.’ For it is He Who, according to the blessed John, ‘taketh away the sin of the world.’ He purifies our souls, as Jeremiah the prophet says in a certain place, ‘Stand in the ways and see, and enquire, and look which is the good path, and ye shall find in it cleansing for your souls.’ Of old time, the blood of he-goats and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled upon those who were unclean, were fit only to purify the flesh; but now, through the grace of God the Word, every man is thoroughly cleansed.

When you eat your meals, remember that you must immediately afterwards pray and read. Have a fixed number of lines of Holy Scripture, and render it as your task to your Lord. On no account resign yourself to sleep until you have filled the basket of your breast with a thread of this weaving. After the Holy Scriptures you should read the writings of learned people, of those at any rate whose faith is well known. You need not go into the mire to seek for gold. You have many pearls. Buy the one pearl with these. Stand, as Jeremiah says, in more ways than one so that you may come on the true way that leads to the Father.

Thus says the Lord: Stand upon the ways and see, and ask about the ancient paths, which is the good way, and walk in it! And you will find refreshment — or purification — for your souls. And they said: We will not walk — or We will not go —. And I set watchmen over you: hear the voice of the trumpet! And they said: We will not hear. Therefore hear — or they heard —, O nations, and know, O congregation — or you who pasture flocks, or according to Symmachus: and know the testimony that is in them —, how great things I will do to them! Hear, O earth! The parable of the Gospel, if it is understood, will furnish the understanding of this passage; in it the good merchant is said to sell all his pearls, so that with their price he may buy the one most precious pearl: namely, that through the patriarchs and prophets we come to him who says: I am the way. We must therefore stand in the prophets, and contemplate most diligently, and ask about the ancient or everlasting paths — which are worn by the footsteps of many saints, which in Greek are more expressively called triboi —, which is the good way in the Gospel, and walk in it; and that way, when it has been found, affords refreshment or purification to the souls of believers. But they, on the contrary, answered: We will not walk in the way of the Gospel, the prophet saying this properly of the faithlessness of the Jews.

There are many ways, and many ways lead to one way. Indeed, it is also said in Jeremiah: 'Stand in the ways of the Lord, and ask for the eternal paths of the Lord, and you will find the way, and you will walk in it.' See what it says, Stand in the ways, and ask for the eternal paths of the Lord, and you will find the one way, and walk in it. See how through many ways we come to one way. This is also said in the gospel in other words, under another meaning of the parable, concerning that merchant who had many pearls, who sold them, and bought one most precious pearl. What it says is this: Stand in the ways, that is, have very many pearls. Stand in the ways, and ask for the eternal paths of the Lord. Beautifully it says eternal, lest we should think that at the coming of Christ the law and the prophets were brought to an end. But see what it says. Stand in the ways, in the law and the prophets. Stand in the ways; do not so believe in the one way that you abandon the many ways; but stand in the ways, and ask for the eternal paths of the Lord. Ask the paths of the Lord, what Jeremiah said, Isaiah, Ezekiel, what the rest of the prophets said. Ask the paths. It is better said in Greek τρίβους (tribous): for a path (semita) is so called from the fact that it is worn (trita) by the heel of those walking. And what is said is this: Ask the paths, that is τρίβους (tribous), which the foot of the Lord wore down: seeing that the Lord too walked in them. But when you have asked for the eternal paths of the Lord, and through those paths you have found the one way, which says 'I am the way and the life and the truth,' walk in it. See the mysteries of the scriptures: see in the simple words of the scriptures very many sacred meanings, in the ways and paths, in the law and the prophets. It did not say, walk, but, stand: do not abandon the law nor the prophets. Yet when you have found those ways, through these ways walk in this one way.

The holy prophets might themselves be considered as "many ways"; our Lord, however, is the truly good way. In fact, listen to his words, "I am the way, the truth and the life." But each of the prophetic ways leads to this way, Moses the lawgiver hinting at this in his words, "The Lord our God will raise up for you from among your brothers a prophet like me." David, king and prophet, and also Isaiah, Micah, Ezekiel and each of the prophets give a glimpse of this way. And as there is one way leading to the biggest cities that we are accustomed to call kingly and royal—whereas some paths do conduct people from both town and country to this one way—so there is one way leading to the Father, the only-begotten Son of God, while the blessed prophets lead people to this one way who choose to travel by the particular path they represent. The prophetic word, therefore, bids Jews to search out the prophetic ways and through them to discover the good way and travel in it.

The Enemy loves platitudes. Of a proposed course of action He wants men, so far as I can see, to ask very simple questions; is it righteous? is it prudent? is it possible? Now if we can keep men asking "Is it in accordance with the general movement of our time? Is it progressive or reactionary? Is this the way that History is going?" they will neglect the relevant questions. And the questions they do ask are, of course, unanswerable; for they do not know the future, and what the future will be depends very largely on just those choices which they now invoke the future to help them to make.

We all want progress. But progress means getting nearer to the place where you want to be. And if you have taken a wrong turning, then to go forward does not get you any nearer. If you are on the wrong road, progress means doing an about-turn and walking back to the right road; and in that case the man who turns back soonest is the most progressive man. We have all seen this when doing arithmetic. When I have started a sum the wrong way, the sooner I admit this and go back and start again, the faster I shall get on. There is nothing progressive about being pig-headed and refusing to admit a mistake. And I think if you look at the present state of the world, it is pretty plain that humanity has been making some big mistake. We are on the wrong road. And if that is so, we must go back. Going back is the quickest way on.
Mere Christianity, Book 1, Chapter 5: We Have Cause to be Uneasy

And at once he adds: 'And I set watchmen over you' — no doubt the choir of the apostles is indicated, according to Ezekiel: Son of man, I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel —, 'and I commanded that you hear the voice of the trumpet, either the commands of the Gospel or the teaching of the apostles, according to that saying of Isaiah: Go up onto a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion; lift up your voice like a trumpet, you who announce to Jerusalem'.

Jeremiah refers to their guides by the term "shepherds," not simply those accorded spiritual guidance but also kings and rulers who have accepted the divine message. This is the way the divine apostles Barnabas and Paul also behaved. When they entered a certain synagogue, they principally engaged the Jews in discussion. But when they perceived their unbelief, they said, "It was necessary to speak the word of God to you first, but since you resist it and pass judgment on yourselves as unworthy of eternal life, we turn to the nations, the Lord having given us this direction. I have placed you as a light for the nations to bring salvation to the ends of the earth." This is where this prophecy finds its fulfillment.

They said: We will not hear, and when invited to the supper they would not come; therefore it is said: Hear, O nations! This the apostles too followed when they speak in Lycaonia: It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you; but since you thrust it away and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. And know, O congregation: by no means the Jewish one, but that of all nations; or, you who pasture flocks: the bishops and presbyters and the whole order of the Church; or, know the testimony that is in them; for the testimony of God is faithful, giving wisdom to little ones. To them the Lord also speaks: Fear not, little flock, and: Behold, I and my children, whom God has given me. 'Know, therefore, how great things I will do to the people that does not believe.'

And in what is added: Hear, O earth, the whole world is called to hear, as we also read at the beginning of Isaiah: Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth: that is, what the Lord is going to do to the people of the Jews.

Behold, I will bring evils upon this people, the fruit of their thoughts — or of their turning away —, because they have not heard my words and have cast away my law. He calls 'evils' the punishments and penalties of those who suffer, not upon the Gentiles, who are called to the truth of the Gospel, but upon the people that answered: We will not hear. And it is going to receive the fruit of its thoughts or of its turning away, as David says: You shall eat the labors of your hands. And the cause is plain: because they did not hear the words of the Lord and cast off his law.

For it was not because He was angry, like a man, as many venture to say, that He rejected their sacrifices; but out of compassion to their blindness, and with the view of suggesting to them the true sacrifice, by offering which they shall appease God, that they may receive life from Him. As He elsewhere declares: "The sacrifice to God is an afflicted heart: a sweet savour to God is a heart glorifying Him who formed it." For if, when angry, He had repudiated these sacrifices of theirs, as if they were persons unworthy to obtain His compassion, He would not certainly have urged these same things upon them as those by which they might be saved. But inasmuch as God is merciful, He did not cut them off from good counsel. For after He had said by Jeremiah, "To what purpose bring ye Me incense from Saba, and cinnamon from a far country? Your whole burnt-offerings and sacrifices are not acceptable to Me;" He proceeds: "Hear the word of the Lord, all Judah.
