These things saith the Lord, the God of Israel, Make straight your ways and your doings, and I will establish you in this place. Put not your trust in lying words, for they will not at all profit you, saying, The temple of the Lord, The temple of the Lord, it is here."

To what purpose do you bring me frankincense from Sheba, and sweet-smelling calamus from a distant land? Your burnt offerings are not accepted, and your victims have not pleased me. That frankincense comes from Sheba no one doubts; whence also that line of Vergil: and a hundred altars glow with Sabaean incense. And that 'calamus', which in Hebrew is called 'cane', for which the Seventy and Theodotion translated 'cinnamon', comes from a distant land, the prophetic word shows, so that we may understand India, from which many spices come by way of the Red Sea. This kind of spice physicians call kassian syringos [pipe cassia]. And the sense is: 'In vain do you bring me spices of sweetest odor for compounding the ointments that are prescribed in the law, and kindle burnt offerings, you who do not do my will in the law', according to what was said above: they have not heard my words and have cast away my law. This, moreover, properly fits those who offer sacrifices from robbery and the stripping of the wretched, and think they redeem their sins by alms from iniquity, though Scripture says: The ransom of a man's soul is his own riches, which are gathered not from iniquity but from labor and righteousness.

Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will put ruins into this people, and they will fall in them — or weakness, and they will be weakened in it —, fathers and sons together, neighbor and kinsman, and they will perish. We see fulfilled all the things with which the Lord threatened that people; for daily they fall in their blasphemies, and they have nothing strong in them, but all is weakness among them. The sons follow the blasphemies of their fathers, and daily receive that imprecation: His blood be upon us and upon our children; and not only they themselves, but also their neighbors and kinsmen, all who follow the law and the prophets according to the letter that kills and not according to the spirit that gives life; and all alike will perish, because alike they have sinned.

Thus says the Lord: Behold, a people comes from the land of the north, and a great nation will rise from the ends of the earth. It will seize arrow and shield — or zibynnam [spear] —; it is cruel — or shameless — and will not have mercy; its voice will sound like the sea, and they will mount upon horses, prepared like a man for battle against you, daughter of Zion. This is properly prophesied of the Babylonians, who are to come against the people of Jerusalem; and the whole array of their armor and the onset of the combatants is described, so that, shaken by the terror of the voice, they may do repentance and appease a most merciful God. Finally, he gives occasion for entreaty when he says: against you, daughter of Zion. We may apply this testimony, in a transferred sense, to a time of persecution, when the whole rage of the devil is stirred up against us, and there is no mercy, and like the waves of a most violent sea they overwhelm those who resist.

We have heard the report of it; our hands have grown feeble; tribulation has seized us, pains as of a woman in labor. The people answers, whom the prophet, nay rather the Lord through the prophet, has threatened with the Babylonians: that before they come they have been overcome by fear, and cannot lift up their hands, and anguish has seized them as pain seizes a woman in labor; than which pain those women who have felt it affirm that nothing is more grievous.

Do not go out into the fields, and do not walk on the road, for the sword of the enemy, terror is all around! The Gospel teaches that one must not go out into the field nor come down from the height of the housetops, but must heed that word: Save yourself on the mountain, to which in Isaiah and Micah we are commanded to run and climb. According to the letter, however, it is commanded that they not go outside, that they not desert the walls, but that they protect themselves with strong fortifications.

Daughter of my people, gird yourself with sackcloth and sprinkle yourself with ashes; make for yourself the mourning for an only-begotten — or a beloved —, a bitter lament — or a pitiable one —, for suddenly the destroyer will come — or misery — upon us — or upon you — ! Since he had said above: Do not go out into the fields, and do not walk on the road, for the sword of the enemy, terror is all around, and had forbidden flight as well, he teaches what they ought to do: namely, that they be converted to repentance and have this as their firmest and safest armor. Where we have said: make for yourself the mourning for an only-begotten, for 'only-begotten' in the Hebrew is written 'iaid', which means 'solitary' rather than 'only-begotten'. For if it were 'beloved' or 'lovable', as the Seventy translated, 'ididia' would be set down, which is also the name God gave to Solomon. And nothing is more grievous than to lose one son, or an only son. And that which we have translated: for suddenly the destroyer will come or misery upon us, the Seventy rendered upon you, whereas God has spoken far more mercifully, testifying that whatever is to come upon his people comes upon himself as well. 'The destroyer', moreover, properly signifies either Nebuchadnezzar or the devil.

I have given you as a strong assayer among my people, and you will know and test their way. All these are princes turning aside — or disobedient —, walking deceitfully — or perversely —, bronze and iron; all of them are corrupted. The bellows has failed in the fire — which the Greeks more expressively call physētēra —, the lead is consumed, in vain has the smelter smelted — or the silversmith —; for their wickednesses have not been consumed. Call them reprobate silver, for the Lord has cast them away! The prophet is given to the unbelieving people as a 'strong' assayer, which in Hebrew is called 'mabsar', which means either 'fortified', according to Aquila, or 'shut in' and 'surrounded', according to Symmachus and the Seventy, like a most strongly fortified city, so that he may fear no ambushes of the people: 'so that, when you have tested', he says, 'and known the way of the transgressing people, you may then understand that silver mixed with bronze can by no means be purified'.

Perhaps he will say to me, who am not reformed even by blows, I know that you are obstinate, and your neck is an iron sinew, the heedless is heedless, and the lawless person acts lawlessly, naught is the heavenly correction, naught the scourges. The bellows are burned, the lead is consumed, as I once reproached you by the mouth of Jeremiah, the founder melted the silver in vain, your evil deeds are not melted away. Can you abide my wrath? says the Lord. Has not my hand the power to inflict on you other plagues also?

For as lead is mixed with metals that are adulterated and debased, so that the foreign matter may be separated, and, if perhaps it has not been purified, all the lead is consumed and reduced to nothing, so all the eloquence of teaching and the prophetic word perishes in those who scorn to hear. Let us speak also of those who, like deaf asps, stop their ears so as not to hear the voices of the charmers. For in vain has the silversmith smelted or the smelter; for their wickednesses have not been consumed. Hence they are called not 'silver' but 'reprobate silver', for the Lord has cast them off. And the princes are those who withdraw from the Lord, or the disobedient, who walk perversely and deceitfully.

And the prophet seeing that all the remedies of this life will have been applied in vain for their healing, and already as it were despairing of their life, declares: "The bellows have failed in the fire, the founder hath melted in vain: for their wicked deeds are not consumed. Call them reprobate silver, for the Lord hath rejected them." And the Lord thus laments that to no purpose has He applied this salutary cleansing by fire to those who are hardened in their sins, in the person of Jerusalem crusted all over with the rust of her sins, when He says: "set it empty upon burning coals, that it may be hot, and the brass thereof may be melted; and let the filth of it be melted in the midst thereof. Great pains have been taken, and the great rust thereof is not gone out, no not even by fire. Thy uncleanness is execrable: because I desired to cleanse thee, and thou art not cleansed from thy filthiness." Wherefore like a skilful physician, who has tried all saving cures, and sees there is no remedy left which can be applied to their disease, the Lord is in a manner overcome by their iniquities and is obliged to desist from that kindly chastisement of His, and so denounces them saying: "I will no longer be angry with thee, and thy jealousy has departed from thee." But of others, whose heart has not grown hard by continuance in sin, and who do not stand in need of that most severe and (if I may so call it) caustic remedy, but for whose salvation the instruction of the life-giving word is suffi- cient-of them it is said: "I will improve them by hearing of their suffering."

And again in like manner does Jeremiah speak: "I set watchmen over you; hearken to the sound of the trumpet; and they said, We will not hearken. Therefore have the Gentiles heard, and they who feed the flocks in them." It is therefore one and the same Father who planted the vineyard, who led forth the people, who sent the prophets, who sent His own Son, and who gave the vineyard to those other husbandmen that render the fruits in their season.
7: And thus did He send prophets prior to the transmigration to Babylon, and after that event others again in greater number than the former, to seek the fruits, saying thus to them (the Jews): "Thus saith the Lord, Cleanse your ways and your doings, execute just judgment, and look each one with pity and compassion on his brother: oppress not the widow nor the orphan, the proselyte nor the poor, and let none of you treasure up evil against his brother in your hearts, and love not false swearing. Wash you, make you clean, put away evil from your hearts, learn to do well, seek judgment, protect the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow; and come, let us reason together, saith the Lord." And again: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips that they speak no guile; depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it." In preaching these things, the prophets sought the fruits of righteousness.

The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Stand in the gate of the house of the Lord and proclaim — or read — there this word, and say: Hear the word of the Lord, all Judah, you who enter by these gates to worship the Lord! This is not found in the edition of the Seventy, but has been added from Theodotion out of the Hebrew. Now the prophet is commanded to stand in the gate of the Lord, through which the multitude of the people enters to pray to the Lord, so that on this occasion they may be able to hear what the Lord commands. By this we understand the hardness of the people of the Jews, in that they held the prophets as liars and madmen, since it is through the occasion and the throng of the place that they are compelled to hear the words of the Lord, and not because they are the words of the Lord.

Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Make good — or direct — your ways and your pursuits — or your devices — and I will dwell with you in this place or I will make you dwell in this place. The most merciful physician desires to heal the wounded with every remedy. But when he says: make good or correct your ways, he shows that they are perverse and have nothing good in them. And because it is natural that each person loves his native soil and holds nothing sweeter than his fatherland, he promises rewards to the obedient. 'I will dwell,' he says, 'with you, so that I may make you secure about your dwelling, or I will found you yourselves' — according to Symmachus — 'with a firm dwelling', who says: and I will establish you in this place.

And now hear concerning faith that is based upon the Stone, and concerning the structure that is reared up upon the Stone. For first a man believes, and when he believes, he loves. When he loves, he hopes. When he hopes, he is justified. When he is justified, he is perfected. When he is perfected, he is consummated. And when his whole structure is raised up, consummated, and perfected, then he becomes a house and a temple for a dwelling-place of Christ, as Jeremiah the Prophet said:—The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord are ye, if ye amend your ways and your works. And again He said through the Prophet:—I will dwell in them and walk in them. And also the Blessed Apostle thus said:—Ye are the temple of God and the spirit of Christ dwelleth in you. And also our Lord again thus said to His disciples:—Ye are in Me and I am in you.

"Do not put your hope in deceptive words that say, 'Here is the temple of the Lord,' " that imply you are his temple. They are only trying to assure you that you will never be left by God as though God would decide to preserve his blessed temple and would save his priests even though they are wicked. No! Do not find hope in those who flatter you with these words. If you have not corrected what you are doing, then you are no temple of God, and God will not save you on account of the sacredness of his temple that is desecrated by you. His soul is disgusted by the multitude of your sacrifices that you offer in your wickedness.

If heaven and earth must pass away, obviously all things that are earthly must also pass away. Therefore the spots that witnessed the crucifixion and the resurrection profit those only who bear their several crosses, who day by day rise again with Christ and who thus show themselves worthy of an abode so holy. Those who say, "the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord," should give ear to the words of the apostle: "you are the temple of the Lord," and the Holy Spirit "dwells in you." Access to the courts of heaven is as easy from Britain as it is from Jerusalem, for "the kingdom of God is within you."

Do not trust in lying words, saying: The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord it is! For if you direct well — or direct — your ways and your pursuits, if you execute judgment between a man and his neighbor, if you do not practice false accusation against the stranger and the orphan and the widow — or do not oppress them — and do not shed innocent blood in this place, and do not walk after strange gods to your own harm, I will dwell with you — or I will make you dwell — in this place, in the land which I gave to your fathers from age to age. This, which the Seventy added at the beginning of this chapter: in words of falsehood, which will not profit you at all, is not found in the Hebrew. He commands both the people of the Jews then and us today, who seem to be established in the Church, not to have confidence in the splendor of buildings and in gilded ceilings and in walls clad with veneers of marble, and say: the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord it is. For that is the temple of the Lord in which true faith dwells, holy conduct, and the choir of all the virtues.

Then what value can our claim to a religious title have for us, what use is it to say we are catholic, to boast that we possess the true faith, to despise the Goths and Vandals, reviling them as heretics, when we are living in a truly heretical depravity? The words of the Divine Scripture addressed to the Jews who trusted in the law are most fittingly applied to us: "How do you say, 'We are wise and the law of the Lord is with us?' . . . Trust ye not in lying words, saying, 'The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, are these.' For if ye thoroughly amend your ways and your doings; if ye oppress not the stranger and the fatherless and the widow and shed not innocent blood in this place, then will I cause you to dwell in this place, in the land that I gave to your fathers for ever and ever.'' By this surely it is shown that if we do not amend our ways, it is useless for us to vaunt our claims to Catholicism.
On the Government of God, Book 7, Chapter 11

Then he adds: 'if you make your ways straight, and your thought does not go off after error, and you follow righteousness and do not commit evil, and do not shed innocent blood by scandalizing every simple person, and do not walk after strange gods by worshipping perverse doctrines which you have feigned out of your own heart to your own harm, then either I will dwell with you in this place, which you call the temple of God, and in the land which I gave to your fathers, namely the apostles and apostolic men, or at any rate with a firm standing I will make you dwell from the beginning to the end.' This can also suit those virgins who boast of their chastity and display purity with a shameless face, while their conscience holds something else, and who do not know that definition of virginity given by the Apostle, that she be holy in body and in spirit. For what does purity of body profit when the mind has been debauched, if she does not have the other virtues which the prophetic word has described?

Behold, you trust in words of falsehood — or lying words —, which will not profit you: to steal, to kill, to commit adultery, to swear falsely, to pour libations to the Baals, and to go after strange gods whom you do not know. And you came and stood before me in this house, in which my name has been called upon, and you said: We are delivered — or we have ceased — because we have done all these abominations. The sins that follow show that they have confidence in the temple in vain. For what does it profit to cross boldly the threshold of the house of God, to stand with neck held high, and to have not only the heart but also the hands polluted with theft, murder, adultery, perjury, sacrilege, and the worship of those gods whom you do not know? No one doubts that this happens spiritually in the Church, when people, considering the prosperity of the present time, do not take account of their sins and think that they are hidden from God, because punishment does not follow at once; nay rather, they break out into such madness that they think themselves delivered because after their evil works they have even withdrawn from the worship of the Lord.

And they come to Jerusalem: and Jesus went into the temple, and began to cast out them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves;  And would not suffer that any man should carry any vessel through the temple.  And he taught, saying unto them, Is it not written, My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer? but ye have made it a den of thieves. [Jeremiah 7:11] And the scribes and chief priests heard it, and sought how they might destroy him: for they feared him, because all the people was astonished at his doctrine.

And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves,  And said unto them, It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves. [Jeremiah 7:11]

Wherefore, brethren, if we do the will of God our Father, we shall be of the first Church, that is, spiritual, that hath been created before the sun and moon; but if we do not the will of the Lord, we shall be of the scripture that saith, "My house was made a den of robbers." So then let us choose to be of the Church of life, that we may be saved.
Second Epistle to the Corinthians (2 Clement), 14

Has this house — or my house —, in which my name has been called upon, become a den of robbers in your eyes? I, I am, I have seen, says the Lord. From this passage, I think, was taken what is in the Gospel: It is written: My Father's house shall be called a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of robbers, or, as is written in another Gospel, a house of trade. The Church of God is turned into a den of robbers when theft, murder, adultery, perjury, sacrilege, the invention of heresy and every crime are at home in it, when princes burn with the torches of avarice and a cheap, or at any rate not cheap, little cloak possesses what were once the riches of kings. Hence he adds: 'I, I am, I have seen, says the Lord; my eyes have beheld what you think hidden; the darkness of your treasuries does not escape my knowledge'. He who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake, now blushes at our riches and says: Woe to you rich, who have your consolation!

Go to my place in Shiloh, where my name dwelt from the beginning, and see what I did to it because of the wickedness of my people Israel! From the past he teaches the present, and to those who say: the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord and who rejoice in the gleam of a costly house he recalls the history of Shiloh, where the tabernacle of God first was, of which it is written in the psalm: and he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, so that, just as that place collapsed into ruins and ashes, so the temple too may fall, since it has been the dwelling of like sins. Therefore, just as Shiloh is an example for the temple, so is the temple for us, when the time of that testimony comes: Do you think the Son of Man, when he comes, will find faith on the earth?

And now, because you have done all these works, says the Lord, and I spoke to you, rising early and speaking, and you did not hear, and I called you and you did not answer, I will do to this house, in which my name has been called upon and in which you have confidence, and to the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh, and I will cast you out from my face, as I cast out all your brothers, the whole seed of Ephraim. This which we have set down: rising early and speaking, is not found in the Seventy. Now God rises early, not because there is any time for him without daybreak, but because after the rest of the night, when the strength of the body has been restored, the soul of men is more vigorous and, in no way occupied with pleasures and the desire for food, is able to hear and to do what is said. Hence we also read this in the psalm: In the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you and will see; and in Isaiah: By night — or at daybreak — my spirit will rise to you, O God, for your precepts are light upon the earth. Hence also the apostle Paul calls them sons of light, and not of night nor of darkness, nor sleepers, as the others too have slept, who do not perceive the commandments of God.

Since, therefore, God called them, rising by night, so that he might free them too from darkness, he threatens them that he will do to the temple in Jerusalem things like those he did to the place Shiloh, where the tabernacle first was, so that like sins may be struck by an equal sentence. And just as the Lord cast out the seed of Ephraim, that is, the ten tribes, which were called Israel and had princes on account of Jeroboam son of Nebat, of the tribe of Ephraim, which was likewise called the tribe of Joseph, so he testifies that he will also cast away Jerusalem and the tribe of Judah with Benjamin. He cast away Shiloh, therefore, and he will cast away the temple too; he cast away the ten tribes, and he will cast away the two as well. Whatever is said to that people, let us understand it of ourselves too, if we do like things.

Just as God knows how to heal, so does he furthermore know how to smite. He knows how to make peace but likewise permits evils. He prefers repentance but moreover commands Jeremiah not to pray for the reversal of ills on behalf of the sinful people. He says, "If they will fast, I still will not listen to their plea." And again: "Do not pray to me on behalf of the people, and do not request on their behalf in prayer and supplication, since I will not listen to them in the time when they shall have invoked me, in the time of their affliction." And further he, the same One who prefers mercy above sacrifice, says, "And do not pray to me on behalf of this people, and do not request that they may obtain mercy, and do not approach me on their behalf, since I will not listen to them in the time wherein they shall have invoked me, in the time of their affliction."

Rightly, then, is it said, "Who shall entreat for him?" It implies that it must be such a one as Moses to offer himself for those who sin. Or such as Jeremiah, who, though the Lord said to him, "Pray not for this people," yet prayed and obtained their forgiveness. For at the intercession of the prophet and the entreaty of so great a seer, the Lord was moved. And Jerusalem, which had meanwhile repented for its sins, had said, "O Almighty Lord God of Israel, the soul in anguish and the troubled spirit cries to you. Hear, O Lord, and have mercy."

And with regard to the deluge again He did the self-same thing, by His acts excusing Himself to Noah. And also to Ezekiel in like manner, when He caused him dwelling in Babylon to see men's evil deeds in Jerusalem. And yet again to Jeremiah, when He said, "Pray not," excusing Himself He added, "Seest thou not what they do?" And everywhere He doeth the selfsame thing, as here also. For what saith He? "The men of Nineveh shall rise up, and shall condemn this generation, because they repented at the preaching of Jonas, and, behold, a greater than Jonas is here."
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 43:3

[Daniel 9:2] "I, Daniel, understood by the books the number of the years concerning which the word of the Lord had come to the prophet Jeremiah, that seventy years would be accomplished for the desolation of Jerusalem." Jeremiah had predicted seventy years for the desolation of the Temple (Jeremiah 29:1-10), at the end of which the people would again return to Judaea and build the Temple and the city of Jerusalem. But this fact did not render Daniel careless, but rather encouraged him to pray that God might through his supplications fulfil that which He had graciously promised. Thus he avoided the danger that carelessness might result in pride, and pride cause offense to the Lord. Accordingly we read in Genesis that prior to the Deluge one hundred and twenty years were appointed for men to come to repentance (Genesis 6:3); and inasmuch as they refused to repent even within so long an interval of time as a hundred years, God did not wait for the remaining twenty years to be fulfilled, but brought on the punishment earlier which He had threatened for a later time. So also Jeremiah is told, on account of the hardness of the heart of the Jewish people: "Pray not for this people, for I will not hearken unto thee" (Jeremiah 7:16). Samuel also was told: "How long wilt thou mourn over Saul? I also have rejected him" (1 Samuel 16:1). And so it was with sackcloth and ashes that Daniel besought the Lord to fulfil what He had promised, not that Daniel lacked faith concerning the future, but rather he would avoid the danger that a feeling of security might produce carelessness, and carelessness produce an offense to God.
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER NINE

You, therefore, do not pray for this people, nor take up praise and prayer for them — or nor ask that they obtain mercy, — and do not withstand me, for I will not hear you. So that the prophet may not seem, in asking, to fail to obtain what he requests, God commands him not to intercede for a sinful people that does no repentance at all. But when he says: and do not resist me, he shows this, that the prayers of the saints can resist the wrath of God. Hence the Lord also speaks to Moses: Let me go, that I may strike this people, and I will make you into a great nation; and in the Psalms it is written: And Phinehas stood and appeased, and the shaking ceased, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness. Aaron too, seizing a censer, stood in the midst between the fire and the people about to burn, and the wrath of God ceased. And lest we think God cruel, since he does not even allow himself to be entreated, he gives the reasons why he does not hear, saying:

You will find at least in the book of Jeremiah the words of God censuring by the mouth of the prophet the Jewish people for doing obeisance to such objects and for sacrificing to the queen of heaven and to all the host of heaven. The writings of the Christians, moreover, show, in censuring the sins committed among the Jews, that when God abandoned that people on account of certain sins, these sins of idol worship also were committed by them.

Do you not see what these are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? The sons gather wood and the fathers kindle the fire and the women sprinkle fat, to make cakes — or chauonas — for the queen — or the host — of heaven, and to pour libations to strange gods and to provoke me to anger. Is it me they provoke to anger? says the Lord, is it not themselves, to the confusion of their own face? 'Do you wish,' he says, 'to hear, prophet, why I said to you: do not pray for this people? They do these things that follow: both within and without and in the streets and in the outlets of Jerusalem the sons carry together wood and the fathers kindle the fire and the women sprinkle fat with flour to make chauonim' — which we have rendered 'cakes' or 'preparations', so that it shows every kind of sacrifice to the queen of heaven, whom we should take to be the moon, or at any rate to the host of heaven, so that we understand all the stars — 'and after this they pour libations to strange gods, not that these exist, but in that under their names they burn incense to demons, and they provoke me to anger by doing these things. Nor do the wretches understand that this contention does not harm me, whom anger never changes, but themselves, to the confusion of their own face and to everlasting disgrace.' Whatever, therefore, we do, we do not harm God, who can never be harmed, but we prepare destruction for ourselves, storing up wrath for the day of wrath. And he set down the different tasks of the sons and of the fathers and of the mothers, or wives, so that there may be no age that has dissented from the impiety.

For "God" is "jealous" and does not wish the soul which he has betrothed to himself in faith to remain in the defilement of sin, but wishes her quickly to be purged, wishes her swiftly to cast off all her uncleannesses, if perhaps anything has stolen upon her. But if she remain in sins and say: we will not hear the voice of the Lord, but doing we will do our own wills and will burn offerings "to the queen of heaven", as is reproached through the prophet: then she too is reserved for that sentence of wisdom which says: "since indeed I called and you would not hear, but mocked my words; therefore I too will laugh at your destruction", or for that which is set before them in the Gospel, the Lord saying: "depart from me into eternal fire, which God has prepared for the devil and his angels".

For this is why He at all threatens punishment; that by fear He may destroy contempt; and when the threat alone is sufficient to cause fear in us, He doth not suffer us to undergo the actual trial. See, for instance, what He saith unto Jeremiah, "Seest thou not what they do? Their fathers light a fire, their children gather sticks together, their women knead dough." It is to be feared lest the same kind of thing be said also concerning us. "Seest thou not what they do? No one seeketh the things of Christ, but all their own. Their children run into uncleanness, their fathers into covetousness and rapine, their wives so far from keeping back their husbands from the pomps and vanities of life, do rather sharpen their appetites for them."

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, my fury and my indignation is kindled — or has dripped — upon this place, upon men and upon beasts and upon the trees of the region and upon the fruits of the earth, and it will be set alight and will not be quenched. He who had said above: Is it me they provoke to anger?, how does he now say: Behold, my fury and my indignation has dripped upon this place? And the sense is: 'I indeed am not angered by nature, but they act in such a way as to provoke me to anger, so that I seem to change my nature. Let them, therefore, feel me angry, which, so far as in them lies, they are trying to bring about.' And beautifully he does not say: 'has been poured out' my fury upon this place, but: has dripped, so as to signify a moderate punishment. But if in a drop of fury there is such harshness, what will happen if the whole downpour is poured out? But 'kindling' too can be understood thus: that what he long did not wish to do, he is compelled to do by the multitude of sins. And when God is angry, both men and the things that are men's will feel a like destruction. 'And it will be set alight', he says — no doubt the fury of the Lord — 'and will not be quenched, because the people do not do the things through which it could be quenched.'

You are blessed who are delivered from the curse. Christ, the Son of God, by his coming has confirmed and completed the law but has taken away the additional precepts, although not all of them, yet at least the more grievous ones. He confirmed the former and abolished the latter, and he has again set the free will of humankind at liberty. He does not subject them to the penalty of a temporal death but gives laws to them according to another constitution. For this reason, he says, "If anyone will come after me, let him come." And again, "Will you also go away?" And besides, before his coming he refused the sacrifices of the people, while they frequently offered them, when they sinned against him and thought he was to be appeased by sacrifices but not by repentance.

HOW HAS THE LORD IN LEVITICUS COMMANDED THAT SACRIFICES AND LIBATIONS BE OFFERED, WHICH ELSEWHERE HE REJECTS? FOR IT IS CLEAR IN LEVITICUS THAT THE LORD COMMANDED THE FATHERS TO OFFER LIBATIONS OR SACRIFICES OR BURNT OFFERINGS: YET HE SAYS THEREFORE THROUGH THE PROPHET JEREMIAH: THEREFORE SAYS THE LORD, GATHER YOUR BURNT OFFERINGS WITH YOUR SACRIFICES, AND EAT FLESH; FOR I DID NOT SPEAK TO YOUR FATHERS, NOR DID I COMMAND THEM, IN THE DAY THAT I BROUGHT THEM OUT OF THE LAND OF EGYPT (Jer. 7:21–22) ABOUT BURNT OFFERINGS AND SACRIFICES. — If you look closely, there is really no question to be raised on this matter; nor should you think the Lord lied or changed, as if he commanded and later denied. For of this kind of sacrifices and drink offerings or burnt offerings, nothing is found that he commanded, regarding those of which he now testifies that he spoke. Notice that there are two kinds of sacrifices: one which was commanded to be offered for each specific kind, and another which was called voluntary. As for that which was commanded to be offered in various kinds, whether for sins or for firstborn, it was prescribed what it was, of what sort, and how it was to be offered. But the voluntary sacrifice was certainly not commanded, because it was left to free choice, so that if anyone wished to offer, he would offer what seemed good to him; for these sacrifices were voluntary. And because they offered these carelessly and rashly, without considering that whoever offers to one greater should offer chosen gifts, it is therefore said to them, I did not command you about these: but if you wish to offer, you ought to offer what is worthy. Therefore it is found that Cain also sinned, when he did not consider that what is better ought to be offered to God. For when they claimed to offer these to appease God, in that very act they provoked God to anger, so that in what they said they were doing well, they sinned by offering unworthy burnt offerings to God. Therefore he says in the prophet Malachi: “If you bring a blind or lame or sick animal as a victim, it is not good. Offer it to your leader or governor; if he will receive you, says the Lord almighty” (Mal. 1:8). From this it is that through Isaiah God complains of the same matter, saying: “What are your sheep of burnt offering to me? Nor in your sacrifices have you honored me. For I did not make you for this purpose, that you should toil over incense, or that you should buy incense for me with silver; nor have I desired the fat of your sacrifices: instead, you have stood before me in your sins and iniquities” (Isa. 1:11). It is therefore clear that complaints arose because, while they were offering voluntary sacrifices, they were not honoring God in them, since they offered what was unworthy, although these were in no way a matter of necessity. For if they had been commanded, they would seem to offer whatever they could by necessity; but when they offered these of their own free will, they ought to have offered such things as would show God’s service in themselves. But because their mind wandered through the desire for idols, they acted in these matters without due thought. Therefore they are reproached in a twofold way, because they dared to offer to God while acting wickedly, and they offered things that were unworthy; since wicked deeds are not redeemed by sacrifices, but by weeping and mercy. Therefore David, when he had sinned, says: “If you had willed it, I would have given sacrifices: surely you will not delight in burnt offerings. The sacrifice to God is a regretful spirit; and a broken and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. 50:18–19). Finally, Samuel says to Saul, who, after he had despised the command of the Lord, thought God could be appeased by a sacrifice: “For,” he says, “God does not desire sacrifice more than that his voice be heard” (1 Sam. 15:22). And Scripture says: “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Hos. 6:6). The Jews, though unjust and without mercy, thought God could be made favorable by offerings; just as even now certain people, despising righteousness, think they are to be praised for their offerings. An offering is therefore good, if righteousness is preserved and mercy is not neglected; because what we ask for ourselves, we must also grant to others.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 103: WHY GOD COMMANDS SACRIFICES YET ELSEWHERE REJECTS THEM

Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Add your burnt offerings to your victims and eat flesh, for I did not speak with your fathers, and I did not command them on the day that I led them out of the land of Egypt, concerning the matter of burnt offerings and victims, but this word I commanded them, saying: Hear my voice, and I will be your God and you will be my people, and walk in every way that I have commanded you, that it may be well with you. Having rejected their temple, he consequently rejects their sacrifices too, and indirectly reproves them because they sacrifice victims not out of reverence for him but out of desire for feasting. But when he says: I did not speak with your fathers, and I did not command them on the day that I led them out of the land of Egypt, about the matter of the burnt offering and of victims, it is clearly understood that he first gave the Decalogue, written on tablets of stone by the finger of God, and that after the offense of idolatry and the head of the calf he afterward commanded that it be done to himself rather than to demons, taking away the pure religion of the commandments of God and granting the blood of victims and the craving for flesh.

It is made clear also from this that the obsolete prescriptions of the law had been imposed because of Israel's limitations. Since they had learned in Egypt how to sacrifice to idols, he wanted to separate them from those practices—in all the prophets he rejects them, remember—yet out of consideration for their limitations he utters this remark, "Eat flesh," that is, Although I reject the sacrifices, I shall not oppose your partaking of flesh. After all, he declares in the law that those wishing to partake of flesh in their own cities and towns should "perform the sacrifice, but pour out the blood on the ground and then partake of the sacrifice," not as though they were offering it as a sacrifice but as ordinary flesh, as part of the prohibition imposed on performing sacred rites outside the designated place.

He has therefore abolished these things, that the new law of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is without the yoke of necessity, might have a human oblation. And again He says to them, "Did I command your fathers, when they went out from the land of Egypt, to offer unto Me burnt-offerings and sacrifices? But this rather I commanded them, Let no one of you cherish any evil in his heart against his neighbour, and love not an oath of falsehood." We ought therefore, being possessed of understanding, to perceive the gracious intention of our Father; for He speaks to us, desirous that we, not going astray like them, should ask how we may approach Him. To us, then, He declares, "A sacrifice [pleasing] to God is a broken spirit; a smell of sweet savour to the Lord is a heart that glorifieth Him that made it." We ought therefore, brethren, carefully to inquire concerning our salvation, lest the wicked one, having made his entrance by deceit, should hurl us forth from our [true] life.
The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter II

And what does this mean my brethren? For it is right for us to investigate the saying of the prophet, and especially on account of heretics who have turned their mind against the law. By Moses then, God gave commandment respecting sacrifices, and all the book called Leviticus is entirely taken up with the arrangement of these matters, so that He might accept the offerer. So through the Prophets, He blames him who despised these things, as disobedient to the commandment saying, ‘I have not required these at your hands. Neither did I speak to your fathers respecting sacrifices, nor command them concerning whole burnt-offerings.’ Now it is the opinion of some, that the Scriptures do not agree together, or that God, Who gave the commandment, is false. But there is no disagreement whatever, far from it, neither can the Father, Who is truth, lie; ‘for it is impossible that God should lie,’ as Paul affirms. But all these things are plain to those who rightly consider them, and to those who receive with faith the writings of the law. Now it appears to me—may God grant, by your prayers, that the remarks I presume to make may not be far from the truth—that not at first were the commandment and the law concerning sacrifices, neither did the mind of God, Who gave the law, regard whole burnt-offerings, but those things which were pointed out and prefigured by them. ‘For the law contained a shadow of good things to come.’ And, ‘Those things were appointed until the time of reformation.’

Therefore, the whole law did not treat of sacrifices, though there was in the law a commandment concerning sacrifices, that by means of them it might begin to instruct men and might withdraw them from idols, and bring them near to God, teaching them for that present time. Therefore neither at the beginning, when God brought the people out of Egypt, did He command them concerning sacrifices or whole burnt-offerings, nor even when they came to mount Sinai. For God is not as man, that He should be careful about these things beforehand; but His commandment was given, that they might know Him Who is truly God, and His Word, and might despise those which are falsely called gods, which are not, but appear in outward show. So He made Himself known to them in that He brought them out of Egypt, and caused them to pass through the Red Sea. But when they chose to serve Baal, and dared to offer sacrifices to those that have no existence, and forgat the miracles which were wrought in their behalf in Egypt, and thought of returning thither again; then indeed, after the law, that commandment concerning sacrifices was ordained as law; so that with their mind, which at one time had meditated on those which are not, they might turn to Him Who is truly God, and learn not, in the first place, to sacrifice, but to turn away their faces from idols, and conform to what God commanded. For when He saith, ‘I have not spoken concerning sacrifices, neither given commandment concerning whole burnt-offerings,’ He immediately adds, ‘But this is the thing which I commanded them, saying, Obey My voice, and I will be to you a God, and ye shall be to Me a people, and ye shall walk in all the ways that I command you.’ Thus then, being before instructed and taught, they learned not to do service to any one but the Lord. They attained to know what time the shadow should last, and not to forget the time that was at hand, in which no longer should the bullock of the herd be a sacrifice to God, nor the ram of the flock, nor the he-goat, but all these things should be fulfilled in a purely spiritual manner, and by constant prayer, and upright conversation, with godly words; as David sings, ‘May my meditation be pleasing to Him. Let my prayer be set forth before Thee as incense, and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice.’ The Spirit also, who is in him, commands, saying, ‘Offer unto God the sacrifice of praise, and pay to the Lord thy vows. Offer the sacrifice of righteousness, and put your trust in the Lord.’

In a manner most germane to this parable, He said by Jeremiah: "Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and ye shall be my people; and ye shall walk in all my ways, which I have commanded you." This is the invitation of God. "But," says He, "they hearkened not, nor inclined their ear." This is the refusal of the people. "They departed, and walked every one in the imagination of their evil heart." "I have bought a field-and I have bought some oxen-and I have married a wife." And still He urges them: "I have sent unto you all my servants the prophets, rising early even before day-light." The Holy Spirit is here meant, the admonisher of the guests. "Yet my people hearkened not unto me, nor inclined their ear, but hardened their neck."
The Five Books Against Marcion, Book 4

And they did not hear nor incline their ear, but they went off in the wills — or desires — and the depravity of their evil heart, and they became backward and not forward, from the day on which their fathers came out of the land of Egypt until this day. 'When I said: Hear my voice and I will be your God and the rest, they did not hear nor incline their ear, but they did the desires of their own heart, and against the judgment of the Apostle, who forgot what lay behind and stretched himself toward what lay before, they did the contrary, so as to desire the past and despise the future.' And when he says: from the day on which their fathers came out of the land of Egypt until this day, he says that they spent all the time in between in offense against the Lord. Hence the grace of the Gospel was also necessary, which saved them not by their own merit but by the mercy of the Lord.

And I sent to you my servants, the prophets, by day, rising at daybreak and sending; and they did not hear me nor incline their ear, but they hardened their neck and wrought worse than their fathers. Just, therefore, is the wrath of the Lord, which has been kindled and has dripped upon a contemptuous and stiff-necked people that refuses to hear the words of God. But how God sends the prophets either by night or at daybreak and by day, we have said above.

When the whole world was oppressed by the darkness of the devil. When the gloom brought on by sin had laid hold of the world. At the last age, when night had already fallen, this sun deigned to bring forth the rising of his birth. Before the light, before the sun of justice shone, he sent the oracle of the prophets as a kind of dawning, as it is written: "I sent my prophets before the light."

And you will speak to them all these words, and they will not hear you; and you will call them, and they will not answer you. And you will say to them: This is the nation that has not heard the voice of the Lord its God nor received discipline; faith has perished and has been taken away from their mouth. 'Do not doubt,' he says, 'that they have hardened their neck and wrought worse than their fathers; behold, I give room for repentance, and I do not speak in order that these things may happen, but because they are going to happen, therefore I foretell them. At least now speak to them with my words, and yet they will not hear you; and you will call them, and they will not answer you; for they will be of such pride that, when you call them to hear, no one will deign to answer. And you will say to them: This is the nation that has not heard the voice of the Lord its God nor received discipline'. Beautifully, as I have already said before, he calls them not at all his people, but a nation. And although this was in part done in the time of the prophets too, and went before in shadow and in image, yet it is more fully fulfilled in Christ, when they refused to receive discipline and despised the voice of their Lord. Hence it is fittingly added: faith has perished, which belongs properly to Christians, and has been taken away from their mouth, namely every confession of the Son of God and of the faith.

But last of all He sent to those unbelievers His own Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, whom the wicked husbandmen cast out of the vineyard when they had slain Him. Wherefore the Lord God did even give it up (no longer hedged around, but thrown open throughout all the world) to other husbandmen, who render the fruits in their seasons—the beautiful elect tower being also raised everywhere. For the illustrious Church is [now] everywhere, and everywhere is the winepress digged: because those who do receive the Spirit are everywhere. For inasmuch as the former have rejected the Son of God, and cast Him out of the vineyard when they slew Him, God has justly rejected them, and given to the Gentiles outside the vineyard the fruits of its cultivation. This is in accordance with what Jeremiah says, "The Lord hath rejected and cast off the nation which does these things; for the children of Judah have done evil in my sight, saith the Lord."

Shear your hair and cast it away, and take up in the open — or upon the lips — a lament, for the Lord has cast off and forsaken the generation of his fury. We read that Job too, on hearing of the death of his sons and daughters, sheared his hair, and among the ancients this was the custom of all who mourned, to shear the locks; but now, on the contrary, to let the hair grow long is the sign of mourning. And all the prophet's lament and lamentation is taken up for this reason, for the Lord has cast off and forsaken the generation of his fury; no doubt he signifies the people of the Jews. And this is properly to be referred to the times of Christ, when faith perished and was taken away from the mouth of the people blaspheming the Lord.

For the sons of Judah have done evil in my sight, says the Lord; they have set their stumbling blocks in the house in which my name has been called upon, to pollute it, and they have built the high places — or the altar — of Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters with fire, which I did not command nor think of in my heart. That the sons of Judah set up a statue of Baal in the temple of God we learn at the beginning of Ezekiel. Now 'high places', which in Hebrew are called 'bamath', or 'altar' of Topheth, which is in the valley of the sons of Hinnom, signifies that place which is watered by the springs of Siloam, and is pleasant and wooded, and to this day offers the delights of gardens. And this error of paganism took hold of all the provinces, so that they sacrificed victims at the heads of springs and in the loveliest groves, and the observance of every depraved superstition was kept. 'Tofeth' in the Hebrew tongue means 'breadth', and it is said to be written in the book of Joshua son of Nun about this place, which is in the valley of the sons of Hinnom and in Hebrew is called 'gehennom'; for 'ge' signifies pharanga, that is, 'valley', and 'hennom' signifies either a man's name or 'grace'. And the Hebrews hand down that 'gehennam' was named from this place, because, namely, the whole people of the Jews perished there by offending God, in which place they also consecrated their sons in fire to idols or offered them as a burnt offering, which he had not commanded them nor ordered by any sanction of the law. But if Jephthah offered his virgin daughter to God, it is not the sacrifice that pleases, but the mind of the one offering; for if a dog or an ass or any unclean animal whatever had first met the father as he returned from the slaughter of the enemy, he ought not to have offered it to God.

Therefore, behold, the days will come, says the Lord, and it will no longer be called Topheth and the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of killing, and they will bury in Topheth because there is no room. And the carcasses of this people will be food for the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth, and there will be none to drive them away. He signifies the time of the siege, which they endured from the ninth year of King Zedekiah to the eleventh year, and that the valley itself will by no means be called 'gehennom', that is, 'valley of hennom', or 'of the sons of Hinnom', but, on account of the killing of very many, 'valley of slaughter'. And so great will the slaughter be that in the place formerly of worship there will be innumerable tombs, and those whom they cannot bury will be torn by birds and devoured by beasts, and there will be no one to drive them away, since he fears the like and is overcome by the duties of burying. We pass quickly over what is plain, so that, wherever there is occasion, we may linger over what is obscure. For the very size of the book can cause weariness to readers; how much more if it were discussed by us at greater length!

And I will make to cease from the cities of Judah and from the streets of Jerusalem the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, and the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride; for the land will be in desolation. When the place of idolatry has been turned into tombs, so that where they had offended God, there their corpses lie unburied, all gladness will be taken away from the city of Jerusalem that once was and from the other cities that were under its dominion, and all things will be filled with sorrow and groaning and desolation.
8: At that time, says the Lord, they shall cast out the bones of the king of Judah and the bones of his princes and the bones of the priests and the bones of the prophets and the bones of those who dwelt in Jerusalem, from their graves. And they shall spread them out to the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which they have loved and which they have served and after which they have walked and which they have sought and worshiped. They shall not be gathered and shall not be buried; they shall be for a dunghill upon the face of the earth. And all who remain of this most wicked family shall choose death rather than life, in all the places that are left, to which I have cast them out, says the Lord of hosts. All the things that the prophetic word describes we see to have happened in our own time, not to Jerusalem alone, which suffered these things from the Chaldeans and the Romans, but to the whole world, so that tears have dried up and everything has been filled with the bones of the dead. And because, according to ancient custom, they used to lay up gold and certain ornaments, whether of women or of men, in tombs, avarice broke these open too and dug them up, so as to expose them to the sky and the light. And therefore first the bones of the kings of Judah and of its princes, of the priests also and of the prophets and of all the people who had been in Jerusalem, were brought out of their tombs, lying open to the sun and the moon and to the sight of all the stars, so that they lay open to the gaze of those whom they had served after forsaking God, and, consumed, were dissolved into a dunghill and ashes; and if anyone of the multitude had been able to escape, to whatever places he came, he would prefer death to life and think destruction the remedy of an unhappy soul.

And pray ye without ceasing in behalf of other men; for there is hope of the repentance, that they may attain to God. For "cannot he that falls arise again, and he that goes astray return?" Permit them, then, to be instructed by you. Be ye therefore the ministers of God, and the mouth of Christ. For thus saith the Lord, "If ye take forth the precious from the vile, ye shall be as my mouth." Be ye humble in response to their wrath; oppose to their blasphemies your earnest prayers; while they go astray, stand ye stedfast in the faith. Conquer ye their harsh temper by gentleness, their passion by meekness. For "blessed are the meek"; and Moses was meek above all men; and David was exceeding meek.
Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians

If you have any hope of salvation; if you have the least thought of God, or any desire for good things to come; if you have any fear of the chastisements reserved for the impenitent, awake without delay, lift up your eyes to heaven, come to your senses, cease from your wickedness, shake off the stupor that enwraps you, make a stand against the foe who has struck you down. Make an effort to rise from the ground. Remember the good Shepherd who will follow and rescue you. Though it be but two legs or a lobe of an ear, spring back from the beast that has wounded you. Remember the mercies of God and how He cures with oil and wine. Do not despair of salvation. Recall your recollection of how it is written in the Scriptures that he who is falling rises and he who turns away returns; the wounded is healed, the prey of beasts escapes; he who owns his sin is not rejected. The Lord willeth not the death of a sinner but rather that he should turn and live.

Doth not David say, Every night I will wash my bed, I will water my couch with my tears; and again, I acknowledge my sin, and mine unrighteousness have I not hid; and yet more, I said, I will confess my sins unto the Lord, and so Thou forgavest the wickedness of my heart. Did not the Prophet answer him when, after the guilt of murder and adultery, penitent for Bathsheba, The Lord also hath put away from thee thy sin? Did not confession deliver the king of Babylon, when condemned after so many sins of idolatry? And what is it that the Lord saith, Shall he who has fallen not arise, and he who has turned not return?

Behold! I promise, I engage, if ye return to your Father with true satisfaction, erring no more, adding nothing to former sins, saying also some humble and mournful words, as, Father, we have sinned before Thee, and are no more worthy to be called Thy sons; straightway shall leave you both that filthy herd, and the unseemly food of husks. Straightway on your return shall the robe be put upon you, and the ring adorn you, and your Father's embrace again receive you. Lo! He saith Himself, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that he turn from his way and live. And again He saith, Shall they fall, and not arise? Shall he turn away, and not return? And the Apostle saith, God is able to make him stand.

God is indeed good to everyone, but he shows his patient endurance especially to those who sin. If you want to hear a paradoxical statement—paradoxical because it is not customary but true for the great piety it reveals—listen. God always seems to be severe to the righteous. But he seems good to sinners and quick to clemency. He restores the one who sinned and fell, and he tells him, "Shall not he who falls get up? Or the one who turns away, shall he not turn back again?" And "Why did the stupid daughter of Judah turn away with a shameless revolting?" And again, "Return to me, and I will return to you."

The very thing I said in the beginning, I say now, that both of these cause us to betray our salvation: placing our courage in our goodness and losing our hope to wickedness. This is why Paul, to protect those who remain in goodness, said, "Let any one who thinks that he stand take heed in fear that he fall." And again: "I am afraid that, after preaching to others, I myself should be disapproved." In order to lift up those who are found fallen in wickedness and to excite them to greater readiness, he bore testimony to the Corinthians. He wrote to them, "I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned before and have not repented." In this way, he revealed that the sinners do not deserve equal pity with the unrepentant. And the prophet said to them, "Shall not he that falls arise, or he that turns away, shall he not turn back again?" Hence, as long as the "today" is said let us not despair but have good hope in the Master. Let us recognize the vast sea of his philanthropy.

Now then is it not strange that, whilst others do not even now despair of thy salvation, but are continually praying that they may have their member restored to them, thou thyself, having once fallen, art unwilling to get up again, and remainest prostrate, all but crying aloud to the enemy: "Slay me, smite me, spare not?" "Does he who falls not rise up again?" speaks the divine oracle. But thou art striving against this and contradicting it; for if one who has fallen despairs it is as much as to say that he who falls does not rise up again. I entreat thee do not so great a wrong to thyself; do not pour upon us such a flood of sorrow. I do not say at the present time, when thou hast not yet completed thy twentieth year, but even if, after achieving many things, and spending thy whole life in Christ thou hadst, in extreme old age, experienced this attack, even then it would not have been right to despair, but to call to mind the robber who was justified on the cross, the labourers who wrought about the eleventh hour, and received the wages of the whole day.

And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Shall he who falls not rise again? And he who has turned away, shall he not return — or shall he not turn away — ? After such great evils he calls to repentance those who were able to remain, or before they come. He has threatened these things; he exhorts them to conversion and gives room for repentance. But what is written according to the Hebrew: and he who has turned away, shall he not turn away, signifies this: that he who has turned away from God, if he is willing to be converted to better things, can also turn the fury of God to better things, and withstand what is coming, and escape the blows by prayers.

They have all abandoned him. There is no one who speaks well and does penance for his sins. They follow their own wills like a horse ready for battle. They bend their tongue as a bow. They invent everything, and there is no truth in them.

Why then has this people in Jerusalem turned away with a contentious turning away? They have laid hold of falsehood and they would not return? 'The more I,' he says, 'called them to repentance, the more they withdrew from me, not so much from eagerness to sin as from eagerness to overcome me. For they have laid hold firmly of falsehood, whether idols or whatever perverse things are contrary to truth and righteousness, and they would not return' — he did not say 'they could not' —, 'but with all eagerness they have pursued wicked things'.

Just as there is no illness that is incurable for our physician, so the heavenly medicine cannot be powerless in any wound or for any length of time. Therefore, the physician testifies that he is always able to restore health to the one converted. He says, "In returning and rest, you shall be saved." Hence God, through Jeremiah, does not cease to reprove the hardheartedness of certain ones. Instead he says in this way: "When people fall, do they not get up again? If they go astray, do they not turn back? Why then has this people turned away in perpetual backsliding? They have held fast to deceit. They have refused to return." God does not punish the sins in the sinner, if the neck of the sinner is not stiffened.

Jeremiah also says, in like manner: "The turtle and the swallow have known her time, and the sparrows of the field have observed the times of their coming, but my people have not known the judgment of the Lord. How do you say, We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us? The meting out is in vain. The scribes are deceived and confounded. The wise men are dismayed and taken, for they have rejected the word of the Lord." Therefore (as I had begun to say), when God had determined to send to people a teacher of righteousness, he commanded him to be born again a second time in the flesh and to be made in the likeness of humankind himself, to whom he was about to be a guide, and companion and teacher. But since God is kind and merciful to his people, he sent him to those very persons whom he hated, that he might not close the way of salvation against them forever but might give them a free opportunity of following God, that they might both gain the reward of life if they should follow him (which many of them do and have done) and incur the penalty of death by their fault if they should reject their King.

Wherefore it were meet exceedingly to admire the consideration of our Lawgiver, in that, when He might bring forward His illustration from among men, and when He might have spoken of Moses and Elias and John, and others like them, who took no thought; that He might touch them more to the quick, He made mention of the irrational beings. For had He spoken of those righteous men, these would have been able to say, "We are not yet become like them." But now by passing them over in silence, and bringing forward the fowls of the air, He hath cut off from them every excuse, imitating in this place also the old law. Yea, for the old covenant likewise sends to the bee, and to the ant, and to the turtle, and to the swallow. And neither is this a small sign of honor, when the same sort of things, which those animals possess by nature, those we are able to accomplish by an act of our choice.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 21:4

I attended and listened; no one speaks what is good, there is none who does repentance over his sin, saying: What have I done? All have turned to their course, like a horse going with a rush to battle. Called back to repentance, they scorn to listen; nor is it enough for them to have offended against the Lord and to have spoken blasphemy, but all, like horses rushing in hot course to battle, do not reflect on their sin nor say: what have I done? By which we understand that these things are said either of the whole human race, because it is prone to vices, or of the time of the Savior, when all have turned aside, together they have become useless; there was none who did good, there was not even one. Hence he himself also cries out mystically: save me, O Lord, for the holy one has failed! But if these things are so, where are those who say that it lies within our will to be free of all sin? No one, he says, speaks what is good, because we shall render account even for an idle word on the day of judgment.

The kite in the heaven has known its time; the turtledove and the swallow and the stork have kept the time of their coming; but my people has not known the judgment of the Lord. For 'kite', which Symmachus translated, the Seventy and Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, 'asida', Aquila 'herodiona' [heron]. And again for 'swallow' Symmachus translated 'cicada', which in Hebrew is called 'sis'. And for what we have put as 'stork', both Aquila and Symmachus translated 'agur', just as it is written in the Hebrew, for which the Seventy translated 'sparrows of the field'. And it is one and the same sense which is also set down at the beginning of Isaiah: the ox has known its owner and the ass the manger of its master, but Israel has not known me and my people has not understood; namely, that even small birds know their seasons and know when, hastening to warm places, they ought to escape the harshness of winter, and again at the beginning of spring come back to their accustomed regions. And here we ought to take 'heaven' for 'the air', which is above.

How do you say: We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us? Truly the lying pen of the scribes has wrought falsehood. He speaks to the scribes and Pharisees, who boast of their knowledge of the law and, writing, write iniquity. And as for what he says:

Nor is it in my opinion unreasonable to add also the following. The Scribes and Pharisees, who held high rank among the Jews, as having the reputation of legal learning, were regarded as wise men. But they were convicted by the very result of not being so in reality. For even the prophet Jeremiah thus somewhere addressed them: "How say ye, that we are wise, and the word of the Lord is with us? The lying cord of the scribe is for emptiness. The wise men are ashamed; they fear and are taken: what wisdom is in. them, because they have rejected the word of the Lord?" Because then they rejected the word of the Saviour, that is, the saving message of the Gospel, or in other language, the Word of God the Father, Who for our sakes became man, they have themselves been rejected.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

THE blessed prophet Jeremiah loudly condemned the ignorance, at once, and pride of the Jews, rebuking them in these words; "How say you that we are wise, and the word of the Lord is with us? In vain is the lying cord of the scribes. The wise men are ashamed: they trembled, and were taken: what wisdom have they, in that they have rejected the Word of the Lord!" For being neither wise, nor acquainted with the sacred Scriptures, though the scribes and Pharisees falsely assumed to themselves the reputation of being learned in the law, they rejected the Word of God. For when the Only Begotten had become man, they did not receive Him, nor yield their neck obediently to the summons which He addressed to them by the Gospel. Because therefore by their wicked conduct they rejected the Word of God, they were themselves rejected, being condemned by God's just decree. For He said, by the voice of Jeremiah, "Call them rejected silver: because the Lord has rejected them." And again, "Shave your head, and cast it away, and take lamentation upon your lips, because the Lord has rejected and thrust away the generation that has done these things." And what these things are, the God of all has Himself declared to us, saying, "Hear, O earth: behold! I am bringing upon this people evils; the fruit of their turning away; because they regarded not My word, and have rejected My law." For neither did they keep the commandment that was given to them by Moses, "teaching for doctrines the commandments of men:" and further, they also rejected the Word of God the Father, having refused to honour by faith Christ, when He called them thereunto. The fruits therefore of their turning away were plainly the calamities which happened to them: for they suffered all misery, as the retribution due for murdering the Lord.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

Then what value can our claim to a religious title have for us, what use is it to say we are catholic, to boast that we possess the true faith, to despise the Goths and Vandals, reviling them as heretics, when we are living in a truly heretical depravity? The words of the Divine Scripture addressed to the Jews who trusted in the law are most fittingly applied to us: "How do you say, 'We are wise and the law of the Lord is with us?' . . . Trust ye not in lying words, saying, 'The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, are these.' For if ye thoroughly amend your ways and your doings; if ye oppress not the stranger and the fatherless and the widow and shed not innocent blood in this place, then will I cause you to dwell in this place, in the land that I gave to your fathers for ever and ever.'' By this surely it is shown that if we do not amend our ways, it is useless for us to vaunt our claims to Catholicism.
On the Government of God, Book 7, Chapter 11

The wise are confounded, terrified and taken, it is not that those who do these things are wise, but he calls them wise so that they may be condemned by their own judgment and, on the contrary, their wisdom may be proved to be folly, as Paul says: you who teach another, do you not teach yourself? And because they have cast away the word of the Lord, therefore there is no wisdom in them. In vain, then, do they boast of knowledge of the law who destroy their teaching by their works.

Finally, whoever wishes fuller proof that mere words are nothing without actions should consider how countless peoples, by failing in good works, have lost the names given them. The twelve tribes of the Hebrews, when they were of old chosen by God, received two holy names, for they were called the people of God, and Israel. We read: "Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, and I will testify against thee." Once the Jews bore both these titles, now they have neither. They who long since left off the worship of God cannot be called God's people, nor can they who denied his Son be given a name that means "Seeing God." So it is written: "But Israel does not know, my people doth not consider."

For this reason on another occasion our God spoke of the people of the Hebrews to the prophet, saying: "Call his name, Not Beloved." And speaking to the Jews themselves: "You are not my people and I am not your God." Moreover, he himself showed clearly why he spoke thus about them, for he said: "They have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of living waters." And again: "They have rejected the word of the Lord and there is no wisdom in them."

But indeed I am afraid that this is true of us now no less than it was of them, since we do not obey the words of the Lord, and our disobedience certainly shows that there is no wisdom in us. Unless perhaps we believe that we act wisely in scorning God, and consider it as a sign of the greatest prudence that we despise Christ's commandments. There is some reason why we should be thought to hold this opinion, for we all sin with as much accord as if we were doing it in pursuit of an elaborately planned policy.
On the Government of God, Book 4, Chapter 1

Therefore I will give their women — or wives — to strangers, their fields to heirs, because from the least to the greatest all are devoted to avarice, from the prophet to the priest all practice falsehood — or iniquity —. And they healed the breaking of the daughter of my people to ignominy, saying: Peace, peace, when there was not peace. They received the wages of their works, so that those who cast away the word of the Lord were themselves cast away by him. 'Their wives,' he says, 'and their possessions I will hand over to the enemy. And lest my sentence be thought cruel, let the hearer recognize the causes: from the least to the greatest all are devoted to avarice — for avarice is the root of all evils —, from the prophet to the priest. Those who ought to restrain others when they sin are the first to be given over to crimes, and all either do iniquitous things, while they plunder the goods of others, or at any rate practice falsehood, so that there is no truth in their mouth.

The arranged time comes to our people; there is peace in the world; and, at the same time, ruin is weighing us down from the enticement of the world, (the destruction) of the reckless people whom you have rent into schism. Either obey the law of the city, or depart from it. You behold the mote sticking in our eyes, and will not see the beam in your own. A treacherous peace is coming to you; persecution is rife; the wounds do not appear; and thus, without slaughter, you are destroyed. War is waged in secret, because, in the midst of peace itself, scarcely one of you has behaved himself with caution. O badly fortified, and foretold for slaughter, you praise a treacherous peace, a peace that is mischievous to you. Having become the soldiers of another than Christ, you have perished.

Do not believe the false prophets who say, "Peace, peace, and there is no peace"; who are always repeating, "The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord." "Your prophets have seen for you false and foolish things; they have not laid bare your iniquity that they might call you to repentance—those who devour God's people like bread have not called on God." Jeremiah announced the captivity and was [punished] by the people. Hananiah, the son of Azzur, broke the bars of wood for the present but was preparing bars of iron for the future. False prophets always promise pleasant things, and please for a fee. Truth is bitter, however, and those who preach it are filled with bitterness. For with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth the Lord's Passover is kept, and it is eaten with bitter herbs.

But what can I do, I who can only wish for peace and have no power to bring it about? Even though the wish may win its reward with God, its futility must still sadden one who cherishes it. When the apostle said, "as much as lies in you, live peaceably with all," he knew quite well that the realization of peace depends on the consent of two parties. The prophet truly cries, "They say Peace, peace: and yet there is no peace." To overthrow peace by actions while professing it in words is not hard. To point out its advantages is one thing, and to strive for it another. People's speeches may be all for unity, but their actions may in fact enforce bondage. I wish for peace as much as any one else; and not only do I wish for it, I ask for it. But the peace that I want is the peace of Christ; a true peace, a peace without rancor, a peace that does not involve war, a peace that will not reduce opponents but will unite friends. How can I term domination peace? I must call things by their right names. Where there is hatred, there let people talk of feuds; and where there is mutual esteem, there only let peace be spoken of. For my part I neither tear the church apart nor separate myself from the communion of the fathers. From my very cradle, I may say, I have been reared on Catholic milk; and no one can be a better churchman than one who has never been a heretic. But I know nothing of a peace that is without love or of a communion that is without peace. In the Gospel I read, "If you bring your gift to the altar and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go your way; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift." If then we may not offer gifts that are our own unless we are at peace with our brothers; how much less can we receive the body of Christ if we cherish enmity in our hearts? How can I conscientiously approach Christ's Eucharist and answer the Amen if I doubt the charity of him who ministers it?

And after these things, like good physicians, they desired to heal the wounds of others with words, they who were themselves pierced through with the wounds of every shameful deed'. This we see daily in our own people too, as the Apostle says: you who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? and the rest.
