When these see sinners and rich men, they desire to heal the breaking of the daughter of the people of God, that is, of the Church, to the ignominy either of those who are deceived or of those who deceive others, so that they say to men covered with every crime: peace, peace, when there is no peace, while the war of their sins hangs over them.

Such, then, should Christ's apostles be preachers of the gospel and not ones who greet on the road. That is, not ones who look for something else, but those who proclaim the gospel out of genuine brotherly love. Let them come to the house and say, "Peace be to this house." They do not only say it with their lips, but they pour out what they are full of. They preach peace, and they have peace. They are not like those of whom it is said, "Peace, peace, and there is no peace." What's the meaning of "Peace, peace, and there is no peace"? They preach it and do not have it. They praise and do not love it. They say, and they do not do. As for you, though, be sure you accept peace, whether Christ is being proclaimed casually or with sincerity.

Were they confounded, because they committed abomination? Nay rather, they were not confounded with confusion, and they did not know how to blush. This is to be read Erōtēmatikōs [as a question], so that the sense is: 'Did they blush in their crimes, did they understand the abominations which they wrought?' 'By no means; but they burst out into such madness that they neither desired to amend their vices through confusion nor to confess their crimes in hope of pardon'.

Therefore they shall fall among those who collapse; in the time of their visitation they shall collapse, says the Lord. These are the rewards of those who did not know how to blush: that those whose dignity was loftier than the peoples should be mingled in the ruins of the people. For from the least to the greatest all are devoted to avarice, and from the prophet to the priest all practice falsehood; and the time of visitation is the approaching captivity.

Gathering I will gather them, says the Lord; there is no grape on the vines and there are no figs on the fig tree; the leaf has fallen, and I have given them things that have passed by. What the time of visitation is, in which the transgressors shall collapse, he teaches more plainly, saying: 'Gathering I will gather them' — no doubt in Jerusalem —, 'so that they may be besieged by the Chaldeans for a long time and endure the evils of famine. When,' he says, 'the seasons pass, and autumn follows summer, and in winter the leaves of the trees fall, you will see everything from afar and from them you will take no food. There is no indeed grape on the vines for you, who do not take the fruit of the vines, and there are no figs on the fig tree for the besieged people, who sees the fruits of its own trees plundered by the enemy. The leaves,' he says, 'will fall when summer and autumn are past. For I have given them things which they would see pass by, so that with the greater grief they would lose the abundance of all things, which they were not permitted to touch'.

Why do we sit still? Come together, and let us enter the fortified city — or the fortified cities — and let us be silent there — or let us be cast out there —, for our Lord has cast us off — or has made us silent — and has given us water of gall to drink; for we have sinned against the Lord. We waited for peace, and there was no good, for a time of healing, and behold, dread. The voice of the people is brought in, answering and confessing its vices and exhorting one another to enter the walled cities, or the one city Jerusalem; for the rest had already been taken. 'And let us be silent', he says, 'there, for our Lord has made us silent — for we have no confidence to pray —, or let us be cast away there or let us be cast out like dung. He himself has made us drink waters of gall, because we turned God, who is sweet, into bitterness. And the cause why we should drink such waters is plain: for we have sinned against the Lord and we waited for peace, we who had done no good work and thought that the time of remedy was at hand for us, when all things were filled with dread and terror'. A change of persons, especially in the prophets, makes the understanding difficult; if these are restored to their own places and causes and times, the things which seemed obscure will become plain.

From Dan was heard the snorting of his horses, at the sound of the neighings of his fighters — or of his cavalry — the whole land was shaken; and they came and devoured — or and they will come and will devour — the land and its fullness, the city and its inhabitants. So the people did not say, as the Seventy translated above: let us enter the fortified cities, but: the fortified city, so as to signify Jerusalem. And indeed he now also adds: the city and its inhabitants. Nebuchadnezzar is described coming with his army from Dan, through Phoenicia, at which place the river Jordan rises; and what the Seventy give as things to come, the Hebrew, in accordance with the truth of the event, records as already done.

For behold, I will send among you serpents, basilisks — or most wicked or, as the Seventy translated, deadly —, for which there is no charm; and they shall bite you, says the Lord, incurably, with the pain of your failing heart. Who those are who come from Dan, and whose snorting was heard, and who reduced the whole land to a wilderness, the same prophetic word shows under another figure, calling them 'serpents', 'most wicked' or 'deadly', and, as Aquila translated, 'basilisks', which are called in Hebrew 'sapphonim'; for which I do not understand what his second edition meant by saying 'watchmen', unless perhaps because of the similarity of the word. For which there is no, he says, charm. For in vain do they pour out prayers to God against the ancient serpent, the twisting snake, who have scorned the commandments of God. Let us use this passage against those who, scorning the sayings of the Savior, are handed over to the adverse powers.

However you should know that the evil of envy is harder to be cured than other faults, for I should almost say that a man whom it has once tainted with the mischief of its poison is without a remedy. For it is the plague of which it is figuratively said by the prophet: "Behold I will send among you serpents, basilisks, against which there is no charm: and they shall bite you." Rightly then are the stings of envy compared by the prophet to the deadly poison of basilisks, as by it the first author of all poisons and their chief perished and died. For he slew himself before him of whom he was envious, and destroyed himself before that he poured forth the poison of death against man: for "by the envy of the devil death entered into the world: they therefore who are on his side follow him." For just as he who was the first to be corrupted by the plague of that evil, admitted no remedy of penitence, nor any healing plaster, so those also who have given themselves up to be smitten by the same pricks, exclude all the aid of the sacred charmer, because as they are tormented not by the faults but by the prosperity of those of whom they are jealous, they are ashamed to display the real truth and look out for some external unnecessary and trifling causes of offence: and of these, because they are altogether false, vain is the hope of cure, while the deadly poison which they will not produce is lurking in their veins. Of which the wisest of men has fitly said: "If a serpent bite without hissing, there is no supply for the charmer." For those are silent bites, to which alone the medicine of the wise is no succour. For that evil is so far incurable that it is made worse by attentions, it is increased by services, is irritated by presents, because as the same Solomon says: "envy endures nothing." For just in proportion as another has made progress in humble submission or in the virtue of patience or in the merit of munificence, so is a man excited by worse pricks of envy, because he desires nothing less than the ruin or death of the man whom he envies. Lastly no submission on the part of their harmless brother could soften the envy of the eleven patriarchs, so that Scripture relates of them: "But his brothers envied him because his father loved him, and they could not speak peaceably unto him" until their jealousy, which would not listen to any entreaties on the part of their obedient and submissive brother, desired his death, and would scarcely be satisfied with the sin of selling a brother. It is plain then thatenvy is worse than all faults, and harder to get rid of, as it is inflamed by those remedies by which the others are destroyed. For, for example, a man who is grieved by a loss that has been caused to him, is healed by a liberal compensation: one who is sore owing to a wrong done to him, is appeased by humble satisfaction being made. What can you do with one who is the more offended by the very fact that he sees you humbler and kinder, who is not aroused to anger by any greed which can be appeased by a bribe; or by any injurious attack or love of vengeance, which is overcome by obsequious services; but is only irritated by another's success and happiness? But who is there who in order to satisfy one who envies him, would wish to fall from his good fortune, or to lose his prosperity or to be involved in some calamity? Wherefore we must constantly implore the divine aid, to which nothing is impossible, in order that the serpent may not by a single bite of this evil destroy whatever is flourishing in us, and animated as it were by the life and quickening power of the Holy Ghost. For the other poisons of serpents, i.e., carnal sins and faults, in which human frailty is easily entangled and from which it is as easily purified, show some traces of their wounds in the flesh, whereby although the earthly body is most dangerously inflamed, yet if any charmer well skilled in divine incantations applies a cure and antidote or the remedy of words of salvation, the poisonous evil does not reach to the everlasting death of the soul. But the poison of envy as if emitted by the basilisk, destroys the very life of religion and faith, even before the wound is perceived in the body. For he does not raise himself up against men, but, in his blasphemy, against God, who carps at nothing in his brother except his felicity, and so blames no fault of man, but simply the judgment of God. This then is that "root of bitterness springing up" which raises itself to heaven and tends to reproaching the very Author Who bestows good things on man. Nor shall anyone be disturbed because God threatens to send "serpents, basilisks," to bite those by whose crimes He is offended. For although it is certain that God cannot be the author of envy, yet it is fair and worthy of the divine judgment that, while good gifts are bestowed on the humble and refused to the proud and reprobate, those who, as the Apostle says, deserve to be given over "to a reprobate mind," should be smitten and consumed by envy sent as it were by Him, according to this passage: "They have provoked me to jealousy by them that are no gods: and I will provoke them to jealousy by them that are no nation."

My pain is above pain, within me my heart is mourning. For this, as we said above, the Seventy joined what is said to the preceding sentence, so as to put: and they shall bite you, says the Lord, incurably, with the pain of your failing heart. But in the Hebrew there is not so much 'pain', which in Greek is called odynē, as meidiama, which we can translate as the 'grimace' of a mouth contracted by pain and having the likeness of a smile. And these things are to be read Emphatikōs [emphatically] as from the person of God, lamenting the overthrow of Jerusalem and not bearing her miseries.
Behold the voice of the crying of the daughter of my people from a land far off! He describes the weeping and wailing of the city of Jerusalem when the enemy had entered.

Is the Lord not in Zion, or is her king not in her? Either the Lord himself is the king, or else 'Lord' refers to the Father, 'king' to the Son, according to that which is written under the name of Solomon: O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the son of the king. But why the voice of crying is in Jerusalem and the crying itself comes from a land far off, the cause is manifest: because the Lord is not in her and her king has withdrawn from her.

Why then have they provoked me to anger with their graven images and with foreign vanities? 'But the Lord has withdrawn from them,' he says, 'because they provoked me, who was their Lord and king, to anger by the worship of idols'.

The harvest is past, the summer is ended; and we are not saved. Again the people speaks, which was shut up in Jerusalem by a long siege, saying that the seasons have changed and the circle of the year has rolled round, and all their hope has been made void and has passed away.

Over the breaking of the daughter of my people I am broken and saddened, astonishment has taken hold of me. God answers that in the affliction of Jerusalem he himself appears afflicted, and, after the likeness of a man, he is broken by astonishment.

Let no one, then, run down the law, as if, on account of the penalty, it were not beautiful and good. Shouldn't he who drives away bodily disease appear as a benefactor? Shouldn't he who attempts to deliver the soul from iniquity even more appear as a friend since the soul is a more precious thing than the body? Besides, for the sake of bodily health we submit to incisions, cauterization and medicinal draughts. He who administers them is called savior and healer. He is called this even though he amputates parts, but he works not from a grudge or ill will toward the patient. He instead acts according to the principles that the art prescribes so that the sound parts may not perish along with them. No one accuses the physician's art of wickedness. In the same way, shouldn't we submit, for the soul's sake, to either banishment, or punishment or bonds, as long as from unrighteousness we shall obtain righteousness?

And just as in the one case we put up with operations and cauterisings and the taking of bitter drugs for the treatment of the body, so also in this case we must receive the cutting effects of words of rebuke and the bitter drugs of blame for the cure of the soul. This is what the prophetic word says by way of rebuke to those who have not received correction: “Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why has not the healing of the daughter of my people gone up?”

In such a state of things as this, “Shall they fall and not arise? Shall he turn away and not return?” Why did the virgin turn shamefully away, though she had heard Christ her bridegroom saying through the mouth of Jeremiah, “And I said, after she had done all these things (committed all these fornications, LXX.), turn thou unto me, but she returned not?” “Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? Why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?” You might indeed find many remedies for evil in Scripture, many medicines to save from destruction and lead to health; the mysteries of death and resurrection, the sentences of terrible judgment and everlasting punishment; the doctrines of repentance and of remission of sins; all the countless illustrations of conversion, the piece of money, the sheep, the son who wasted his substance with harlots, who was lost and was found, who was dead and alive again. Let us not use these remedies for ill; by these means let us heal our soul.

Is there no resin in Gilead, or is there no physician there? Why then has the scar of the daughter of my people not closed over? Not only in the present passage, but also in many other testimonies of the Scriptures we find the resin of Gilead put for repentance and medicine; and we find that God now wonders why the wounds of Jerusalem have by no means been healed and the scars have not yet drawn over the skin, because there are no prophets or priests by whose medicine they ought to be healed.
9: Now is the time to quote the words of the prophet and to say, “Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people.” Though they are wrapped in profound silence and lie stunned by their misfortune, robbed of all sense of feeling by the fatal blow, I at all events must not let such a fall go unlamented. If, to Jeremiah, it seemed that those whose bodies had been wounded in war, were worthy of innumerable lamentations, what shall be said of such a disaster of souls? “My slain men,” it is said, “are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle.” But I am bewailing the sting of the real death, the grievousness of sin and the fiery darts of the wicked one, which have savagely set on fire souls as well as bodies.

What should we do? Let us allow a spring of tears to flow every day, day and night. Let us, too, say with the weeping Jeremiah, the great prophet, "Who will give some water to my head, and a spring of tears to my eyes? I would weep for my sins day and night." Let us first of all confess our sins before this.… which is full of terror and trembling tears. Let us invoke the goodness and mercy of our God, while we are in this exile of tears, before death overtakes us.

Let us collect ourselves, I exhort you. There are daily wars, submersions of towns, innumerable destructions all around us, and on every side the wrath of God is enclosing us as in a net. As though we were well-pleasing to him, we are secure. We all make our hands ready for unjust gains and not for helping others. We are all ready to plunder, but no one is ready to protect. Each one of us has much anxiety over how he may add to his wealth. No one has anxiety over how he may save his own soul. One fear possesses all, that we should not become poor. No one is in anguish and trembling out of fear that we should fall into hell. These things call for lamentation, these call for accusation, for eternal damnation. I do not wish to speak of these things, but I am constrained by my grief. Forgive me. I am forced by sorrow to utter many things, even those that I do not wish to say. I see that our wound is grievous, that our calamity is beyond comfort, that woes have overtaken us that exceed the consolation. We are undone. "O that my head were waters and mine eyes a fountain of tears," that I might lament. Let us weep, beloved, let us groan.
ON THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS 23:8-9

Who will give water to my head, and to my eyes a fountain of tears? And I will weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people. 'If I,' he says, 'were turned wholly into weeping, and there were not drops of tears at all but the abundance of a river, still I could not worthily weep for the slain of the daughter of my people. For so great are the evils that by their greatness they surpass all grief over them'. And this can be understood as much from the person of the prophet as from that of the Lord.

You exclaim, "How fitting it was for Jeremiah, with the chorus of the prophets and all the saints, to cry out, 'Who will give water to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes,' that he might bewail the sins of the foolish people, because the church of Christ expelled the teachers of the Pelagian error." If you wish to weep wholesomely, weep for this, that you are involved in that error, and let your tears wash you clean of the new plague. Are you ignorant, or have you forgotten or do you wish not to know that the holy, the one, the Catholic church was also signified by the word Paradise?

Isaac: Not every kind of shedding of tears is produced by one feeling or one virtue. For in one way does that weeping originate which is caused by the pricks of our sins smiting our heart, of which we read: "I have laboured in my groanings, every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears." And again: "Let tears run down like a torrent day and night: give thyself no rest, and let not the apple of thine eye cease." In another, that which arises from the contemplation of eternal good things and the desire of that future glory, owing to which even richer well-springs of tears burst forth from uncontrollable delights and boundless exultation, while our soul is athirst for the mighty Living God, saying, "When shall I come and appear before the presence of God? My tears have been my meat day and night," declaring with daily crying and lamentation: "Woe is me that my sojourning is prolonged;" and: "Too long hath my soul been a sojourner." In another way do the tears flow forth, which without any conscience of deadly sin, yet still proceed from the fear of hell and the recollection of It hat terrible judgment, with the terror of which the prophet was smitten and prayed to God, saying: "Enter not into judgment with Thy servant, for in Thy sight shall no man living be justified." There is too another kind of tears, which are caused not by knowledge of one's self but by the hardness and sins of others; whereby Samuel is described as having wept for Saul, and both the Lord in the gospel and Jeremiah in former days for the city of Jerusalem, the latter thus saying: "Oh, that my head were water and mine eyes a fountain of tears! And I will weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people." Or also such as were those tears of which we hear in the hundred and first Psalm: "For I have eaten ashes for my bread, and mingled my cup with weeping." And these were certainty not caused by the same feeling as those which arise in the sixth Psalm from the person of the penitent, but were due to the anxieties of this life and its distresses and losses, by which the righteous who are living in this world are oppressed. And this is clearly shown not only by the words of the Psalm itself, but also by its title, which runs as follows in the character of that poor person of whom it is said in the gospel that "blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven:" "A prayer of the poor when he was in distress and poured forth his prayer to God."
The First Conference of Abbot Isaac, Chapter 29

The unrighteous man then, in every respect corrupts his body; stealing, committing adultery, cursing, being drunken, and doing such like things. Even as Jeremiah, the prophet, convicts Israel of these things, crying out and saying, ‘Oh, that I had a lodge far off in the wilderness! then would I leave my people and depart from them: for they are all adulterers, an assembly of oppressors, who draw out their tongue as a bow; lying and not truth has prevailed upon the earth, and they proceed from iniquities to iniquities; but Me they have not known.’ Thus, for wickedness and falsehood, and for deeds, in which they [proceed] from iniquity to iniquity, he reproves their practices; but, because they knew not the Lord, and were faithless, he charges them with unrighteousness.

For they are all adulterers, an assembly of transgressors, and they have stretched out their tongue like a bow of falsehood and not of truth; they have grown strong in the land, for they have gone forth from evil to evil, and they have not known me, says the Lord. Sinners pass from evil to evil when they exchange idol for idol and go over from sins to sins, or at any rate pass from the evil of the siege to captivity. And of the saints indeed it is said: they shall go from strength to strength, but of sinners: they have gone forth from evil to evil. And the cause of all their miseries is that they did not know the Lord, and that it is an assembly of men transgressing and arming their tongue like a stretched bow for blasphemy; and they have grown strong in the land, so that they deserve to hear: earth you are and into earth you shall go.

Who will give me in the wilderness a lodging place of wayfarers? And I will forsake my people and withdraw from them. LXX: who would give me in the wilderness a last dwelling, that I may leave my people and withdraw from them? 'It is better,' he says, 'to dwell in the farthest wilderness than to abide among such great crimes of men'. Hence the Savior also said in the Gospel: how long shall I bear with you? And in another place it is written: at that time he who understands shall sit and be silent, for it is a most evil time.

They were fabricating deceit, engaging in blackmail, leveling false accusations against neighbors. For this is what he says, "Deceit, not faith, prevails over the land, for they proceed from evil to evil." Because of this he exposes their evil, which never changes as they move "from evil to evil," immediately adding the reason they neglect the divine law: because "they do not know me, says the Lord."

Let each one guard himself from his neighbor, and let him not have confidence in any brother of his, for every brother supplants with supplanting, and every friend walks deceitfully, and a man will mock his brother, and they will not speak the truth; for their tongue has learned to speak falsehood — or for they have taught their tongue to speak falsehood —. They have labored to act wickedly — or they have acted wickedly and have not ceased, so as to be converted —. Your dwelling is in the midst of deceit; in deceit — or usury upon usury and deceit in deceit; — they have refused — or they would not — to know me, says the Lord. This passage is to be used in a time of persecution and distress, when faith is either rare or none, when neither brother nor neighbor is to be trusted and his enemies are those of his household, when, according to the Gospel, the father will hand over the son and the son the father, and two are divided against three and three against two.

And what he adds: they have taught their tongue to speak falsehood or their tongue has learned to speak falsehood, shows that the habit of lying is in a manner turned into nature, and that they act with zeal so as to do wicked things.

What are we to do with such a useful member? From it we pray to God, we confess our sins, we give praise, we sing to God with one voice in harmony, and in our daily lives, we either show mercy when we converse with others, or we give counsel. What are we to do now? Our very tongue offers you service. What are we to do so that we do not sin with our tongue? Especially since it has been said: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue," and again it has been said: "I have seen many fall by the edge of the sword, but not as many as by the tongue." Again it has been said: "The tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. Consider how a great forest is set on fire by a small spark." Again the same Lord said: "They have taught their tongue to speak lies." Oh, they have taught it! For habit causes it to speak lies; even if you do not wish to, it speaks lies. Just as if you turn a wheel once, having pushed it with your hand, it runs because of its shape and roundness and by its own unstable and almost natural course, so too does our tongue; it does not need to be taught to speak lies. For already, once started, it runs by itself to what it can more easily move toward. Sometimes you have something in your heart, and it speaks something else out of habit.

For what sinner defiles himself unwillingly by adulteries and fornication? Who against his will prepares plots against his neighbour? Who is driven by unavoidable necessity to oppress a man by false witness or cheat him by theft, or covet the goods of another or shed his blood? Nay rather, as Scripture says, "Mankind is diligently inclined to wickedness from his youth." For to such an extent are all inflamed by the love of sin and desire to carry out what they like, that they actually look out with watchful care for an opportunity of committing wickedness and are afraid of being too slow to enjoy their lusts, and glory in their shame and the mass of their crimes, as the Apostle says in censure, and seek credit for themselves out of their own confusion, of whom also the prophet Jeremiah maintains that they commit their flagitious crimes not only not unwillingly nor with ease of heart and body, but with laborious efforts to such an extent that they come to toil to carry them out, so that they are prevented even by the hindrance of arduous difficulty from their deadly quest of sin; as he says: "They have laboured to do wickedly."
The Third Conference of Abbot Theonas, Chapter 1

The insincere are to be admonished to learn how heavy is the labor of deception. They endure it with guilt. They are afraid of being found out. They are ever seeking dishonest defenses. They are agitated by fearful suspicions. But there is nothing safer to defend than sincerity, nothing easier to say than truth. For, when obliged to defend its deceit, the heart is wearied with hard labor. For it is written, "The labor of their own lips shall cover them." For what now fills them then covers them, since it then presses down with sharp retribution one whose soul it now elevates with a mild uneasiness. It is said through Jeremiah, "They have taught their tongue to speak lies, and weary themselves to commit iniquity." Said more plainly: "They who might have been friends of truth without labor, labor to sin."
The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part III, Chapter XI

And as for what follows: your dwelling is in the midst of deceit, in deceit, the word is properly directed to the prophet, that he dwells in the midst of a lying people — or, as the Seventy translated: usury upon usury and deceit upon deceit — and that they daily increase their crimes and by no means repent of their former deed, but heap new crimes upon past ones; doing these things, they act with all eagerness so as not to know the Lord, who commanded that these things should not be done.

Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I will melt — or I will test by fire — and try them; for what else shall I do in the face of the daughter of my people? Or for I will act in the face of the wickedness of the daughter of my people. Whenever we are subject to distresses, we receive evils from God and are tested by persecutions, so that whatever adulterated matter is in us may be smelted out by the heat of tribulations and miseries: for the silver of the Lord is tested by fire, proved in the earth, purified sevenfold.

Their tongue is a wounding arrow, it has spoken deceit; with his mouth he speaks peace with his friend and secretly lays snares for him. Shall I not visit upon these things, says the Lord, or on such a nation shall my soul not take vengeance? Every heretic who wounds the hearts of his hearers, of those who do not know what is written: keep your heart with all watchfulness, possesses a wounding arrow and speaks in deceit, and while with his mouth he promises peace to his neighbor, he secretly sets snares.

As for the following verses, in which he says: shall I not visit upon these things, says the Lord, or on such a nation shall my soul not take vengeance? He makes frequent use of them in this prophet, so that, when he has enumerated the evil works one by one, he infers that he does justly what he does.

Upon the mountains I will take up — or take up — weeping and lamentation, and over the beautiful places — or the paths — of the desert a wailing, because they are burned up — or they have failed — because there is no man — or human being — passing through. And they have not heard the voice of the possessor — or of substance —; from the bird of the heaven to the beasts they have migrated and withdrawn. When the Babylonian comes upon them and lays everything waste, the desolation of the province is prophesied: that there is wailing on the mountains, weeping in the desert or in the paths of the wilderness, that all things have failed and been burned up, and there is no one to walk through the land, all having been slain, and nothing has remained that can breathe and live. Hence for 'possessor' the Seventy translated 'of substance', which in Hebrew is called 'macne'; and 'substance' here is not taken for ousia, that is, 'essence', but for 'wealth' and 'riches'. And what he adds: from the bird of the heaven to the beast they have withdrawn and departed, shows this, as we have often said: that all things feel the wrath of God, and not only the birds of the air but also the fish of the water fail. According to tropology, weeping is taken up upon the mountains and lamentation over the beautiful places of the desert when the princes of the Church sin and nothing of the substance of God is found in her, nor is the voice of the Lord who possesses the Church heard through holy and apostolic men, and from the bird of the heaven to the beasts, that is, from those who can ascend on high down to the irrational and all the simpler ones, they have withdrawn from the assembly of God.

And I will give Jerusalem into heaps of sand — or into exile — and into lairs of dragons, and the cities of Judah I will give into desolation, because there is no inhabitant. When churchmen and all the teachers have failed, then Jerusalem is given into exile or into heaps of sand, so that heretical speech prevails in her and she is made a lair of dragons and her cities are reduced to a wilderness, and there is in her no dwelling of the divine word and of him who says: I will dwell and walk among them, and I will be their God.

Who is the wise man who may understand this, and to whom the word of the mouth of the Lord may come, and who may declare it: why the land has perished and is burned up like a desert, because there is none who passes through? And the Lord said: Because they have forsaken my law, which I gave them, and have not heard my voice and have not walked in it, and have gone after the perversity of their heart and after the Baals, whom they learned from their fathers. The prophet asks whether he can find anyone of the wise in Jerusalem, and of those to whom the word of God comes and who can declare the will of the Lord and give the reasons why Judea has been reduced to a wilderness and, all having been slain, no one has remained to pass through it.

And he brings in the Lord answering and giving the reasons: because they had forsaken his law, which he had given them, and had not heard his voice nor done what had been commanded, but had gone after the perversity of their heart. Therefore we must trust not in our own will but in the Lord; for the heart in men is perverse, and from our heart come forth the worst thoughts. And after the Baals, he says, they have gone, whom they learned from their fathers. Bahal is the idol of the Sidonians and is of the singular number, but Bahalim of the plural number. Therefore neither the error of parents nor that of ancestors is to be followed, but the authority of the Scriptures and the command of God who teaches.

I was then about sixteen years of age. I did not know the true God. I was taken as a captive to Ireland with many thousands of people, and deservedly so, because we had turned away from God and did not keep his commandments and did not obey our priests, who used to remind us of our salvation. The Lord brought over us the wrath of his anger and scattered us among many nations, even unto the utmost part of the earth, where now my insignificance is placed among strangers.

Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will feed them, this people, with wormwood — or with distresses — and I will give them water of gall for drink, and I will scatter them among the nations which neither they nor their fathers have known, and I will send the sword after them until they are consumed. This can be prophesied both of the near time, when they were taken captive by the Chaldeans, and properly of this present time, when they have been scattered among the nations which neither they nor their fathers had known, and, divided through the whole world, have been fed with wormwood, or with necessities and distresses. And they have received water of gall for drink, which either signifies the greatness of their evils and the everlasting yoke of captivity, or else means that, through ignorance of the law of God, they are going to receive Antichrist instead of Christ. And the sword is sent after them, so that they are consumed even to destruction, or else a sword which divides them and does not allow them to be of one accord in evil, so that they perish in this, that they are evil.

I was then about sixteen years of age. I did not know the true God. I was taken as a captive to Ireland with many thousands of people, and deservedly so, because we had turned away from God and did not keep his commandments and did not obey our priests, who used to remind us of our salvation. The Lord brought over us the wrath of his anger and scattered us among many nations, even unto the utmost part of the earth, where now my insignificance is placed among strangers.

It is our part too henceforth to mourn, or rather we have need to say this every day. We profit nothing by our prayers, nothing by our advice and exhortation, it remaineth therefore that we weep. Thus did Christ; after having many times exhorted those in Jerusalem, when they profited nothing, He wept at their hardness. This also do the Prophets, and this let us do now. Henceforth is the season for mourning and tears and wailing; it is seasonable for us also to say now, "Call for the mourning women, and send for the cunning women, that they may cry aloud" (Jer. ix. 17); perhaps thus we shall be able to cast out the malady of those who build splendid houses, of those who surround themselves with lands gotten by rapine.
Homily on the Gospel of John 64

Thus says the Lord of hosts: Consider — or understand — and call the mourning women, and let them come, and send to those who are wise, and let them hasten — or let them speak —, let them make haste and take up a lamentation over us — or over you — and let our eyes — or your — bring down tears and our eyelids — or your — flow with waters, for a voice of lamentation has been heard from Zion or in Zion. On account of the coming captivity and overthrow of Jerusalem he bids the mourning women be called, who in times of grief are accustomed, with a tearful voice and beating their arms with their hands, to provoke the people to tears; for this custom remains to this day in Judea, that women with hair loosened and breasts bared, with a measured chant, stir everyone to weeping. And God joins himself to them with the feeling of one who suffers with them, or the prophet does, so as to say that whatever the people endures, he himself endures and feels. But as for what he adds: for a voice of lamentation has been heard from Zion, what this voice is follows at once.

How are we laid waste and confounded exceedingly? Because we have forsaken the land, for our tents have been thrown down — or we have cast away —. This is the voice of those lamenting Zion: how are we laid waste and confounded exceedingly? And at once they answer themselves and set out the causes of the devastation, saying: because we have forsaken the land through our own fault and sin, and our tents have been thrown down, which they once possessed as if passing by. Let the crowds of those who once believed say this too in persecution: that they have been laid waste and confounded for this reason, because they have forsaken the land of the Lord and deserted their tents.

Hear therefore, O women, the word of the Lord, and let your ear take up the speech of his mouth, and teach your daughters lamentation, and each woman her neighbor wailing, for death has come up through our windows, it has entered our houses, to destroy the little ones from outside, the young men from the streets! In the preceding section he had said: call the mourning women, and let them come, and send to those who are wise, and let them hasten; now he speaks as if to women present, to the condemnation of the priests and teachers and of all the men, so that, since these cease from teaching, the women may hear the word of the Lord and take up the words of his mouth and teach their daughters and their neighbors wailing and the causes of tears, for death, he says, has come up through our windows, it has entered our houses. Although this can also be understood spiritually, in that the death of sins enters through all the senses to the destruction of the soul, yet it can also be understood of the onslaught of the Babylonians: that so great is their strength and speed in fighting that they do not wait to unbar the doors, but climb up through the windows and roofs to lay waste the houses of Jerusalem. And the little ones perish who are outside and go out of Jerusalem, and the young men, to whom John also writes, who do not enter by the strait and narrow way that leads to life, but walk through the streets, of which it is written: how broad and spacious is the way that leads to death!

One window is one sense: through this the bridegroom looks. Another window is another sense: and through this too the bridegroom carefully gazes. For through what senses does the word of God not look? But what it is to look through the windows, and how the bridegroom gazes through them, the following example will teach. Where the bridegroom does not look, there death is found climbing up, as we read in Jeremiah: Behold, death has climbed up through your windows. When you have looked upon a woman to lust after her, already death has climbed up through your windows.
HOMILIES ON THE SONG OF SONGS, HOMILY 2

But we may understand the windows to be the bodily senses, through which either death or life enters into the soul; for so does it signify when the prophet Jeremiah speaks concerning sinners, saying: "Death has climbed up through your windows." How does death climb up through the windows? If the eyes of a sinner should look upon a woman, and he should commit adultery with her in his heart, thus death has entered into the soul through the windows of the eyes.
COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 3

Amid so many passions of this body of ours, amid so many enticements of this world, who indeed can keep his footstep safe and undefiled? The eye looks back and leads the mind's perception astray, the ear hears and turns one's attention away, a whiff of fragrance hinders thought, a kiss of the mouth introduces guilt, a touch kindles the fire of passion. "Death has entered in through the window," the prophet said. Your eye is your window. If you look at a woman to lust after her, death has entered in; if you listen to the harlot's words, death has entered in; if licentiousness takes hold of your senses, death has gone in.

The prophet says, "Death is come up through the windows." Surely he does not mean actual windows—otherwise we could shut our windows and never die. But the bodily senses—sight, hearing, and so on—are windows to us and death enters us through them if we sin with them.

These are the windows of which Jeremiah also says: Death has entered through our windows; for the enemies desire to enter through all our senses, and to take the city of a good conscience, and to run about through our fortifications, and to destroy the houses which we have built for ourselves by good works. And they do all things entering through the windows like a thief, for they do not enter openly, that they may shoot in the dark at the upright of heart.

For Jeremiah says: 'Death has entered through your windows.' Now we have five windows: that is, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. If therefore I have looked at a woman to lust after her, I have already committed adultery with her in my heart; and death has entered through my window, that is, through sight. If the lyre or the organ or the reed-pipe as it were dissolves me, death has entered through my hearing. But if I touch something soft, and am unstrung by the softness of the body, death has entered through my touch, and the rest likewise.

By "windows" he refers to the error of their thinking: through them they gave entrance to the error and the blow inflicted by it. You would not be wide of the mark to call the body's senses "windows"—sight, taste, smell, hearing and touch. Both life and death can enter through these. For example, the person who looks with restraint reaps life, while the one looking immoderately gains death. The truthful tongue procures salvation for the soul, while the lying one brings about ruin; and likewise with the rest, as you can easily learn.

Speak: Thus says the Lord: And the carcass of man shall fall — or the corpses of men — like dung upon the face of the region — or of the field — and like hay behind the back of the reaper, and there is none who gathers. The Hebrew word that is written with three letters, 'daleth, beth, res' — for it has no vowels in the middle —, if it is read, according to the context and the judgment of the reader, as 'dabar', means 'word'; if as 'deber', 'death'; if as 'dabber', 'speak'. Hence the Seventy and Theodotion joined it to the previous section, so as to say: to destroy the little ones from outside, the young men from the streets, by death. But Aquila and Symmachus translated lalēson, 'speak', so that God commands the prophet to speak what follows: thus says the Lord and the rest. And the sense is: when death has come up through our windows and has entered the houses of Jerusalem, and the little ones and the young men have perished from outside and from the streets, then their carcass, or the corpses of the dead, will be as it were for a dunghill upon the face of the earth and like stubble that is left behind the back of the reapers and, being useless, is not gathered. By these things he wishes to show that there will be so great a slaughter in Jerusalem and around the city that there will be no one to bury those who fall.

Let us therefore, brethren, be of humble mind, laying aside all haughtiness, and pride, and foolishness, and angry feelings; and let us act according to that which is written (for the Holy Spirit saith, "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, neither let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him that glorieth glory in the Lord, in diligently seeking Him, and doing judgment and righteousness"), being especially mindful of the words of the Lord Jesus which He spake, teaching us meekness and long-suffering. For thus He spoke: "Be ye merciful, that ye may obtain mercy; forgive, that it may be forgiven to you; as ye do, so shall it be done unto you; as ye judge, so shall ye be judged; as ye are kind, so shall kindness be shown to you; with what measure ye mete, with the same it shall be measured to you." By this precept and by these rules let us establish ourselves, that we walk with all humility in obedience to His holy words. For the holy word saith, "On whom shall I look, but on him that is meek and peaceable, and that trembleth at My words?"
Clement's First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 13

Let us therefore, brethren, be of humble mind, laying aside all haughtiness, and pride, and foolishness, and angry feelings; and let us act according to that which is written (for the Holy Spirit saith, "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, neither let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him that glorieth glory in the Lord, in diligently seeking Him, and doing judgment and righteousness"), being especially mindful of the words of the Lord Jesus which He spake, teaching us meekness and long-suffering. For thus He spoke: "Be ye merciful, that ye may obtain mercy; forgive, that it may be forgiven to you; as ye do, so shall it be done unto you; as ye judge, so shall ye be judged; as ye are kind, so shall kindness be shown to you; with what measure ye mete, with the same it shall be measured to you."

What is the philosophy that the apostle bids us shun? This, then, "the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God." "The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain." Let no one therefore glory on account of pre-eminence in human thought. For it is written well in Jeremiah, "Let not the wise person glory in his wisdom, and let not the mighty person glory in his might, and let not the rich person glory in his riches. But let him that glories glory in this, that he understands and knows that I am the Lord, that executes mercy and judgment and righteousness on the earth: for in these things is my delight, say the Lord."

The only true salvation is if Christ saves me, for then I will be saved. The horse is a false hope for deliverance. False also are all others besides God for salvation. On account of this I might say to him, "Save me, Lord, and I will be saved," and I say this if I can say also the next words after every boast that is renounced. For you are my boast or when I fulfill the commandment that says, "Let not the wise person boast in his wisdom, and let not the strong person boast in his strength, or the rich person in his riches; let him who boasts boast in this, to understand and know that I am Lord." Blessed is one who has renounced every boast here below, such as in so-called noble birth and in beauty and in corporeal things, in riches, in vainglory, since he is content with one boast, that he may say, For you are my boast.

"Let not the wise person glory in his wisdom or the strong person in his strength," for that which is worth boasting about is not ours but is the gift of God. The wisdom is from him, and the strength is from him and so with the rest.
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 10:19

We must trust in God only, and in him we must glory. In Jeremiah: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the strong man glory in his strength, nor let the rich man glory in his riches. But let him that glories glory in this, that he understands and knows that I am the Lord, who does mercy, and judgment, and righteousness upon the earth, because in them is my pleasure, says the Lord."
Treatise XII. Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews 3:10

No sensible person, then, will be proud of his wisdom or of possessing the other goods I have mentioned but will follow the excellent advice of blessed Anna and of the prophet Jeremiah: "Let not the wise person glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong person glory in his strength, and let not the rich person glory in his riches." But what is true glory, and what makes a person great? "In this," says the prophet, "let him that glories, glory that he understands and knows that I am the Lord." This constitutes the highest dignity of humankind, this is his glory and greatness. Truly it is to know what is great and to cleave to it, and to seek after glory from the Lord of glory.

Thus says the Lord: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong man glory in his strength, and let not the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this: to know — or to understand — and to know me, that I am the Lord, who do mercy and judgment and righteousness on the earth! For these things please me — or for in these is my will —, says the Lord. All the pride of men is taken away, while their wisdom and strength and wealth are reckoned as nothing, and this is the only glorying: that one should know and understand that he himself is the Lord, who does mercy and judgment and righteousness upon the earth; that all things are governed by the providence and righteousness of God, and that the things which seem to us to have no reason are full of righteousness and reason. For these things alone please God, and in these is his will. Where then are those who say that man is governed by his own will, and that the power of free will was so given that the mercy and righteousness of God were taken away? Hence also the Apostle, taking up this testimony, sets down the example: let him who glories, glory in the Lord.

Moreover, the experience of the Vandals was not dissimilar: when our people went against them in Spain and had as much confidence in a complete victory as they had recently against the Goths, the same overweening pride engulfed them in the same disastrous ruin. Then the words of the prophet were fulfilled for our army: "The Lord shall reject thy confidence and thou shalt not prosper in it."

For we trusted in our own wisdom and strength against the command of the Lord, who said: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither the mighty man in his might, but let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the Lord."

So we have not been conquered undeservedly, for the enemy sought better aid than we did. While we prided ourselves on arms and auxiliaries, on the side of the enemy the Book of the Divine Law opposed us. To its help most of all the fear and terror of the Vandals then resorted, to oppose to us the Divine Word and to open up to those who came against them in rivalry the writings of the Sacred Book which may be called the very voice of God.
On the Government of God, Book 7, Chapter 11

"Each one looking not to his own interests but to those of others," "that one may not glory in his prudence," for the virtue of the humble is not to boast of their knowledge, since it is common to all. In repressing the mind's audacity, it is helpful not to despise others or to assume a special knowledge or holiness ourselves.

If you glory in wisdom, by that very fact you lose wisdom. "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong man glory in his strength." And the cause of this is given in Ezekiel, where it is said: "You, full of wisdom and beauty, were in the delights of the paradise of God: you lost your wisdom on account of your beauty."

For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God.  For it is written, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and will bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent.  Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?  For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.  For the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom:  But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness;  But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God.  Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men.  For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called:  But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;  And base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are:  That no flesh should glory in his presence.  But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption:  That, according as it is written, He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord. [Jeremiah 9:24]

Now I Paul myself beseech you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, who in presence am base among you, but being absent am bold toward you:  But I beseech you, that I may not be bold when I am present with that confidence, wherewith I think to be bold against some, which think of us as if we walked according to the flesh.  For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war after the flesh:  (For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)  Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ;  And having in a readiness to revenge all disobedience, when your obedience is fulfilled.  Do ye look on things after the outward appearance? If any man trust to himself that he is Christ's, let him of himself think this again, that, as he is Christ's, even so are we Christ's.  For though I should boast somewhat more of our authority, which the Lord hath given us for edification, and not for your destruction, I should not be ashamed:  That I may not seem as if I would terrify you by letters.  For his letters, say they, are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible.  Let such an one think this, that, such as we are in word by letters when we are absent, such will we be also in deed when we are present.  For we dare not make ourselves of the number, or compare ourselves with some that commend themselves: but they measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves among themselves, are not wise.  But we will not boast of things without our measure, but according to the measure of the rule which God hath distributed to us, a measure to reach even unto you.  For we stretch not ourselves beyond our measure, as though we reached not unto you: for we are come as far as to you also in preaching the gospel of Christ:  Not boasting of things without our measure, that is, of other men's labours; but having hope, when your faith is increased, that we shall be enlarged by you according to our rule abundantly,  To preach the gospel in the regions beyond you, and not to boast in another man's line of things made ready to our hand.  But he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord. [Jeremiah 9:24] For not he that commendeth himself is approved, but whom the Lord commendeth.

So that, as it is written: Let him who glories, glory in the Lord. This is written in the prophet Jeremiah (Jer. 9:24). Worthy is what the prophet says, that we should glory in God; because he who glories in the Lord will not be able to be confounded; for his works and his magnificence appear in the things he has done. And therefore, he says, let them be confounded in their idols, which do not send rain and did not make heaven and earth: in like manner also those who glory in men, whom they surely know to be of no power; wherefore Scripture also says: Vain is hope in man (Jer. 17:5).

Forasmuch then as our turning away from God is our own act, and this is evil will; but our turning to God is not possible, except He rouses and helps us, and this is good will,—what have we that we have not received? But if we received, why do we glory as if we had not received? Therefore, as "he that glorieth must glory in the Lord," it comes from His mercy, not their merit, that God wills to impart this to some, but from His truth that He wills not to impart it to others. For to sinners punishment is justly due.
ON THE MERITS AND FORGIVENESS OF SINS, AND ON THE BAPTISM OF INFANTS 2:31

Let us joyfully celebrate the coming of our salvation and redemption. Let us celebrate the festal day on which the great and eternal day came from the great and eternal day into this our very short temporal day. He has been made for us righteousness, sanctification, and redemption: so that, as it is written, He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.

For as many of this race as are delivered by God's grace are certainly delivered from the condemnation in which they are already held bound. Whence, even if none should be delivered, no one could justly blame the judgment of God. That, therefore, in comparison of those that perish few, but in their absolute number many, are delivered, is effected by grace, is effected freely: thanks must be given, because it is effected, so that no one may be lifted up as of his own deservings, but that every mouth may be stopped, and he that glorieth may glory in the Lord.

Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will visit upon everyone who have the foreskin circumcised, upon Egypt and upon Judah and upon Edom and upon the sons of Ammon and upon Moab and upon all who are shorn about the hair, dwelling in the desert; for all the nations have the foreskin, but all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart. In part, the peoples of many nations, and especially of those that border on Judea and Palestine, are circumcised to this day, and above all the Egyptians and the Edomites, the Ammonites and the Moabites, and the whole region of the Saracens, which dwells in the wilderness and of whom it is said: upon all who are shorn about the hair, dwelling in the desert. Judah, therefore, who is mingled with the nations written above, ought not to glory because he does not have the foreskin but is circumcised by the law of God, since others too do these things who do not keep the commandments of the law and do not know the God of Israel. Nor is circumcision, which was given as a sign, of any profit unless the commandments of the Lord are fulfilled; just as the long hair also signifies a nation, not strength of body and the bravery of fighters. And what follows: all the nations have the foreskin, but all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart, has this sense: whereas, apart from the Egyptians, Edomites, Ammonites and Moabites, and the Ishmaelites dwelling in the wilderness, of whom for the most part a portion is circumcised, all the other nations in the whole world are uncircumcised in the flesh, the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart, not in flesh; and this uncircumcision leads to death, for that one is of the flesh, this of the spirit.

The ancient Scriptures therefore teach the benefit of spiritual circumcision and that bodily circumcision makes no difference. For it is not the Gentiles who are accused of being uncircumcised but the Jews, who were physically circumcised but whose heart was uncircumcised.

But perhaps the novelty of the saying may deter not only the Jews but also some of our brethren. For Paul seems to presume impossible things, in that he introduces "circumcision of the heart." For how can it come about that a member be circumcised which, hidden by the inner organs, lies concealed even from the very sight of men? Let us return, then, to the prophetic utterances, so that, while you pray, these matters about which we inquire may from there become clear. The prophet Ezekiel says: "Every stranger uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh shall not enter into my sanctuary." And likewise elsewhere the prophet, reproaching them no less, says: "all the strangers are uncircumcised in flesh, but the sons of Israel are uncircumcised in heart." It is signified, therefore, that unless one has been circumcised in heart and circumcised in flesh, "he shall not enter into the sanctuary" of God.
10: Hear the word which the Lord has spoken concerning you, house of Israel! Thus says the Lord: Do not learn according to the ways of the nations, and do not be afraid of the signs of heaven, which the nations fear, for the laws of the peoples are vain! He speaks properly against those who venerate the heavenly bodies and suppose that the human race is ruled by those which have been set as signs of years, seasons, months and days, and that earthly things are governed by the causes of heavenly ones. And in saying: the laws or the statutes of the peoples are vain, he shows that all human wisdom is futile and has no usefulness in itself.

For he has cut wood from the forest, the work of the craftsman's hands with the adze; with silver and gold he has adorned it, with nails and hammers he has fastened it, that it may not come apart — or may not be moved —. They are fashioned after the likeness of a palm tree and will not speak; carried, they will be lifted, because they cannot walk. Do not therefore fear them, for they can do neither evil nor good. A description of the idols which the nations venerate. He has cut wood, he says, from the forest — the material of idols, then, is cheap and perishable — the work of the craftsman's hands — since the craftsman is mortal, mortal therefore are those things too which he fashions —; with silver and gold he has adorned it, so that by the gleam of both materials he may deceive the simple. And this error has passed down even to us, so that we think religion lies in riches. With nails and hammers he has fastened it, that it may not come apart or that it may not be moved. How great is the power of idols, which cannot stand by themselves unless they are fastened with nails and hammers? Fashioned after the likeness of a palm tree, they have the beauty of metals and are adorned by the art of painting, but they possess no usefulness that would yield any fruit to the craftsman. And they will not speak — for they have nothing living in them, those of whom it is written: they have a mouth and will not speak; they have ears and will not hear —; carried, they will be lifted. Stronger is he who carries than the things which are carried; nay rather, in him there is sense, in this a shape without sense. Do not therefore fear them, for they can do neither good nor evil. For many of the Gentiles are accustomed to worship some demons so that they may do no harm, and to entreat others so that they may grant benefits; whence also that line of Vergil: a black beast to Winter, a white one to the favoring Zephyrs. Whatever we have said of idols can be referred to all the doctrines which are contrary to the truth. For they too promise mighty things and fashion out of their own heart an image of vain worship; they boast great things, and to deceive all the simple they hold fast the gaze of the unskilled with thoughts golden, as it were, and with speech gleaming with the splendor of silver, and they are raised aloft by their inventors; in them there is no usefulness, and their worship belongs properly to the nations and to those who do not know God.

Therefore we ought to believe that God is good, eternal, perfect, almighty and true, such as we find him in the Law and the Prophets and the rest of the Holy Scriptures, for otherwise there is no God. For he who is God must be good, seeing that fullness of goodness is of the nature of God. God, who made time, cannot be in time. Again, God cannot be imperfect, for a lesser being is plainly imperfect, seeing that it lacks somewhat whereby it could be made equal to a greater. This, then, is the teaching of our faith—that God is not evil, that with God nothing is impossible, that God does not exist in time, that God is beneath no being. If I am in error, let my adversaries prove it.

These tokens so declare the nature of the Son, that by them you may know both that the Father is eternal, and that the Son is not diverse from Him; for the source of generation is He Who is, and as begotten of the Eternal, He is God; coming forth from the Father, He is the Son; from God, He is the Word; He is the radiance of the Father's glory, the expression of His substance, the counterpart of God, the image of His majesty; the Bounty of Him Who is bountiful, the Wisdom of Him Who is wise, the Power of the Mighty One, the Truth of Him Who is true, the Life of the Living One.

There is none like you, O Lord; great are you, and great is your name in might. Who will not fear you, O king of the nations? For yours is the beauty; among all the wise of the nations and in all their kingdoms there is none like you. The wise and the foolish alike shall be proved; the teaching of their vanity is wood; silver wrapped — or drawn out — is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz, the work of the craftsman and of the hand of the coppersmith; blue and purple are their clothing; the work of craftsmen — or of the wise — are all these things. But the Lord is the true God; this is the living God and the everlasting king. At his indignation the earth will be shaken, and the nations will not endure his threatening. These words are not found in the Seventy, but in most copies they have been added from Theodotion's edition, and although according to the letter they seem clear, according to the anagōgēn [the higher, spiritual sense] they hold great difficulty. For none of those gods which are fashioned by heretical art is like the true God. All will fear him who is king of the nations; for the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and from it we advance to love. Yours, he says, is the beauty; in truth there is comeliness, in falsehood ugliness. Although the heretics seem to themselves to be wise according to the wisdom of the world, which is destroyed, yet in all the kingdoms in which they tear the Church apart there is none like you, as the divine word says: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject.

The fear of God arises in us from the consideration of divine power. Whence in Jeremiah: "There is none like unto thee, O Lord; thou art great, and thy name is great in might: who would not fear thee, O king of nations?" He sets forth first the magnitude of divine power, when he says: "There is none like unto thee, O Lord"; whence in the book of Wisdom: "As a drop of morning dew, so is the whole world before thee." Therefore who would not fear thee, unless he be impious and foolish?

The fear of God arises in us from the consideration of divine power. "Who would not fear thee, O king of nations? For thine is the glory: among all the wise men of the nations and in all their kingdoms, who is like unto thee?" Therefore who would not fear thee, unless he be impious and foolish? If a man is impious, he is in need of punishment; if he is foolish, he is in need of understanding.

They are at once wise and foolish; their teaching, according to the quality of their talent, is either cheap and is compared to wood, or is like silver because of the charm of its eloquence; it is brought from Tarshish — either it is a region of India, as Josephus would have it, or else the whole sea is called Tarshish and has a likeness to the sky — and yet it is wrapped in the artifice of words; for if it were laid open, it could not deceive. And gold from Uphaz. Gold is called by seven names among the Hebrews, of which one is called 'ophaz', which we can call 'obryzum' [refined gold], so that it may gleam on the surface of the idols, which within is wood and of cheap material. They are covered with blue and purple, so that by their surface they may deceive the eyes, while they promise themselves the color of the heavens and the heavenly kingdoms; and yet all these things are works of the wise, who are thought wise in the world, but before God are foolish.

But the Lord our God is the true God — all those, therefore, are lies — and he himself is the living God — so those which are fashioned are dead — and the everlasting king — the shadows of the heretics prevail for a time, but in the long run they decay —; at his indignation the earth will be shaken — those who have earthly works and fashion earthly images — and the nations will not endure: by no means the people of the Lord, but the multitude of the nations, which cannot bear God's threatening.

Who would doubt that God has made these things, who spoke through the Prophet, saying: 'Who has measured the waters in the hollow of His hand, and marked off the heavens with a span, enclosed the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance, who has directed the Spirit of the Lord, or who has been his counselor or instructed Him?' (Isaiah 40:12). We also read elsewhere: Because it holds the circuit of the earth and has made the earth as nothing. And Jeremiah says: The gods who have not made the heavens and the earth shall perish from the earth, and from under these heavens. The Lord who made the earth in His power, and established it in His wisdom, and by His understanding stretched out the heavens, and caused a multitude of waters to be in the heaven (Jeremiah 10:11). And he added: Man is made foolish by his knowledge (ibid., 14). For anyone who follows the corruptible things of the world, and from these things believes that they can grasp the truth of divine nature, how can they not be bewitched by the cunning craftiness of disputation?

But if heretics deny that either the heavens or the earth were made by you, O Lord, let them take heed of the abyss into which they are hurling themselves by their own madness. The prophet writes, "Perish the gods that have not made heaven and earth." Shall he then perish, O Arian, who had found and saved that which had perished?

Next, he adduces what indeed is the greatest token of divinity; "of Whom are all things." For this implies also that those others are not gods. For it is said, "Let the gods who made not the heaven and the earth perish." Then he subjoins what is not less than this, "and we unto Him." For when he saith, "of Whom are all things," he means the creation and the bringing of things out of nothing into existence. But when he saith, "and we unto Him," he speaks of the word of faith and mutual appropriation, as also he said before, "but of Him are ye also in Christ Jesus."

Thus therefore you shall say to them: The gods who did not make the heavens and the earth, let them perish from the earth and from those things which are under heaven! These words are to be said to the false gods and to those which have been put together by artifice — for they made neither the heavens nor the earth —, words which the fellow workers of Christ, who are called God's and the Lord's, for the most part frame through the Church's teaching.

In reading what is said in this Psalm of Christ and of the Church, he would find that what is there foretold is fulfilled in the present state of the world. He would see the idols of the nations perishing from off the earth, and he would find that this is predicted by the prophets, as in Jeremiah, "Then shall ye say unto them, The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth shall perish from the earth, and from under heaven;" and again, "O Lord, my strength, and my fortress, and my refuge in the day of affliction, the Gentiles shall come unto Thee from the ends of the earth, and shall say, Surely our fathers have inherited lies, vanity, and things wherein there is no profit. Shall a man make gods unto himself, and they are no gods? Therefore, behold, I will at that time cause them to know, I will cause them to know mine hand and my might; and they shall know that I am the Lord." Hearing these prophecies, and seeing their actual fulfillment, I need not say that he would be affected; for we know by experience how the hearts of believers are confirmed by seeing ancient predictions now receiving their accomplishment.

Ye heard when Jeremiah was being read before the reading of the Apostle, if ye listened; ye saw therein the times in which we now live. He said, “The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth, let them perish from the earth, and from under the heaven.” He said not, The gods that have not made the heavens and earth, let them perish from the heaven and from the earth; because they never were in heaven: but what did he say? “Let them perish from the earth, and from under the heaven.” As if, while the word earth was repeated, the repetition of the word heaven were wanting (because they never were in heaven): he repeateth the earth twice, since it is under heaven. “Let them perish from the earth, and from under the heaven,” from their temples. Consider if this be not now taking place; if in a great measure it hath not already happened: for what, or how much, hath remained? The idols remained rather in the hearts of the pagans, than in the niches of the temples.

The prophet of God, having taken up as it were three excellences of His—His strength, His wisdom, and His understanding—assigns to each of them a work proper to it: to the strength the earth, to the wisdom the inhabited world, and to the understanding the heaven. For listen to the passage as it says: "The Lord who made the earth in His strength, who set upright the inhabited world in His wisdom, and in His understanding stretched out the heaven." And we too, as regards our earth (for it was said to Adam, "Earth you are, and to earth you shall depart"), have need of the strength of God, and apart from the power of God we are not able to accomplish these things, all that is not according to "the mind-set of the flesh." And when "the members that are upon the earth" have been put to death, then there will be what is according to the will of the Spirit, since "by the Spirit the deeds of the flesh," according to the apostle, are put to death. "The Lord," then, "who made the earth in His strength." And if you come also to this earth, if you are able to see what is written in Job, as we found in the more accurate copies, that He set it "upon nothing," you will see that by the strength of God it lies at the very midmost point.

I come also to the inhabited world. I know of a soul that is inhabited, I know of a soul that is desolate. For if it does not have God, if it does not have Christ, who said, "I and my Father will come to him, and we will make our abode with him," if a soul does not have the Holy Spirit, it is desolate. But it is inhabited when it has been filled with God, when it has Christ, when the Holy Spirit is in it. And these things are said in the Scriptures in various and diverse ways—that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are in the soul of a human being. David, at any rate, in the psalm of confession, asks the Father concerning these spirits, saying: "With a governing spirit uphold me," "renew an upright spirit in my inward parts," "and take not your Holy Spirit from me." What are these three spirits? The governing one is the Father, the upright one is Christ, and the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit—these to establish that the inhabited world is inhabited in no other way than in the wisdom of God. For "wisdom will help the wise man more than ten rulers who are in the city." "But he who despises wisdom and instruction is wretched, and his hope is empty, and his labors are unprofitable, and his works are useless," says the Wisdom inscribed to Solomon. On this account, so far as is possible, since the inhabited world is set upright in the wisdom of God, let us ourselves also wish to have our own inhabited world set upright, which has perhaps fallen. For this inhabited world has fallen when we came to the place of affliction; this inhabited world has fallen when "we sinned, we acted impiously, we did wrong," and it needs to be set upright. It is God, then, who has set upright the inhabited world. But if you do not take "who has set upright the inhabited world" in this way, but understanding the inhabited world more commonly, seek from what condition He is the one who set the inhabited world upright, seek the fall of the inhabited world, so that having found its fall you may see its being set upright. If, then, anyone is in this inhabited world, if you understand the inhabited world in that way, before being set upright it had fallen. And if it has fallen, it is clear that it needs to be set upright, but no one who has not fallen needs to be set upright. And if it was set upright, let us see—it is clear that each of those in the inhabited world has fallen from sin. And "the Lord is the one who sets upright those who have been broken down," and "He supports all who are falling," "in Adam all die," and thus the inhabited world has fallen and needs to be set upright, so that "in Christ all" may be made alive.
