So then I have rendered the matters concerning the inhabited world in two ways, in one place showing with respect to each single person how each soul is either an inhabited world or a desolation, and in another place setting the discourse upon the inhabited world itself.

"And in His understanding He stretched out the heaven." It was not by chance that he took up understanding in connection with the heaven. For you will find it said in the Proverbs: "God in wisdom founded the earth, and He prepared the heavens in understanding." There is, then, a certain understanding of God, which you should not seek except in Christ Jesus. For all such things as are of God, Christ is. He Himself is the wisdom of God, He Himself the power of God, He Himself the righteousness of God, He Himself sanctification, He Himself redemption; thus He Himself is the understanding of God. But the underlying subject is one, and by conceptions the many names apply to different aspects. And you do not conceive the same thing about Christ when you conceive Him as wisdom and when you conceive Him as righteousness. For when you conceive Him as wisdom, you take up the knowledge of things divine and human; and when as righteousness, the power that distributes according to desert in the whole; and when as sanctification, that which brings it about that those who believe and are devoted to God become holy. Thus, then, you will conceive Him also as understanding, when it is the knowledge of goods and evils and things that are neither. Since, then, it is distinguished for those who dwell in heaven or for those who bear the heavenly man, having separated the evils from the goods, so that that heaven may no longer be defiled—because the heaven has been stretched out by the understanding of God—neither the one who is a righteous heaven (and the righteous man too is heaven, as has been said). "And He stretched out the heaven by His understanding."

How, then, is the heaven stretched out? By wisdom stretching it out. And it is made clear that wisdom stretches out in the words "since I stretched out words and you did not attend," and it speaks of there being a certain stretching-out of words; thus the heaven is stretched out. And in the one hundred and third psalm it is said, "who stretches out the heaven like a curtain," and our soul too, previously contracted, is stretched out, so that it may be able to contain the wisdom of God. But let us return to what is before us. We were speaking about the heaven having come to be in understanding. And we say that those who bear the heavenly man are themselves also heaven. For if it is said to the one who sins, "Earth you are, and to earth you shall depart," would it not be said to the righteous man, whose is the kingdom of the heavens, "Heaven you are, and to heaven you shall depart"? Or rather, on account of the earthy man will it be said to the one who bears "the image of the earthy," "Earth you are, and to earth you shall depart," but on account of the heavenly man, when you have borne "the image of the heavenly," it will no longer be fitting to say it—"Heaven you are, and to heaven you shall depart"? Each of us, then, has works heavenly and works earthly. Earthly are the works which bring down to the earth akin to them the one who lays them up as treasure upon the earth and does not lay up treasure in heaven. Again, to the regions akin to the works, those in heaven, they lead up the one who lays up treasure in heaven, the one who has borne "the image of the heavenly," the things done according to virtue.

The Lord, who makes — or made — the earth by his might, prepares the world by his wisdom, and by his prudence stretches out the heavens. At his voice he gives a multitude of waters in the heaven, and lifts up — or brings out — the mists from the ends of the earth; he has made lightnings into rain, and brings out the wind — or the winds — from his treasuries. Every man has become foolish from knowledge; every craftsman is confounded in his carved image, for what he has cast is false, and there is no spirit in them. They are vain and works worthy of laughter; in the time of their visitation they will perish. Not like these is the portion of Jacob; for he who formed all things, he it is, and Israel is the rod of his inheritance; the Lord of hosts is his name. He who makes the earth by his might is God the Father. And he makes it by his might, that is, by the Lord the Savior; for Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. He himself is also the prudence in which he stretches out the heaven. For he himself spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created, saying to the Son: Let us make man after our image and likeness!

"And He brought up clouds from the end of the earth." This saying fell to us recently also in the psalm, and we were saying how God "brought up clouds from the end of the earth." Which things it is necessary to take up again—for those who know, for the clarification and reminder of what has been said, but for those who have forgotten or were not present, for the plain understanding of this, whether it be revealed and made manifest or however it may be understood. And we were saying that the saints are clouds. For the phrase "your truth is unto the clouds" cannot be referred to the lifeless clouds; but the truth of God is unto the clouds, which hear the commandment of God and know where they should send forth rain and from what places they should withhold it. For, as of clouds which exist, to which God gives command not to rain or to rain, it is written, "I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it." Now in the case of these clouds, when there is no rain, God does not command the clouds not to rain rain upon the vineyard or upon the land, but no cloud appears at all, as is written in the third book of Kingdoms, where, during the time of the drought, no cloud appeared; but when, according to the word of the prophecy of Elijah, the rain was about to come, a trace of a cloud appeared "like the trace of a man," and it became a cloud producing the rain. But as of clouds that do exist, yet are ordered not to rain when the soul happens to be unworthy of the rain, it is said, "I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it." Therefore each of the saints is a cloud. Moses was a cloud, and as a cloud he said: "Attend, O heaven, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words of my mouth. Let my utterance be awaited like rain." If he were not a cloud, he would never have said, "Let my utterance be awaited like rain, and let my words come down like dew." As a cloud he says: "As a shower upon the grass, and as snowfall upon the herbage; because I have called upon the name of the Lord." Thus, as a cloud, Isaiah too says: "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, because the Lord has spoken." And since he too was a cloud, and called those who prophesied together with him clouds, he says, prophesying: "I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it."

And if it has been understood by us who the clouds are, let us see how God is the one who brings up "clouds from the end of the earth." How from "the end of the earth"? The Savior says, "He who wishes to be first among you shall be last of all." Paul kept this commandment, and he was last in this world. Therefore he says: "For I think that God has exhibited us the apostles as last, as men doomed to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world and to angels and to men." If, then, anyone keeps the commandment of the Savior and becomes last as regards this life, this man becomes a cloud. And God brings up clouds not from the foremost of the earth, not from men of consular rank does He bring up clouds, not from rulers does He bring up clouds, not from the rich; for "blessed are the poor, because yours is the kingdom of God." Do you see how from the last God brings up and gives bodily form to the clouds? On this account, if we wish to become clouds, upon which the truth of God arrives, let us become last of all and say, in works and in disposition, "For I think that God has exhibited us the apostles as last"; and even if I am not an apostle, it is possible for me to become last, so that God, bringing up clouds from "the end of the earth," may bring me up.

"And He made lightnings into rain." Those skilled in these matters say that the generation of lightnings comes from the clouds rubbing against one another. For what happens with the fire-striking stones on the earth, so that when two stones strike together fire is produced, this they say happens also in the case of the clouds. When the clouds strike together during storms, the lightning is produced. Therefore, for the most part, the lightning occurs together with thunder, the thunder manifesting the sound of the collision of the clouds, and the lightning generating the light.

If you have understood the illustration, look with me also at the spiritual cloud. Moses was a cloud, Jesus the son of Nave was a cloud. These, indeed, converse with one another, and from their words lightning is produced. Jeremiah was a cloud, Baruch was a cloud. They discourse with one another, the lightning came from the words of Jeremiah and the words of Baruch. Thus, if you can, gather from the Scriptures in what manner the lightning comes. And in the new covenant Paul and Silvanus were two clouds. They came together, the lightning of the epistle came to be.

God, then, "made lightnings into rain, and brought forth winds from His treasuries." Are, then, these winds in treasuries? Or is not their nature apparent, when they blow upon the earth, in what manner it subsists? But there are certain treasuries of winds, treasuries of spirits: "a spirit of wisdom and understanding, a spirit of counsel and strength, a spirit of knowledge and piety," "a spirit of the fear of God," "a spirit of power and love and self-control." And you yourself can gather these winds from the Scriptures. These spirits are in treasuries; who are the treasuries? "In whom are the treasuries of wisdom and knowledge hidden"? These treasuries are in Christ. From there, then, come these winds, these spirits, so that one may be wise, another faithful, another may have knowledge, and another may have taken up whatever gift of God: "for to one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit."

"He brought up," then, "clouds from the end of the earth, and made lightnings into rain, and brought forth winds from His treasuries." And we too, on account of God, hope to arrive at these treasuries. And since there are many treasuries, perhaps according to the ranks of those who are raised up there will be places of rest in the treasuries of God. What I mean is such as this. The resurrection of the dead comes about in certain ranks; for the apostle says, "but each in his own rank." And since the ranks are not jumbled together as it may chance, this rank will be in a certain treasury of God, and that rank in another treasury of God, and a third, another rank, will be in yet another treasury. All these treasuries, however, have one treasury, in which they dwell. Therefore it is said in Paul: "in whom are the treasuries both of wisdom and of knowledge hidden." And just as I acquire the "one precious pearl" through the many pearls, so I come to the treasury of the treasuries, the Lord of lords, the King of kings, when I have become worthy of the spirits from the treasuries of God; for "He brought forth winds from His treasuries."

At his voice he gives a multitude of waters in the heaven. For all the teaching of the Lord flows from heavenly things, as David says: A willing rain you will set apart, O God, for your inheritance, and it was weakened; but you have perfected it. And he lifts up — or brings out — the mists from the ends of the earth. The mists or clouds, which the Lord commanded not to rain a shower upon Israel, are brought out from the extremities of the earth; one of these mists said: For I think that God has displayed us apostles as last, as men destined to death, because we have been made a spectacle to this world, both to angels and to men. He has made lightnings into rain. For when the shower of teachings has come from heaven and has sated the parched hearts of men, then you will find flashes and the bright lightnings of wisdom. And he brings out the winds from his treasuries, in which are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

"Every man was made foolish from knowledge." If every man was made foolish from knowledge, and Paul too is a man, Paul was made foolish from knowledge; for "knowing in part and prophesying in part," he was made foolish from knowledge; "seeing through a mirror," seeing in an enigma, seeing and grasping a small fraction, and, if one may say so, an infinitesimal fraction of things. But you will understand from the contrary "every man was made foolish from knowledge." There are sins of Jerusalem, and sins also of Sodom, but by comparison with the worse sins of Jerusalem, the sins of Sodom are righteousness; for it says, "Sodom was justified from you." As, then, the sins of Sodom are not righteousness but injustice, yet as compared with the greater injustice it is righteousness, so, from the contrary, knowledge—the knowledge that belongs to Paul—as compared with that knowledge which is in the heavens, as compared with the perfect knowledge, is foolishness. On this account "every man was made foolish from knowledge." Some such thing, I think, Ecclesiastes was grasping when he said: "I said, I will become wise; and it withdrew from me, far beyond what it was, and a deep depth—who will find it?"

The discourse is about to venture something and to say that the one who came to sojourn in this life emptied himself, so that by his emptying the world might be filled. And if that one who came to sojourn in this life emptied himself, that very emptying was wisdom. "For the foolish thing of God is wiser than men." If I had said, "the foolish thing of God," how would the fault-finders have accused me? How would they have blamed me? How would I have been charged—while the other things said, which are reckoned even by them to be noble, were approved, but this, as they suppose, not being nobly said—because I said "the foolish thing of God"? But now Paul, as one who is wise and has apostolic authority, dared to say that all the wisdom upon earth, both that in himself and that in Peter and the apostles, all that has come to sojourn in the world, is "the foolish thing of God." For as compared with that wisdom which no place upon earth can contain, as compared with that supra-celestial wisdom, this thing that has come to sojourn is the foolish thing of God. But this "foolish thing of God is wiser than men." Than which men? I do not mean than the foolish, but it is wiser even than the wise men. And even if you name the wise men of this age, whether rulers or prophets, than the rulers of this age "the foolish thing of God," which I have expounded, "is wiser than men."

The discourse is about to say something paradoxical, that "the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God," and "God made foolish the wisdom of the world." Did He, then, in wisdom make foolish the wisdom of the world? And can the wisdom of the world contain the wisdom, so as to be proved foolish? For does the wisdom of God contend against the wisdom of the world, in order to be tested against it? But there is need of some little thing, which is the little foolish thing of God, so that by this small foolish thing of God the wisdom of the world may be made foolish and refuted; for the wisdom of this world did not endure the wisdom of God. As, for example—so that you may understand that "the foolish thing of God" "made foolish the wisdom of the world"—let it be granted that I am contending, I who seem to know many things and more, against someone senseless and uninstructed and understanding nothing and not contending on behalf of noble words of any sort whatever. Do I, then, have need of dialectic against that man, or of deeper speculations, if his notions are foolish? Do I not have need of one little word slightly sharper than his diction, so that I may be able to refute his foolishness? Thus, in order that the wisdom of this world may be made foolish, there is no need of the wisdom of God contending against it (for it itself is below), but the foolish thing of God suffices, since "the foolish thing of God is wiser than men, and the weak thing of God is stronger than men." And my Savior and Lord took up all the contrary things, so that by the contraries he might dissolve the contraries, and that we might be made strong from the weakness of Jesus and made wise from the foolish thing of God, and, being introduced through these things, might be able to ascend to the wisdom, to the strength of God, Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the might unto the ages. Amen.

The psalmist writes, "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me. It is high; I cannot attain unto it." In another: "When I thought how I might know this, it was too painful for me until I went into the sanctuary of God and considered their latter end." And later in the same psalm, "I was as a beast before you; nevertheless I am continually with you." And Jeremiah says, "Every person is become brutish and without knowledge."

Every man has become foolish from knowledge. Though it be Paul, though Peter, though Moses and Abraham, in comparison with God all their wisdom will be counted as nothing; whence also the foolishness of God is wiser than men. Every craftsman is confounded in his carved image, he who has fashioned images out of his own heart, and what he has cast is false. But if every man is foolish from knowledge, everything that he has made is foolish and false. And there is no spirit in them. It should be noted that in this passage too 'wind' and 'spirit' are called by one name among the Hebrews, 'ruha'; but he means the spirit of sanctification, which cannot be found in the minds of heretics.

In the second word: You shall not make a graven image, all false and superstitious inventions of errors are prohibited. Every error is nothing other than a fiction of the mind. For imagination produces error by clouding reason and making what is not appear to be. All false and superstitious inventions of errors arise either from the wicked audacity of philosophical investigation, or from a perverse understanding of Sacred Scripture, or from a disordered affection of human carnality. Concerning such men, however, who devise, or defend, or imitate these or similar errors, Jeremiah says: Every man has become foolish by his own knowledge, that is, by his own investigation and excessive philosophy; every craftsman has been confounded by his graven image: their works are vain and worthy of ridicule, and in the time of their visitation they shall perish. We must therefore stand upon what the lights of faith dictate, and whatever is opposed to this, we ought to abominate entirely as a graven image.

The first brightness, namely that of philosophical knowledge, is great according to the opinion of worldly men: but it is easily eclipsed, unless a man guards himself from the head and tail of the dragon. If anything is interposed between him and the sun of justice, he suffers an eclipse of foolishness. "Every man is made foolish by his knowledge," namely occasioned by it, not caused by it. He who trusts in philosophical knowledge and esteems himself on account of this and believes himself to be better, has been made foolish—namely, when through this knowledge without any further light he believes himself to apprehend the Creator: just as if a man should wish to see the heavens or the body of the sun by candlelight.

They are vain and a work worthy of laughter. For who would not laugh when he has looked closely at the images of the heretics? For either what they say is rustic, and it is wood; or it is composed in fine speech, and it is found to be silver; or else it is feigned out of their own mind, and in vain they promise the image of gold. In the time of their visitation they will perish. Heresy prevails for a time, so that all the elect may become manifest and be proved; but when the visitation of God has come and his eye has looked upon foolish things, all things fall silent.

Not like these is the portion of Jacob, that is, of those who supplanted the Jews and daily destroy the heretics. But the portion of the saints is God, of whom the prophet says: The Lord is my portion. For he who formed all things, he it is, who made and molded all things, both in mind and in body, and Israel is the rod of his inheritance. Everyone who is 'upright in God' or 'discerns God with the mind' is the scepter of his inheritance, whose name is 'the Lord almighty' or 'of powers'; for this is what 'the Lord of hosts' means, which in the Hebrew is written 'the Lord sabaoth'.

Gather out of the land your confusion, you who dwell under siege, for thus says the Lord: Behold, I will cast far away the inhabitants of the land at this turn, and I will afflict them, that they may be found. LXX: She has gathered from outside her substance, she who dwells in a stronghold, for thus says the Lord: Behold, I will supplant the inhabitants of this land and afflict them, that they may be found. Jerusalem is commanded to gather whatever substance she has outside into the most strongly fortified city and to prepare provisions for a long siege; for he is threatening no longer, as before, about a future and distant time, but now about the captivity close at hand, which is about to come at any moment. 'Gather,' he says, 'both from outside and from the land, that is, from the fields, your substance into confusion. For whatever you have is worthy of confusion; and although you prepare these things, learn the words of the Lord concerning them: Behold, I at this turn, that is, at this time, will cast or hurl as from a sling far away the inhabitants of the land, this one'. For this the Seventy translated: I will supplant and make fall; for this Hebrew word, that is 'cole', Aquila and Symmachus translated sphendonisō [I will sling], and the sense is: 'As from a sling I will hurl them with all force, and so I will cause them to be besieged, and so I will afflict and hem them in, that all may be found in the city and be unable to escape the evil'.

Woe is me over my crushing, my most grievous wound! LXX: Woe over your crushing, your most grievous wound! According to the Hebrew, Jerusalem herself speaks, because she is grievously afflicted and bears an incurable wound; but according to the Seventy, the prophet speaks to Jerusalem and laments her over her crushing and her own wound.

But I said: Truly this is my infirmity — or my wound — and I will bear it or it has seized me. Jerusalem herself speaks: 'Whatever I suffer, I suffer through my own fault; I understand my wound, which has seized me, or I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him'.

My tabernacle is established, all my cords are broken — or all my skins are torn apart —, my sons have gone out from me — or my sheep — and they are not; there is no one to stretch out my tent any more — or there is no more place for my tabernacle — and to raise up my skins. Jerusalem laments the overthrow of her city as so easy that you would think it not the razing of the walls and all the fortifications to the ground, but the taking down of a tabernacle and a tent. 'My tabernacle,' she says, 'that is, my dwelling, has suddenly been taken away. All my cords are broken — she keeps the metaphoran [metaphor] of the tabernacle — or all my skins are torn apart. My sons have gone out from me or my cattle'; this, added by the Seventy, does not stand according to the history; for in a long siege how could sheep and cattle have been carried off from Jerusalem, when, even if there had been any, famine had consumed them? 'And they do not', she says, 'subsist or they are not'; for they were not carried over into Chaldea, but a great part of them was killed and utterly destroyed. 'There is no one to stretch out my tent any more: there is no one to restore me and lay the foundations of my walls, which have been leveled to the ground'.

For the shepherds have acted foolishly and have not sought the Lord; therefore they have not understood, and all their flock has been scattered. Through the metaphor of shepherds and sheep the guilt of the princes and the scattering of the people are described. For because the princes acted foolishly and did not seek the Lord, whom they ought to have sought with their whole heart, therefore they did not see the evils that were coming, or did not understand the Lord, and the whole multitude of Jerusalem has been scattered hither and thither.
He refers to the kings and priests as [stupid] shepherds because they were the guardians of this wandering people.

A voice of hearing, behold, comes, and a great commotion from the land of the north, to make the cities of Judah a desolation and a dwelling of dragons — or a lair of ostriches and, as Symmachus translated, of sirens —; for this in the Hebrew 'thannim' is set down. The words of the prophet: 'Behold,' he says, 'the sound and roaring of the Babylonian as he comes is heard, and a great commotion, or earthquake, from the land of the north, to reduce all the cities of Judea to desolation, their inhabitants slain, and to make dragons and all venomous creatures dwell in place of men, or ostriches'; this animal too is at home in desolation, and is born and nourished in deserts; or else we can understand sirens, certain monsters and phantoms of demons. All these things, which both the past and the present discourse have described, let us refer to the times of the Church's persecution, when the tabernacles of the Lord are overthrown and every dwelling of the Church is reduced to desolation. And that all these things come to pass is the fault of the shepherds, who have acted foolishly and have not sought the Lord nor understood him; and therefore the whole flock has been scattered.

"All are governed by their own free choice." What Christian can bear to hear this? For if not one, or a few or many, but all of us are governed by our own free choice, what becomes of the help of God? How do you explain the proverb that "A person's goings are ordered by the Lord?" Or "A person's way is not in himself"? Or "No one can receive anything, unless it be given him from above"? And elsewhere, "What do you have that you did not receive?"

I know, O Lord, that his way is not man's, nor is it a man's to walk and to direct his steps. Let the new preachers blush, who say that each one is ruled by his own will, when this prophet too says: his way is not man's, and David sings in a lyric song: By the Lord shall a man's steps be directed, and he will greatly desire his way. Or else this is the sense: 'What we suffer from the Babylonians comes not from dread of them, but from our desert and from your indignation'.

Unless God works in us, we cannot be partakers of any virtue. For indeed, without this Good, nothing is good. Without this Light, nothing is bright. Without this Wisdom, nothing is wise. Without this Justice, nothing is right. For the Lord says through the mouth of Isaiah, "I am, I am the Lord, and there is no one besides me who saves," and through Jeremiah, "I know, O Lord, that the way of a person is not in him. Neither is it in a person to direct his way."

Jeremiah, explaining that humankind receives wisdom from God, states, "I know, O Lord, that the way of a person is not his. Neither is it of a person … to direct his way." Again the Lord proclaims through the same prophet that God effects the conversion of a heart to him and says, "I will bring them again into this land. And I will build them up again and not pull them down. And I will plant them and pluck them up. And I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the Lord. And they shall be my people and I will be their God, because they shall return to me with whole heart."

It is clear, therefore, from what was said at first and what was added, that the verse "I know, Lord, that the people's way is not their own," neither subjects our free will to nature's enslavement nor submits our affairs to an ordained necessity. Instead, it expressly teaches us that the Lord God keeps his hand on the tiller of the universe and wisely directs it. He provides blessings but also corrects with justice whenever he perceives that despite his extended long-suffering we persist in evildoing.

This the general of our forces learned when he entered as a captive the same city of the enemy that he had boasted he would enter that same day as victor. He proved indeed the words of the prophet: "For a man's way is not his own, nor is it in his own power to walk and direct his steps.'' Since he thought his actions were under his own control, he could neither direct his steps nor find the way of safety. So we read: "He poureth contempt upon the prince and causeth him to wander in the wilderness where there is no way. . . . He has been brought to nothing, even as the waters which run continually." In him, indeed, in addition to his actual misfortune, the present judgment of God was clearly shown. He has endured all the sufferings that he had boasted he would inflict on others. Because he trusted that the enemy could be taken without God's aid and consent, he has himself been captured; he claimed foreknowledge and wisdom and has met with disgrace for his presumption; he himself has worn the chains he prepared for others.
On the Government of God, Book 7, Chapter 10

Chasten me, O Lord, but yet in judgment and not in your fury, lest perhaps you bring me to nothing! Pour out your indignation upon the nations which have not known you, and upon the provinces — or generations — which have not called upon your name, for they have devoured Jacob and consumed his place, and his beauty — or pastures — they have scattered or reduced to desolation. We read this passage in the Psalm: O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury, nor chasten me in your wrath! And the sense is: 'We deserve indeed all that we endure, and we deserve much greater things than we suffer; yet this I beseech, that you chasten me as a father, not as an adversary, that you amend me as a son and do not punish me as an enemy; for you chastise every son whom you receive, and through every pain and scourge you amend Jerusalem. But the enemies, who have not known you, and the provinces or regions, which have not called upon your name, ought by no means to feel your judgment, but your indignation. For you handed us over that we might be amended. But they made their yoke heavy; they did not spare the old man and they afflicted the little ones; they ate us up and utterly devoured us, and reduced Jerusalem to such desolation that they scattered everything of both public and private buildings and killed your people'.

The inspired author knows the usefulness of discipline and understands that the Lord is exercising loving-kindness in applying it to human beings. This is the reason he asks to have a share in it. God exercises goodness in applying correction, and correction produces knowledge. Likewise the prophet Jeremiah begs, "Correct us, O Lord, but in just measure, not in anger, lest you make us few." Thus, a sick person who longs for health goes in search of a cure through cutting by steel and burning.
11:
According to the recorded coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, His sojourn came about bodily in a certain universal way, shining upon the whole world, when "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us." For "there was the true Light which enlightens every man coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through Him, and the world knew Him not. He came unto His own, and His own received Him not." Yet one must know that even earlier He sojourned, though not bodily, in each of the saints, and that after this His visible coming He sojourns among us again. And if you wish to receive a demonstration of these things, attend to the passage: "The word which came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Hear," and what follows. For what is "the word which came from the Lord," whether to Jeremiah or to Isaiah or to Ezekiel or to whomever, other than He who was in the beginning with God? I know of no other word of the Lord than this, concerning which the evangelist has said, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

And this too we must know, that it is above all when it is possible to profit from them that the coming of the Word is to each one. For what benefit is it to me if the Word has sojourned in the world, but I do not have Him? On the contrary, even if He has not yet sojourned in the whole world, grant that I have come to be among the prophets—I have the Word. And I would say that Christ came to Moses, to Jeremiah, to Isaiah, to each of the righteous, and that what was said by Him to the disciples, "Behold, I am with you all the days until the consummation of the age," was in fact fulfilled and came to pass even before His coming; for He was with Moses and He was with Isaiah and with each of the saints. How could those men have spoken the word of God if the Word of God had not sojourned in them? These things are especially necessary to be known by us who belong to the Church, who wish the God of the Law and of the Gospel to be the same, and Christ to be the same both then and now unto all ages. But there will be those who sever the Godhead older than the coming of the Savior—so far as their own supposition goes—from the Godhead proclaimed by Jesus Christ. But we know one God both then and now, one Christ both then and now. These things because of "the word which came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying."

The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Hear the words of this pact — or covenant — and speak to the men of Judah and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel. It is not, indeed, set down in the heading at what time, or under which king and in which year of his, this prophecy was made; but we understand either that it is to be joined to the former prophecy and its time, or certainly that this word of the Lord came to the prophet some interval of time after the former prophecy. It is to be noted, moreover, that the word 'berith' Aquila and Symmachus always translated 'pact', the Seventy and Theodotion 'covenant'. Properly, however, the word is now directed to Jerusalem and to the men of the tribe of Judah.

What then are we also to hear? "Hear the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem." We are men of Judah because of Christ; for it is plain that our Lord "has arisen out of Judah," and if I establish, according to Scripture, that the name of Judah refers to Christ, then the men of Judah will not be the Jews who disbelieve in Christ, but ourselves, as many as believe in Christ. "Judah, may your brothers praise you. Your hands are upon the back of your enemies"—"may they praise you." His brothers did not praise that Judah, the son of Jacob. But this Judah his brothers will praise, since this Judah says, "I will declare your name to my brothers, in the midst of the church I will hymn you." It is not said with reference to that Judah. "Your hands are upon the back of your enemies": where is that Judah found laying his hands upon the back of his enemies? The narrative has recorded nothing of the sort concerning him. But if you understand the coming of the Lord Jesus abolishing the devil, stripping off "the principalities and powers" and making a show of them and triumphing over them in the wood, you see how upon this Judah the prophecy that says this has been fulfilled: "Your hands are upon the back of your enemies." If this is so, and the word now speaks "to the men of Judah," to whom would it be speaking except to those who believe in Christ, called in a certain manner Judah too because of the tribe of Judah?

"To the men of Judah" the word is spoken, and "to the inhabitants of Jerusalem." This is the church. For the city of God is the church, the Vision of peace; in her is the peace which He brought us, if indeed we are children of peace, and it is multiplied and seen.

"Hear," then, "the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Cursed is the man who will not hear the words of the covenant which I commanded your fathers." Who most of all hears "the words of the covenant which God commanded the fathers"? Is it those who believe in Him, or those who are shown not even to believe Moses by the very fact that they have not believed in the Lord? For the Savior says to those men: "If you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote concerning me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?" Therefore those men have not believed in Moses, but we who believe in Christ believe the covenant given through Moses, and it is spoken to us, that we may not become accursed: "Cursed is the man who will not hear the words of the covenant which I commanded the fathers." Those men, then, have this—to be accursed. For they did not hear "the covenant which God commanded the fathers."

"In the day," He says, "when I brought them up out of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace." Us too God has led out "of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace," especially according to him who has understood what is written in the Revelation of John, that the place "where their Lord was crucified is called spiritually Sodom and Egypt." For if it "is called spiritually Egypt," and this Egypt is not that Egypt which is spiritually called Egypt, for this one is perceptible to the senses, it is clear that if you understand the Egypt which is spiritually so called and go out from it, you are the one who has gone out "of the land of Egypt and out of the iron furnace," and it is said to you: "Hear my voice and do according to all" these things.

Then there is a promise of God to those who hear, if they do what He has commanded, saying: "And you shall be to me a people, and I will be to you a God." Not everyone who says he is the people of God is the people of God; that people, then, which had promised to be the people of God, heard "you are not my people" in the words "for you are not my people," and it was said to that people "not my people," and again this people was called a people. For "they moved me to jealousy with what is no god"—and He speaks concerning those men—"they provoked me to anger with their idols; and I will move them to jealousy with what is no nation, with a nation without understanding I will provoke them to anger."

We, then, have become a people to God, and "the righteousness of God is to the people," to the people from the nations. For this people is born all at once, as it is also said in the prophet: "Has a nation been born at once?" And a nation was born at once, when the Savior had come and in one day five thousand believed, and on another day three thousand were added. And it is possible to see a whole people being born by the word of God, and the barren woman, who formerly did not bear, bearing all at once, to whom it is said: "Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear, break forth and cry out, you who are not in travail, for many are the children of the desolate one, more than of her who has the husband." The church is desolate—desolate of the law, this one was desolate of God. But that synagogue was said to have a husband, the law.

Cursed be the man who will not hear the words of this pact, which I commanded your fathers in the day in which I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace, saying: Hear my voice and do all that I command you, and you shall be my people and I will be your Lord. Not because of the privileges of race, not because of the injury of circumcision and the idleness of the sabbath, but because of obedience does God become the God of the people of Israel, and Israel his people. And here, indeed, he speaks as to servants, that they may please God; but in the Gospel the Lord says to the disciples: You, he says, are my friends, if you do what I command you. No longer do I call you servants, because the servant does not know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, because all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. And when they have become friends, from friends they pass over into sons; for as many as received him, to them he gave power to become sons of God. Hence he commands friends and sons: Be perfect, as your Father is perfect, enjoining likeness, not equality. And there it is obedience to the commandments, here likeness to God. And what he says: in the day in which I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace, gives us to understand that the oven and the iron furnace, kindled, signify the greatness of tribulation and punishment, not some place of punishment made ready out of the material of iron.

What then does God promise me? "You shall be to me a people, and I will be to you a God." He is not the God of all, but only of those to whom He grants Himself, just as He granted Himself to that patriarch to whom He said, "I am your God," and again to another, "I will be your God," and concerning others, "I will be their God." When, then, do we attain—I speak of each individual—to God being our God? But if you wish to learn whose God He is and to whom He grants the invocation of Himself, "I," He says, "am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob." And the Savior, expounding this very thing, says: "God is not the God of the dead but of the living." Who is the dead? The sinner, who does not have the One who said, "I am the Life," the one who has dead works, the one who has not yet repented from dead works, concerning which the apostle says: "Not again laying a foundation of repentance from dead works." If, then, "God is not the God of the dead but of the living," and we know who is the living one—that it is he who lives his life according to Christ and abides with Him—then, if we wish that God may be ours, let us renounce the works of deadness, that He may fulfill His promise which says: "And I will be to you a God, that I may establish my oath which I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey." For observe that He says: "I will establish my oath which I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey," as though He had not yet given them "the land flowing with milk and honey." For this is not the land which God promised "flowing with milk and honey," but it is that one concerning which the Savior taught, saying: "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth."

Then to what was said beforehand by the Lord the prophet answers—to the words "Cursed is the man who will not hear the words of this covenant"—and he says: "And I answered and said, So be it, Lord." What is "So be it, Lord"? Cursed is he who will not abide in the words of this covenant.

This was the reason why He sent not Jeremiah only into Egypt, but also Ezekiel into Babylon, and they did not refuse to go. For when they found their Master love the people exceedingly, they continued themselves to do so likewise. Much as if a right-minded servant were to take compassion upon an intractable son when he saw his father grieving and lamenting about him. And what was there that they did not suffer for them? They were sawn asunder, they were driven out, they were reproached, they were stoned, they underwent numberless grievances. And after all this they would run back to them.… And for the people of the Jews, Jeremiah has composed Lamentations in writing. And when the general of the Persians had given him liberty to dwell securely, and with perfect freedom, wherever he pleased, he preferred above dwelling at home the affliction of the people, and their hard durance in a strange land.

That I may raise up the oath which I swore to your fathers, that I would give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as it is this day. The fathers are seen to receive when the sons receive, and the promise to Abraham is fulfilled in his posterity. A land moreover streaming with milk and honey we ought to take hyperbolically, for an abundance of all things, as in that line: let honey flow for them, and let the rough bramble bear amomum, and again: and he held back the wine running everywhere in streams; or else, tropologically, let us understand the land streaming with milk and honey as the Church of Christ, in which, as little ones and sucklings, we are brought up through faith, so that we may be able to take solid food.

And I answered and said: Amen, O Lord, for which LXX: So be it, O Lord — for this is what 'amen' signifies — is what they translated. The Lord had said: I swore to your fathers that I would give them a land streaming with milk and honey, as is proved today by the facts themselves. The prophet, loving his people, takes up the voice of the Lord and longs that what has been given may be true and may endure forever. Hence he says: 'Truly, O Lord, you have fulfilled what you promised; or So be it, O Lord, that is: may what you have given remain always!'

"And the Lord said to me: Read these words in the cities of Judah and outside Jerusalem." And to those outside we read the words of God, calling them to salvation. "Hear the words of this covenant and do them."

And the Lord said to me: Cry out — or read — all these words in the cities of Judah and outside Jerusalem, saying: Hear the words of this pact and do them! The most merciful God frequently foretells what is to come, so that the mind that is hard to believe may at last be softened. And he foretells it both in the city of Jerusalem and outside in the countryside, so that those whose peril is common may have the same penitence.

For, testifying, I testified to your fathers in the day in which I brought them out of the land of Egypt, even to this day; rising early I testified and said: Hear my voice! And they did not hear nor incline their ear, but each one went away in the perversity of his evil heart; and I brought upon them all the words of this pact, which I commanded them to do. Up to this point it is not found in the LXX, and what follows: and they did not do it, was placed by them and joined to the end of the preceding passage, in which it is written: Hear the words of this pact and do them! And they did not do it. But what it means to rise early and frequently press the words of God upon them through the prophets, and to bring them out of Egypt, and often to admonish them and to say: Hear my voice, and that they went away after the perversity of their heart, and that afterwards he renders to them what they deserve to receive, we have already said before.

When he was giving the law, he added this to the law, for he said, "Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them," and he also promises there and again here how he will deem worthy of all care those who keep the divine commandments. And he reminds them also of the things spoken to their ancestors and of their ancestors' disobedience. For they turned their ear away, he says, and every one went in the direction of his own evil heart. And he says here "direction" not as meaning "uprightness" but rather the evil that arises immediately in their malice. For they have not turned from this evil but have journeyed constantly in it. "And I brought on them all the words of this covenant that I commanded them to do, and yet they did not do." He gave them over to noteworthy punishments; sometimes they served the Ammonites, other times the Moabites and still other times other foreigners.…The phrase "a band has been found" means "they have banded themselves together and joined themselves with their ancestors and they travel down the road of their ancestors' wickedness." He indicates as much also through the things that are brought against them. "And behold, they go after foreign gods, in order to serve them." They do these things in transgression of the covenant that was given to them. For this reason I will surround them with misfortunes of all kinds, and those who weep I will not deem worthy to be spared. They will not even enjoy any help from the gods who are revered by them.

"And they did not do them. And the Lord said to me: A conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem." Are we going to repent over the sins spoken of concerning the men of Judah, knowing that we are men of Judah because of Christ who was prophesied and spoken of? For perhaps, since there are among us certain sinners who act contrary to right reason, for this reason the prophet says: "A conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem." For when there is found, in certain persons who bear the name of the church, a bond of injustice and a bond of sins, so that to them may be applied what is said of the sinner, "and each one is bound tight by the cords of his own sins," God would say: "A conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah." But let no conspiracy be found among us. And how is a conspiracy not found among us, even if until now there is a conspiracy in certain persons? "Loose every bond of injustice, undo the knots of forced dealings, tear apart every unjust contract. Break your bread for the hungry."

And the Lord said to me: A conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem. They have turned back to the former iniquities of their fathers, who would not hear my words; and these, therefore, have gone after foreign gods to serve them. The house of Israel and the house of Judah have made void my pact, which I made with their fathers. For 'conspiracy', which we have translated following Symmachus, Aquila and the Seventy and Theodotion translated syndesmon, which we can call 'a binding-together'. Hence also Athaliah, when she discovered that a plot was being prepared against her in the temple, spoke with the same word: Conspiracy, conspiracy. Properly, however, Scripture employs this word when one strives toward wrongdoing not by a sudden and chance sin but by prepared plots and conspiracy, and when with like mind and one zeal they act so as to despise the commandments of God.

"A conspiracy," then, "has been found among the men of Judah and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem. They have turned back to the injustices of their fathers of former times." "They have turned back to the injustices"—of whom? He does not say simply "of the fathers." What is the addition? "They have turned back to the injustices of their fathers of former times." We were saying that these things are spoken to us and to those among us who sin. How then have those among us who sin turned back not "to the injustices of the fathers," but "of their fathers of former times"? Perhaps, then, our fathers are twofold, and there is among us the worse kind of fathers; for before we believed we were sons, so to speak, of the devil, as the evangelic word shows, saying: "You are of your father the devil," but when we believed, we became sons of God. When, therefore, we sin, we turn back to the injustices not simply of the fathers, but of the former fathers. And to establish that our fathers are twofold, I will make use of statements from the forty-fourth Psalm which run thus: "Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and the house of your father." He calls Him father, "forget the house of your father"; for as a father He says, "Hear, O daughter." Therefore our fathers are twofold. But "forget the house of your father," the former one. If, having forgotten your former house, you again turn back to the sins, you have done the sins here spoken of.

"They have turned back to the injustices of their fathers of former times." I was saying that the devil too was formerly our father, before God became our father, if indeed even now the devil is not our father; which we will also establish from the catholic epistle of John, in which it is written: "Everyone who commits sin has been begotten of the devil." If "everyone who commits sin has been begotten of the devil," then, as it were, we have been begotten of the devil as many times as we sin. Wretched, then, is this one who is always being begotten of the devil, just as, on the other hand, blessed is he who is always being begotten by God. For I will not say that the righteous man has been begotten by God once, but that he is always being begotten at each good deed, in which God begets the righteous man. If, then, I direct you to the Savior—that the Father did not beget the Son and then release Him from His begetting, but always begets Him—I will establish something similar also in the case of the righteous man. Let us see who our Savior is. "The radiance of glory." The radiance of the glory has not been begotten once and is not being begotten; but insofar as the light is productive of the radiance, to that extent the radiance of the glory of God is begotten. Our Savior is the wisdom of God. And wisdom is "the radiance of eternal light." If, then, the Savior is always begotten, and for this reason He says, "Before all the hills He begets me"—not "before all the hills He has begotten me," but "before all the hills He begets me"—and the Savior is always begotten by the Father, so also you, if you have the spirit of adoption, God always begets you in Him at each deed, at each thought, and being thus begotten you become ever a son of God being begotten in Christ Jesus; to whom is the glory and the might unto the ages of ages. Amen.

And he says that both fathers and sons, with one mind and an equal resolve, neglecting God, worshiped idols, namely both Israel and the house of Judah, that is, both the ten tribes and the two, whose rule was in Jerusalem, so that those who had one zeal in contempt of God may have an equal punishment in enduring captivity.

Though God justly does not hear those who do not hear him, the demons will be unable to save the just in those who burn incense to them, whenever the time of troubles arrives. Thus, whenever God does not listen, it is dangerous to seek help from demons. But one must depend on God, who has turned away from us due to sins, yet who does not disregard the great and lasting refuge in himself.

Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will bring upon them evils from which they will not be able to go out; and they will cry to me and I will not hear them. And the cities of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem will go and cry to the gods to whom they pour libations; and these will not save them in the time of their affliction. God does not hear in the time of need and distress, because they too would not hear the voice of the Lord. This Saul also suffered; for when, dreading the ranks of the Philistines, he had not deserved to receive the word of the Lord, he turned to the pythoness, so as to learn from idols what he ought to have wrung from the Lord by the insistence of prayer and of tears. Through these things we learn that, even if the Lord does not hear, we must by no means cease, nor flee for refuge to demons. They cannot help their worshipers; but we must flee to the help of the Lord, who, though angered, is quickly turned and changes his sentence, if those too with whom he has been angry are changed. And all that is now said pertains to the tribe of Judah and the city of Jerusalem, upon whom captivity is pressing.

Theodore: Sometimes holy Scripture is wont by an improper use of terms to use "evils "for "affliction;" not that these are properly and in their nature evils, but because they are imagined to be evils by those on whom they are brought for their good. For when divine judgment is reasoning with men it must speak with the language and feelings of men. For when a doctor for the sake of health with good reason either cuts or cauterizes those who are suffering from the inflammation of ulcers, it is considered an evil by those who have to bear it. Nor are the spur and the whip pleasant to a restive horse. Moreover all chastisement seems at the moment to be a bitter thing to those who are chastised, as the Apostle says: "Now all chastisement for the present indeed seemeth not to bring with it joy but sorrow; but afterwards it will yield to them that are exercised by it most peaceable fruits of righteousness," and "whom the Lord loveth He chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom He receiveth: for what son is there whom the father doth not correct?" And so evils are sometimes wont to stand for afflictions, as where we read: "And God repented of the evil which He had said that He would do to them and He did it not." And again: "For Thou, Lord, are gracious and merciful, patient and very merciful and ready to repent of the evil," i.e., of the sufferings and losses which Thou art forced to bring upon us as the reward of our sins. And another prophet, knowing that these are profitable to some men, and certainly not through any jealousy of their safety, but with an eye to their good, prays thus: "Add evils to them, O Lord, add evils to the haughty ones of the earth;" and the Lord Himself says "Lo, I will bring evils upon them," i.e., sorrows, and losses, with which they shall for the present be chastened for their soul's health, and so shall be at length driven to return and hasten back to Me whom in their prosperity they scorned. And so that these are originally evil we cannot possibly assert: for to many they conduce to their good and offer the occasions of eternal bliss, and therefore (to return to the question raised) all those things, which are thought to be brought upon us as evils by our enemies or by any other people, should not be counted as evils, but as things indifferent.

For according to the number of your cities were your gods, O Judah, and according to the number of the ways of Jerusalem you have set up altars of confusion for pouring libations to the Baals. Let us read the books of Kings and of Chronicles, and we shall find that Judah and Jerusalem did far worse things than Israel, so that as many cities as they had, so many kinds of idols they also had, and as many as were the streets and street-corners in the city of Jerusalem, so many altars they had, to their own confusion, on which they sacrificed victims to the idols of the Baals.

Or having sins unrepented they ask mercy, which thing it is impossible to receive, not only if themselves ask it, but although others having much confidence towards God entreat for them, like as even Jeremiah praying for the Jews did hear, "Pray not thou for this people, because I will not hear thee." But if all things are there, and thou ask things expedient, and contribute all thine own part, and exhibit an apostolical life, and have concord and love towards thy neighbor, thou wilt obtain on thy entreaty; for the Lord is loving towards man.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 60:2

"How then do they not obtain all things?" Because many are causes of their failing. For either they often ask things inexpedient. And why marvellest thou, if this is the case with some others, whereas it was so even with Paul, when he heard, "My grace is sufficient for thee; for my strength is perfected in weakness." Or they are unworthy to be reckoned with them that heard these words, and contribute not their own part, but He seeks for such as are like them; therefore He saith "of you," of the virtuous, of them that show forth an angelic rule of life. Or they pray against them that have aggrieved them, seeking for redress and vengeance; and this kind of thing is forbidden, for, "Pray," saith He, "for your enemies." Or having sins unrepented they ask mercy, which thing it is impossible to receive, not only if themselves ask it, but although others having much confidence towards God entreat for them, like as even Jeremiah praying for the Jews did hear, "Pray not thou for this people, because I will not hear thee."
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 60:2

You, therefore, do not pray for this people, and do not take up praise and prayer for them, for I will not hear in the time of their crying to me, in the time of their affliction! Jeremiah is commanded not to wish to entreat the Lord for those against whom the sentence has already been completed, lest his prayer should seem weak and should not be heard because of their own crimes. 'Do not', he says, 'pray for them, nor take up praise, striving, by recounting the clemency of the ancient history with which I have always had mercy on him, and by praising me, to change my sentence! For even if you do this, I will not hear those who are forced to ask me in the time of necessity'. From which we learn that it is in vain for anyone to ask on behalf of another, when the one for whom God is asked does not deserve to receive.

And the other half shall be split toward the west and the sea, with a very great chasm: this is the people of the circumcision, to whom God speaks through the prophet: Why has my beloved done abomination in my house? Shall vows and holy flesh take away your wickedness from you, or will you escape by these? This beloved did abomination in the house of God, so that she crucified the Son of God and heard: The Lord called your name a shady olive tree and a wooded beauty; and your branches became useless, which were broken off from the good root, so that we might be grafted in their place.

What is it that my beloved has done many crimes in my house? Will holy flesh take away from you your wickednesses, in which you have gloried? A rich olive, beautiful, fruitful, comely, the Lord called your name; at the sound of a great speech a fire blazed up in it, and its thickets were burned up. He calls beloved and most dear the people of Judah, which set up idols in his temple and worshiped them, and thinks that in it it appeases the wrath of God if it sacrifices many offerings, and glories in the multitude of sacrifices, which cannot take away the wickednesses of sins. He compares Jerusalem, or the whole people of the Jews, to a beautiful and fruitful olive, which, exalted through pride, by no means acted humbly nor understood its creator and ruler, but, lifted up through pride and having spoken grandly, was set on fire by the fire of the Lord, so that its branches or thickets were burned up and reduced to nothing, that is, the whole people was destroyed by the sword of the adversaries. This sense is found in another place too, where it is said to Jerusalem: I planted you a fruit-bearing vine, wholly true; how have you been turned into bitterness, O alien vine? When its walls are torn down and the boar from the forest lays it waste and all the beasts devour its fruits, let us say this passage to the princes of the churches: What is it that my beloved has done many crimes in my house? Or else to the rich, who, while they plunder what belongs to others and do not take away the wickednesses of their heart, think that they merit the clemency of God: Will holy flesh take away from you your wickednesses, in which you have gloried? But now the names of those who make offerings are recited publicly, and the redemption of sins is turned into praise, nor do they remember that widow in the Gospel who, by casting two coins into the treasury, surpassed the gifts of all the rich.

And the Lord of hosts, who planted you, has spoken evil against you for the evils of the house of Israel and of the house of Judah, which they did to themselves to provoke me, pouring libations to the Baals. 'A rich olive,' he says, 'beautiful, fruitful, your Lord called you, and he planted you; but because at the sound of the great speech of God a flame came down upon you and consumed all your branches, therefore he who had planted you has now spoken evil against you, not out of the injustice of his sentence nor out of a sudden perversity of speech, but for the evils which the house of Israel and the house of Judah did to themselves and zealously carried out, pouring libations to the Baals, so as to provoke me to anger'. And although God can do what he wills, he gives his reasons, lest he should seem to act unjustly, according to that which is written: that you may be justified in your words and may overcome when you are judged.

If there are oracles of God in the Law and the Prophets, in the Gospels and the Apostles, then whoever is being made a disciple by the oracles of God will need to inscribe God as his teacher; for "he who teaches man knowledge" is God, as it is also written in the Psalms. And the Savior too testifies that no one should be inscribed as a teacher upon the earth, saying, "And do not call anyone teacher upon the earth; for one is your teacher, the Father who is in the heavens." But "the Father who is in the heavens" teaches either by himself, or through Christ, or in the Holy Spirit, or through Paul, let us say, or through Peter, or through some other of the saints — only let the Spirit of God and the Word of God be present and teach. And for what purpose have I said these things? Because the prophet says, "Make it known to me, Lord, and I will know"; for I will not know unless you make it known to me; but if, when you make it known to me, I know, "then I will see their practices" and I will understand what each one does and of what disposition he is.
That the Jews would fasten Christ to the cross.… Also in Jeremiah: "Come, let us cast the tree into his bread, and let us blot out his life from the earth."
Treatise XII. Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews 2:20

Jeremiah, too, said, "Show me, O Lord, and I shall know. Then I saw their plots. And I was carried as a meek lamb to be the victim. They devised counsels against me, saying, 'Let us put wood on his bread and cut him off from the land of the living, and his name shall be remembered no more.' " Now the wood signifies the cross and the bread his body, because he is himself the food and life of all who believe in the flesh that he put on and by which he hung on the cross.

Listen to Jeremiah and be convinced: "I was as a meek lamb that is carried to be a victim. Did I not know it?" (Read it thus as a question, as I have put it. For he who said, "You know that after two days the Passover shall be here, and the Son of man will be delivered up to be crucified," did he not know?) "I was a meek lamb that is carried to be a victim. Did I not know it?" (What sort of lamb? Let John the Baptist interpret, when he says, "Behold the lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world!") "They devised a wicked counsel against me, saying (Was it that he who knew the counsels did not know their result? And what did they say?): "Come, and let us put wood on his bread." (If the Lord shall count you worthy, hereafter you shall learn that his body, according to the Gospel, bore the figure of bread.) "Come, and let us put wood on his bread, and cut him off from the land of the living (Life is not cut off. Why do you toil to no purpose?) And let his name be remembered no more."

He was led to the cross, and the life of the whole world hung suspended from its wood. Would you care to have this, too, confirmed by the testimony of prophets? Listen to what Jeremiah has to say about it: "Come, and let us put wood on his bread, and let us cut him off from the land of the living." Moses again, lamenting over them, remarked, "And your life shall be hanging suspended before your eyes, and you shall fear by day and by night, neither shall you trust your life."

But you, O Lord, have shown me and I have known; then you showed me their pursuits. And I was like a gentle lamb that is carried to be a victim, and I did not know that they had devised counsels against me: Let us put wood into his bread and crush him from the land of the living, and let his name be remembered no more! But you, O Lord of Sabaoth, who judge justly and test the reins and the heart, let me see your vengeance on them! For to you I have revealed my cause. This is the consensus of all the churches, that they understand these words to be spoken by Christ under the person of Jeremiah: that the Father showed him how he ought to speak, and showed him the pursuits of the Jews, and that he himself, like a lamb led to be a victim, did not open his mouth and did not know — 'sin' is understood, according to what is said by the Apostle: who, though he had not known sin, was made sin for us —, and that they said: Let us put wood into his bread — namely the cross into the body of the Savior; for he it is who says: I am the bread that came down from heaven, — and let us root him out — or crush him — from the land of the living! For this crime they devised in their mind, to blot out his name forever. But on the contrary, according to the mystery of the body he had assumed, the Son speaks to the Father and calls down his judgment, while he praises his righteousness and invokes God as the inspector of reins and heart, that he himself may render to the people what it deserves, and he says: let me see your vengeance on them — namely on those who persist in crime, and not on those who turn to repentance; of these he says on the cross: Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they do —, and he reveals to the Father and lays open his cause, that he was crucified through no fault of his own but by the crime of the people, saying: Behold, the prince of this world comes and finds nothing in me. The Jews and our Judaizers understand these words to be spoken in the person of Jeremiah, and they maintain that he endured these things from the people because of his prophecy of things to come and because of the impending evils of the captivity. But I do not know how they can prove that Jeremiah was crucified, since Scripture does not record it, unless perhaps they devised it and did not do it.

The careful student of the sacred books, moreover, may gather not a few similar passages from the prophets, as where He calls Himself a chosen shaft, and a servant of God, and a light of the Gentiles. Isaiah also says, "From my mother's womb hath He called me by my name, and He made my mouth as a sharp sword, and under the shadow of His hand did He hide me, and He said to me, Thou art My servant, O Israel, and in thee will I be glorified." And a little farther on: "And my God shall be my strength, and He said to me, This is a great thing for thee to be called My servant, to set up the tribes of Jacob and to turn again the diaspora of Israel. Behold I have set thee for a light of the Gentiles, that thou shouldest be for salvation to the end of the earth." And in Jeremiah too He likens Himself to a lamb, as thus: "I was as a gentle lamb that is led to the slaughter." These and other similar sayings He applies to Himself. In addition to these one might collect in the Gospels and the Apostles and in the prophets a countless number of titles which are applied to the Son of God, as the writers of the Gospels set forth their own views of what He is, or the Apostles extol Him out of what they had learned, or the prophets proclaim in advance His coming advent and announce the things concerning Him under various names. Thus John calls Him the Lamb of God, saying, "Behold the Lamb of God which taketh away the sins of the world."
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 1:23

If we examine the declaration about Jesus who is pointed out by John in the words, "This is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world," from the standpoint of the dispensation itself of the bodily sojourn of the Son of God in the life of people, we will assume that the lamb is none other than his humanity. For he was "led as a sheep to the slaughter and was dumb as a lamb before its shearer," saying, "I was as an innocent lamb being led to be sacrificed."
COMMENTARY ON ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 6:35

These are the prophet's words. Then let us see what the Savior says in the prophet: "I, like an innocent lamb led to be sacrificed, did not know. Against me they devised a device, saying, Come and let us cast wood into his bread, and let us wipe him out from the land of the living, and his name shall no more be remembered." As the prophet Isaiah also says, Christ "was led as a sheep to slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth." There, then, Isaiah speaks about him, but here Christ says about himself, "I, like an innocent lamb led to slaughter to be sacrificed, did not know." He did not say what he did not know. For he has not said, "I did not know evils"; he has not said, "I did not know good things"; nor has he said, "I did not know sin"; but simply, "I did not know." To you, then, he has left it to examine what he did not know. And learn what he did not know from this: "the one who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf"; for to know sin is to sin, just as to know righteousness is to act righteously. Therefore the one who proclaims the things concerning righteousness and does not act righteously has not known righteousness.

"Against me they devised a device, saying, Come and let us cast wood into his bread." That the Jews crucified him is clear, and we proclaim this with boldness. But how you are to fit this to "they devised a device against me, saying, Come and let us cast wood into his bread" is a work to understand. The bread of Jesus is the word by which we are nourished. Since, therefore, while he was teaching among the people, they wished to add the stumbling-block to his teaching by crucifying him, they said, "Let us cast wood into his bread." For whenever the crucifixion of the teacher is attached to the word of Jesus' teaching, wood has been cast into his bread. Let those men, then, having plotted out of conspiracy, say, "Come and let us cast wood into his bread." But I will say something more paradoxical: the wood cast into his bread has made the bread better. I take an example from the Law of Moses: the wood cast into the bitter water made it sweet. Thus the wood of the passion of Jesus Christ, coming into the word, has made his bread sweeter. Indeed, before the wood came into his bread, when it was only bread and there was no wood in his teaching, "his voice did not go out into all the earth." But since the bread took on power through the wood cast into it, on account of this the word of his teaching has been distributed throughout the whole inhabited world. And then the wood was the symbol of the passion of Jesus, through which the bitter water becomes sweet; for I say that the Law, when it is not understood, is bitter water, but if the wood of Jesus comes and the teaching of my Savior arrives, the Law of Moses, when it is read and understood, is sweetened and becomes most delightful.

They said, then, "Come and let us cast wood into his bread."

And they also say, "Let us wipe him out from the land of the living, and his name shall no more be remembered." Thus they killed him, as though obliterating his name. But Jesus knows how he dies and for what reason. Therefore he says, "Unless the grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit"; so that the death of Jesus becomes an ear of wheat, making what was sown many times multiplied and abundant. So that, if by hypothesis he had not been crucified nor died, the grain of wheat would have remained alone, and many would not have come from it. Attend, then, to his wording, whether he did not mean to say this: "The grain of wheat, unless it falls into the earth and dies, remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit." The death of Jesus bore all these as fruit; and if his death bore so many as fruit, how many will the resurrection bear as fruit?

While then the better, the great and worthy and divine sacrifice was not yet available for men, it was necessary for them by the offering of animals to pay a ransom for their own life, and this was fitly a life that represented their own nature. Thus did the holy men of old, anticipating by the Holy Spirit that a holy victim, dear to God and great, would one day come for men, as the offering for the sins of the world, believing that as prophets they must perform in symbol his sacrifice, and shew forth in type what was yet to be. But when that which was perfect was come, in accordance with the predictions of the prophets, the former sacrifices ceased at once because of the better and true Sacrifice.

This Sacrifice was the Christ of God, from far distant times foretold as coming to men, to be sacrificed like a sheep for the whole human race. As Isaiah the prophet says of him:

"As a sheep he was led to slaughter, and as a lamb dumb before her shearers."

And he adds:

"4. He bears our sins and is pained for us; yet we accounted him to be in trouble, and in suffering and in affliction. 5. But he was wounded on account of our sins, and he was made sick on account of our iniquities, the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and with his stripe we are healed. ... 6. And the Lord hath given him up for our iniquities ... .9 for he did no sin himself, nor was guile found in his mouth.''

Jeremiah, another Hebrew prophet, speaks similarly in the person of Christ: "I was led as a lamb to the slaughter."

John Baptist sets the seal on their predictions at the appearance of our Saviour. For beholding Him, and pointing Him out to those present as the one foretold by the prophets, he cried: "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.''

Since then according to the witness of the prophets the great and precious ransom has been found for Jews and Greeks alike, the propitiation for the whole world, the life given for the life of all men, the pure offering for every stain and sin, the Lamb of God, the holy sheep dear to God, the Lamb that was foretold, by Whose inspired and mystic teaching all we Gentiles have procured the forgive ness of our former sins, and such Jews as hope in Him are freed from the curse of Moses, daily celebrating His memorial, the remembrance of His Body and Blood, and are admitted to a greater sacrifice than that of the ancient law, we do not reckon it right to fall back upon the first beggarly elements, which are symbols and likenesses but do not contain the truth itself.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter 10

And hearken unto the prophet who also proclaimed our Lord with his simple teaching, and who likened Him unto a lamb and a sheep, the most innocent of all animals: "Like a lamb was He led to the slaughter, and like a sheep before the shearer He was silent." The lion and the wolf and bear are crafty, together with the other wild beasts, because craftiness was mingled with their evil nature when they were made; but sheep and lambs and ewes are simple and innocent in their ways and movements, and to them was our Lord likened, and by their name are believers called. Our Lord did not liken Himself unto a lion, which bringeth suffering and death, and He did not call His flocks by the names of wild animals, which by the nature in which they were created are cunning in respect of evil things, but He was called "lamb" and "sheep", and being meek like unto them He was led to suffering and to death, for "like a sheep before his shearer He was silent", and thus He in His humility opened not His mouth.
13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 5 -- Second Discourse on Simplicity
