He wishes the one who gives "glory to God" to give "glory to God" while there is light, since the glory of God cannot be proclaimed once it has grown dark and darkness has come. When, then, does it grow dark, and when does the darkening not occur? "Work while the light is in you." "The light is in" you if you have in you the one who said: "I am the light of the world." As long as this rises for you, glorify God; but know that a certain darkening can occur, and one must not let this darkening remain, but must give glory to God before it grows dark.

Perhaps we shall understand what is written by using an evangelical saying spoken by the Savior which runs thus: "Work while it is day; night comes when no one is able to work." He named there this present age "day" (but I necessarily added the "there"; for I know that in other places other things again are indicated) — he named, then, this present age "day," but darkness and night the consummation, because of the punishments. For "why do you desire the day of the Lord? And this is darkness and not light," says the prophet Amos. If you see what the gloom is after the consummation of the world, that which follows when almost the whole race of men is punished for the things they have sinned, you will see that then that which surrounds has grown dark, and no one any longer is able to glorify God, seeing that the word of God commanded even the righteous, saying: "Go, my people, enter into your chamber, shut your door, hide yourself for a little while, until the wrath of my anger pass by." And at the same time, in these words, let anyone who is able observe that he said: "a little while." But that "little while" is little for God; it is not little for a man; for one must see that for each thing there is something little and something great. And from an example I shall demonstrate that for each thing there is something little or great. For every animal such-and-such an amount of food is little in comparison with its constitution, and such-and-such an amount of food is much again in comparison with its constitution. And thus what is little for a man is great for another animal. What is little, for example, for a man is much for a child. Thus the whole time of human life is little, even the time of the long-lived man, in comparison with the whole of the entire present age. So indeed the "little" of God is much in comparison with us, and a whole age is the "little" of God. If, then, it is said: "Go, my people, enter into your chambers, shut your door, hide yourself for a little while," that "little" must be thought to be spoken not in relation to the condition of the one commanded to go and to enter into his chambers, but in relation to the condition of the one who commands these things, for whom that which is much for this man is little. For if, "until the wrath of the anger" of God "pass by," some must enter into their chambers, and there are those for whom "the sins are not forgiven, not only throughout this whole age but also throughout the whole age to come," it is clear that the "little" is extended alongside the things that have been said.

"Give," therefore, "glory to the Lord our God." How do we give glory to the Lord our God? It is not in voices and little phrases that I seek the giving of glory to the Lord our God, but in deeds the one who gives glory to the Lord God gives glory to him. Glorify God in self-control (sōphrosynē), in righteousness, in doing good glorify God; give glory to God in courage and endurance, give glory to God in piety and holiness and the remaining virtues. And if these things are so, and one glorifies God in this way, then if I state the opposite, do not think that I am blaspheming; for I will bring forward the Scripture as a witness of those things too. The self-controlled man glorifies God, the one who lives licentiously dishonors God. For, like Nebuchadnezzar, he overturns the temple of God and "corrupts the temple of God" and "through the transgression of the law dishonors God" (this too is an apostolic expression). The sinner, then, clothes God with dishonor. And questions are raised concerning providence, so that some doubt whether providence exists; but providence is nothing other than [what is questioned] on account of evil. Take away the evil, and you do not stumble against providence. But up and down those who stumble against providence say these things: why are there so many adulterers and so many effeminate men, why are there so many godless and impious people? And it is the sinners who beget dishonor for providence, stumbling-blocks against God, blasphemy against the one who created the world. Some, then, do give glory to God, but they do not give glory to God who do the things opposite to the glory of God through their sins.

"Give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains." There are certain dark mountains, there are certain luminous mountains; but since there are both. The luminous mountains are the holy angels of God, the prophets, Moses the servant, the apostles of Jesus Christ. All these are luminous mountains, and I think it is concerning these that it has been said in the Psalms: "His foundations are in the holy mountains." But what sort of mountains are dark? Those who raise up high things against the knowledge of God. The devil is a dark mountain; the rulers of this age who are being brought to nothing are dark mountains; and the demon, the epilepsy (moon-affliction), was a mountain, and it was a dark mountain, concerning which the Savior said: "You shall say to this mountain." For when the discussion concerned the epilepsy and the disciples said, "Why were we not able to cast it out?", the Savior answers that "if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you shall say to this mountain," concerning which you put forward the question, concerning which you inquired, "you shall say to this mountain: Move from here to there, and it shall move." "From here" — away from the man; "there" — to its own proper place. Those, then, who stumble do not stumble upon luminous mountains, but upon dark mountains, whenever they come to be with the devil and his angels, the dark mountains.

"And you shall wait for light." Now "and you shall wait for light" can be joined to "give glory to the Lord our God." If you give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, before your feet stumble upon dark mountains," it is clear that, even if it does grow dark, "you shall wait for the light" and the light shall receive you in succession. But another might say (I do not know whether he is thinking soundly or not) that even those who stumble "upon dark mountains" shall wait beside the dark mountains, waiting for the light of mercy; for this is what "and you shall wait for light" would seem to mean. But when one comes upon the dark mountains, let us see what is there: "the shadow of death." Where the dark mountains are, there is the shadow of death, begotten from those very dark mountains; "and they shall be set in darkness."

'But if', he says, 'you refuse to hear me, secretly' — according to Aquila 'in darkness' — 'the soul will weep, mine' — or, according to the Seventy, 'yours' — 'before the face of pride, so that not even groaning and weeping may be free, lest the eyes of the victors be offended'. But we can also interpret this passage thus: the Savior speaks: 'Work while it is day; the night will come, when no one can work any longer'. Of this time there is also the prophecy of Isaiah: For the stars of heaven and Orion and all the adornment of heaven will not give light, and they will be darkened at the rising of the sun, and the moon will not give light. Zephaniah too agrees in the same words, saying: A day of tribulation and distress, a day of misery and perdition, a day of darkness and whirlwind, a day of cloud and gloom. Before, therefore, the time of judgment arrives and our feet stumble upon the dark mountains, namely the adverse powers that are set over torments and tortures, let us do repentance, lest, waiting for light, we be wrapped in the darkness of night; and let us know that, unless we do this, the soul either of God or of the prophet will weep before the face of our pride, who refuse to hear the words of God. Hence the prophet himself also says:

Give glory to the Lord our God, before it grows dark and before your feet stumble upon the misty — or dark — mountains! You will wait for light, and there will be the shadow of death, and they will be placed in darkness — or, according to the Hebrew: and he will set it in the shadow of death and in gloom —. But if you do not hear, in secret the soul will weep, mine — or yours — before the face of pride or injury. Those to whom the divine word had said: Hear and perceive with your ears and do not be lifted up, he now calls to repentance, that, before they are led to Babylon and their feet stumble upon the dark or misty mountains, they should give glory to God. Hence sinners too are often told: Give glory to God! And that Babylon and the whole region of the Chaldeans are called misty or dark mountains we read at the beginning of Isaiah, against Babylon, where it is written: Upon the misty mountain lift up a sign, which in Hebrew is called 'neseptha'. This therefore he commands: that, before they are led into captivity and feel the evils of servitude, they should do repentance, since, when they wait for light, they are to sit in darkness.

"But if you do not hear in secret, your soul shall weep before the face of insolence." Of those who hear, some hear in secret, but others, even if they hear, do not hear in secret. What then is it to hear in secret, other than "but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom, which God foreordained before the ages for our glory"? And again elsewhere it is said that "the greater part of the works of God are in hidden things." If I hear the law, either I hear in secret or I do not hear in secret. The Jew does not hear the law in secret; therefore he is circumcised openly, not knowing that "the Jew is not the one in the open, nor is circumcision that which is in the open in the flesh." But he who hears about circumcision in secret shall be circumcised in what is hidden; he who hears in secret the things enacted by law concerning the Passover eats of the lamb Christ (for "Christ our Passover has been sacrificed"), and knowing what sort of thing the flesh of the Word is, and knowing that "it is true food," he partakes of it; for he heard about the Passover in secret. But this great mass of the Jew, for this reason, killed the Lord Jesus and is even today guilty of the murder of Jesus, since he heard neither the law nor the prophets in secret. If you read about the unleavened bread, it is possible to hear in secret, it is possible to hear the commandment openly. As many of you (for the Passover is near) as keep the unleavened bread, the bodily unleavened bread, do not hear the commandment that says: "If you do not hear in secret, your soul shall weep." And concerning the Sabbath, women who have not heard the prophet do not hear in secret, but hear openly. They do not wash on the day of the Sabbath, they return "to the poor and weak elements," as though Christ had not sojourned among us, the one who perfects us and carries us over from the elements of the law to the perfection of the Gospel.

Therefore let us take heed as we read the law and the prophets, lest we ever fall under the prophecy that says: "But if you do not hear in secret, your soul shall weep before the face of insolence." As many of you as observe the Jewish fast, as though not understanding the day of atonement, keep it after the sojourn of Jesus Christ. You did not hear about the atonement in secret, but you heard openly; for to hear about the atonement in secret is to hear how God made Jesus a propitiation concerning our sins, and that "he is the propitiation concerning our sins, and not concerning ours only, but also concerning the whole world." And even if evangelical parables are read and the hearer is of those outside, he will not hear them in secret. But if the hearer is an apostle or one of those who enter "into the house" of Jesus, he approaches Jesus, and he inquires also about the obscurity of the parable, and Jesus interprets it, and that hearer of the Gospel comes to hear it in secret, so that his soul may not weep; for the soul of those who do not hear in secret weeps.

Why, marvelously, did he not say: you shall weep, if you do not hear in secret, but rather: "your soul shall weep"? There is a certain weeping of the soul alone weeping, and perhaps the Savior teaches us that weeping when he says: "There shall be the weeping." And even if he says: "Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep," he speaks concerning that weeping, which the prophet here also threatens, saying: "But if you do not hear in secret, your soul shall weep before the face of insolence." For when you are treated with insolence, then you shall weep and your eyes shall bring down tears, "because the flock of the Lord has been crushed." If someone now looks at the affairs of the Jews and compares them with the ancient things, he will see in what manner "the flock of the Lord has been crushed." For this was once the flock of the Lord, and since they judged themselves unworthy, the word was turned to the nations. If, then, that flock of the Lord was crushed, ought not we, the wild olive, grafted contrary to its own nature into the cultivated olive of the fathers, to fear all the more, lest this "flock of the Lord" too be crushed? For it is destined to be crushed at some time, according to what was said by the Savior, when "because lawlessness is multiplied, the love of the many shall grow cold." For concerning whom is the word? Is not "the love of the many shall grow cold" said concerning those called Christians? Concerning whom is the word, that "yet when the Son of Man comes, will he then find faith upon the earth"? Is it not concerning us? Therefore let us take heed to ourselves in all that we do, so that day by day this flock of God may be made better, may be made healthy, may be healed, and that all crushing may depart from our souls, so that we may be perfected in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the might unto the ages. Amen.

Weeping, Jerusalem shall weep — or weeping, it shall weep — and my eye shall shed a tear, and I cannot conceal my grief in silent groans; but the whole cause of the torments is that the flock of the Lord has been taken captive. Let us say to the Jews and to our own Judaizers, who follow only the simple and killing history: Unless you hear secretly, that is, in mystery or in darkness, which God has made his hiding place, and, according to Solomon, so as to understand a parable and a dark saying, the soul will weep, the prophet's or their own, before the face of pride, while through contumacy they resist God. Hence there will also be continual weeping and perpetual tears, because the flock of the Lord has been taken captive and corrupted by the true Nebuchadnezzar.

The cities of the south are shut up, that is, the tribe of Judah and Jerusalem, which, lying next to the desert, faces toward the south, and there is none who opens them, surrounded as they are by siege. All Judea has been carried away — or all Judah — with exile complete, or 'it has received what it deserved, and it has been fulfilled in it'; for so the Seventy translated. He raves in this place who understands the king as Christ and the mighty as angels or apostles, as if they were to take on the body of humility and sit in the dust and lose — either the king or the mighty — from their head the crown and the glory of strength. He also interprets the shut cities of the south as hell, as cities opened to no one, and says that all the glory of Judah was carried away when there was fulfilled in the passion: All have turned aside, together they have become useless; there is none who does good, there is not even one. The Hebrew word 'gebira' Aquila and Symmachus translated 'mistress' and 'lady'; the Seventy thought it was 'geburoth' and said 'the mighty'.

Say to the king and to the mistress — or say to the king and to the mighty —: Humble yourselves, sit down, for there has come down — or there has been taken away — from your head the crown of your glory! The cities of the south are shut up, and there is none who opens; all Judea has been carried away — or all Judah has been carried away — with exile complete — or captivity —. The prophet is commanded to speak to King Jeconiah and to his mother, whom he calls lady and mistress or queen, that they should humble themselves and sit in the dust; for they have lost the royal dignity and are to be handed over to the Babylonian king.

Lift up your eyes and see those who are coming — or you who are coming — from the north! Where is the flock that was given to you, your glorious herd? What will you say when he visits you? For you teach them against yourself and instruct them to your own head. The inhabitants of Jerusalem are commanded to lift up their eyes and see the Chaldeans coming from the region of the north; and the city herself is questioned, and it is said to her: 'Where is the flock that was given to you, your glorious herd? Where is your people, which you had received from God? Where is that multitude, so great and glorious that you would have believed the crowd of a whole province gathered into one place? What will you say when he visits you, the Lord, with his rod, and hands you over to the Babylonian enemies, whom you yourself taught against you, either to your own head or from the beginning, so that you fled to their help and followed their idols — they who, under the pretext of your friendship, learned by what road they should come to you?' Let the negligent Church hear this, that she herself teaches her adversaries how they can seize her in a spiritual captivity and tear her herd with the cruelty of beasts.

Will not pains seize you like a woman in labor? But if you say in your heart: Why have these things come upon me? Because of the multitude of your iniquity your more shameful parts have been uncovered, your soles have been polluted — or have been dishonored —. 'While you do not know it, as a sudden childbirth seizes a woman, so a sudden captivity will seize you. But if you wish to complain and ask why you have been handed over to enemies, hear plainly that the multitude of your iniquity has done these things to you, so that, as of a harlot woman whose garments have been lifted, your ignominy has been uncovered and your fornications have been shown in public'. By these things we learn that, so long as sins are lesser, God acts patiently and waits for our repentance; but if we choose to join offenses to offenses and to make a heap of sins, our shameful parts will be uncovered and our soles will be shown to all, either in the present age or in the future. For there is nothing hidden that will not be made manifest, when that word of Daniel will be fulfilled: These shall rise to eternal life and those to reproach and to everlasting confusion.

For as the prophet speaks," If the Ethiopian changes his skin, or the leopard his spots," then will they be willing to think religiously who have been instructed in irreligion. You, however, beloved, on receiving this, read it by yourself. If you approve of it, read it also to the brethren who happen to be present, that they, too, on hearing it, may welcome the council's zeal for the truth and the exactness of its sense and may condemn that of Christ's foes, the Arians, and the futile pretenses, which for the sake of their irreligious heresy they have been at the pains to frame among themselves.

Afterwards he came to Cilicia, and, on meeting with a certain Gelasius, showed him the creed which only an Arian, or a thorough disciple of Arius, could subscribe. Then, indeed, I was yet more confirmed in my alienation from him. I felt that the Ethiopian will never change his skin, nor the leopard his spots, nor a man nurtured in doctrines of perversity ever be able to rub off the stain of his heresy.

And if, "they could not," is put, instead of, "they would not," do not marvel, for He saith also in another place, "He that is able to receive it, let him receive it." So in many places He is wont to term choice, power... And what saith the Prophet? "If the Ethiopian shall change his skin, or the leopard his spots, this people also shall be able to do good, having learned evil." He saith not that the doing of virtue is impossible to them, but that because they will not, therefore they cannot.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 68

By the reading of the prophet the eunuch of Candace, the queen of Ethiopia, is made ready for the baptism of Christ. Though it is against nature, the Ethiopian does change his skin, and the leopard his spots.

Then immediately quickening her pace, she began to move along the old road that leads to Gaza, that is, to the "power" or "wealth" of God, silently meditating on that type of the Gentiles, the Ethiopian eunuch, who, in spite of the prophet, changed his skin and, while he read the Old Testament, found the fountain of the gospel.

If the Ethiopian can change his skin or the leopard its spots, you too will be able to do good, when you have learned evil. This testimony is used against the Church by those who desire to assert diverse natures, and they say that the blackness or the variegation of sins is so great that they cannot pass into whiteness and the beauty of a single color, not attending to what follows: and you will be able to do good, when you have learned evil. For whatever is learned is not of nature but of effort and of one's own will, which through excessive habit and love of sinning is in a manner turned into nature. But this, which is impossible for men, is possible for God: so that it is by no means the Ethiopian and the leopard who are seen to change their nature, but he who works in the Ethiopian and the leopard, as the Apostle says: I can do all things in him who strengthens me, Christ. Hence also in another place: I labored, he says, more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which is in me, and: I live, now not I, but Christ lives in me. And again we read it written: What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you glory as if you had not received it? For these reasons let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches, nor the chaste man in his chastity, knowing that in all these things it is the power of Christ, not of those who glory in their virtues.

Chus in the Hebrew tongue is interpreted 'Ethiopian,' that is, black and dark, who has such a soul as he has a body, of whom Jeremiah says: 'If the Ethiopian will change his skin, or the leopard his spots.' So this Chusi signifies his black and Ethiopian enemy, Saul. And he says this: As the Ethiopian cannot change his skin, so this man too cannot change his character. Twice he came into my hands, I could have killed him. Whose blood I could have shed, I wished rather to overcome him by kindness; but his malice cannot be conquered. For just as the Ethiopian's skin cannot be changed, so too his malice cannot be changed.

Also, he showed so much love in his religion that, leaving behind a queen's court, he came from the farthest regions of the world to the Lord's temple. Hence, as a just reward, while he sought the interpretation of something that he was reading, he found Christ, whom he was seeking. Furthermore, as Jerome says, he found the church's font there in the desert, rather than in the golden temple of the synagogue. For there in the desert something happened that Jeremiah declared was to be wondered at, an Ethiopian changed his skin, that is, with the stain of his sins washed away by the waters of baptism, he went up, shining white, to Jesus.

And I will scatter them like stubble that is snatched away by the wind in the desert. This is your lot and the portion of your measure from me, says the Lord or and the portion of your disobedience against me. 'Because through excessive habit of evils they could not change their nature — not by the fault of the Creator, but by the pursuit of ingrained wickedness —, therefore I will scatter them like stubble snatched away by the wind into the wilderness, according to what is written elsewhere: like the dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth'.

Because you have forgotten me and trusted — or hoped — in falsehood, therefore I too have bared — or will bare and will uncover — your thighs — and hinder parts — before your face, and your ignominy will appear, your adulteries and your neighing, the wickedness — or estrangement — of your fornication. The cause of the scattering of Jerusalem is that she has forgotten God and trusted or hoped in falsehoods. He who, apart from God, trusts in the things of the world forgets God. Hence his thighs or hinder parts are uncovered, so that he may see his own ignominy, and the things that ought to be behind may come to the front, and he himself may perceive what he has done, and his ignominy may appear not only to himself but to all. Your adulteries, he says, and your neighing shows not lust alone but the madness of lust, after the manner of mares that are eager for coupling, as in that line of Vergil: hippomanes, as the shepherds call it by a true name, a sticky venom drips from the groin. Let us ask Jesus that neither in the present age nor in the future he uncover our thighs and hinder parts, but that he blot out our iniquities and not let all our crimes appear.

And he makes an apostrophe to Jerusalem herself: that this is her lot and this the portion which she herself has chosen, a measure heaped up and full and running over, or the portion of her disobedience, by which she would not acquiesce to the Lord; for with what measure she has measured, it will be measured back to her.

But if even real virgins, when they have other failings, are not saved by their physical virginity, what shall become of those who have prostituted the members of Christ and have changed the temple of the Holy Spirit into a brothel? Immediately they should hear the words, "Come down and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground—there is no throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans. You shall no more be called tender and delicate. Take the millstone and grind meal. Uncover your locks, make bare your legs, pass over the rivers. Your nakedness shall be uncovered. Yes, your shame shall be seen." Shall she come to this after the bridal chamber of God the Son, after the kisses of him who is to her both kinsman and spouse? Yes, she of whom the prophetic utterance once sang, "At your right hand stands the queen in gold of Ophir," shall be made naked, and her skirts shall be discovered on her face.

"After committing many transgressions," he says, "you were not prepared to have recourse to repentance. I shall no longer demonstrate longsuffering. Instead, I will inflict punishment." It is better, therefore, to live according to the divine laws. But since we who are human will most likely fall at some point, we ought to have recourse to the remedies of repentance, and through them placate the judge and escape the experience of the punishments he threatens. May we for our part continue to not experience them, thanks to the grace and lovingkindness of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Upon the hills in the field I have seen your abominations. Woe to you, Jerusalem! You will not be cleansed — or because you have not been cleansed — after me; how long yet? 'Not only in the midst of the city of Jerusalem but on every hill and in all regions I have seen your idols'; hence it is said to her: 'Woe to you, Jerusalem, because you have not been cleansed after me, so that, though you boasted that you followed my footsteps and paraded the confession of my name, yet you have never been purified, because you have forgotten me and hoped in falsehoods'. Hence he rebukes her and says: How long yet? And the sense is: 'How long shall I wait for you? How long shall I bear it? How long will you forget me to the end and despise my precepts?' He commits fornication on the hills and in the fields and is never cleansed, who, with neck erect through pride, is not humbled under the mighty hand of God but trusts in his own crimes and vices.
14: It will serve us to remember that what is called the Word came to certain persons, as "the word of the Lord which came to Hosea, the son of Beeri," and "the word which came to Isaiah, the son of Amoz, concerning Judah and concerning Jerusalem," and "the word that came to Jeremiah concerning the drought." We must inquire how this Word came to Hosea, and how it came also to Isaiah the son of Amoz, and again to Jeremiah concerning the drought. The comparison may enable us to find out how the Word was with God. We will generalize by simply looking at what the prophets said, as if that were the Word of the Lord or the Word that came to them. May it not be … that … the Son, the Word, of whom we are now theologizing, came to Hosea, sent to him by the Father, historically, that is to say, to the son of Beeri, the prophet Hosea.… Similarly the Word comes also to Isaiah, teaching the things that are coming on Judea and Jerusalem in the last days. So also it comes to Jeremiah lifted up by a divine elation.… Thus to find out what is meant by the phrase "the Word was with God," we have adduced the words used about the prophets, how he came to Hosea, to Isaiah, to Jeremiah.… We have to add that in his coming to the prophets he illuminates the prophets with the light of knowledge, causing them to see things that had been before them but that they had not understood until then.
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 2:1

The word of the Lord which came to Jeremiah concerning the words of the drought. All things are in accord with the wrath of God; hence the sun also sets at noon upon sinners, and the moon and the other stars do not give their light, and we must suppose that in the time of the siege there were no rains, so that the besieged endured a dearth of water. For the city uses a single spring, that of Siloam, and this not a perennial one, and to the present day a dearth of rains causes a lack not only of crops but also of water to drink.

Judea has mourned — or Judah — and its gates have fallen — or have been made empty — and have been darkened — or have been made dark — upon the earth, and the cry of Jerusalem has gone up. Its elders sent their lesser ones — or younger ones — to the water; they came to draw — or to the wells — and did not find water; they brought back their vessels empty. They were confounded and afflicted — or they blushed — and covered their heads; because of the desolation of the land — or and the works of the land, because they have failed —, because no rain came — or there was no rain — upon the land, the farmers were confounded, they covered their heads. In the time of drought, when the multitude suffers a famine of hearing and learning the word of God, Judea mourns, 'boasting' that it formerly had the worship of God and the 'confession' of the true faith; and its gates are either emptied or fall, which we ought to refer to the senses, through which instruction is conceived by the soul. Then all things are darkened and wrapped in darkness, and in Jerusalem it is by no means reason and the word of teaching that reign, but clamor and confusion.

The elders also, who ought themselves to go to draw the waters, send the younger ones, in whom there are no gray hairs of wisdom, and therefore they come to the wells and do not find the waters which, as the history relates, the patriarchs found. They bring back their vessels empty, the younger ones, that is, not because there were no waters, but because they could not find them. They were confounded and afflicted — or they blushed — and covered their heads — because they could not say with the Apostle: 'But we all, with unveiled face, behold the glory of the Lord' — because of the desolation of the land or and the works of the land have failed, through which we advance to the knowledge of God. And the cause is plain: because no rain came upon the land. For the clouds were commanded not to rain a shower upon it. The farmers also, one of whom says: You are God's husbandry, God's building and: We are God's fellow workers, cover their head and are confounded, understanding that without the grace and help of God they strive in vain.

For the hind also — or the hinds — gave birth in the field — or they gave birth — and forsook — or they forsook —, because there was no grass. And the wild asses stood on the crags, they drew in the wind like dragons; their eyes failed, because there was no grass or hay. Great is the barrenness when even the hinds give birth in the field and forsake their young because there is no grass or hay, so that they, which by the scent of their nostrils draw serpents out of their holes and kill venomous creatures, do not enjoy the food of grace; and when the wild asses also, of which it is written: Who has sent out the wild ass free into the wilderness?, leaving the plains and the open country, stand on the crags and cannot run, and draw in the wind after the likeness of dragons, and their eyes fail and cannot see the clear light, since rational food has been withdrawn. This drought often happens in the churches, when both stags and wild asses are found among the peoples and waste away through a dearth of teachers: there are those who could learn, and there are none who could teach.

If our iniquities have answered — or have withstood — us, O Lord, act for your name's sake, for many are our turnings away — or our sins —. Against you we have sinned, O expectation of Israel, his Savior in the time of tribulation. If we are in doubt why the rains do not come down upon the land, why all things wither with dryness, let us hear: our iniquities have withstood us; 'therefore, O Lord, not according to our works but according to your holy name, overcome our many turnings away. For against you we have sinned, whom the secrets of the heart do not deceive, and we wait for you, who are the true hope and expectation of Israel and save him in the time of tribulation, according to that which is written: To the Lord I cried when I was in tribulation, and he heard me'. Let us too say, in the time of drought and dearth of waters: 'Against you we have sinned and have done evil before you; we wait for your coming, you who save Israel not by its own merit but by your clemency.'

Why will you be like a settler in the land and like a traveler turning aside to lodge? Why will you be like a wandering man or a mighty one who cannot save? LXX: why have you become like a stranger in the land and like a native turning aside to lodge? Will you be like a man asleep and like a man who cannot save? The Jews understand this passage thus: 'Why do you separate yourself from your people and, like a traveler, for the refreshment of a single hour not care what lodging you use, but, being about to pass on to other places, not save your people and forsake the temple once renowned?' Our people, however, think that it is said of the future dispensation of Christ: that he was to be a pilgrim in the land and to use the hospitality of the earth for a short time, and, like a man passing through and strong, having left Israel, to make for the multitude of the Gentiles, so as to pass from place to place, from people to people, from the temple to the Church.

Again, the Scriptures speak of God as asleep when the psalmist says, "Arise! Why do you sleep, O Lord?" He does not say this to make us suspect that God sleeps. This would be the utmost madness. By the word sleep the psalm shows God's patience and forbearance toward us. Another prophet has said, "You will not be like a person who sleeps, will you?" Do you not see that we need much help from our understanding and reason when we are searching into the treasure house of the divine Scriptures? If we listen to the words only, if we do not think but take the words as they come, not only will those absurdities follow, but many a conflict will be seen in what has been said.

But what is said according to the Seventy: Will you be like a man asleep and like a man who cannot save? sets down a likeness, not the truth of the matter, according to that which is written: Arise, why do you sleep, O Lord?, not that the Lord sleeps, of whom it is said: He who keeps Israel will not slumber nor sleep, but that he seems to sleep to those whom he forsakes. Finally, in what follows too, it is not written: 'a man asleep', who cannot save, but: 'like a man'; in both, anthrōpopathōs [in human terms].

But you are in us, O Lord, and your name has been invoked upon us; do not forsake us or do not forget us! 'You who among the Jews will be like a stranger and a traveler and a wandering man, forsaking your ancient dwelling, dwell in us, and your name has been invoked upon us, so that we are called Christians; therefore do not forsake us nor forget us, to whom the mouths of all the prophets have sung of your future coming'.

Hence it is that they are always writing, and always altering their own previous statements, and thus they shew an uncertain faith, or rather a manifest unbelief and perverseness. And this, it appears to me, must needs be the case with them; for since, having fallen away from the truth, and desiring to overthrow that sound confession of faith which was drawn up at Nicaea, they have, in the language of Scripture, `loved to wander, and have not refrained their feet;' therefore, like Jerusalem of old, they labour and toil in their changes, sometimes writing one thing, and sometimes another, but only for the sake of gaining time, and that they may continue enemies of Christ, and deceivers of mankind.
LETTER TO THE BISHOPS OF EGYPT 1:6

Thus says the Lord to this people: because it has loved — or they have loved — to move its feet and has not rested — or they have not spared — and it has not pleased the Lord — or and God was not well pleased in them —, now he will remember their iniquities and will visit their sins. When the people says: 'Why have you become like a stranger and a traveler and a wanderer, so as to forsake your dwelling?', the Lord answers the people that was once his own: 'Do you wish to know the reason? Listen to what is said: because the people has loved to move its feet and has not withdrawn them from the fetter of sins, or has not rested and could not stand, therefore I too have forsaken it, and I have no good pleasure in it'. He, then, who long delayed and through patience was unwilling to punish sinners, since they persisted in wickedness, will remember their iniquities and will visit the sins of those who are, as it were, sick and do not perceive God, so that they may cease to sin any more. But it should be noted in the holy Scriptures that it is always the feet of sinners that are moved, while to the saints it is said, with Moses: But you, stand here with me, and elsewhere it is written: Praise the Lord, you servants, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God!

Although God is by nature good, yet he is also just, and as the case requires. He knows how to heal but also how to strike. He brings peace, but he brings about evil. He desires repentance, yet he commands Jeremiah not to intercede for the sinful people, since, he says, even if they fast, I will not hear their prayer.

In the Gospel, the Savior commends the unjust steward because, although he defrauded his master, he acted wisely for his own interests. The heretics in this instance pursued the same course. When they saw how great a matter a little fire had kindled, and that the flames applied by them to the foundations had by this time reached the housetops and that the deception practiced on many could no longer be hid, they asked for and obtained letters of commendation from the church, so that it might appear that until the day of their departure they had continued in full communion with it. Shortly afterward the distinguished Anastasius succeeded to the pontificate. But he was soon taken away, for it was not fitting that the head of the world should be struck off during the episcopate of one so great. He was removed, no doubt, that he might not seek to turn away by his prayers the sentence of God passed once for all. For the words of the Lord to Jeremiah concerning Israel applied equally to Rome: "Pray not for this people for their good. When they fast, I will not hear their cry. When they offer burnt offering and oblation, I will not accept them. But I will consume them by the sword and by the famine and by the pestilence."

And the Lord said to me: Do not pray for this people for good! When they fast, I will not hear their prayers, and if they offer burnt offerings and victims, I will not accept them, for by the sword and by famine and by pestilence I will consume them. It is foolish to pray for one who has sinned unto death, as John says: There is a sin unto death; I do not say that one should pray for that. All iniquity is sin, and there is a sin not unto death. Fasts and prayers and victims and burnt offerings profit only when we withdraw from vices and weep for our former sins; but if, persisting in our crimes, we think that we can buy the ears of God with vows and sacrifices, we greatly err, judging God to be unjust. For he who has once been destined for the sword and famine and pestilence cannot be rescued by any prayers. Hence the prophet too is told not to ask in vain for what he cannot obtain.

And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God — or you who are, Lord God —, the prophets say to them: You shall not see the sword, and famine shall not be among you, but he will give you true peace in this place. And the Lord said to me: The prophets prophesy falsely in my name. I did not send them, and I did not command them, nor did I speak to them; a lying vision and deceitful divination and the seduction of their own heart they prophesy to you. Let the teachers hear this who promise prosperity to those who sin and persist in their vices, who say to the rich: 'You shall not see the sword of God's torments, and famine shall not be among you. For you will be filled with the words of God, and the Lord will give you most true peace in the place of the Church, or of Jerusalem'. But that, according to the Hebrew, he said three times: Ah, ah, ah, answers to what came before, where the Lord had threatened, saying: by the sword and by famine and by pestilence I will consume them.

Since, then, the prophets, nay rather the false prophets, promised false things, the Lord therefore spoke through Jeremiah: 'Do not listen to the words of the false prophets, who were not sent by me but came of their own will! Hence they are by no means to be called prophets but diviners, they who speak seduction to the people'. For it is much better to amend sins through fear of punishments than, through hope of prosperity, to fall under the divine sentence.

Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who prophesy in my name, whom I did not send, saying: Sword and famine shall not be in this land: by sword and famine those prophets shall be consumed. And the peoples to whom they have prophesied shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem because of famine and sword, and there shall be none to bury them, they and their wives, their sons and their daughters, and I will pour out upon them their own evil or their own evils. Let the false prophets beware, who by promising prosperity trip up the people of God, lest they themselves perish and the deceived people be destroyed by a like ruin, and they lie in the streets of Jerusalem and, trampling on the precepts of the Lord, perish by famine and sword, and there be none to bury them nor to cover their disgrace with the dust of repentance. For the prophets themselves and the people, and their wives, and sons and daughters, and their whole generation will be on the dunghill without any undertaker. How many lie in the streets of Jerusalem! How many do we see unburied receiving their own evils, which they suffer as the Lord pours them out!

And you shall say this word to them: Let my eyes shed a tear — or let your eyes shed tears — through night and day, and let them not be silent — or let them not cease —, for the virgin daughter of my people has been crushed with a great crushing, with a most grievous blow, exceedingly. This passage is understood in two ways: either that God himself laments his people and his eyes do not cease to weep, or at any rate that he commands that the eyes of the peoples should flow with tears; and that what must be lamented is no light thing, since the virgin daughter of his people has been struck with the greatest crushing and an intolerable blow. Others think that these things are said in the person of the prophet.

If I go out into the fields, behold, those slain by the sword, and if I enter the city, behold, those wasted with famine — or the pain of famine —! The prophet also and the priest have gone off into a land which they did not know. A just cause for lamenting, that the virgin has been crushed, the daughter struck and the people destroyed. 'For if,' he says, 'I wish to go outside, I shall see the slain; if to enter the city, I shall behold those wasted and scarcely clinging to their bones through the necessity of famine'. And what wonder is it to say this of the common people and the ignoble crowd, when the prophets also and the priests, who prophesied prosperity to others and who ought to have opened the commandments of the law, themselves went into a land which they did not know and endured the evil of captivity? Let our prophets and priests hear this: that because of their negligence there is no security either within or without, since they both scandalize those who are without and allow those who are within to perish by famine, and those who were the authors of sinning become companions in the torments.

And blessed Daniel the prophet, the divine Ezekiel (who was both prophet and priest) and many other priests in addition to them shared in these misfortunes. For God provided for those profane exiles and sent along also prophets that could be pedagogues and teachers so that the exiles might not incline entirely to godlessness.

Have you utterly cast off Judah, or has your soul abhorred Zion? Why then have you struck us, so that there is no healing? We waited for peace, and there is no good, and for a time of healing, and behold, turmoil! The prophet marvels that the Lord has so suddenly cast off Judah and Jerusalem, that is, the kingdom of the two tribes, in which were the religion of God and the ceremonies of the temple, and has struck them with so great a blow that no medicine can be applied. 'We waited', he says, 'for peace and for a time of healing, and there is no good at all, but, on the contrary, turmoil, so that where formerly there had been the worship of God and tranquility, there all things were filled with seditions and the roar of the enemy'. If ever, therefore, our Zion too and our Judah is cast off and the soul of God abhors it, let us by no means marvel, but rather let us say what follows:

We have acknowledged, O Lord, our impieties, the iniquity of our fathers, because we have sinned against you. 'Both we', he says, 'and our fathers, with the same madness, neglected the precepts of God, and the measure of our forefathers has been filled up in us, so that whatever had been lacking in them was completed by our heap'. Hence it is also said of Judas: Let the iniquity of his fathers return to remembrance in the sight of the Lord, and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out! Let it be over against the Lord always, and let the memory of them perish from the earth!

Do not give us over to reproach for your name's sake, nor bring upon us the dishonor of the throne of your glory! Remember, do not make void your covenant with us! Let us consider the throne of God's glory to be not only the temple of Judea, which has often been destroyed, but every saint, in whom, according to that which is written: You have dashed his throne to the ground, it is dashed down and destroyed when he has offended God by a multitude of sins; but nevertheless he who has perished by his own fault is upheld by the clemency of the Lord, which is exchanged for the severity of the sentence if the Lord makes void his pact, by which he has promised that we shall be saved.

What a state the person is in who has deserted the easy yoke and the light burden of Christ to subject himself once again to the yoke of demons and to bear the burden of the heaviest sin! How can this be after we have known that the heart of those who worship idols is ashes and their life more worthless than clay, and after we have said, "Our ancestors possessed false idols, and none of them can bring rain"?

Are there among the graven images of the nations any that rain, or can the heavens give showers? Are you not the Lord God, whom we have awaited? For you have made all these things. After many and varied discourses he returns to the title of the prophecy, in which it is written: the word of the Lord which came to Jeremiah concerning the words of the drought. So what he says is this: 'Since the images of demons cannot rain, nor can the heavens of themselves give their shower, therefore you, O Lord our God, whom we have always awaited, to whom we have turned our hopes and vows, you give your rain! For all things are yours, and whatever is good cannot be given without you, whose it is'. Let us say this also against the heretics, who cannot bestow the rain of doctrines, and who, though they promise that they are heavens and boast that it is written of them: The heavens declare the glory of God, nevertheless cannot give the showers of doctrine. For it is God alone who instructs his people and bestows the diversities of grace on those who await him.
15: And the Lord said to me: if Moses and Samuel stand before me — or against me —, my soul is not toward this people. For we read that these men withstood the wrath of the Lord on behalf of the people and turned aside a sentence that was already impending. 'Even if', he says, 'they stand either in my sight or against me' — to one of whom God said: Let me alone, and I will strike this people —, 'yet I will not hear, because the crimes of the offending people are complete'.
Cast — or send — them out from my face, and let them go forth! Sinners withdraw from God not in place but in will, although we read that both Adam and Cain were cast out from the face of God.

Hence the Truth says: "When you stand to pray, forgive if you have anything in your hearts." We show the virtue of forgiveness more clearly if we bring forward one testimony from the Old Testament. Certainly when Judea had offended the justice of its Creator through its demanding sins, the Lord, forbidding His prophet from prayer, says: "Do not take up praise and prayer for them. If Moses and Samuel stood before me, my soul would not be toward this people." What is it that, with so many fathers passed over and left aside, Moses and Samuel alone are brought forward, whose wondrous power of obtaining is shown, while even they are said to be unable to intercede? As if the Lord were saying openly: I do not even hear those whom I by no means despise on account of the great merit of their petition. What then is it that Moses and Samuel are preferred to the other fathers in petition, except that these two alone in the entire sequence of the Old Testament are read to have prayed even for their enemies? One is assailed with stones by the people, and yet he entreats the Lord for the one who stoned him; the other is cast down from leadership, and yet when asked to pray, he confesses saying: "Far be this sin from me against the Lord, that I should cease to pray for you." "If Moses and Samuel stood before me, my soul would not be toward this people." As if He were saying openly: I do not even now hear those on behalf of friends, whom I know by the merit of their great virtue to pray even for enemies. Therefore the power of true prayer is the loftiness of charity. And then each person obtains what he rightly asks, when his mind in petition is not darkened by hatred of an enemy.

And if they say to you: where shall we go forth?, you will say to them: thus says the Lord: those for death, to death, and those for the sword, to the sword, and those for famine, to famine, and those for captivity, to captivity! And I will visit upon them four kinds, says the Lord: the sword for slaying, and dogs for tearing, and the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth for devouring and scattering. The prophecy of Ezekiel also shows four plagues to which the people of the Jews was handed over: the sword, pestilence from famine, beasts, captivity. Among the beasts, moreover, understand the dogs and the birds as well, to which they were handed over for their bodies to be torn and devoured and scattered. For it could not happen that, once the Creator was neglected, the whole creation should not rise up against sinners.

And I will give them over to ferment — or commotion and distresses — to all the kingdoms of the earth because of Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, for all that he did in Jerusalem. We read in the book of Chronicles that Manasseh, after his captivity and repentance, returned to Jerusalem and reigned; but just as the merits of the saints descend to their posterity, as in the case of David and the rest, so the outrages of sinners reach their posterity, if their children and grandchildren have done similar things. But what he says: 'I will give them over to ferment or commotion and distresses of the whole earth', was both fulfilled in part under the Babylonians and is now being fulfilled in full, since the impious people imitated a most wicked king, one who filled Jerusalem from gate to gate with the blood of the righteous. From this we learn that peoples are very often destroyed by the crime of kings and princes and of those set over them.

He forecasts what would happen after the return, what would happen to them under the Macedonians and the destruction that would be inflicted on them by the Romans. He brings out that the first fate would happen to them owing to the impiety committed by Manasseh. Yet he is not an unjust judge, nor does he require an account of them for others' faults. He submits them to the evils prophesied as sharers in impiety and enthusiastic supporters of their wicked king.

We wish to understand the words spoken to Jerusalem with much menace, which run thus: "Who will spare you, O Jerusalem? Or who will be sorrowful for you? Or who will turn aside to ask after your peace? You have turned away from me, says the Lord. You shall go backward, and I will stretch out my hand against you and destroy you, and I will no longer let you go. And I will scatter them in a dispersion." Then: "I have been made childless." Perplexity has seized me. I take as an illustration a man who has been declared an enemy of the one who reigns upon the earth, because for such a person it is not permitted even to impart mercy, lest anyone seem to give offense to the king who has condemned him. And it is not permitted even to show mercy to such a one; some go still further and do not even show sorrow over him, lest by showing sorrow they seem to be displeased with the sentence passed by the king. If you have grasped this, look with me at the one condemned by God on account of his own many sins, and consider such a person: though there are legions of angels appointed to help the nature of human beings, he is pitied by none. For each of the angels, seeing that the one who has condemned him is God, that the one from whom he has turned away is the Creator, that the nature of the sins is such that the good God was compelled — so to speak — to bring the verdict against the one who has sinned, each of those who see does not spare, does not show sorrow, does not pity, does not turn back to intercede for peace toward such a one.

Let this Jerusalem, then (for so it shall be spoken according to the letter), have sinned against my Jesus, and have done such things, that Jesus should say concerning her: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often would I have gathered your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not. Behold, your house is left to you." Let this Jerusalem be forsaken, as she has been forsaken. Let the angels who ever help Jerusalem — through whom also the law of Moses was ordained, "ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator" — let them forsake Jerusalem and say: her sins have become great, they have killed Jesus, they have laid their hands upon Christ. As long as the sins were still smaller, we could still make request and intercede concerning them, we could spare Jerusalem; who will spare her in this case? "If a man sinning sins against another man, then they shall pray for him; but if he sins against the Lord, who shall pray for him?" "Jerusalem has sinned a sin; therefore she has become an object of tossing." And it is said to this very one first: "Who will spare you, O Jerusalem? And who will be sorrowful for you?" We do not show sorrow over Jerusalem and over her calamities and over the things that befell all that people; "for by their trespass salvation has come to us, to provoke them to jealousy." Since their trespass became so great a sin that it was said by the voice of the Lord, "Who then will spare you" — I too say to her who killed my Jesus — "Who will spare you, O Jerusalem? And who will be sorrowful for you?"

I pass over from the letter — although I have had a road, which the word has given — to each soul that has already been counted worthy to see peace; for after the divine lessons you have become Jerusalem, having formerly been Jebus. The history says that the name of that place was Jebus, and afterward it changed its name and became Jerusalem. Jebus, the children of the Hebrews say, is interpreted "trodden down." Jebus, then, the soul trodden down by the opposing powers, has been changed and become Jerusalem, "Vision of peace." If, then, when you have been changed from Jebus into becoming Jerusalem, you have sinned and "trodden down the Son of God and counted the blood of the new covenant a common thing" (as she did, so also you), and are in grievous sins, it will be said also concerning you: "Who will spare you, O Jerusalem? And who will be sorrowful for you?" — if you become such as to betray Jesus. Each of us when he sins, and especially if he sins the greater sins, sins against Jesus. And if he is also an apostate, then all the more does he do to Jesus spiritually the things which Jerusalem did to him bodily. Therefore, "of how much worse punishment do you think he will be counted worthy who has trodden down the Son of God and counted the blood of the covenant a common thing, by which he was sanctified, and has insulted the Spirit of grace?" If you have trodden down the Son of God and insulted the Spirit of grace, who "will spare you? Who will be sorrowful for you? Who will turn aside to ask after the things that make for your peace?" The very Son of God, who asks after the things that make for your peace, the soul of the sinner has betrayed; who is able to intercede, turning back again concerning peace? Knowing, then, that "it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened and have tasted the heavenly gift and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, to renew them again to repentance, since they crucify again for themselves the Son of God and put him to open shame" — let us do everything, so that it may not be said also concerning us: "Who will spare you, O Jerusalem? And who will be sorrowful for you? Or who will turn aside to ask after your peace?"

For who will have pity on you, Jerusalem? or who will grieve for you? or who will go to ask for your peace? For when God has been offended no one can intercede for the outrages of sinners, because a creature cannot be as merciful as the Maker, nor can a stranger spare outsiders as the Lord spares his own.

And to each interpretation of Jerusalem what follows will also fit: "You have turned away from me, says the Lord. You shall go backward." That you have turned away from the Son of God, and because of having turned away from the Son of God you have turned away from God — what need is there even to say it? And since Jerusalem in Judea turned away from Christ — from which we must understand all the Jews — for this reason "you shall go backward." For there was a time when she did not go backward, but forward; but now she goes backward, and "they turned in their hearts to Egypt," clearly so that they might go backward. But concerning what "you shall go backward" means, or what it is to reach forward to the things that are ahead, we shall present it thus. The righteous man "reaches forward to the things that are ahead, forgetting the things that are behind." Clearly the one disposed contrary to the righteous man remembers the things behind and does not reach forward to the things that are ahead. But he who remembers the things behind disobeys Jesus who teaches and says: "Let him not turn back to take up his garment"; he disobeys Jesus who says: "Remember Lot's wife"; he disobeys Jesus who says: "No one who has put his hand to the plow and turned back to the things behind is fit for the kingdom of God." And in the law also it is written that the angels said to Lot who had gone out from Sodom: "Do not look around to the things behind, nor stand in all the surrounding country; escape to the mountain, lest you be swept away with them." And this too has a meaning worthy of an angelic spirit: "Do not look around to the things behind" — ever reach forward to the things ahead. You have left Sodom, do not turn to Sodom. You have left vice and sin, do not turn back to it, "nor stand in all the surrounding country." And even if you keep the first commandment which says, "Do not look around to the things behind," it does not suffice you for salvation, unless you also hear the second commandment which says, "Nor stand in all the surrounding country." For one who has begun to make progress must not stand in the surrounding country of Sodom, even if he has passed beyond Sodom, but having passed beyond standing in the surrounding country he must be saved to the mountain, according to the "Do not look around to the things behind, nor stand in all the surrounding country; escape to the mountain, lest you be swept away with them." If you wish not to be swept away with the Sodomites, never turn to the things behind, nor stand in the surrounding country of Sodom, nor be anywhere else than at the mountain; for there alone is it possible to be saved. And the mountain is the Lord Jesus, to whom is the glory and the might unto the ages. Amen.

You have forsaken me, says the Lord; you have gone backward. The reason is given why no one should have pity on Jerusalem, or grieve for her, or entreat for her peace: that, although according to the Apostle she ought, forgetting what lies behind, to have stretched forward to what lies before, she on the contrary turned back and longed for the meats of Egypt.

And I will stretch out my hand over you and kill you; I have labored, being entreated — or entreating —, for which the Seventy translated: I will by no means forgive them any longer. An outstretched hand is the sign of one who strikes; the killing of sinners signifies wrath brought to completion. But what he added: I have labored, being entreated or entreating, has a twofold sense: that God has already grown faint from often forgiving them, and that he is weary from always calling them to salvation.

And I will scatter them with a winnowing fan in the gates of the land — or of my people —; I have killed and destroyed my people, and yet they have not turned back from their ways. 'What does it profit that I am entreated so often, when they do not turn back from their most wicked ways nor do repentance? For I scattered them as with a winnowing fan, to purge my threshing floor, and I scattered them in the gates of the land, so that in a manner they might tread the thresholds of hell, and I have killed and destroyed my people, so that, compelled by the necessity of evils, they might avoid the evils that were impending'.

There are also other sorts of vengeance, with which some who have overpassed the bounds of wickedness are smitten in this life, as we read that Dathan and Abiram or Korah were punished, or above all, those of whom the Apostle speaks: "Wherefore God gave them up to vile passions and a reprobate mind:" and this must be counted worse than all other punishments. For of these the Psalmist says: "They are not in the labours of men; neither shall they be scourged like other men." For theyare not worthy of being healed by the visitation of the Lord which gives life, and by plagues in this world, as "in despair they have given themselves over to lasciviousness, unto the working of all error unto uncleanness," and as by hardening their hearts, and by growing accustomed and used to sin they have got beyond cleansing in this brief life and punishment in the present world: men, who are thus reproved by the holy word of the prophet: "I destroyed some of you, as God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, and you were as a firebrand plucked out of the burning: yet you returned not to Me, saith the Lord," and Jeremiah: "I have killed and destroyed thy people, and yet they are not returned from their ways."

Her widows have been multiplied to me above the sand of the sea; I have brought upon them, upon the mother of the young man, a destroyer at noon; I have sent terror suddenly upon the cities. God desires to save sinners by various remedies, so that those who had despised him when he coaxed them may fear him when he threatens. The widows were multiplied above the sand of the sea when their husbands had been slain; the mothers, having lost their children, felt the destroyer not at night and through ambushes, but in broad daylight, to show the open force of a stronger adversary. 'I have sent', he says, 'upon the cities' — no doubt those of Judah and of the sinful people — 'terror suddenly, so that, the more sudden the evil was, the more difficult escape would be'.

"In that day, saith the Lord, the sun shall go down at noon, and there shall be darkness over the earth in the clear day; and I will turn your feast days into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation," plainly announced that obscuration of the sun which at the time of His crucifixion took place from the sixth hour onwards, and that after this event, those days which were their festivals according to the law, and their songs, should be changed into grief and lamentation when they were handed over to the Gentiles. Jeremiah, too, makes this point still clearer, when he thus speaks concerning Jerusalem: "She that hath born [seven] languisheth; her soul hath become weary; her sun hath gone down while it was yet noon; she hath been confounded, and suffered reproach: the remainder of them will I give to the sword in the sight of their enemies." Those of them, again, who spoke of His having slumbered and taken sleep, and of His having risen again because the Lord sustained Him, and who enjoined the principalities of heaven to set open the everlasting doors, that the King of glory might go in, proclaimed beforehand His resurrection from the dead through the Father's power, and His reception into heaven.

The Scriptures prophesied that at noon in Christ's passion there should be darkness. In Amos it says, "And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord, the sun shall set at noon, and the day of light shall be darkened. I will turn your feast days into grief and all your songs into lamentation." Also in Jeremiah: "She is frightened that has borne children, and her soul has grown weary. Her sun has gone down while as yet it was noon. She has been confounded and accursed. I will give the rest of them to the sword in the sight of their enemies." Also in the Gospel: "Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the earth even to the ninth hour."
Treatise XII. Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews 2:23

What more can now be said respecting the crime of the Jews, than that they were then blinded and seized with incurable madness, who read these things daily and yet neither understood them nor were able to be on their guard so as not to do them? Therefore, being lifted up and nailed to the cross, Jesus cried to the Lord with a loud voice and of his own accord gave up his spirit. At the same hour there was an earthquake. The veil of the temple, which separated the two tabernacles, was torn into two parts. The sun suddenly withdrew its light, and there was darkness from the sixth even to the ninth hour. Of this event the prophet Amos testifies, "And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord that the sun shall go down at noon, and the daylight shall be darkened. I will turn your feasts into mourning and your songs into lamentation." Also Jeremiah: "She who brings forth is afraid and vexed in spirit. Her sun is gone down while it was yet noon. She has been ashamed and confounded. The residue of them will I give to the sword in the sight of their enemies."

She is weakened — or has cast away or has been made empty —, who bore seven — or very many —, her soul has fainted; the sun has set for her while it was still day — or midday —; she is confounded and has blushed. And her remnant I will give to the sword in the sight of their enemies, says the Lord. We have often said that the Hebrew word 'saba' means either 'seven' or 'oath' or 'very many'. Hence the translation also differs, Aquila, the Seventy and Theodotion translating 'seven', Symmachus 'very many'. She, then, who was rich in children was suddenly made childless, and perished in broad daylight, and was confounded in her own desolation. 'But the remnant of the people', he says, 'I will hand over to the sword, so that no one may escape death and the wrath of God'. Others refer it to the synagogue, which was weakened so that the multitude of the Church might grow, according to what is written: The barren has borne seven — or very many — and she who had many children has been weakened. Hence also there has set for her the sun of righteousness, in whose wings is healing, and therefore she is covered with eternal confusion, losing her people by the spiritual sword.

Physicians of bodies, being present with the sick and always devoting themselves to the care of the ailing according to the intent of the medical art, look upon dreadful things and touch loathsome ones; from the misfortunes of others they reap their own griefs, and their life is always in the midst of hardship. For they are never with the healthy, but always with the wounded, with those who have festering sores, with those full of pus, of fevers, of manifold diseases. And if anyone wishes to make ready the practice of medicine, he will not be indignant nor neglect the intent of the art which he has taken up, whenever he is among such people as we have described.

I have spoken this preface because the prophets too are, as it were, physicians of souls, and they always spend their time where those who need healing are; for "it is not the healthy who have need of a physician, but those who are ill." And what physicians suffer at the hands of the intemperate sick, this the prophets and the teachers also suffer at the hands of those who do not wish to be healed. For thence they are hated, as though they gave orders contrary to the preference of the desire of the sick, as though they hindered from luxury and pleasure those who, even in their sicknesses, wish not to receive what befits their sicknesses. So the intemperate among the sick flee from their physicians, often even reviling them and speaking evil of them and doing every possible thing that an enemy might do to an enemy. For these people forget that the physicians come as friends, since they look only at the toilsomeness of the regimen, at the toilsomeness of the physicians' stroke with the iron, and not at the end that comes after the toil; and they hate them as fathers of toils only, and not of toils that bring those who are treated to health.

That people, then, was sick; manifold diseases were in the people that had been called the people of God. God sent them physicians, the prophets. One of the physicians was Jeremiah too; he reproved the sinners, wishing to turn back those who were doing evil. But they, when they ought to have listened to what was said, accused the prophet, and accused him before judges who were much like themselves. And the prophet was always in lawsuits at the hands of those who, so far as his prophecy was concerned, were being healed, but who, because of their own disobedience, were not being healed. Concerning these things he says at one point: "And I said, I will not speak, nor will I name the name of the Lord. And it became like a burning fire, blazing in my bones, and I am unstrung on every side and cannot bear it." And at another point he says, seeing himself always brought to trial, reviled, accused, borne false witness against: "Woe is me, mother, as what have you borne me?" He said "a man" not judging but "being judged," and not passing judgment but "being disputed against by all the earth." And since the sick did not listen to him when he counseled them well and after the manner of a physician, he says, "I did not profit." And since, when he was lending the spiritual silver pieces, those to whom he spoke were unwilling to listen, that they might be profited by what they heard, he says, "Neither did anyone owe me, nor did I owe."

But I have said these things by way of anticipation, before I expound the words "I did not owe, nor did anyone owe me." For the text is twofold: in most copies it reads "I did not profit, nor did anyone profit me," but in the most accurate ones, which agree with the Hebrew, it reads "I did not owe, nor did anyone owe me." One must therefore both expound what is worn smooth by use and current in the churches, and not leave unexpounded what comes from the Hebrew Scriptures. He was proclaiming the word, then, and no one accepted what was said. Like a physician he was expending his remedies, though the sick were intemperate and fulfilling their own desires. As if he too were saying, "I did not profit, nor did anyone profit me." Perhaps there is a reciprocal feeling, on account of the love-toward-humanity of the one profited toward the one who profited him, so that the speaker too comes to be profited, since "blessed is the one who speaks into the ears of those who hear." This profit, then, a teacher might receive from hearers who advance and are made better; he might be profited by having fruits in them. ⟨Not having this from the Jews, Jeremiah says:⟩ "No one profited me." For if the speaker ought to have fruit in himself, but the hearer misconstrues and remains outside of what is said, then it is said, "No single one profited me"; since he does not have this profit which he would have received from the hearer, once profited, becoming a cause of advancement and blessedness for the one who profited him. And besides, everyone who teaches, by the very act of teaching, the more intelligent the learner is, is profited in the things he teaches, in the things he learns. And speakers become better regarding the lessons they hand on, when the hearers are intelligent and do not simply accept, but test in return and question and examine the intent of what is said. ⟨Neither, then, did I profit, nor did anyone profit me.⟩

But since another exposition is also necessary on account of the more accurate copies, which read thus: "I did not owe, nor did anyone owe me," we shall expound the saying as it stands thus also. The one who renders to all their debts—to whom fear, fear; to whom the tax, the tax; to whom the tribute, the tribute; to whom the honor, the honor—and who renders to all their dues, so as not to owe the dues toward anyone, honoring ⟨parents⟩ as parents, so to speak, brothers as brothers, sons as sons, bishops as bishops, presbyters as presbyters, deacons as deacons, believers as believers, catechumens as catechumens—if he renders all the dues, he did not owe. But if he owes indeed to do a due, and has not done it, he cannot say, "I did not owe"; for owing, he did not render it. How then shall I expound also "nor did anyone owe me"? I indeed was lending and wished to give the spiritual riches, but they turned away from what was said and did not present themselves receptive, so as to owe; therefore no single one owed me. For who accepted what was said, so that from accepting it he might become a debtor of what he heard, and be required, as a debtor of what was said, to pay the interest? It is better, then, in this respect for the hearer to receive rational silver from the speaker and to owe, than, not accepting nor receiving, not even to owe. For "nor did any single one owe me" is set among reproaches.

As for "Woe is me, mother, as what a man have you begotten me, being judged and disputed against in all the earth"—I do not think it so fitting for the other prophets to say this as for Jeremiah; for most of the prophets, after certain periods of time, after their wickedness, after their sins, changed and began to prophesy, but Jeremiah prophesies from childhood. And it is possible to give an example from the writings. Isaiah did not hear "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the mother's womb I sanctified you, I have set you as a prophet unto the nations"; nor did he say, "I do not know how to speak, because I am too young," but when he saw the vision recorded in his prophecy, he saw and said: "Woe is me, wretched that I am, because having unclean lips I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips, and I have seen with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth," "and there was sent," he says, "to me one of the Seraphim, and he touched my lips and said: Behold, I have taken away your iniquities, and this will cleanse your sins." After the sins, then, which he had formerly committed, Isaiah later became worthy of the Holy Spirit and prophesied. And in another you would find something similar. But not so Jeremiah; for while still in swaddling-clothes, adorned with the prophetic Spirit, he prophesied from childhood; wherefore he said (for I expound first the common sense): "Woe is me, mother, as what a man have you begotten me, being judged and disputed against by all the earth?"

But one of those before me applied himself to the passage, saying that he spoke these things not to his bodily mother, but to the mother who gives birth to prophets. And who gives birth to prophets but the wisdom of God? He said, then, "Woe is me, mother," "as what have you borne me," O wisdom? And the children of wisdom are recorded in the Gospel too: "And wisdom sends out her children."
