This was not intended to be a specific number for the servants of God, but only indicates a multitude too great for human computation. These are the thousands and tens of thousands of which we read in the Psalms: "The chariot of God is attended by ten thousands; thousands of them that rejoice. The Lord is among them" (Psalm 68:17). And in another place: "He who maketh His angels spirits, and His ministers a flaming fire" (Psalm 104:4). Now the duty of angels is twofold: the duty of one group is to bestow rewards upon just men; the duty of the other is to have charge over individual calamities.

"...The court was in session, and the books were opened." The consciences of men, and the deeds of individuals which partake of either character, whether good or bad, are disclosed to all. One of the books is the good book of which we often read, namely the book of the living. The other is the evil book which is held in the hand of the accuser, who is the fiend and avenger of whom we read in Revelation: "The accuser of our brethren" (Revelation 12:10). This is the earthly book of which the prophet says: "Let them be written on earth" (Jeremiah 17:13).
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER SEVEN

Finally, when the Lord would for their speedy fall turn away His merciful countenance from the people, whom He had chosen out of all nations, the giver of the law interposes on their behalf and cries out: "I beseech Thee, O Lord, this people have sinned a great sin; they have made for themselves gods of gold; and now if Thou forgivest their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me out of Thy book which Thou hast written. To whom the Lord answered: If any man hath sinned before Me, I will blot him out of My book." David also, when complaining in prophetic spirit of Judas and the Lord's persecutors, says: "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living;" and because they did not deserve to come to saving penitence because of the guilt of their great sin, he subjoins: "And let them not be written among the righteous." Finally in the case of Judas himself the meaning of the prophetic curse was clearly fulfilled, for when his deadly sin was completed, he killed himself by hanging, that he might not after his name was blotted out be converted and repent and deserve to be once more written among the righteous in heaven. We must therefore not doubt that at the time when he was chosen by Christ and obtained a place in the Apostolate, the name of Judas was written in the book of the living, and that he heard as well as the rest the words: "Rejoice not because the devils are subject unto you, but rejoice because your names are written in heaven." But because he was corrupted by the plague of covetousness and had his name struck out from that heavenly list, it is suitably said of him and of men like him by the prophet: "O Lord, let all those that forsake Thee be confounded. Let them that depart from Thee be written in the earth, because they have forsaken the Lord, the vein of living waters." And elsewhere: "They shall not be in the counsel of My people, nor shall they be written in the writing of the house of Israel, neither shall they enter into the land of lsrael."
The Second Conference of Abbot Joseph, Chapter 25

Then again there is a prayer that runs thus: "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my boast. Behold, they say to me, 'Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come.' But I have not grown weary in following after you, and I have not desired the day of man, you know it." To him alone who came for the sake of those who are sick, the physician who says, "Those who are strong have no need of a physician, but those who are sick," everyone who wishes to be cured of the sickness of his soul may confidently say, "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed." But if anyone else besides him professes the healing of souls, you would not be speaking truly if you said to that one, "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed." For that woman too who "had a flow of blood" spent "all that she had" on the physicians, and "was not able to be healed by any of them"; for to none of those was it reasonable to say, "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed," but only to the one whom it suffices to touch "the fringe of his garment." I say therefore to this one: "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed"; for if you heal, the end will follow upon the healing that comes from you, the cure, so that I may be saved. But however many others may save, I shall not be saved; but the only and true salvation is if Christ saves, since then I shall be saved. "A horse is false for salvation," and false too are all the other things apart from God for salvation. Therefore I would say to him: "Save me, O Lord, and I shall be saved." And I say this, if I am also able to say what follows by having renounced every boast, so that I may say, "For you are my boast," or when I fulfill the commandment that says, "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches, but rather let him who boasts boast in this, to understand and to know that I am the Lord." Blessed therefore is he who has renounced all boasting here below, such as in what is called nobility of birth and in beauty and in bodily things, in wealth, in glory, and who is content with one boast, so that he may say, "For you are my boast."
He says to him who alone is the true physician, "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed. Save me, and I shall be saved. You are my praise and my hope."

Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, since you are my praise! Many physicians in the Gospel had treated the woman with the issue of blood, who had spent all her substance on them, and yet she could be cured by none except by him who is the true physician and in whose wings is healing. Hence now too the prophet, having suffered reproaches from the people and having been often beset by plots, desires to be healed and to be saved by him who is his true praise and his true medicine.

No evil person does good. And if no evil person does good, how could an evil person make himself good? He who is eternally good can make an evil person good. "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed: save me, and I shall be saved."

So, the reason that we, being bad, have a good Father is in order that we may not always remain bad. No bad person can make a good one. If no bad person can make a good one, how can a bad person make himself good? The only one who can make a good person out of a bad one is the one who is always good. "Heal me, Lord," he says, "and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved."

Behold, they say to me: where is the word of the Lord? Let it come! But I was not troubled, following you as shepherd — or I have not labored following you — and I have not desired the day of man; you know. What went out from my lips was right in your sight — or is before your face —. Do not be a terror to me, my hope in the day of affliction, or do not become a stranger to me, sparing me in the worst day! Those who do not think that what has been spoken will come say to the prophet: where is the word of the Lord? let it come!, judging the delay to be a setting aside of the sentence.

Further, also, it is written concerning the Sabbath in the Decalogue which [the Lord] spoke, face to face, to Moses on Mount Sinai, "And sanctify ye the Sabbath of the Lord with clean hands and a pure heart." And He says in another place, "If my sons keep the Sabbath, then will I cause my mercy to rest upon them." The Sabbath is mentioned at the beginning of the creation [thus]: "And God made in six days the works of His hands, and made an end on the seventh day, and rested on it, and sanctified it." Attend, my children, to the meaning of this expression, "He finished in six days." This implieth that the Lord will finish all things in six thousand years, for a day is with Him a thousand years. And He Himself testifieth, saying, "Behold, to-day will be as a thousand years." Therefore, my children, in six days, that is, in six thousand years, all things will be finished. "And He rested on the seventh day." This meaneth: when His Son, coming [again], shall destroy the time of the wicked man, and judge the ungodly, and change the-sun, and the moon, and the stars, then shall He truly rest on the seventh day. Moreover, He says, "Thou shalt sanctify it with pure hands and a pure heart." If, therefore, any one can now sanctify the day which God hath sanctified, except he is pure in heart in all things, we are deceived. Behold, therefore: certainly then one properly resting sanctifies it, when we ourselves, having received the promise, wickedness no longer existing, and all things having been made new by the Lord, shall be able to work righteousness. Then we shall be able to sanctify it, having been first sanctified ourselves. Further, He says to them, "Your new moons and your Sabbath I cannot endure." Ye perceive how He speaks: Your present Sabbaths are not acceptable to Me, but that is which I have made, [namely this,] when, giving rest to all things, I shall make a beginning of the eighth day, that is, a beginning of another world. Wherefore, also, we keep the eighth day with joyfulness, the day also on which Jesus rose again from the dead. And when He had manifested Himself, He ascended into the heavens.
The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter XV

"Behold, they say to me, 'Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come.' But I have not grown weary in following after you." Jesus says to you, "Take up your cross, and follow me," and "Leave all things, and follow me," and "Whoever will not forsake his father and his mother and follow after me is not worthy to be my disciple." If, then, you become such a one as to follow Jesus always, you will indeed follow, and however far you follow you will not grow weary; for "there shall be no toil in Jacob, nor shall trouble be seen in Israel." There is no weariness for the one who follows Jesus; the very act of following takes away the weariness. For this reason he himself says—so that we may toil no longer, having toiled before we began to follow him—"Come to me, all you who toil and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." If, then, though toiling we come to him and follow him, we shall say, "But I have not grown weary in following after you."

And to this it follows that we should also speak of the words "I have not desired the day of man." There is a certain day of man, and there is a certain day of God. Let each one of us desire the day of the resurrection of the saints, not that day of which it is written: "Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord; and this day is darkness and not light." Who is it that says, "And I have not desired the day of man"? The plain sense of the passage will convict us, that we have desired the day of man. Often, when we have fallen sick and have come to imagine death upon our departure, we entreat the brethren who watch over us and say: Ask for me a respite, ask that I may remain in this life. In saying these things we do not desire the holy day of God, but the day of man. Wherefore, having laid aside the love of life and the desiring of a human day, let us seek to see that day in which we shall attain the blessedness that is in Christ Jesus, to whom belong the glory and the might unto the ages. Amen.

For I love those presbyters and deacons who when they have performed their mission will not allow themselves to remain absent any longer from their duties. For the prophet says, I have not been weary in following thee. And who can be weary in following Jesus, when He Himself says, Come unto Me all ye that labour, and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Let us therefore never cease from following Jesus, which if we do we shall never fail, for He gives strength to them that follow Him. The more nearly you approach to the Source of power the stronger you will be. Often, while we are thus following Him, the adversaries say to us, Where is the word of the Lord? let it come now. But let us not grow weary in following Him, let us not be turned aside by meeting with this crafty question. It was said to the prophet, when he was thrown into prison, when he was cast into the pit of mire, Where is the word of the Lord? let it come now. But he followed him so much the more, and therefore attained the prize, and received the crown; for following Jesus he was not weary; for there is no weariness in Jacob, neither shall sorrow be in Israel.

But while they are saying these things, he says: 'I was not troubled, nor did I labor, following you as shepherd, or walking in your footsteps; nor was I content to stop there, but I have not desired the day of man, either a longer life or any of the prosperities of this world'. And he calls the same one as witness whom he calls as judge: you have known. There follows: what went out from my lips was right in your sight, meaning that he never lied, that he said nothing contrary to the will of the Lord.

The Lord has indeed made every day—not only has made but also continues to make. I mean, he makes every day as follows: he makes his sun rise on the good and the bad and sends rain on the just and the unjust. So we are not to imagine that this ordinary kind of day, which is common to good and bad alike, is meant in this place, where we heard, "This is the day that the Lord has made." What particular sort of day can it be when it says, "Let us exult and be joyful in it"? What sort, but a good one? What sort, but a very choice, lovable, desirable one, the sort about which Jeremiah said, "And I have not yearned for the day of men, you know it well"?

Next we come to the passage where His brethren—that is to say, His relations according to the flesh—urge Him to go up to the feast-day, in order that He may have an opportunity of making Himself known to the multitude. And here, again, how supremely elevated is the tone of His reply! "My time is not yet come, but your time is alway ready. The world cannot hate you; but me it hateth, because I testify of it that the works thereof are evil." So it is the case, then, that "your time is alway ready," because ye desire that kind of day to which the prophet refers when he says, "But I have not laboured following Thee, O Lord; and the day of man I have not desired, Thou knowest:" that is to say, to soar to the light of the Word, and to desire that day which Abraham desired to see, and which he did see, and was glad.
The Harmony of the Gospels, Book 4, Chapter 10

For it is but little for a monk to have once made his renunciation, i.e., in the early days of his conversion to have disregarded the present world, unless he continues to renounce it daily. For to the very end of this life we must with the prophet say this: "And I have not desired the day of man, Thou knowest." Wherefore also the Lord says in the gospel: "If any man will come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me."

Do not, he says, be a terror to me, my hope in the day of affliction! This is clear according to the Hebrew; but according to what the Seventy translated, saying, do not become to me as a stranger, sparing me in the evil day, the sense is: 'do not spare me in the present world, which is evil, but render to me according to my sins, so that I may have everlasting rest! for I know that it is written: whom the Lord loves, he reproves; and he scourges every son whom he receives'. But the evil day is either the whole world or the day of judgment for those who are tormented on account of their sins.

Let those who persecute me be confounded, and let me not be confounded! Let them tremble, and let me not tremble! Bring upon them the day of affliction, and crush them with a double crushing! The prophet calls down imprecations against those who taunt him with the word of the Lord and say, where is the word of the Lord? let it come: that those who persecute him may be confounded, and may blush and return to salvation; that they, who lie, may tremble, and not he, who foretells true things; and that, when the day of vengeance has come, he may crush them with a double crushing, famine and sword.

But they certainly have to labour, and when they attack men, exert themselves in no lesser degree in order to secure from each one that victory which they want to obtain, and there is hurled back upon them the same confusion which was awaiting us had we been worsted by them; as it is said: "The head of their compassing me about, the labour of their own lips shall overwhelm them;" and: "His sorrow shall be turned on his own head;" and again: "Let the snare which he knoweth not come upon him, and let the net which he hath hidden catch him, and into that very snare let him fall;" viz., that which he contrived for the deception of men. They then themselves also come to grief, and as they damage us so are they also in like manner damaged by us, nor when they are worsted do they depart without confusion, and seeing these defeats of theirs and their struggles, one who had good eyes in his inner man, seeing also that they gloated over the downfall and mischances of individuals, and fearing lest his own case might furnish them with this kind of delight, prayed to the Lord saying: "Lighten mine eyes that I sleep not in death: lest mine enemy say, I have prevailed against him. They that trouble me will rejoice if I be moved;" and: "O My God, let them not rejoice over me; let them not say in their hearts, Aha, Aha, our very wish; neither let them say; we have devoured hint." and: "They gnashed their teeth upon me. Lord, how long wilt Thou look on this?" for: "he lieth in wait secretly as a lion in his den: he lieth in wait to ravish the poor;" and: "He seeketh from God his meat." And again when all their efforts are exhausted, and they have failed to secure our deception, they must "be confounded and blush" at the failure of their efforts, "who seek our souls to destroy them: and let them be covered with shame and confusion who imagine evil against us." Jeremiah also says: "Let them be confounded, and let not me be confounded: let them be afraid, and let not me be afraid: bring upon them the fury of Thy wrath, and with a double destruction destroy them." For no one can doubt that when they are vanquished by us they will be destroyed with a double destruction: first, because while men are seeking after holiness, they, though they possessed it, lost it, and became the cause of man's ruin; secondly, because being spiritual existences, they have been vanquished by carnal and earthly ones. Each one then of the saints when he looks on the destruction of his foes and his own triumphs, exclaims with delight: "I will follow after mine enemies and overtake them: and I will not turn until they are destroyed. I will break them and they shall not be able to stand: they shall fall under my feet," and in his prayers against them the same prophet says: "Judge thou, O Lord, them that wrong me: overthrow them that fight against me. Take hold of arms and shield: and rise up to help me. Bring out the sword and shut up the way against them that persecute me: say to my soul, I am thy salvation." And when by subduing and destroying all our passions we have vanquished these, we shall then be permitted to hear those words of blessing: "Thy hand shall be exalted over thine enemies, and all thine enemies shall perish." And so when we read or chant all these and such like passages found in holy writ, unless we take them as written against those spiritual wickednesses which lie in wait for us night and day, we shall not only fail to draw from them any edification to make us gentle and patient, but shall actually meet with some dreadful consequence and one that is quite contrary to evangelical perfection. For we shall not only not be taught to pray for or to love our enemies, but actually shall be stirred up to hate them with an implacable hatred, and to curse them and incessantly to pour forth prayers against them. And it is terribly wrong and blasphemous to think that these words were uttered in such a spirit by holy men and friends of God, on whom before the coming of Christ the law was not imposed for the very reason that they went beyond its commands, and chose rather to obey the preCepts of the gospel and to aim at apostolical perfection, though they lived before the dispensation of the time.
First Conference of Abbot Serenus, Chapter 21

Thus says the Lord to me: go and stand in the gate — or in the gates — of the sons of the people, through which [gate] — or through which [gates] — the kings of Judah go in and go out, in all the gates of Jerusalem, and you shall say to them: hear the word of the Lord, kings of Judah and all Judah — or Judea — and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, who go in through these gates! 'Since', he says, 'they scorn to hear your words and do not come to you to inquire what the sentence of God may be, go you to the most frequented place, either of the gates of the temple or of those of the city, through which the kings and all the common people go in and go out, so that they may be compelled by necessity to hear, and you may preach the word of God out of season and in season, and no excuse may remain to them that they did not do it because they did not hear'.

Thus says the Lord: guard your souls, and do not carry weights on the sabbath day, nor bring them in through the gates of Jerusalem! And do not cast out loads from your houses on the sabbath day, and you shall do no work, and sanctify the sabbath day, as I commanded your fathers! And they did not hear, nor did they incline their ear, and they hardened their neck — and what is not found in the Hebrew: above their fathers —, that they might not hear me and might not receive instruction. And it shall be, he says, if you hear me, says the Lord, so as not to bring in loads through the gates of this city on the sabbath day, and if you sanctify the sabbath day, so as not to do any work on it, there will enter through the gates of this city kings and princes sitting upon the throne of David and mounting in chariots and on horses, they and their princes, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and this city will be inhabited forever. And they will come from the cities of Judah and from round about Jerusalem and from the land of Benjamin and from the plains and from the hill country and from the south, bringing burnt offering and victims — or incense offerings — and sacrifice — or manna — and frankincense, and they will bring in an offering — or praise — into the house of the Lord. But if you will not hear me, to sanctify the sabbath day and not to carry a load and not to bring it in through the gates of Jerusalem on the sabbath day, I will kindle a fire in its gates, and it will devour the houses of Jerusalem and will not be extinguished. Lest I should tear in pieces the precept of the sabbath renewed through Jeremiah, I have chosen to set it out whole, so that we may know everything together. He guards his soul who does not carry the weights of sins on the day of 'rest' and of sabbath, nor bring them in through the gates of Jerusalem, which we ought to take as the virtues.

And do not, he says, cast out loads from your houses — for they are not to be carried, but utterly cast away — and do no work — either servile work or that of which it is written: food for the belly and the belly for foods; but God will destroy both it and them —, but that work is to be worked of which the Savior speaks: 'work the work that does not perish!' Sanctify, he says, the sabbath day, so that we may spend all the time of our life in sanctification, as our fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob did.

And when God had commanded these things, they did not incline their ear — that of the mind, surely, not of the flesh —, but they hardened their neck, rejecting the yoke of the law and, by metaphoran [metaphor], bearing the likeness of untamed animals.

Let us see what is the reward of those who do not carry loads on the sabbath day and who sanctify it. There will enter, he says, through the gates of this city kings, whose heart is in the hand of God and who reign over their bodies, and princes sitting upon the throne of David, so that they imitate the example of Christ, and mounting in chariots and on horses, of which it is written: the chariot of God is ten thousandfold, manifold, thousands of those who rejoice; the Lord is among them in Sinai, in the holy place, and elsewhere: your riding is salvation: every man who 'confesses' God and who dwells in Jerusalem, of which it has been said: was made in Salem, that is, in peace, his place, and his dwelling in Zion; and the Church of God will be inhabited forever.

And they will come from the cities of Judah and from round about Jerusalem, of which we have already spoken, and from the land of Benjamin, who is the 'son' 'of power' and 'of the right hand', and from the plains, which in Hebrew is called 'sefela' and signifies the plain understanding of the history, and from the hill country, namely the lofty doctrines, and from the south, of which it is written, God will come from the south, whence comes heat and full light, and where all cold is driven out. Bringing, he says, burnt offerings — consecrating themselves to God — and a victim or incense, so that they may say: a sacrifice to the Lord is a troubled spirit, and: we are the good odor of Christ in every place, and elsewhere: let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight; and sacrifice, for which the Seventy put the Hebrew word itself, 'manaa', which by a very bad custom, nay rather by the carelessness of scribes, is read in our books as 'manna'; and frankincense, of which it has been said, to what purpose do you bring me frankincense from Sheba?; and they will bring in an offering, which in Hebrew is called 'thoda' and can be rendered as 'thanksgiving', and which the Seventy translated as 'praise'. Into the house of David: no doubt, into the Church. These are the rewards of those who sanctify the sabbath and are weighed down by no weight.

'But if', he says, 'you will not hear my precepts, and do the things which I commanded not to be done, I will kindle a fire in its gates' — that is, of Jerusalem: that fire of which it is said, all committing adultery, like an oven, their hearts —, 'which will devour the houses or streets of Jerusalem' — which the Seventy translated as amphoda, Aquila and Symmachus as bareis, that is, 'towered houses', and which are called in Hebrew 'armanoth' — 'and this burning will never be extinguished', as the Apostle says: the fire will test what sort each one's work is, and again: if anyone's work is burned, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire. But if our Judaizers reject the figurative explanation, they will be compelled either to be Jews and, with the observance of the sabbath, to circumcise their foreskins, or else to find fault with the Savior, who on the sabbath commanded the paralytic to carry his bed, as the evangelist says: for this reason the Jews sought all the more to kill him, not only because he was breaking the sabbath, but also because he said that God was his own Father, making himself equal to God.
18:
There are two visions of Jeremiah that have just been read, one following the other. The former of these contains what concerns the clay vessel in the potter's hand, which admits of restoration after being broken (for it is possible for it to be remolded); but the other vision contains what concerns the earthen jug, which, once shattered, admits of no cure. For when it was clay, if it was broken — even if it had already been given its shape — since it was clay, it was possible for it to become a second lump and to be fashioned a second time; but when, after being clay, it has already become earthenware and has been hardened by fire, then it was not possible, after the shattering of the earthenware, for any cure to come to it. What, then, these things intend, let us first consider by way of reflection, and then, if it be granted, let us examine them according to the letter. As long as we are in this life, we are being shaped — that I may so name it, on account of our clay vessel — in a potter's fashion, and we are shaped either according to vice or according to virtue. Yet we are shaped in such a way as to admit both that our vice may be shattered, so that a new and better creature may come to be, and that our progress may be dissolved after its shaping into a clay vessel. But when, after the present age, we arrive, having come to the end of life, and then, once fired — whether by the fire of the flaming darts of the evil one we become whatever we become, or by the divine fire (since indeed "our God is a consuming fire") — if, I say, we come to be under such or such a fire, whatever we become, if we are shattered, whether we were shattered and have perished from having become good vessels, or from having become wretched vessels, we are not created anew, nor does our structure admit of improvement. For this reason, as long as we are here, being as it were in the potter's hand, even if the vessel falls from his hands, it admits of cure and of being created anew. Let this much, then, be said somewhat more readily at hand, before we examine in argument what remains, concerning the two kinds of vessels: the clay one, not yet turned to potsherd, and the second, which has already become a potsherd.

But let us look, from the wording itself, at what is said about the clay vessel in the potter's hand, and how the very Word in the prophet, the Lord who prophesies in him, gives occasions — and others not slight — for the interpretation of the things concerning the molded thing in the potter's hand. "The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Arise and go down to the house of the potter." Jeremiah is above; he has ascended beyond the clay vessels. The clay vessels are below, and the nature that governs the clay vessels, condescending together with the things governed, is below. For this reason the word spoken to Jeremiah from the Lord says to him: "Arise and go down to the house of the potter, and there you shall hear my words." To Moses it is said, "Go up onto the mountain and hear"; to Jeremiah it is said, "Go down to the house of the potter and hear." For each of those who hear a word is either taught about the things above or learns about the things below. If I am taught the lower things, I descend by the word, that I may see the lower things; but if I learn the higher things, I ascend by the word to the higher things, that I may behold the things there.

But that all of you, so far as you are able, may follow along for yourselves with what is being said, I shall use an example, and one from Scripture, and in addition to the example I shall set forth a clarity that brings light to the interpretation that has been given. "In the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, of things heavenly and things earthly and things under the earth, and every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is unto the glory of God the Father." And there is a certain wisdom concerning each of these: a wisdom concerning the heavenly things, how the heavenly things are ordered; a wisdom concerning the things under the earth, since there is a wisdom of God also concerning the ordering of the things under the earth, and likewise concerning the earthly things. If I am going to have room for the wisdom concerning the heavenly things, I ascend to the heavenly things, as Moses ascended to the summit of the mountain, that the voice from heaven might become audible to him, according to what is written. For he was about to be taught heavenly forms of worship; for there was a shadow and a representation of heavenly mysteries in the laws of worship that have been recorded, as the apostle taught, saying: "who serve a representation and shadow of the heavenly things." As, then, when I am about to be taught concerning the heavenly things I ascend, so, if there be need for me to learn about the things under the earth, even should I become a prophet, I descend. And perhaps for this reason Samuel, when he was taught the things under the earth, went down below and came to be in Hades — not being judged so as to be in Hades, but that he might become a spy and a beholder of the mysteries of the things under the earth. Such too can be the things said by the apostle concerning wisdom, distinguished by the knowing of "what is the breadth and length and depth and height." You are going to know the height: you ascend by the word to the height; you are going to know the things between the height and the depth: you know the breadth and the length. Everywhere, guided by the word that teaches concerning all things, the mind that is able to follow the Son of God reaches. And it follows by renouncing the world and taking up the cross; for he is able to follow Jesus who is able to say: "to me the world has been crucified, and I to the world."

It was needful to explain the "Go down to the house of the potter, and there you shall hear my words." For it was needful to compare it with the "Go up and you shall hear my words." For of those who hear, some ascend that they may be taught — and they ascend not altogether bodily; while others descend and yet keep the soul above, in order to see the loftiest word concerning the lowest things. My Lord Jesus Christ himself both ascended and descended; "for he who ascended is himself also the one who descended above all the heavens." If, then, you too are going to understand the one who ascended most high as the word concerning the highest things, and the one who descended into the lowest things as him who teaches concerning the lowest things, "do not say: Who shall ascend into heaven? — that is, to bring Christ down; or, Who shall descend into the abyss? — that is, to bring Christ up from the dead. But what does the Scripture say? The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart," through which you ascend into heaven. And concerning the ascent, "the word is near you," and concerning the lowest things, "the word is near you"; for what else than the word that is everywhere can the holy one have within himself? For "the kingdom of heaven is within you."

"Get up and go to the potter's house, and there you will hear my words." Here we have a parable about a potter meant to call Israel to repentance. As the potter makes from clay any vessel he likes, so God can easily change their state of events, turning disaster into joy. If Israel does not give up its hypocrisy, the Lord will frighten them with great calamities.

The lowest type, and one which is "love" at all only by an extension of the word, is that which an artist feels for an artefact. God's relation to man is pictured thus in Jeremiah's vision of the potter and the clay, or when St. Peter speaks of the whole Church as a building on which God is at work, and of the individual members as stones. The limitation of such an analogy is, of course, that in the symbol the patient is not sentient, and that certain questions of justice and mercy which arise when the "stones" are really "living" therefore remain unrepresented. But it is an important analogy so far as it goes. We are, not metaphorically but in very truth, a Divine work of art, something that God is making, and therefore something with which He will not be satisfied until it has a certain character. Here again we come up against what I have called the "intolerable compliment". Over a sketch made idly to amuse a child, an artist may not take much trouble: he may be content to let it go even though it is not exactly as he meant it to be. But over the great picture of his life--the work which he loves, though in a different fashion, as intensely as a man loves a woman or a mother a child--he will take endless trouble--and would, doubtless, thereby give endless trouble to the picture if it were sentient. One can imagine a sentient picture, after being rubbed and scraped and re-commenced for the tenth time, wishing that it were only a thumb-nail sketch whose making was over in a minute. In the same way, it is natural for us to wish that God had designed for us a less glorious and less arduous destiny; but then we are wishing not for more love but for less.

The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Arise and go down into the potter's house, and there you shall hear my words! And I went down into the potter's house, and behold, he was doing a work upon the wheel — or stones —. And the vessel that he was making from clay with his hands was broken; and turning — or and again — he made it another vessel, as it had pleased in his eyes to make it. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Can I not do with you as this potter, O house of Israel? says the Lord; behold, as clay in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel! Suddenly — or in sum — I will speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to root it out — or to take it away — and to destroy and to ruin it. If that nation repents of its evil, which I have spoken against it, I too will repent of the evil which I thought to do to it. And suddenly — or in sum — I will speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to build and to plant it. If it does evil in my eyes, so as not to hear my voice, I will repent of the good which I spoke of, to do to it. Through all the senses, indeed, one arrives at judgment and understanding of mind, through hearing, smell, taste, touch; but what is seen with the eyes is retained more in the mind. Hence the prophet is ordered to go to the potter's house and there to hear the Lord's commands.

The prophet, then, goes down to the house of the potter and recounts what he beheld, saying: "And behold, he was doing a work upon his hands, and the vessel which he was making of the clay fell apart in his hands; and again he made it into another vessel, as it pleased him to make it." But I do not know what the prophet saw when he came to the potter. For he saw the potter working; the vessel that had been made was of clay; the vessel fell apart. Why did he not say precisely: he let the vessel go out of his hand — nor did he lay the cause upon the potter? But since the word is about ensouled vessels, which fall apart of themselves, for this reason it is said: "the vessel fell apart from his hands." Take heed, then, to yourself as well, lest, while being in the potter's hand and still being molded, you fall apart from his hands by your own doing. For "no one snatches out of his hands," according to what is said in the Gospel according to John. Yet it is not written that, as no one snatches, so no one falls apart out of his hands; for free will is free. And I say: no one shall snatch out of the shepherd's hand, no one is able to take us out of God's hand; but we ourselves, by being negligent, are able to fall apart from his hands.

The prophet Jeremiah addresses the Jews in these words: "And I went down to the potter's house. Behold, he made a work on the stones. The vessel that he made in his hands was broken. Again he made another vessel, as it pleased him to make it. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying, 'Cannot I do to you as this potter, O house of Israel? Behold, you are like the clay of the potter in my hands.' " For I call your attention to this, that, as I said, after human transgression the great Hand was not content to leave as a trophy of victory its own work, debased by the evil one, who wickedly injured it from motives of envy, but moistened and reduced it to clay, as a potter breaks up a vessel, that by the remodeling of it all the blemishes and bruises in it may disappear, and it may be made afresh faultless and pleasing.

When, therefore, God speaks of an irremediable calamity, he does not say vessels of the potter, but an earthen vessel; when, for instance, he wished to teach the prophet and the Jews that he delivered up the city to an irremediable calamity, he bade him take an earthen wine-vessel, and crush it before all the people, and say, "Thus shall this city be destroyed, be broken in pieces." But when he wishes to hold out good hopes to them, he brings the prophet to a pottery, and does not show him an earthen vessel, but shows him a vessel of clay, which was in the hands of the potter, falling to the ground: and brings him to it saying, "If this potter has taken up and remodelled his vessel which has fallen, shall I not much rather be able to restore you when you have fallen?" It is possible therefore for God not only to restore those who are made of clay, through the laver of regeneration, but to bring back again to their original state, on their careful repentance, those who have received the power of the Spirit, and have lapsed.

'And when,' he says, 'I had set out and had gone down into the potter's house, he was doing a work upon the wheel', which the Seventy, led astray by the ambiguity of the word, translated 'stones'; for 'abanim', according to the nature of the context and the difference of pronunciation, is used both for an 'instrument', that is, the potter's 'wheel', and for 'stones'.

By his passion, therefore, Christ made perfect that human flesh that had been brought down to death by the first man's sin and restored it by the power of his resurrection. Sitting on God's right hand, he placed it in the highest heavens. In view of this, the apostle says, "Who has raised us up together and has made us sit together in the heavenly places." It was he, you see, who was the potter mentioned by the prophet Jeremiah: "The vessel that had fallen from his hand and was broken, he again raised up with his hands and formed anew, as it seemed good in his eyes." So it seemed good to him to raise the mortal and corruptible body he had assumed from the rocky tomb, and, rendering it immortal and incorruptible, to place it no longer in an earthly environment but in heaven at his Father's right hand.

'And when,' he says, 'I saw a vessel being made from clay, it was suddenly broken', God's providence bringing this about, so that the craftsman's hand, without knowing it, should by its own mistake figure forth a parable. And again that potter, who had lost the vessel of clay as the wheel was running, made another for himself, as it seemed good to him.

"And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Shall I not be able to do to you as the potter, O house of Israel? says the Lord." Each one understands the things written according to his ability, the one more superficially, as though drawing his understanding from them from a surface spring, the other more deeply, as one drawing up from a well. And both can be helped, since the same thing is for one a spring and for the other a well. The Gospel bears witness, when it recounts the things concerning the Samaritan woman; for there the same thing is named "spring" and "well," and in turn it is sometimes called a spring and sometimes a well. Let him who is able take note, that he may know that the same thing in its substance is for the superficial one a spring, but for the deeper one a well. This is for me a preface to the account that is coming, concerning the clay vessel that fell apart from the potter's hand and was again molded. Some have viewed these things more simply and have understood them. I shall set before you their account and interpretation; after this, if we have anything deeper, this too we shall recount. It is possible, they say, that here the things concerning the resurrection are indicated. For if the clay vessel fell apart from the potter's hands, and from the same material of the same clay he makes "it into another vessel as it pleased him before him," then the potter — God — of our bodies, the Craftsman of our structure, when this falls apart and is shattered for whatever cause, is able to take it up and renew it and make it a more beautiful and better "other vessel, as it pleased him before him to make."

Let this account too have its charm.

And at once the Lord says to the prophet: 'If a potter,' he says, 'has this power, that from the same clay he makes again what had been broken, shall I not be able to do this in you, who, as far as lies in you, seem to have perished?'

What do you mean, Paul? Am I to be subject to God in the same way the clay is to the potter? Yes, Paul says. For the distance between God and man is as great as the distance between the potter and the clay. Rather the distance is not merely as great but much greater. The potter and the clay are of one and the same substance. It is just as Job said: "I admit it as for those who dwell in houses of clay, because we are ourselves formed from the same clay." If a man seems more beautiful to look upon than clay, this difference was not produced by a change of nature but by the wisdom of the craftsman. Why? Because you are no different from the clay. If you refuse to believe this, let the coffins and the cremation urn convince you. And you will know that this is the truth if you have gone to visit the tombs of your ancestors. Therefore, there is no difference between the clay and the potter.

But let us hear the Lord himself recounting and saying: "Shall I not be able to do to you as the potter, O house of Israel? says the Lord. Behold, as the clay of the potter, so are you in my hands. At the end I will speak against a nation and a kingdom, to remove them and to destroy them; and that nation shall turn from their evils of which I spoke against it, and I will repent of the evils which I purposed to do to them. And at the end I will speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to build it up and to plant it, and they shall do wicked things before me, so as not to hear my voice, and I will repent concerning the good things which I said I would do to them, says the Lord." This concerning the house of the potter we see to be referred not to any of the individuals, but to two nations; for, beginning, he says that he is going to speak about nations, that he may suggest something to those able to hear hidden mysteries: "At the end I will speak against a nation." Seek both the end and the former nation, against which he speaks the things of destruction on account of their sins; and having spoken the things of destruction on account of the sins, he nonetheless promises that if they repent, he will repent concerning the evils which he said he would do to them. And again he speaks concerning another, a second nation, that a whole nation be "built up and planted"; and since this nation that is built up and planted has a good promise, but is able to sin, he says, after speaking these things, if they should depart from the good works: "I will repent concerning the good things which I said I would do to them."

What, then, are the two nations — the one first named, to which the word threatens, and the second, to which it promises? Yet he threatens in such a way that, if it should repent, he does not carry out the things of the threat. He promises in such a way that, if the second nation should fall away and become unworthy of the promises, they should not obtain them. Concerning two nations especially is set forth the whole economy of God for the human beings in the world. That first nation, Israel, came to be first; second, from the sojourn of Christ, this present nation. To the former God threatened what he threatened, and we see the things of the threat against the former nation: it has come to be in captivity, their city was razed, the sanctuary was destroyed, the altar has been thrown down, nothing is any longer preserved of the things once held holy among them. For God said to that nation: Repent — and they did not repent. After these things were said to them, God speaks to this second nation the things concerning its being built up. But he sees that this nation too are human beings, able again to fall away. For this reason he threatens this one also and says: Even though I foretold the things concerning the building and the things concerning the planting and the husbandry, yet this nation too is going to sin, and to this one, having sinned, the same things will befall which were said to those others on account of the sins, and they will suffer them if they do not repent. Search the whole Scripture, and you will find most things spoken concerning these two nations. God chose the fathers, gave them a promise, led out a people from the race of the fathers out of Egypt, was long-suffering with them as they sinned, disciplined them as a father, brought them in, gave them a land of promise, sent them prophets at various times, disciplined them and turned them back from their sins. He was ever long-suffering, sending those who would heal, until the chief physician should come — the prophet surpassing prophets, the physician surpassing physicians. When he had come, they betrayed and killed him, saying, "Away, away with such a one from the earth; crucify, crucify him." Immediately a visitation came upon the nation; the place where my Jesus was crucified was made desolate; God chose another nation. See how great is the harvest, even if the laborers are few. And in another way too God orders that the dragnet always be cast upon the sea of this life, and fish of every kind are gathered; he sends "the many fishermen"; he sends "the many hunters," and they hunt from "every mountain," they hunt from "every hill." See how great is the economy concerning the salvation of the nations. "See, then, the kindness and severity of God: toward" the former nation, which also fell, "severity, but toward you," the second nation, promises and "kindness, if you continue in the kindness; since you too will be cut off." For the axe did not then lie against the root of the trees for that time only. The axe is ready to come again; and "the axe lies against the root of the trees," my Jesus was saying then, prophesying concerning Israel, against which the axe was. He himself was the axe of the unfruitful tree, and he said: "Already the axe lies against the root of the trees." As many trees as were there not producing fruit were cut down and cast into the fire and punished. But now another farmland has come to be, corresponding to the former, concerning which it is said: "Having brought them in, plant them on the mountain of your inheritance, in the prepared dwelling place of yours." God brought his nation into the mountain of his inheritance. The mountain I seek not as the Jews do, thus in inanimate materials. The mountain is Christ. In this we were planted, upon it we were kept. See, then, even if he be long-suffering, lest the master of the house, coming, should say: "For three years already I come to this fig tree and it has borne no fruit; cut it down; why does it even use up the ground?" For he uses up the good ground, Christ, the mystery of the Church, who comes to the assembly and does not bear fruit.

It was not as though it were unknown that He had promised in their behalf that things should be thus, and then the years were diminished and also were increased, but as known; for He knew the measure of that which was to come, and on account of His mercies He gave a time for repentance that men might be without excuse; and men despised the longsuffering of God, and when they heard that there was much time until the wrath which was promised should come, becoming bold they sinned before Him and said: "That which the prophets say is prophesied for a remote time." On account of this when there arose a disputing concerning these things in the days of Ezekiel the prophet and they said: "That which hath been prophesied is for a remote time," He said to Ezekiel: "As I live," saith the Lord of dominions, "there shall not again be a delay to My words, for the word which I shall speak I shall shortly accomplish." And He cut off that which He had foretold, to give to men a time for repentance, that perhaps they might repent; but they despised the longsuffering of God and did not repent, and He also changed the time which He had appointed and decreed to them. And it was not done as if it were not known, but as it is written: "Woe to him that destroyeth! Ye were not destroyed; and who hath spoken falsely, and He did not speak falsely against you. For when ye have wished to destroy ye have been destroyed, and when ye have wished to speak falsely it hath been spoken falsely against you." Again it is written in Jeremiah: "If I shall speak against a people and against a kingdom, to pluck up and to break down and to destroy them and to cause them to perish, and that nation shall turn from its wickedness, I also will make false My word, and I will turn away from them everything which I have spoken against them." Again Jeremiah said: "If I shall speak concerning a people and concerning a kingdom to build and to plant, and that people shall do iniquity before Me, I also will make false My word, and I will turn from it the good thing which I have spoken to benefit it."

And though they promise themselves prosperity, they will afterwards endure evils; while, on the other side, the saints fear and do not sin, and therefore by no means die by the sword, because they said: Evils will draw near to us, and the punishments which our sins have deserved will come upon us; of which God speaks more fully in Jeremiah: I will take it up and speak against a nation and a kingdom, to take it away and destroy it; if that nation turns from its evils, I too will repent of the things that I had thought to do to it. God, therefore, is not changed, who is always immutable; but we change him by our conversion. He rages, he is angry, he threatens, and says that he will inflict punishments: If we repent, he too will repent of his sentence. Again, according to the same Jeremiah, he promises prosperity: If we grow slack through negligence, he too will repent of his pledge, and will change what he promised. Of this we can have an example in the Ninevites and in Jerusalem, of whom the one were set free from the punishments that hung over them, the other lost what had been promised to their fathers.

And to signify free will, he says that he announces both evils to this or that nation and kingdom and, again, good things; and yet that what he himself has foretold does not come about, but that the contrary happens, so that good things befall the evil, if they repent, and evils befall the good, if after the promises they have turned to sins. And we say this not because God does not know that this or that nation or kingdom will do this or that, but because he leaves man to his own will, so that he may receive either rewards or punishments by his own desert. Nor will what befalls be wholly man's at once, but belongs to the grace of him who has bestowed all things; for the freedom of the will must be preserved in such a way that the grace of the giver excels in all things, according to that prophetic word: Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain; unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it has watched in vain. For it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.

[Daniel 4:27] "'Wherefore, O king, let my counsel meet with thy favor, and make up for thy sins by deeds of charity, and thine iniquities by showing mercy to the poor. Perhaps God will forgive thy transgressions.'" Since he had previously pronounced the sentence of God, which of course cannot be altered, how could he exhort the king to deeds of charity and acts of mercy towards the poor? This difficulty is easily solved by reference to the example of King Hezekiah, who Isaiah had said was going to die (Isaiah 38:1); and again, to the example of the Ninevites, to whom it was said: "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be destroyed" (Jonah 3:4). And yet the sentence of God was changed in response to the prayers of Hezekiah and the city of Nineveh, not by any means because of the ineffectualness of the judgment itself but because of the conversion of those who merited pardon. Morever in Jeremiah God states that He threatens evil for the nation (Jeremiah 18:7-8), but if it does that which is good, He will alter His threats to bestow mercy. Again, He affirms that He directs His promises to the man who does good; and if the same man thereafter works evil, He says that He changes His decision, not with regard to the men themselves, but with regard to their works which have thus changed in character. For after all, God is not angered at men but at their sins; and when no sins inhere in a man, God by no means inflicts a punishment which has been commuted. In other words, let us say that Nebuchadnezzar performed deeds of mercy toward the poor in accordance with Daniel's advice, and for that reason the sentence against him was delayed of execution for twelve months. But because he afterwards while walking about in his palace at Babylon said boastingly: "Is this not the great Babylon which I myself have built up as a home for the king by the might of my power and the glory of my name?" therefore he lost the virtue of his charitableness by reason of the wickedness of his pride.

"It may be that God will forgive thy sins." In view of the fact that the blessed Daniel, foreknowing the future as he did, had doubts concerning God's decision, it is very rash on the part of those who boldly promise pardon to sinners. And yet it should be recognized that indulgence was promised to Nebuchadnezzar in return, as long as he wrought good works. Much more, then, is it promised to other men who have committed less grievous sins than he. We read in Jeremiah also of God's direction to the people of the Jews, that they should pray for the Babylonians, inasmuch as the peace of the captives was bound up with the peace of the captors themselves (Jeremiah 29:7).
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER FOUR

You may as well accuse God of falsehood because he said by the mouth of Jonah: "Yet three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown." But God will reply by the mouth of Jeremiah, "At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to break down and to destroy it; if that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do to them. And at what instant I shall speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it; if it does evil in my sight, that it obeys not my voice, then I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit them." Jonah, on a certain occasion, was indignant because, at God's command, he had spoken falsely; but his sorrow was proved to be ill founded, since he would rather speak truth and have a countless multitude perish than speak falsely and have them saved.

And that we may not fancy that the Lord granted this specially to the Ninevites, He continually affirms by Jeremiah that He will do the same in general towards all, and promises that without delay He will change His sentence in accordance with our deserts; saying: "I will suddenly speak against a nation and against a kingdom to root out and to pull down and to destroy it. If that nation repent of the evil, which I have spoken against it, I also will repent of the evil which I thought to do to them. And I will suddenly speak of a nation and a kingdom, to build up and to plant it. If it shall do evil in My sight, that it obey not My voice: I will repent of the good that I thought to do to it." To Ezekiel also: "Leave out nota word, if so be they will hearken and be converted every one from his evil way: that I may repent Me of the evil that I thought to do to them for the wickedness of their doings." And by these passages it is declared that we ought not obstinately to stick to our decisions, but to modify them with reason and judgment, and that better courses should always be adopted and preferred, and that we should turn without any delay to that course which is considered the more profitable. For this above all that invaluable sentence teaches us, because though each man's end is known beforehand to Him before his birth, yet somehow He so orders all things by a plan and method for all, and with regard to man's disposition, that He decides on everything not by the mere exercise of His power, nor according to the ineffable knowledge which His Prescience possesses, but according to the present actions of men, and rejects or draws to Himself each one, and daily either grants or withholds His grace.
The Second Conference of Abbot Joseph, Chapter 25

Do not despair of salvation, God is saying. Even if I condemn a nation and threaten ultimate punishment, if I see their repentance, I extend mercy instead of inflicting punishment. If I promise an abundance of blessings, but they scorn me and embrace wickedness, I shall not fulfill the promise of blessings. Knowing this, then, do not despair of better things, but apply repentance and reap salvation.

If only the sinner would have recourse to repentance as quickly as God is willing to change that fixed sentence. Listen to the Lord through the prophet promise the greatest hope to the human race: "Finally I shall speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to root out and destroy them. If that nation shall turn from all of their evil deeds, I also shall repent of the evil that I thought to do to them." Behold how great is our God's goodness to us, and learn whether he will refuse his mercy, since he longs to change his sentence if we are converted. Therefore, let us turn to him, dearly beloved, and not wish to defer the amendment of our ways until the end of our life.

"At the end I will speak against a nation or also against a kingdom." It will seem that "the end" is said simply. But it is said in this way. In the "I will speak against a nation or a kingdom," the "end" is of this sort: "I will raze" is said to the former nation as the "end"; to the second nation, "I will build you up." And again, "I will uproot" is said to the former ones, and "I will plant" to the second. Is it, then, that because the "end" has been spoken, the end must come to pass? God, though he does not repent, is said in Scripture to repent. And let us attend to the wording, that if we are able to give a defense of how these things are said, we may accept the account. "At the end I will speak," he says, "against a nation or against a kingdom, to remove them and to destroy them; and if that nation should turn from their evils of which I spoke against it, then I will repent concerning the evils which I purposed to do to them. And at the end I will speak concerning a nation or a kingdom, to be built up and to be planted, and they shall do wicked things before me, so as not to hear my voice, and I will repent concerning the good things which I said I would do to them." Concerning the repentance of God we are required to give a defense; for it seems to be a thing to be censured and unworthy — not only of God but even of the wise man — to repent. For I do not conceive of a wise man repenting; but the one who repents, so far as the customary use of the word goes, repents over not having deliberated well. But God, being foreknower of the things to come, cannot deliberate ill and, on account of this, repent. How, then, has the Scripture introduced him saying "I will repent" — not yet do I speak of what is said in the Books of Kingdoms in the "I repent that I anointed Saul as king," and what is said of him generally: "and repenting over the evils."

But see what we are taught concerning God generally. In one place, "God is not as a man, to be torn apart, nor as a son of man, to be threatened," and we learn through this wording that God is not as a man; but through another, which says that God is as a man: "that the Lord your God disciplined you, as if a man should discipline his son," and again, "he bore with the ways of his son as a man does." So then, when the Scriptures speak of God theologically in himself and do not interweave his economy with human affairs, they say that he is not as a man. For "of his greatness there shall be no end," and "he is fearful above all gods," and "praise him, all you angels of God; praise him, all his hosts; praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all you stars and light." And gathering countless other passages from the sacred writings you would find those to which you will fit the "God is not as a man." But when the divine economy is interwoven with human affairs, it bears the human mind and manner and expression. And just as we, if we converse with a two-year-old child, lisp on account of the child — for it is not possible for us, keeping the dignity of the mature man's age and speaking to children, without condescending to their speech, to understand the children — understand something of this sort for me concerning God also, when he orders the affairs of the human race, and especially of those who are still infants. See how we mature men also alter our words toward babies, and we name bread to them in a peculiar way, and we name the act of drinking by another expression, not using the mature speech which we use toward our grown-up peers, but some other childish and infantile expression. And if we name garments to the children, we assign to them other names, as it were fashioning a childish name. Are we, then, at that time imperfect? And if someone should hear us conversing with children, will he say that this old man has become foolish, that this man has forgotten his beard, the age of a man? Or is it granted, by way of accommodation, that one conversing with a child should not speak with the speech of an old man, nor with a complete one, but with a childish one?

And God indeed speaks to children; "behold," says the Savior also, "I and the children whom God has given me." It might be said to the old man who speaks to the child childishly — or, that I may say it more emphatically, infantilely — that you bore with the ways of your son and put on the manner of the infant and took up his condition. So, then, understand for me also the Scripture saying: "The Lord your God bore with your ways, as if a man should bear with the ways of his son." And it seems that those who translated from the Hebrew, not finding the word established among the Greeks, coined this one too, as in the case of many others, and made the "the Lord your God bore with your ways" (that is, he put on your ways), "as if a man should bear with the ways" (according to this example which I have given) "of his son." Since, therefore, we repent, when he converses with us who repent God says: I repent; and in threatening us he does not make a show of being a foreknower, but as speaking to infants he threatens. He does not make a show that he foreknew "all things before their coming to be," but as, that I may so name it, playing the part of the infant, he pretends not even to know the things to come. And so he threatens a nation on account of its sins and says: "If the nation repents, I too will repent." O God! When you threatened, did you not know whether the nation would repent or would not repent? And what? When you promised, did you not know whether the man — or the nation to which the word is addressed — would remain worthy of the promises, or would not remain? But he makes no show of it.

And many such human things you would find in the Scripture, as also the "Speak to the sons of Israel; perhaps they will hear and repent." This God did not say as one doubting, the "perhaps they will hear"; for God does not doubt, so as to say the "perhaps they will hear and repent," but that he may to a great degree make manifest your free will, and that you may not say: If he foreknew me as one perishing, I must perish; if he foreknew me as one to be saved, I must altogether be saved. He makes no show, then, of knowing about what is going to be concerning you, that he may preserve your free will by not having anticipated nor foreknown whether you will repent or not. And he says to the prophet: "Speak, perhaps they will repent." For countless other such things you will find said concerning God bearing with the ways of man. If you hear of the wrath of God and his anger, do not think the anger and the wrath to be passions of God. They are economies in the use of expressions, for the turning back and bettering of the infant; since we too make toward the children a face that is fearful not from disposition but by way of economy. If we keep the graciousness of the soul toward the infant in our face, and make manifest the tender affection which we have toward it, not distorting ourselves nor, as it were, changing toward its correction, we destroy it and make it worse. So, then, God also is said both to be angry and to be wrathful, that you may turn back and be bettered. And in truth he is neither angry nor wrathful; but you shall suffer the things of wrath and the things of anger, coming to be in pains hard to endure on account of your vice, when he disciplines you by what is called the wrath of God.

I affirm that "wickedness" in this context does not signify something that can be referred to the Creator's nature, as though he were evil, but to his authority, because he is a judge. It was in view of this that he declared, "It is I who create evils," and, "Behold, I send evils against you." These are not evils of ill doing but evils of vengeance—and I have already cleared away the ill repute of these by showing them to be fit and proper for a judge. As then, though described as evils, they are no matter of disrepute in a judge, nor by being so described do they stigmatize the judge as evil, so also "wickedness" in this context must now be understood as that which, deriving from those judiciary evils, is along with them proper to a judge.… As then his purpose, being a just one, was not evil, he had decided on it for justice's sake, not from wickedness. Yet the Scripture has described the punishment itself as "wickedness" because of the well-deserved evil of what they were to suffer.

"Let each one turn back, then, from his evil way, and make your practices better." Sometimes the more simple-minded say: blessed were the men of old, because they heard the Lord through the prophet saying, "and the Lord spoke to them." And to us now the Lord speaks through the things that are written: "Let each one turn back from his evil way"; the Lord himself converses with you, declaring, "and make your practices better." But those to whom the hortatory words concerning repentance were spoken made an answer, and let us see what they answered, so that we too may not answer in such a way. What, then, do they say in reply? "We will play the man, for we will go after our own backslidings, and each of us will do the pleasing things of his evil heart." And even if you do not say it in words, but your life is such that you sin, you too in effect say, through your evil deeds after the hortatory words, "We will play the man, for we will go after our own backslidings, and each of us will do the pleasing things of his evil heart." And what is "we will go after our own backslidings"? Those who have begun to put "their hand to the plow" and "who stretch forward to the things that are before" in their plowing, while "forgetting the things behind," have turned away from base things. Whenever, then, someone who has put "his hand to the plow" turns to the things behind, he will go "after his own backslidings"; for he will go after those things from which he turned away, and he runs back again to those sins which he had left behind. And so, of those who hear these things — whether catechumens who have left behind the gentile life, or believers who have already advanced in "stretching forward to the things that are before" — if the life has become depraved, they say nothing else than this very thing: "we will go after our own backslidings, and each of us will do the pleasing things of his heart" — not simply, but "of his evil heart, we will do." For there is an evil heart, and there is a good heart. Let no one, then, go "after his own backslidings," nor let him do "the pleasing things of his evil heart."

"Therefore," to those who answer thus, "the Lord says: Ask now among the nations: who has heard such dreadful things as the virgin Israel has done exceedingly?" And these things too will seem to have been said simply. But if the Church from among the nations turns to God in the manner it ought, it will be said: "Ask now among the nations: hear the dreadful things which the virgin Israel has done exceedingly." For let us compare the life of those who sinned with the life of those who turned back and believed, and we shall know that the former did dreadful things in killing "the Lord of glory," while the latter, when those had done dreadful things, turned to him who was taken away and put to death by them for the sins of the world. "Ask," then, "among the nations: who has heard such dreadful things as the virgin Israel has done exceedingly?"

Next, after the discourse concerning the two nations — the former, to which the threat is given, and the second, to which the promise is given — he says (he said, that is, to the former ones): "And now I have spoken to the men of Judah and to those who dwell in Jerusalem; thus says the Lord: Behold, I am molding evils against you." Because these things which I am molding against you are in my hand, they can fall apart. Make these things fall apart from my hand, so that the evils which I am molding against you I may change and make into good things. You would not find, "Behold, I am molding good things against you," and the things said correspondingly after them, so that after this he might make manifest that the good things which he molds he releases from his hands, that he may make them evil. But he molds evils according to the example that has been mentioned, and, molding evils, he orders them wisely (apart from the interpretation that has been given for the "it fell from my hands"), so that, if it should fall, even the end of the evils being molded may come to be of a kind I do not know.

Now therefore say to the man of Judah and to the inhabitant of Jerusalem, saying: These things — or thus — says the Lord: Behold, I am fashioning evil against you and devising a device against you; let each one turn back from his evil way, and make straight your ways and your pursuits! And they said: We have despaired — or we will be strong —; for we will walk after our own thoughts, and each one of us will do the depravity — or what has pleased his evil heart —. Therefore thus says the Lord: Ask among the nations: who has heard such horrible things as the virgin of Israel has done exceedingly? The Lord fulfills the parable which he had taught both by sight and by words, and says: 'Behold, I am fashioning evil against you, as a potter fashions clay' — evil, however, in the sense of Isaiah, who says: making peace and creating evil, not that it is evil in itself, but that it seems to be evil to those who suffer it — 'and devising a device against you' — that is, to pass sentence according to desert —; 'change your works and make straight your ways, so that the punishment too may be changed into prosperity!'

'But they, on the contrary,' he says, 'said: We will be strong' — in their evil works, that is, or, according to Aquila, we have despaired, and according to Symmachus, we have failed, both of which offend God, that one should either think that he can by no means be saved, or should have failed in spirit for appeasing God — 'and after our own thoughts,' he says, 'we will walk.' Where, then, is the power of free will and the judgment of one's own will apart from the grace of God, when it is a grave offense against God to follow one's own thoughts and to do the will of a depraved heart?

Therefore he adds, saying: 'Ask among the nations and all the peoples round about, who has done, who has heard, while serving idols, what the virgin of Israel has done exceedingly.' And he calls her a virgin because she had served the one God, as the prophet says: God is known in Judea, his name is great in Israel.

"Shall the breasts fail from the rock, or the snow from Lebanon? Or shall water be turned aside that is borne violently by the wind? For my people have forgotten me; they have burned incense in vain, and they shall grow weak in their ways, the everlasting paths, so as to walk in tracks that have no way for journeying, so as to make their land a desolation and a perpetual hissing." He has here spoken of differences of waters: first in "shall the breasts fail from the rock?"; second in "or the snow from Lebanon?"; third in "or shall water be turned aside that is borne violently by the wind?" These three kinds of waters are the springs of the waters which the soul of the righteous, likened to the deer, longs for, so that each one may say: "As the deer longs for the springs of the waters, so my soul longs for you, O God." Who, then, has become a deer, an enemy to the race of serpents, suffering nothing from their venom, as is recounted concerning the deer? Who has so thirsted for God as to say, "My soul thirsted for the living God"? Who has so thirsted for the breasts of the rock? "And the rock was Christ." Who has so thirsted for the Holy Spirit as to say, "As the deer longs for the springs of the waters, so my soul longs for you, O God"? If we do not thirst for the three springs of the waters, we shall find not even one spring of the waters. The Jews seemed to have thirsted for one spring of the waters, God; but since they did not thirst for Christ and the Holy Spirit, they cannot drink even from God. Those from the heresies seemed to have thirsted for Christ Jesus; but since they did not thirst for the Father, who is the God of the Law and the Prophets, therefore they do not drink even from Jesus Christ. And those who keep one God, but set at naught the prophecies and did not thirst for the Holy Spirit that is in the prophets, therefore do not drink even from the paternal spring, nor from him who cried out in the temple and said, "If anyone thirst, let him come to me and drink."

Therefore "the breasts from the rock" do not fail. But those men "forsook the spring of the water of life"; it was not the spring of the water of life that forsook them; for God removes himself far from no one, but "those who remove themselves far from him shall perish"; rather God draws near to some and meets the one who comes to him. When, at any rate, the son who had devoured the substance returned, the father met him. And he promises through the prophets, saying, "I will be nearer to them than the tunic to their skin." For "I am a God who draws near," he says, "and not a God from afar off, says the Lord." Therefore "the breasts shall not fail from the rock," the waters of Jesus, "nor the snow from Lebanon," the paternal waters. For frankincense (libanos) too is a sacred incense according to the Law of God, and it is offered upon the altar, "clear frankincense, equal part to equal part." And the mountain is called by the same name as this frankincense, and there is snow coming down from Lebanon, just as the water of the Holy Spirit, concerning which it is said, "Shall water be turned aside that is borne violently by the wind?" For indeed it is borne by the wind. The water of the Holy Spirit is not "turned aside," it does not flee, but each of us, by sinning, himself becomes a fugitive from drinking of the Holy Spirit.

Will the snow of Lebanon fail from the rock of the field? Or can the cold waters that burst forth and flow down be torn away? LXX: Will breasts fail from the rock, or snow from Lebanon?
